Unit 1: How the Web and Backends Work

What a backend is, what happens between typing an address and seeing a page, HTTP messages, methods, status codes, headers, cookies, REST and JSON, and the tools you will use all guide long.

When you open an app, two programs cooperate. The frontend (the client) runs on your device: it draws buttons and text and reacts to taps. The backend (the server) runs on a computer somewhere else, always on, and does the things that must not live on a user's device: storing data, enforcing rules, checking who you are, talking to other services.

What a backend is responsible for

JobWhy it cannot live in the frontendWhere this guide teaches it
Store and query dataData must be shared between users and survive when a device is lost.Unit 6 (databases)
Business rulesAnyone can edit frontend code in DevTools. Prices, permissions and limits must be enforced where users cannot touch them.Units 4 and 5
Authentication and authorization"Who are you" and "what may you do" can only be decided by code you control.Unit 7
SecretsAPI keys, database passwords and signing keys would be public if shipped to browsers.Units 7 and 10
IntegrationsPayments, email, SMS and maps APIs need secret credentials.Unit 8
Heavy or scheduled workImage processing, reports, nightly jobs should not run in a user's tab.Unit 8
Reliability and scaleLogging, monitoring, restarts, many users at once.Unit 10
The golden rule of backend workNever trust the client. Everything that arrives in a request (body, URL, headers, cookies) can be forged by anyone with curl. Validate every input, check permission on every action, and assume requests may be malicious or simply buggy.

What a request goes through on the server

Kinds of backends you will meet

KindReturnsExample
REST / JSON APIData as JSON for a separate frontend or mobile appThe API you build in Unit 11
Server-rendered siteFinished HTML pagesA blog with templates (EJS)
Real-time serverA live stream of messagesChat, notifications, live scores
GraphQL / RPC APIExactly the fields the client asked forLarge apps with many clients
Worker / job processorNothing to a user: runs tasks from a queueSending 10,000 emails
MicroservicesMany small backends talking to each otherBig companies' platforms
Serverless functionsOne function per request, run by a cloudAWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers

Almost everything above is built from the same pieces: HTTP, a language runtime, a framework, a database and a few security rules. Learn those pieces once, in Node.js and Express, and you can read backends in any language.

Why Node.js and Express

  • One language (JavaScript) in browser and server, so frontend developers can build backends and share code such as validation rules.
  • Excellent at I/O-heavy work: APIs spend most of their time waiting for databases and networks, which Node's event loop handles without needing a thread per request (Unit 3).
  • Huge ecosystem: npm is the largest package registry.
  • Express is the most widely used Node web framework: small, unopinionated, and the foundation many other frameworks copy or build on. Learning it teaches you the ideas (routing, middleware) behind all of them.
  • Honest limits: CPU-heavy work blocks the event loop (use worker threads, Unit 3), and Node gives you freedom but little structure, so you must organise code yourself (Unit 5).
What was verifiedEvery example in this guide that can run was run, with Node.js 22.22 and Express 5.3, against a real PostgreSQL 16 and Redis 7. Grey boxes are the real output. The few things that could not run in the build environment (Docker, MongoDB, cloud services) are marked Not run here so you always know which is which.
DNS
The phone book of the internet. Turns example.com into an IP address such as 93.184.216.34. Results are cached by your OS, router and ISP (the "TTL" says for how long).
IP address + port
The IP finds the machine; the port finds the program on it. Your Express app listens on a port (3000 in this guide).
TCP
A reliable, ordered byte stream between two machines. Established with a three-step handshake. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 run on top of it.
TLS
Encrypts the stream and proves the server is who it says (certificates). This is what the padlock means. HTTP + TLS = HTTPS. Always use it in production (Unit 10).
localhost
The name for your own computer (127.0.0.1). When you develop, client and server are both on your machine.

Commands in this guideTerminal blocks starting with $ show a command followed by its real output. The copy button copies only the commands. On Windows PowerShell, curl may be an alias for another command: type curl.exe instead, or use Git Bash or WSL.

HTTP is a text protocol (in version 1.1) with a very simple shape: a start line, some header lines, a blank line, and an optional body. Every request and every response has the same shape.

POST /items HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:3000
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 15

{"name":"cup"}
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /items/3
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 22

{"id":3,"name":"cup"}
PartRequestResponse
Start lineMETHOD path VERSIONVERSION status reason
HeadersMetadata: who, what formats, credentials, body typeMetadata: body type, caching, cookies to set, where to go
Blank lineA single empty line (CRLF CRLF) ends the headers.
BodyOptional. POST, PUT, PATCH usually have one. GET does not.Optional. HTML, JSON, an image, nothing at all (204).

Proof: talk HTTP by hand over a raw TCP socket

No browser, no fetch, no curl. This script starts a tiny Node HTTP server, opens a plain TCP connection to it with node:net, types an HTTP request as text, and prints the bytes that come back. \r\n is the line ending HTTP requires (carriage return + line feed).

import http from "node:http";
import net from "node:net";

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.setHeader("Content-Type", "text/plain");
  res.end("hello");
});
await new Promise((r) => server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", r));
const { port } = server.address();

const socket = net.connect(port, "127.0.0.1");
socket.write("GET /anything HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n");

let raw = "";
for await (const chunk of socket) raw += chunk;       // read until the server closes the connection
console.log(JSON.stringify(raw.split("\r\n"), null, 1));
server.close();
[ "HTTP/1.1 200 OK", "Content-Type: text/plain", "Date: Fri, 23 Oct 2026 03:54:23 GMT", "Connection: close", "Content-Length: 5", "", "hello" ]

Each element of the array is one line of the response, in order: the status line, the headers the server added by itself (Date, Content-Length and so on), the empty string that is the blank line, and finally the body. HTTP really is just this.

Statelessness, and the versions of HTTP

  • HTTP is stateless: each request is independent. The server does not remember the previous one. Anything that must persist between requests (who is logged in, what is in the cart) has to travel with every request (a cookie or token) or live in a database. This one fact shapes all of authentication (Unit 7) and scaling (Unit 10).
  • HTTP/1.1 (1997): text format, one request at a time per connection, with keep-alive to reuse connections.
  • HTTP/2 (2015): same meaning, but a binary format with many requests multiplexed over one connection and compressed headers.
  • HTTP/3 (2022): same meaning again, running over QUIC (UDP) for faster connections on bad networks.
  • Your Express code does not change between versions. Usually a reverse proxy such as nginx or a CDN speaks HTTP/2 or 3 to browsers and HTTP/1.1 to your app.

The method says what you want to do to the resource named by the path. Using the right one is how APIs stay predictable.

MethodMeaningBody?SafeIdempotentTypical success
GETRead a resource or listNoYesYes200
POSTCreate a new resource, or run an actionYesNoNo201 + Location, or 200
PUTReplace a resource completely (or create at a known URL)YesNoYes200 or 204
PATCHChange part of a resourceYesNoNot guaranteed200
DELETERemove a resourceRareNoYes204
HEADLike GET but headers only, no bodyNoYesYes200
OPTIONS"What may I do here?" Used by browsers for CORS preflightNoYesYes204
Safe
Does not change anything on the server. Browsers, crawlers and caches may call safe methods freely, so a GET must never delete or modify data.
Idempotent
Doing it once or ten times leaves the server in the same state. Retrying a failed PUT or DELETE is safe; blindly retrying a POST may create duplicates (Unit 5 shows idempotency keys).

GET, HEAD, POST
  • PUT replaced the whole item: you must send every field. PATCH sent only what changed.
  • DELETE returned 204 No Content (success, nothing to send back). Asking for the item again gave 404.
  • curl -I (capital I) sends a HEAD request: headers without a body.
  • OPTIONS was answered automatically by Express, with an Allow header listing the methods that route supports.
Common beginner mistakesUsing GET with query parameters to change data. Using POST for everything. Sending PUT with only some fields (that is PATCH). Forgetting the Content-Type header so the server cannot parse the body.

The status code is a three-digit number summarising the outcome. The first digit is the class. Clients, browsers, caches and monitoring tools all act on it, so choose it deliberately. Never return 200 with an error message inside: that hides failures from every tool.

ClassMeaningWho is at fault
1xxInformational (rarely seen)-
2xxSuccess-
3xxRedirection: look somewhere else, or use your cached copy-
4xxClient error: the request was wrongThe caller
5xxServer error: the request was fine, the server failedYou
CodeNameUse it when
200OKSuccess with a body (GET, PUT, PATCH, most POSTs).
201CreatedA POST created something. Add a Location header with its URL.
202AcceptedWork was queued and will finish later (Unit 8).
204No ContentSuccess with nothing to return (DELETE, some PUTs).
301Moved PermanentlyThe URL changed forever. Clients and search engines update.
302 / 303 / 307 / 308Temporary / See Other / Temporary (keep method) / Permanent (keep method)302 is the common temporary redirect. 307 and 308 keep POST as POST.
304Not ModifiedYour cached copy is still valid (conditional GET with ETag).
400Bad RequestMalformed or invalid input: broken JSON, missing field, wrong type.
401UnauthorizedNot authenticated: no or bad credentials. (The name is misleading: it means "unauthenticated".)
403ForbiddenAuthenticated, but not allowed to do this.
404Not FoundNo such resource or route. Also used to hide that a private resource exists.
405Method Not AllowedThe path exists but not for this method. Send an Allow header.
409ConflictState conflict: duplicate email, edit based on an old version.
410GoneExisted once, deleted deliberately.
413Payload Too LargeBody or upload exceeds your limit.
415Unsupported Media TypeContent-Type you cannot read.
422Unprocessable ContentSyntax is fine but the values fail validation (many APIs use this instead of 400).
429Too Many RequestsRate limit hit. Send Retry-After.
500Internal Server ErrorAn unexpected bug. Log it, hide the details from the client.
501Not ImplementedThe server does not support that functionality.
502Bad GatewayA proxy got an invalid reply from your app (often: your app is down).
503Service UnavailableOverloaded or in maintenance. Send Retry-After.
504Gateway TimeoutA proxy waited too long for your app.

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost:3000/status/418

$ curl -i localhost:3000/old
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: /json
Vary: Accept

Content-Length: 39

Connection: keep-alive

Moved Permanently. Redirecting to /json
$ curl -sL localhost:3000/old
{"ok":true,"now":"a fixed time"}
  • -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' throws the body away and prints only the status code: the standard way to script health checks.
  • /old answered 301 with a Location header. By default curl does not follow redirects; -L (last command) makes it follow to /json and show that final response.
  • 418 is "I'm a teapot", an April Fools code. Express happily sends any code you give it; it does not judge.

Headers are Name: value lines carrying metadata. Names are case-insensitive. Node lowercases them for you (req.headers['content-type']).

HeaderDirectionPurpose
HostrequestThe site being asked for (required in HTTP/1.1).
Content-TypebothFormat of the body: application/json, text/html; charset=utf-8, multipart/form-data, application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
Content-LengthbothBody size in bytes. Missing when the body is streamed (Transfer-Encoding: chunked).
AcceptrequestFormats the client can handle: application/json, text/html.
AuthorizationrequestCredentials: Bearer <token> or Basic <base64>.
Cookie / Set-Cookierequest / responseThe browser's memory: the server sets, the browser returns it on every later request.
User-AgentrequestClient software. Never trust it for security.
OriginrequestWhere a browser page came from. The basis of CORS (Unit 5).
LocationresponseWhere to go (redirects) or where the new resource lives (201).
Cache-Control, ETag, If-None-MatchbothCaching and conditional requests (below and Unit 5).
Access-Control-Allow-*responseCORS permissions for browsers (Unit 5).
Retry-AfterresponseSeconds to wait (429, 503).
X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-ProtorequestAdded by proxies: the real client IP and original protocol (Unit 10).
Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-PolicyresponseSecurity headers (Unit 7).

Content types you will handle as a backend

Content-TypeSent byExpress parser
application/jsonfetch / API clientsexpress.json()
application/x-www-form-urlencodedClassic HTML forms (name=Ana&age=20)express.urlencoded()
multipart/form-dataForms with file uploadsmulter or busboy (Unit 5)
text/plain, application/octet-streamRaw text and binaryexpress.text(), express.raw()

Seeing what a client sends

$ curl -s localhost:3000/headers
{"host":"localhost:3000","user-agent":"curl/8.5.0","accept":"*/*"}
$ curl -s localhost:3000/headers -H 'Authorization: Bearer abc123' -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'X-Request-Id: 7'
{"host":"localhost:3000","user-agent":"curl/8.5.0","authorization":"Bearer abc123","accept":"application/json","x-request-id":"7"}
$ curl -s 'localhost:3000/echo?sort=date&limit=10' -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"hi"}'
{"method":"POST","path":"/echo","query":{"sort":"date","limit":"10"},"body":{"title":"hi"},"type":"application/json"}

The playground's /headers route simply returns req.headers. Notice the lowercase names, and that custom headers (X-Request-Id) arrive as-is. The /echo route shows how a URL's query string, the JSON body and the content type each arrive on the request object (you will meet req.query and req.body in Unit 4).

Cookies: the server's note to the browser

Because HTTP is stateless, a server that wants to recognise a returning browser hands it a small note with Set-Cookie. The browser sends it back in a Cookie header with every later request to that site.

$ curl -i -c jar.txt localhost:3000/cookie/set
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: theme=dark; Max-Age=3600; Path=/; Expires=Fri, 23 Oct 2026 04:56:38 GMT; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 20
ETag: W/"14-6HGypq1tN9iQe/zbsH3AcBNFy+M"
Date: Fri, 23 Oct 2026 09:30:00 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"set":"theme=dark"}
$ curl -s -b jar.txt localhost:3000/cookie/read
{"cookieHeader":"theme=dark"}
$ curl -s localhost:3000/cookie/read
{"cookieHeader":""}
Cookie attributeEffect
HttpOnlyJavaScript on the page cannot read it (document.cookie). Protects session cookies from XSS theft.
SecureOnly sent over HTTPS.
SameSite=Lax|Strict|NoneWhether it is sent on cross-site requests. A main defence against CSRF. None requires Secure.
Max-Age / ExpiresHow long it lives. Without either it is a session cookie, deleted when the browser closes.
Path, DomainWhich URLs and hosts receive it.
GotchaCookies are sent automatically by the browser, even on requests triggered by other sites. That convenience is the reason CSRF exists (Unit 7). They are also limited to about 4 KB each, so store an id, not data.

Caching in one real example: ETag and 304

Express adds an ETag (a fingerprint of the body) to responses. A client that already has the content sends it back in If-None-Match; if nothing changed the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body, saving bandwidth.

$ curl -i localhost:3000/etag
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: no-cache
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 20
ETag: W/"14-IEL9wYI9q/fc5WhVokqFEMN2HRg"
Date: Fri, 23 Oct 2026 09:30:00 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"stable":"content"}
$ etag=$(curl -sI localhost:3000/etag | grep -i '^etag' | cut -d' ' -f2 | tr -d '\r'); curl -i localhost:3000/etag -H "If-None-Match: $etag"
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
Cache-Control: no-cache
ETag: W/"14-IEL9wYI9q/fc5WhVokqFEMN2HRg"
Date: Fri, 23 Oct 2026 09:30:00 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

The second command first fetches the ETag, then repeats the request with If-None-Match set to it. The server compared fingerprints, found them equal, and answered 304 Not Modified with no body. Browsers do this automatically for cached resources. Unit 5 covers Cache-Control in depth.

JSON in five lines

{
  "id": 42,
  "title": "Buy milk",
  "done": false,
  "tags": ["home", "urgent"],
  "owner": { "id": 7, "name": "Ana" },
  "dueDate": null
}
  • Six value types: string (double quotes only), number, boolean, null, array, object. No undefined, no functions, no comments, no trailing commas.
  • JSON has no date type. Send dates as ISO 8601 strings: "2026-10-23T09:30:00Z".
  • In JavaScript: JSON.stringify(value) turns a value into text, JSON.parse(text) turns text back (and throws on invalid JSON).
const note = { id: 42, title: "Buy milk", due: new Date("2026-10-23T09:30:00Z"), secret: undefined, tags: ["home"] };
const text = JSON.stringify(note);
console.log(text);                                  // Date became a string, undefined vanished
console.log(JSON.parse(text).due instanceof Date);  // false: you get a string back
console.log(JSON.stringify(note, null, 2));         // pretty printed
try { JSON.parse("{'bad': 'quotes'}"); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ":", e.message); }
{"id":42,"title":"Buy milk","due":"2026-10-23T09:30:00.000Z","tags":["home"]} false { "id": 42, "title": "Buy milk", "due": "2026-10-23T09:30:00.000Z", "tags": [ "home" ] } SyntaxError: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2)

REST: designing APIs around resources

REST is a style, not a standard: model your API as resources (nouns) identified by URLs, and use the HTTP methods as the verbs. Most "REST APIs" follow a small set of conventions.

GoalRequestSuccess
List notesGET /notes200 + array
One noteGET /notes/42200 + object, or 404
Create a notePOST /notes + JSON body201 + Location + the new note
Replace a notePUT /notes/42 + full body200
Change some fieldsPATCH /notes/42 + changed fields200
Delete a noteDELETE /notes/42204
A user's notesGET /users/7/notes200 + array
Search and pageGET /notes?q=milk&limit=10&page=2200 + array and paging info
An action that is not CRUDPOST /notes/42/archive200 or 204
Do
  • Plural nouns: /notes, /users
  • Lowercase, hyphens: /reading-lists
  • Nest only one level: /users/7/notes
  • Return the right status code
  • Use the same error shape everywhere
  • Version when you break things: /v1/...
Avoid
  • Verbs in paths: /getNotes, /createUser
  • GET that changes data
  • 200 with {"{ error: ... }"} inside
  • Deep nesting: /a/1/b/2/c/3/d
  • Leaking internal ids or database columns you did not mean to publish
  • Different shapes for the same thing on different routes
REST constraintIn practice
Client-serverFrontend and backend evolve separately, joined only by the API.
StatelessEvery request carries what the server needs (token). No server-side conversation memory, so any server instance can answer.
CacheableResponses say whether they may be cached (Cache-Control, ETag).
Uniform interfaceResources, standard methods, standard status codes, self-describing messages.
Layered systemProxies, caches and gateways can sit in between without the client knowing.
REST versus the restGraphQL lets a client ask for exactly the fields it needs through one endpoint, and gRPC uses a compact binary protocol between services. REST with JSON remains the default for public and web APIs. Unit 8 shows GraphQL working.

Which Node.js version

LineStatus in October 2026End of life
Node 22 (Jod)LTS (maintenance). The version every example in this guide was run on.30 April 2027
Node 24 (Krypton)LTS (active)30 April 2028

Use an LTS (long-term support) version for anything real. Even-numbered releases become LTS; odd ones never do. Everything in this guide works on Node 22 and later; where a feature needs something newer or is still experimental it says so. Dates are from the Node.js release schedule and may change: check nodejs.org.

1

Install Node.js

winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS

Or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org. To switch versions easily, install fnm (winget install Schniz.fnm) or nvm-windows, then fnm install 24 and fnm use 24. Close and reopen the terminal afterwards so the new PATH is picked up.

brew install node@24
# or, to switch versions easily:
brew install fnm
fnm install 24
fnm use 24

Or use the installer from nodejs.org. Homebrew's node@24 may need brew link or a PATH line: the command prints exactly what to add.

curl -fsSL https://fnm.vercel.app/install | bash
# open a new terminal, then:
fnm install 24
fnm use 24

Distribution packages (apt install nodejs) are often old. A version manager (fnm, nvm) or NodeSource packages give you a current LTS and let you switch per project.

node runs JavaScript. npm (Node Package Manager) installs libraries and ships with Node. node -p "expr" evaluates an expression and prints it: a quick calculator that also proves Node works. Your versions will differ from the output above.

Terminal basics you will needcd folder moves into a folder, cd .. goes up, ls (macOS/Linux/PowerShell) lists files, pwd shows where you are, Ctrl+C stops a running program (your server), and the Up arrow recalls the last command. Unit 2: JavaScript for the Backend

A complete tour of modern JavaScript syntax as you will use it on a server: values, operators, control flow, functions, objects, arrays, classes, errors, async code, text and dates, and TypeScript in a nutshell. Every snippet was run.

JavaScript was made for browsers; Node.js lets the same language run anywhere, including on servers. There are four ways to run code with Node.

WayCommandUse it for
A filenode app.jsReal programs. Add --watch to restart on every save.
The REPLnode (then type; Ctrl+D to leave)Trying a snippet. Read-Eval-Print Loop.
One expressionnode -p "1 + 2"Quick calculations, scripts in shell one-liners.
One statementnode -e "console.log('hi')"Tiny scripts (-p also prints the result).
 
$ node -p "[1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2)"
[ 2, 4, 6 ]
$ node -e "console.log(process.argv.slice(1))" a b c
[ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]
$ echo 'console.log("from a file:", 6 * 7)' > hello.js
$ node hello.js
from a file: 42
// A comment: ignored by the computer, written for people.
/* A block comment can
   span several lines. */

const name = "Ana";                 // a statement ends with a semicolon (usually optional, see below)
let count = 3;
console.log(`Hello ${name}, you have ${count} messages`);   // template literal: backticks + ${expression}

// blocks group statements; variables declared with let/const live only inside their block
if (count > 2) {
  const bonus = 10;
  count += bonus;
}
console.log(count);
// console.log(bonus);   // ReferenceError: bonus is not defined (it died with the block)
Hello Ana, you have 3 messages 13

Semicolons, and the one place they bite

JavaScript inserts missing semicolons automatically (ASI). You may write with or without them, but pick one style and let Prettier enforce it. The danger is a line that starts with (, [ or a backtick: the previous line then continues into it.

const a = 1
const b = 2
const result = a + b
;[1, 2].forEach((n) => console.log(n))   // a leading semicolon protects a line that starts with [

console.log(result)
1 2 3

Now the real trap. Nothing separates the two statements below, so JavaScript reads them as one: "text"(function () {...})(), which tries to call a string.

const value = "text"
(function () { console.log("never runs") })()
file:///app/app.mjs:2 (function () { console.log("never runs") })() ^ TypeError: "text" is not a function at file:///app/app.mjs:2:1 Node.js v22.22.0 [process exited with code 1]

Strict mode and modules

  • ES modules (files using import/export, .mjs files, or a package with "type": "module") are always in strict mode: silent mistakes become errors (assigning to an undeclared variable, duplicate parameter names). Old CommonJS files (require) are sloppy unless they start with 'use strict'.
  • Use ES modules for new code. Node treats a .js file as a module only if the nearest package.json says "type": "module" (Unit 3 explains both systems).
  • Identifiers are case-sensitive (name is not Name), may contain letters, digits, _ and $, and cannot start with a digit. Convention: camelCase for variables and functions, PascalCase for classes, UPPER_SNAKE for constants.
"use strict";
try {
  undeclaredVariable = 5;       // a typo in sloppy mode silently creates a global
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.name + ":", e.message);
}
console.log(typeof this, "(top-level this in a module is undefined)");
ReferenceError: undeclaredVariable is not defined undefined (top-level this in a module is undefined)

let, const and var

KeywordScopeReassignHoistingUse?
constblockNoUsable only after its line (temporal dead zone)Default choice
letblockYesSame dead zoneWhen the value changes (counters, accumulators)
varfunctionYesExists from the top as undefinedNever in new code

const protects the variable, not the value it points to: a const array can still be pushed to.

const port = 3000;
// port = 4000;                       // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
const list = [1, 2];
list.push(3);                         // allowed: the array changes, the variable still points to the same array
console.log(port, list);

let total = 0;
for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) total += i;   // i exists only inside the loop
console.log(total);

try { console.log(early); let early = 1; } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ":", e.message); }   // dead zone
var legacy = "hoisted";                    // var leaks out of blocks
{ var leaked = "I escaped the block"; }
console.log(leaked);
3000 [ 1, 2, 3 ] 6 ReferenceError: Cannot access 'early' before initialization I escaped the block

The types

TypeExampleNotes
string"a", 'b', `c ${1}`Immutable text (UTF-16).
number42, 3.14, NaN, InfinityOne 64-bit float type for integers and decimals. Safe integers up to 253-1.
bigint9007199254740993nArbitrary-size integers. Cannot mix with numbers in arithmetic.
booleantrue, false
undefinedundefined"No value yet": missing property, uninitialised variable, function with no return.
nullnull"Intentionally empty".
symbolSymbol("id")A unique key. Rare in app code.
object{}, [], functions, dates, mapsEverything else. Compared by reference, not content.
 
const samples = ["text", 42, 10n, true, undefined, null, Symbol("s"), {}, [], () => {}, new Date(0), NaN];
for (const v of samples) console.log(String(typeof v).padEnd(10), Array.isArray(v) ? "array" : v instanceof Date ? v.toISOString() : String(v).slice(0, 25));

console.log(0.1 + 0.2, 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);         // floating point: decimals are approximate
console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, 2 ** 53 + 1); // beyond 2^53 integers lose precision
console.log(9007199254740993n + 1n);                // bigint is exact
console.log({} === {}, [1] === [1]);                // objects compare by identity, not content
string text number 42 bigint 10 boolean true undefined undefined object null symbol Symbol(s) object [object Object] object array function () => {} object 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z number NaN 0.30000000000000004 false 9007199254740991 9007199254740992 9007199254740994n false false

Truthy, falsy and equality

In a condition, every value is converted to true or false. Exactly eight falsy values exist: false 0 -0 0n "" null undefined NaN. Everything else is truthy, including "0", "false", [] and {}.

const falsy = [false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN];
console.log(falsy.map((v) => Boolean(v)).every((b) => b === false));       // true
console.log(Boolean("0"), Boolean([]), Boolean({}), Boolean(" "));          // all true

// === compares value AND type. == converts first, with confusing rules. Always use ===.
console.log(1 === "1", 1 == "1", null == undefined, null === undefined, 0 == "", "0" == false);
console.log(NaN === NaN, Number.isNaN(NaN), Object.is(NaN, NaN));          // NaN is not equal to itself

// Conversions you will meet when reading request data (everything arrives as a string!)
console.log(Number("42"), Number(""), Number("4x2"), parseInt("42px"), parseFloat("3.14abc"), +"7");
console.log(String(123), (255).toString(16), (0.5).toFixed(2), Number("12").toString().padStart(4, "0"));
console.log(Boolean("false"), !!"", Array.from("abc"), [..."hi"]);
true true true true true false true true false true true false true true 42 0 NaN 42 3.14 7 123 ff 0.50 0012 true false [ 'a', 'b', 'c' ] [ 'h', 'i' ]
Backend trapQuery strings, form fields, headers and environment variables are always strings. req.query.limit is "10", not 10, so "10" + 5 is "105". Convert and validate every value at the edge of your app (Unit 5 uses Zod for this). Also, process.env.DEBUG = "false" is a truthy string.
GroupOperatorsNotes
Arithmetic+ - * / % ** ++ --% is remainder. ** is power. + also joins strings.
Comparison=== !== < > <= >=Avoid ==. Comparing strings is alphabetical, numbers numeric.
Logical&& || !Return one of the operands, not a boolean (short-circuit).
Nullish?? ??=Fall back only for null/undefined.
Optional chaininga?.b a?.[0] fn?.()Stops at null/undefined with undefined instead of throwing.
Assignment= += -= *= /= ||= &&= ??=Compound forms update in place.
Ternarycond ? a : bAn expression that picks a value.
Spread / rest...xSpread expands, rest collects.
Othertypeof instanceof in delete void ,"k" in obj tests a key.
 
console.log(7 / 2, Math.trunc(7 / 2), 7 % 3, 2 ** 10, -7 % 3);
console.log("5" + 2, "5" - 2, "5" * "2", JSON.stringify([] + []), 1 + true);        // + joins strings, the others convert to numbers

// && and || return one of their operands: very common in real code
const user = { name: "Ana", nick: "", age: 0 };
console.log(user.nick || "anonymous");        // "" is falsy, so the fallback wins
console.log(user.nick ?? "anonymous");        // "" is not null/undefined, so it is kept
console.log(user.age || 18, user.age ?? 18);  // 18 vs 0: ?? protects legitimate zeros
console.log(user.name && user.name.toUpperCase());

// optional chaining: safe access to things that might not exist
const config = { db: { host: "localhost" } };
console.log(config.db?.host, config.cache?.host, config.cache?.host ?? "no cache", config.run?.());

// logical assignment
let retries; retries ??= 3; retries ||= 5; retries &&= retries + 1;
console.log(retries);

// ternary and a few others
const label = user.age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";
console.log(label, "name" in user, typeof user.missing, delete user.age, user);
3.5 3 1 1024 -1 52 3 10 "" 2 anonymous 18 0 ANA localhost undefined no cache undefined 4 minor true undefined true { name: 'Ana', nick: '' }
PrecedenceMultiplication binds tighter than addition, && tighter than ||. Do not memorise the table: add parentheses whenever a reader would have to think. Mixing ?? with || or && without parentheses is a syntax error on purpose.
function describe(statusCode) {
  if (statusCode >= 500) return "server error";
  else if (statusCode >= 400) return "client error";
  else if (statusCode >= 300) return "redirect";
  else if (statusCode >= 200) return "success";
  return "informational";
}
console.log([200, 301, 404, 503, 101].map(describe));

// switch compares with ===, falls through without break, and default catches the rest
function methodKind(method) {
  switch (method) {
    case "GET":
    case "HEAD":
      return "read";                  // two cases sharing one result
    case "POST":
    case "PUT":
    case "PATCH":
    case "DELETE":
      return "write";
    default:
      return "unknown";
  }
}
console.log(["GET", "DELETE", "TRACE"].map(methodKind));

// an object lookup is often cleaner than a long switch
const messages = { 400: "Bad Request", 404: "Not Found" };
console.log(messages[404] ?? "Unknown", messages[999] ?? "Unknown");
[ 'success', 'redirect', 'client error', 'server error', 'informational' ] [ 'read', 'write', 'unknown' ] Not Found Unknown

Loops

LoopIteratesUse for
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)A counterWhen you need the index or a custom step.
for (const x of iterable)Values of arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, generatorsThe everyday loop. Works with await.
for (const k in object)Keys of an object (including inherited)Rarely. Prefer Object.keys/entries.
while (cond) / do ... whileUntil a condition failsWhen you do not know the count (read until done).
 
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) console.log("for", i);

const fruits = ["apple", "pear", "fig"];
for (const f of fruits) console.log("of", f);
for (const [i, f] of fruits.entries()) console.log("entries", i, f);        // index and value together
for (const ch of "héy") console.log("char", ch);

const scores = { ana: 3, raj: 5 };
for (const key in scores) console.log("in", key, scores[key]);               // keys
for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(scores)) console.log("entries", k, v);   // clearer

let n = 3;
while (n > 0) { n--; if (n === 1) continue; console.log("while", n); }      // continue skips the rest of this round

outer: for (let a = 0; a < 3; a++) {                                         // a label lets break leave BOTH loops
  for (let b = 0; b < 3; b++) {
    if (a * b === 2) break outer;
    console.log("pair", a, b);
  }
}
for 0 for 1 for 2 of apple of pear of fig entries 0 apple entries 1 pear entries 2 fig char h char é char y in ana 3 in raj 5 entries ana 3 entries raj 5 while 2 while 0 pair 0 0 pair 0 1 pair 0 2 pair 1 0 pair 1 1
GotchaUse for...of for arrays, not for...in: for...in gives string indexes and can include inherited properties. And array.forEach(async (x) => await ...) does not wait for the async work. Use for...of with await (Unit 2, async entry).

Three ways to write a function

// 1. declaration: hoisted, so you can call it before its line
console.log(add(2, 3));
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

// 2. function expression: a function stored in a variable
const multiply = function (a, b) { return a * b; };

// 3. arrow function: short, no own `this`, great for callbacks
const square = (n) => n * n;                 // one expression returns automatically
const makeUser = (name) => ({ name, admin: false });   // wrap an object literal in () to return it
const greet = (name) => {                    // a block body needs an explicit return
  const text = `Hi ${name}`;
  return text;
};
console.log(multiply(3, 4), square(5), makeUser("Ana"), greet("Raj"));

console.log(add.name, square.name, add.length, typeof add);   // functions are objects: they have properties
5 12 25 { name: 'Ana', admin: false } Hi Raj add square 2 function

Parameters

function listen(port = 3000, host = "localhost") {          // default values
  return `${host}:${port}`;
}
console.log(listen(), listen(8080), listen(undefined, "0.0.0.0"));

function sum(...numbers) {                                   // rest: collects the remaining arguments into an array
  return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
console.log(sum(), sum(1, 2, 3));

function createUser({ name, role = "viewer", ...rest }) {   // destructured options object: self-documenting calls
  return { name, role, extra: rest };
}
console.log(createUser({ name: "Ana", age: 30 }));

const args = [4, 5, 6];
console.log(Math.max(...args), sum(...args));                // spread: expands an array into arguments
localhost:3000 localhost:8080 0.0.0.0:3000 0 6 { name: 'Ana', role: 'viewer', extra: { age: 30 } } 6 15
Options objectsWhen a function takes more than two or three parameters, accept one object: createUser({ name, role }). Call sites then read like documentation and argument order stops mattering.

Scope and closures

Scope is where a name is visible. Inner functions can see the variables around them. A closure is an inner function that keeps those outer variables alive after the outer function has finished. Servers use closures constantly: middleware factories, counters, caches, configuration.

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;                         // private: nothing outside can touch it directly
  return {
    increment: () => ++count,
    value: () => count,
  };
}
const a = makeCounter(), b = makeCounter();
a.increment(); a.increment(); b.increment();
console.log(a.value(), b.value());       // two separate counters, each with its own hidden count

// a function that returns a configured function: this is exactly how Express middleware factories work
function requireRole(role) {
  return (user) => user.role === role ? "allowed" : "denied";
}
const adminOnly = requireRole("admin");
console.log(adminOnly({ role: "admin" }), adminOnly({ role: "guest" }));

const once = (fn) => { let done = false, result; return (...args) => (done ? result : (done = true, result = fn(...args))); };
const init = once(() => { console.log("expensive setup"); return 42; });
console.log(init(), init());             // setup ran once
2 1 allowed denied expensive setup 42 42

Functions are values: higher-order functions

const apply = (fn, x) => fn(x);                          // takes a function
const double = (n) => n * 2;
console.log(apply(double, 21));

const compose = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduceRight((v, f) => f(v), x);   // returns a function
const slug = compose((s) => s.replaceAll(" ", "-"), (s) => s.toLowerCase(), (s) => s.trim());
console.log(slug("  Hello Big World "));

// callbacks: a function you hand over to be called later
[3, 1, 2].toSorted((a, b) => a - b).forEach((n) => console.log("item", n));
setTimeout(() => console.log("later"), 10);
console.log("now");
42 hello-big-world item 1 item 2 item 3 now later

this: what it is and why arrows matter

this is decided by how a function is called: obj.method() gives this = obj; a plain call gives undefined (strict mode); new makes a new object; call/apply/bind set it explicitly. Arrow functions have no this of their own: they use the one around them.

const server = {
  name: "api-1",
  regular() { return this?.name; },
  arrow: () => typeof this,                 // module top level: this is undefined
  delayed() { setTimeout(() => console.log("arrow keeps this:", this.name), 5); },
};
console.log(server.regular());               // called as server.method(): this is server
const detached = server.regular;
console.log(detached());                     // called alone: this is undefined
console.log(detached.call({ name: "other" }), detached.bind({ name: "bound" })());
console.log(server.arrow());
server.delayed();                            // arrow inside a method inherits the method's this

class Logger {
  prefix = "[log]";
  log = (msg) => `${this.prefix} ${msg}`;    // arrow field: stays bound even when passed around
}
const { log } = new Logger();
console.log(log("works detached"));
api-1 undefined other bound undefined [log] works detached arrow keeps this: api-1
The classic bugPassing a method as a callback (app.get('/', controller.list)) loses this. Fix with an arrow wrapper, .bind(controller), or by writing controllers as plain functions (the style used in this guide).

An object is a bag of key: value pairs. Almost everything in a backend is one: a request, a database row, a config, a JSON response.

const key = "email";
const user = {
  id: 1,
  name: "Ana",
  [key]: "ana@example.com",             // computed key: the name comes from a variable
  address: { city: "Pune", zip: "411001" },
  greet() { return `Hi, I am ${this.name}`; },   // method shorthand
  get label() { return `${this.name} <${this.email}>`; },   // getter: looks like a property
};

console.log(user.name, user["email"], user.address.city, user.greet(), user.label);
user.age = 30;                           // add
user.name = "Ana K.";                    // change
delete user.age;                         // remove
console.log("age" in user, Object.hasOwn(user, "name"));

const id = 7, role = "admin";
console.log({ id, role });               // shorthand: { id: id, role: role }

console.log(Object.keys(user.address), Object.values(user.address), Object.entries(user.address));
console.log(Object.fromEntries([["a", 1], ["b", 2]]));      // entries back into an object
Ana ana@example.com Pune Hi, I am Ana Ana <ana@example.com> false true { id: 7, role: 'admin' } [ 'city', 'zip' ] [ 'Pune', '411001' ] [ [ 'city', 'Pune' ], [ 'zip', '411001' ] ] { a: 1, b: 2 }

Destructuring: unpack values into variables

const user = { id: 1, name: "Ana", address: { city: "Pune" }, tags: ["a", "b", "c"] };

const { name, id } = user;                              // pull properties out by name
const { name: fullName, role = "viewer" } = user;       // rename, and a default for missing values
const { address: { city } } = user;                     // nested
const { id: _ignored, ...others } = user;               // rest: everything else
console.log(name, id, fullName, role, city, Object.keys(others));

const [first, , third, ...remaining] = ["x", "y", "z", "w", "v"];   // arrays go by position
console.log(first, third, remaining);

let a = 1, b = 2;
[a, b] = [b, a];                                         // swap without a temp variable
console.log(a, b);

function handle({ method, url = "/", headers: { host } = {} }) {   // in parameters, with defaults at each level
  return `${method} ${host ?? "no-host"}${url}`;
}
console.log(handle({ method: "GET", headers: { host: "api.test" } }), handle({ method: "POST" }));
Ana 1 Ana viewer Pune [ 'name', 'address', 'tags' ] x z [ 'w', 'v' ] 2 1 GET api.test/ POST no-host/

Spread, copies and immutability

Assigning an object to another variable copies the reference, not the object. {...obj} makes a shallow copy (nested objects are still shared). structuredClone() makes a deep copy.

const original = { name: "Ana", prefs: { theme: "dark" } };
const alias = original;                                  // same object
const shallow = { ...original };                         // new top level, shared prefs
const deep = structuredClone(original);                  // fully independent

original.name = "Changed";
original.prefs.theme = "light";
console.log(alias.name, shallow.name, deep.name);        // Changed Ana Ana
console.log(shallow.prefs.theme, deep.prefs.theme);      // light dark   (the shallow copy shares nested objects)

// merging and overriding: later keys win
const defaults = { port: 3000, debug: false };
const fromEnv = { port: 8080 };
console.log({ ...defaults, ...fromEnv, extra: true });

// non-mutating "update": the pattern behind many state-handling libraries
const updated = { ...original, name: "New" };
console.log(updated.name, original.name);

const locked = Object.freeze({ a: 1, nested: { b: 2 } });
try { locked.a = 99; } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ":", e.message); }   // strict mode (modules) throws; sloppy scripts ignore it silently
locked.nested.b = 3;                                     // freeze is shallow: nested objects stay editable
console.log(locked, Object.isFrozen(locked));
Changed Ana Ana light dark { port: 8080, debug: false, extra: true } New Changed TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'a' of object '#<Object>' { a: 1, nested: { b: 3 } } true
Prototypes in one sentenceEvery object has a hidden link to a prototype object where it looks for properties it does not have itself; that is how methods like .toString() and class inheritance work. You rarely touch prototypes directly: class (below) is the friendly syntax over them.

Arrays are ordered lists. The backbone of everyday JavaScript is a handful of methods that take a function: learn these and most loops disappear.

MethodReturnsMutates?Purpose
map(fn)new arrayNoTransform every item
filter(fn)new arrayNoKeep items where fn is truthy
reduce(fn, start)one valueNoFold the list into a total, object, anything
find(fn) / findIndex / findLastitem / indexNoFirst (or last) match, else undefined / -1
some(fn) / every(fn)booleanNoAny / all match
includes(x) / indexOf(x)boolean / indexNoMembership by value
push pop shift unshiftlength / itemYesAdd or remove at the end or start
splice(i, n, ...add)removed itemsYesCut and insert in the middle
slice(a, b)new arrayNoCopy a range
sort(cmp) / reverse()same arrayYesOrder in place
toSorted toReversed toSpliced withnew arrayNoNon-mutating versions (Node 20+)
flat(depth) / flatMap(fn)new arrayNoFlatten nested lists
join(sep) / concat / at(i)string / array / itemNoat(-1) is the last item
Array.from / Array.of / Array.isArrayarray / boolean-Create and test
Object.groupBy(arr, fn)objectNoGroup items by a key (Node 21+)
 
const orders = [
  { id: 1, customer: "ana", total: 40, paid: true },
  { id: 2, customer: "raj", total: 15, paid: false },
  { id: 3, customer: "ana", total: 25, paid: true },
  { id: 4, customer: "lee", total: 90, paid: true },
];

console.log(orders.map((o) => o.total));                              // transform
console.log(orders.filter((o) => o.paid).map((o) => o.id));           // keep, then transform: chain them
console.log(orders.find((o) => o.total > 50)?.customer);              // first match
console.log(orders.some((o) => !o.paid), orders.every((o) => o.total > 10));

const revenue = orders.filter((o) => o.paid).reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total, 0);   // fold into one number
console.log(revenue);

// reduce can build any shape: here, a total per customer
const byCustomer = orders.reduce((acc, o) => {
  acc[o.customer] = (acc[o.customer] ?? 0) + o.total;
  return acc;
}, {});
console.log(byCustomer);

console.log(Object.groupBy(orders, (o) => (o.paid ? "paid" : "unpaid")).unpaid);
[ 40, 15, 25, 90 ] [ 1, 3, 4 ] lee true true 155 { ana: 65, raj: 15, lee: 90 } [ { id: 2, customer: 'raj', total: 15, paid: false } ]

Sorting, copying and the mutation traps

console.log([10, 9, 1, 100].sort());                       // default sort is TEXT order: [1, 10, 100, 9]
console.log([10, 9, 1, 100].sort((a, b) => a - b));        // numeric: negative = a first, positive = b first

const people = [{ n: "Zed", age: 30 }, { n: "Amy", age: 25 }, { n: "Bob", age: 30 }];
console.log(people.toSorted((a, b) => b.age - a.age || a.n.localeCompare(b.n)).map((p) => p.n));   // two keys; toSorted keeps the original intact
console.log(people.map((p) => p.n));                       // untouched

const list = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
console.log(list.slice(1, 3), list.at(-1), list.indexOf(4), list.includes(9));
const removed = list.splice(1, 2, "a", "b", "c");          // from index 1 remove 2 items, insert three
console.log(removed, list);

console.log([[1, 2], [3, [4]]].flat(), [[1, 2], [3, [4]]].flat(Infinity), ["a b", "c"].flatMap((s) => s.split(" ")));
console.log(Array.from({ length: 4 }, (_, i) => i * i), Array(3).fill(0), [..."abc"].reverse().join(""));

console.log([...new Set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3])]);

Mutation trapssort(), reverse(), splice() and push() change the array they are called on. If that array is shared (a cache, module-level data), use toSorted(), toReversed(), toSpliced() or copy first with [...arr]. Also, sort() without a comparator sorts numbers as text.

Regular expressions

A regex is a pattern for matching text, written /pattern/flags. Backends use them to validate input, parse log lines and rewrite URLs.

PieceMeaningPieceMeaning
.any character\d \w \sdigit, word char, whitespace
^ $start, end of text[abc] [^abc] [a-z]one of, none of, range
* + ?0+, 1+, 0 or 1{2,4}between 2 and 4 times
(...)capture group(?<name>...)named group
a|ba or b\bword boundary
gflag: all matchesi m uignore case, multiline, unicode
 
const email = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/;
console.log(email.test("ana@example.com"), email.test("not an email"));

const log = "2026-10-23 ERROR db: connection refused (code 5432)";
const m = log.match(/^(?<date>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}) (?<level>[A-Z]+) (?<rest>.*)$/);
console.log(m.groups);                                   // named groups come back as an object

console.log("a1b22c333".match(/\d+/g));                  // g: every match
console.log([..."k1=v1;k2=v2".matchAll(/(\w+)=(\w+)/g)].map(([, k, v]) => [k, v]));
console.log("Hello World".replace(/o/g, "0"), "john smith".replace(/\b\w/g, (c) => c.toUpperCase()));
console.log("2026-10-23".replace(/(\d+)-(\d+)-(\d+)/, "$3/$2/$1"));   // $1.. refer to capture groups
console.log("a, b;c  d".split(/[,; ]+/));
true false [Object: null prototype] { date: '2026-10-23', level: 'ERROR', rest: 'db: connection refused (code 5432)' } [ '1', '22', '333' ] [ [ 'k1', 'v1' ], [ 'k2', 'v2' ] ] Hell0 W0rld John Smith 23/10/2026 [ 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' ]
ReDoSA badly written pattern such as /(a+)+$/ can take exponential time on crafted input and freeze your server (a "regular expression denial of service"). Never run a complicated regex on unbounded user input, and prefer simple patterns plus length limits.
UseWhen
MapKey-value storage where keys can be anything, you add and delete often, and you need the size and insertion order. Ideal for caches and counters keyed by user input (it is immune to the __proto__ key tricks that affect plain objects).
SetA list with no duplicates and fast membership tests (has).
WeakMap / WeakSetAttach data to an object without keeping it alive: the entry vanishes when the object is garbage collected.
Plain objectA fixed record with known fields (the shape of JSON).
 
const hits = new Map();
for (const path of ["/", "/api", "/", "/", "/api"]) hits.set(path, (hits.get(path) ?? 0) + 1);
console.log(hits, hits.size, hits.has("/api"), hits.get("/missing"));
hits.delete("/api");
for (const [path, count] of hits) console.log(path, count);
console.log([...hits.keys()], Object.fromEntries(hits), new Map(Object.entries({ a: 1 })));

const seen = new Set([1, 2, 3]);
seen.add(3).add(4);                                          // adding a duplicate does nothing
console.log(seen, seen.has(2), seen.size);
const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]), b = new Set([2, 3, 4]);
console.log(a.intersection(b), a.union(b), a.difference(b));   // set algebra (Node 22+)

// a tiny in-memory cache with expiry, the Map pattern you will write constantly
const cache = new Map();
const setCache = (k, v, ttlMs) => cache.set(k, { v, until: Date.now() + ttlMs });
const getCache = (k) => { const e = cache.get(k); if (!e) return; if (e.until < Date.now()) { cache.delete(k); return; } return e.v; };
setCache("user:1", { name: "Ana" }, 50);
console.log(getCache("user:1"));
setTimeout(() => console.log(getCache("user:1")), 80);        // expired by now: undefined
