Iterators and generators

Anything you can loop over with for...of (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets) follows the iterator protocol. A generator function (function*) writes your own iterable: it pauses at every yield and resumes on demand. Node streams and async iteration (below) build on this idea.

function* range(start, end, step = 1) {
  for (let n = start; n < end; n += step) yield n;        // pause here, hand a value out, continue later
}
console.log([...range(0, 10, 3)]);

function* ids() { let id = 1; while (true) yield id++; }    // infinite, yet harmless: values are made only when asked
const gen = ids();
console.log(gen.next(), gen.next().value, gen.next().value);

for (const n of ids()) { if (n > 3) break; console.log("id", n); }

const iterable = { *[Symbol.iterator]() { yield "a"; yield "b"; } };   // any object can be made iterable
console.log([...iterable], Array.from(iterable));
[ 0, 3, 6, 9 ] { value: 1, done: false } 2 3 id 1 id 2 id 3 [ 'a', 'b' ] [ 'a', 'b' ]

A class is a template for objects that share behaviour and carry their own data. Backends use classes for services, custom errors, repositories and anything holding state with methods.

class Account {
  static count = 0;                          // belongs to the class, not to instances
  #balance = 0;                              // private field: only code inside the class can touch it
  owner;                                     // public field

  constructor(owner, opening = 0) {
    this.owner = owner;
    this.#balance = opening;
    Account.count++;
  }

  deposit(amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) throw new RangeError("Amount must be positive");
    this.#balance += amount;
    return this;                             // returning this allows chaining
  }

  get balance() { return this.#balance; }    // read-only from outside (no setter)

  static compare(a, b) { return a.#balance - b.#balance; }

  toString() { return `${this.owner}: ${this.#balance}`; }
}

const a = new Account("Ana", 100).deposit(50).deposit(25);
const b = new Account("Raj");
console.log(a.balance, `${a}`, Account.count, Account.compare(a, b) > 0);
try { a.balance = 5; } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ":", e.message); }   // getter only: modules are strict, so this throws
175 Ana: 175 2 true TypeError: Cannot set property balance of [object Object] which has only a getter

Private means private. Touching #balance from outside the class is not a runtime error you can catch, it is a SyntaxError that stops the file before anything runs:

class Account { #balance = 100; }
const a = new Account();
console.log(a.#balance);
file:///app/app.mjs:3 console.log(a.#balance); ^ SyntaxError: Private field '#balance' must be declared in an enclosing class Node.js v22.22.0 [process exited with code 1]

Compare this with the older convention of naming a field _balance, which is only a polite request.

Inheritance and custom behaviour

class Animal {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
  speak() { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  constructor(name, breed) {
    super(name);                              // must call the parent constructor before using this
    this.breed = breed;
  }
  speak() { return `${super.speak()}: woof`; }   // override, reusing the parent version
}
const d = new Dog("Rex", "lab");
console.log(d.speak(), d instanceof Dog, d instanceof Animal, Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog) === Animal);
console.log(d.constructor.name, d);

// Prefer composition when "has a" fits better than "is a": pass collaborators in
class Mailer { send(to, msg) { return `mail to ${to}: ${msg}`; } }
class SignupService {
  constructor(mailer) { this.mailer = mailer; }          // dependency injection: easy to swap in tests
  register(email) { return this.mailer.send(email, "welcome!"); }
}
console.log(new SignupService(new Mailer()).register("ana@example.com"));
Rex makes a sound: woof true true true Dog Dog { name: 'Rex', breed: 'lab' } mail to ana@example.com: welcome!

When something goes wrong, JavaScript throws an error. A thrown error travels up through the callers until a catch handles it; if nobody does, the process crashes. Good backends decide deliberately which errors to handle and which to let crash.

function parseConfig(text) {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(text);                          // throws SyntaxError on invalid JSON
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof SyntaxError) {
      console.log("bad config:", err.message);
      return {};                                       // recover with a default
    }
    throw err;                                         // unknown problem: do not swallow it
  } finally {
    console.log("finally always runs (cleanup goes here)");
  }
}
console.log(parseConfig('{"port": 3000}'));
console.log(parseConfig("{port: 3000}"));

// the built-in error types
const attempts = [
  () => null.name,                                     // TypeError
  () => undefinedVariable,                             // ReferenceError
  () => new Array(-1),                                 // RangeError
  () => decodeURIComponent("%"),                       // URIError
  () => { throw new Error("my own"); },                // plain Error
];
for (const fn of attempts) {
  try { fn(); } catch (e) { console.log(`${e.name.padEnd(14)} ${e.message}`); }
}
finally always runs (cleanup goes here) { port: 3000 } bad config: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2) finally always runs (cleanup goes here) {} TypeError Cannot read properties of null (reading 'name') ReferenceError undefinedVariable is not defined RangeError Invalid array length URIError URI malformed Error my own

Custom errors, cause and error handling design

class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, { status = 500, code = "INTERNAL", cause } = {}) {
    super(message, { cause });                         // cause chains the original error
    this.name = this.constructor.name;
    this.status = status;                              // an HTTP status the web layer can use later
    this.code = code;
  }
}
class NotFoundError extends AppError {
  constructor(what) { super(`${what} not found`, { status: 404, code: "NOT_FOUND" }); }
}

function findUser(id) {
  if (id !== 1) throw new NotFoundError(`User ${id}`);
  return { id, name: "Ana" };
}

try {
  findUser(9);
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e instanceof NotFoundError, e instanceof AppError, e instanceof Error);
  console.log(e.name, e.status, e.code, e.message);
}

try {
  try { JSON.parse("oops"); }
  catch (low) { throw new AppError("Could not load settings", { code: "SETTINGS", cause: low }); }   // wrap, never lose the root cause
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.message, "<-", e.cause.name);
}

const all = new AggregateError([new Error("a failed"), new Error("b failed")], "several things failed");
console.log(all.errors.map((x) => x.message), typeof new Error("x").stack);
true true true NotFoundError 404 NOT_FOUND User 9 not found Could not load settings <- SyntaxError [ 'a failed', 'b failed' ] string
Two kinds of errorsOperational errors are expected problems at runtime: bad input, a missing record, a network timeout, a full disk. Handle them and answer politely (a 400, a 404, a retry). Programmer errors are bugs: calling a function with the wrong type, reading a property of undefined. You cannot recover meaningfully; log, then let the process restart (Unit 10 covers this). Mixing the two is how servers end up in half-broken states.
Never use an empty catch {}, throw strings (throw "oops" has no stack trace), or wrap a big block in one try just to be safe: you will hide the real bug. You can write catch { ... } without a variable when you do not need the error.

Why async exists

Waiting for a disk, a database or another server is slow compared with the CPU. JavaScript runs your code on one thread, so instead of blocking while it waits, it starts the operation, moves on, and comes back when the result arrives. Nothing else can run while your own synchronous code is running, so a busy loop freezes every user at once.

Three generations of the same idea

const wait = (ms, value) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms, value));

// 1. Callbacks: pass a function to be called later. Convention in Node: (error, result)
function fetchUserCb(id, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => (id > 0 ? callback(null, { id }) : callback(new Error("bad id"))), 5);
}
fetchUserCb(1, (err, user) => console.log("callback:", err, user));

// 2. Promises: an object that stands for a future value. States: pending, fulfilled, rejected.
const fetchUserP = (id) => new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => (id > 0 ? resolve({ id }) : reject(new Error("bad id"))), 10);
});
fetchUserP(2)
  .then((user) => { console.log("promise:", user); return user.id * 10; })   // a returned value feeds the next .then
  .then((n) => console.log("chained:", n))
  .finally(() => console.log("promise done"));
fetchUserP(-1).catch((e) => console.log("promise error:", e.message));

// 3. async/await: the same promises, written like normal top-to-bottom code
async function main() {
  await wait(30);
  try {
    const user = await fetchUserP(3);
    console.log("await:", user);
    await fetchUserP(-1);                        // rejection becomes a normal exception
  } catch (e) {
    console.log("caught with try/catch:", e.message);
  }
  return "main finished";                        // an async function always returns a promise
}
console.log(await main());
callback: null { id: 1 } promise: { id: 2 } chained: 20 promise done promise error: bad id await: { id: 3 } caught with try/catch: bad id main finished
  • async in front of a function makes it return a Promise (a returned value becomes the fulfilled value, a thrown error becomes the rejection).
  • await pauses that function only until the promise settles; other work keeps running. It works inside async functions and at the top level of ES modules.
  • Forgetting await is the most common bug: you get a pending Promise object instead of the value, and errors escape unhandled.

Running things at the same time

Awaiting in a loop runs one task after another (slow if they are independent). Start them all, then await together.

CombinatorResolves whenRejects whenUse for
Promise.all([...])all succeed (array of results)the first one failsIndependent calls that are all required
Promise.allSettled([...])all finish, success or notneverReport on each; partial success is fine
Promise.race([...])the first to settleif that first one rejectsTimeouts
Promise.any([...])the first successall fail (AggregateError)Fastest replica wins
 
const wait = (ms, value) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms, value));
const task = async (name, ms, fail = false) => { await wait(ms); if (fail) throw new Error(name + " failed"); return name; };
const timed = async (label, fn) => { const t = Date.now(); const r = await fn(); console.log(label.padEnd(12), JSON.stringify(r), Date.now() - t < 140 ? "fast (parallel)" : "slow (one by one)"); };

await timed("sequential", async () => { const out = []; for (const ms of [60, 60, 60]) out.push(await task("t" + ms, ms)); return out; });
await timed("Promise.all", () => Promise.all([task("a", 60), task("b", 60), task("c", 60)]));

const results = await Promise.allSettled([task("ok", 5), task("bad", 5, true)]);
console.log(results.map((r) => r.status === "fulfilled" ? r.value : "rejected: " + r.reason.message));

console.log(await Promise.race([task("slow", 80), task("quick", 10)]));
console.log(await Promise.any([task("x", 5, true), task("y", 20)]));
try { await Promise.all([task("a", 5), task("b", 5, true)]); } catch (e) { console.log("all rejected with:", e.message); }

// a timeout: race a task against a timer. AbortSignal.timeout is the built-in way for fetch and friends
const withTimeout = (p, ms) => Promise.race([p, new Promise((_, rej) => setTimeout(rej, ms, new Error("timed out")))]);
try { await withTimeout(wait(200), 30); } catch (e) { console.log(e.message); }
sequential ["t60","t60","t60"] slow (one by one) Promise.all ["a","b","c"] fast (parallel) [ 'ok', 'rejected: bad failed' ] quick y all rejected with: b failed timed out
forEach does not awaititems.forEach(async (x) => { await save(x); }) starts all the saves and returns immediately: nothing waits for them and their errors are lost. Use for (const x of items) await save(x) to go one by one, or await Promise.all(items.map(save)) to go in parallel. For thousands of items, process in batches so you do not open thousands of connections at once.

The event loop order

When the current code finishes, Node runs the queued microtasks (promise callbacks, the code after an await) and process.nextTick callbacks before it moves on to the next macrotask (timers, I/O callbacks). Unit 3 shows the full phase diagram. Here is the order in a CommonJS file, where nextTick goes first:

setTimeout(() => console.log("5 timeout 0"), 0);              // macrotask: last
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3 promise"));      // microtask
process.nextTick(() => console.log("2 nextTick"));           // runs before promises
(async () => { console.log("1b sync part of an async function"); await null; console.log("4 after await"); })();
console.log("1 sync");
1b sync part of an async function 1 sync 2 nextTick 3 promise 4 after await 5 timeout 0

The same file as an ES module prints the promise lines before nextTick, because an ES module is itself evaluated inside a promise job:

setTimeout(() => console.log("5 timeout 0"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("promise"));
process.nextTick(() => console.log("nextTick"));
console.log("sync");
sync promise nextTick 5 timeout 0
What to rememberSynchronous code first, then microtasks, then timers and I/O. Do not rely on the relative order of nextTick and promises; prefer promises, and avoid nextTick in application code.

Async iteration and errors that nobody caught

const wait = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

async function* pages() {                      // an async generator yields values over time
  for (let page = 1; page <= 3; page++) { await wait(5); yield { page, items: [page * 10, page * 10 + 1] }; }
}
for await (const p of pages()) console.log("got", p.page, p.items);   // for await consumes it

for await (const value of [wait(10).then(() => "first"), "plain value"]) console.log(value);   // also works on arrays of promises
got 1 [ 10, 11 ] got 2 [ 20, 21 ] got 3 [ 30, 31 ] first plain value
async function save() { throw new Error("database is down"); }
save();                         // nobody awaits it and nobody catches it
setTimeout(() => console.log("never printed"), 100);
file:///app/app.mjs:1 async function save() { throw new Error("database is down"); } ^ Error: database is down at save (file:///app/app.mjs:1:31) at file:///app/app.mjs:2:1 Node.js v22.22.0 [process exited with code 1]
Since Node 15an unhandled promise rejection terminates the process with exit code 1, exactly like an uncaught exception. That is the right default: always await or .catch() every promise. Express 5 does this for you in route handlers (Unit 4).

A module is a file with its own scope. Code in other files can use only what the module exports. Node supports two systems:

ES modules (ESM)CommonJS (CJS)
Syntaximport x from "./x.js"
export const a = 1		const x = require("./x")
module.exports = { a }
Enabled by.mjs file, or .js with "type": "module" in package.json.cjs file, or .js with no type (the default!)
Standard?Yes, same as browsers. Use for all new code.Older Node-only system, still in many packages.
LoadingStatic, analysed before running; supports top-level awaitSynchronous, at the moment require runs
File extensionsRequired in relative imports (./math.js)Optional
__dirname / __filenameUse import.meta.dirname / import.meta.filenameAvailable as globals

A tiny project with four files shows every form:

// Named exports: importers must use these exact names
export const TAX_RATE = 0.18;
export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

// A default export: one "main thing" per file; importers choose the local name
export default class Calculator {
  total = 0;
  add(n) {
    this.total += n;
    return this;
  }
}

console.log("math.js is running (this line runs only once, however often it is imported)");
// CommonJS: the original Node module system
const path = require("node:path");

function slugify(text) {
  return text.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, "-");
}

module.exports = { slugify, dir: path.basename(__dirname), file: path.basename(__filename) };
import Calculator, { add, TAX_RATE } from "./math.js";   // default + named, file extension is required
import * as math from "./math.js";                        // everything as a namespace object
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";                   // built-in modules use the node: prefix
import legacy from "./legacy.cjs";                        // ESM can import CommonJS

console.log(add(2, 3), TAX_RATE, new Calculator().add(5).add(6).total);
console.log(Object.keys(math));
console.log(legacy.slugify("Hello Big World"), legacy.file);

// import.meta replaces __dirname and __filename in ES modules
console.log(import.meta.url.endsWith("/main.js"), import.meta.filename.endsWith("main.js"), import.meta.dirname.length > 0);
console.log(readFileSync(new URL("./package.json", import.meta.url), "utf8").includes("modules-demo"));

// dynamic import: load a module later, on demand, returns a promise
const { default: Calc2 } = await import("./math.js");     // top-level await works in ES modules
console.log(Calc2 === Calculator, "same module instance, not run again");
$ node main.js
math.js is running (this line runs only once, however often it is imported)
5 0.18 11
[ 'TAX_RATE', 'add', 'default' ]
hello-big-world legacy.cjs
true true true
true
true same module instance, not run again
// A CommonJS file that uses an ES module through require() (supported in Node 22.12+)
const { add } = require("./math.js");
console.log("require(esm):", add(40, 2));
$ node old-style.cjs
math.js is running (this line runs only once, however often it is imported)
require(esm): 42

Rules of thumb

  • Named exports (export const x) give good editor autocomplete and force consistent names. Default export suits a file with exactly one main thing. Many teams use named exports everywhere.
  • Imports are live bindings and read-only: you cannot reassign an imported name, but the exporting module can change it.
  • A module runs once, the first time it is imported; later imports reuse the same instance. Module-level variables are therefore shared state (handy for a database pool, risky for per-request data).
  • Import the built-ins with the node: prefix (node:fs, node:path) so they can never be confused with an npm package of the same name.
  • Circular imports (a imports b which imports a) can leave a value undefined at the moment you use it. Break the cycle by moving shared code into a third module.
  • Since Node 22.12, a CommonJS file can require() an ES module (as shown above) as long as the module does not use top-level await. Older 22.x releases printed an experimental warning.

JSON

JSON is the text format APIs speak. It looks like a JavaScript object, but it is stricter: keys and strings need double quotes, no comments, no trailing commas, and only these values: object, array, string, number, true, false, null.

const user = { id: 1, name: "Ana", tags: ["a", "b"], joined: new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 9, 23)), skip: undefined, fn() {}, nan: NaN };

const text = JSON.stringify(user);
console.log(text);                                       // undefined and functions vanish, NaN becomes null, Date becomes an ISO string
console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: [1, 2] }, null, 2));   // pretty print with 2 spaces
console.log(JSON.stringify(user, ["id", "name"]));           // keep only these keys

const back = JSON.parse(text);
console.log(back.joined, typeof back.joined);                // a plain string now: Dates do not survive a round trip
console.log(JSON.parse('{"when":"2026-10-23T00:00:00.000Z"}', (k, v) => (k === "when" ? new Date(v) : v)));   // reviver fixes that

class Money { constructor(c) { this.cents = c; } toJSON() { return { amount: this.cents / 100 }; } }   // control your own shape
console.log(JSON.stringify({ price: new Money(1999) }));

try { JSON.parse("{'bad': 1}"); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ":", e.message); }
// circular references cannot be serialised
const loop = {}; loop.self = loop;
try { JSON.stringify(loop); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ":", e.message.split("\n")[0]); }
{"id":1,"name":"Ana","tags":["a","b"],"joined":"2026-10-23T00:00:00.000Z","nan":null} { "a": 1, "b": [ 1, 2 ] } {"id":1,"name":"Ana"} 2026-10-23T00:00:00.000Z string { when: 2026-10-23T00:00:00.000Z } {"price":{"amount":19.99}} SyntaxError: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2) TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON

Dates and time

The built-in Date stores a single moment as milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC (the "epoch"). Its constructor and local-time methods are full of traps. The safe rules for servers:

  • Store and transmit UTC in ISO 8601 form: 2026-10-23T09:30:00.000Z (the Z means UTC). Convert to a person's time zone only when displaying.
  • Use Date.now() for "now in ms", new Date().toISOString() for strings, and Date.UTC(...) for fixed dates.
  • Months are zero-based (0 is January). new Date("2026-10-23") is read as UTC, but new Date("2026-10-23T00:00") (no Z) is read as local time.
  • For heavy calendar maths use a library (date-fns, luxon, dayjs) or the new Temporal API once it ships in your Node version.
const d = new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 9, 23, 9, 30));         // month 9 = October
console.log(d.toISOString(), d.getTime(), d.getUTCFullYear(), d.getUTCMonth(), d.getUTCDay());   // getUTCDay: 5 = Friday

const addDays = (date, n) => new Date(date.getTime() + n * 86_400_000);   // 1_000 separators make big numbers readable
console.log(addDays(d, 10).toISOString(), (addDays(d, 10) - d) / 86_400_000, "days apart");
console.log(new Date("not a date").getTime(), Number.isNaN(new Date("nope")));   // invalid dates are silent: check them

// Intl: locale-aware formatting that ships with Node
console.log(new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-GB", { dateStyle: "full", timeZone: "UTC" }).format(d));
console.log(new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { timeStyle: "short", timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata" }).format(d));
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }).format(1234567.891));
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("de-DE", { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" }).format(1234.5));
console.log(new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat("en", { numeric: "auto" }).format(-1, "day"), new Intl.PluralRules("en").select(1));
console.log((1234.5678).toLocaleString("en-US", { maximumFractionDigits: 1 }));
2026-10-23T09:30:00.000Z 1792747800000 2026 9 5 2026-11-02T09:30:00.000Z 10 days apart NaN false Friday, 23 October 2026 3:00 PM ₹12,34,567.89 1.234,50 € yesterday one 1,234.6

Numbers and money

Never store money as a float0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Keep money as integer cents (or use a decimal library, or a database NUMERIC column) and convert only for display.
console.log(Math.round(2.5), Math.round(-2.5), Math.floor(-2.5), Math.ceil(2.1), Math.trunc(-2.9), Math.abs(-3));
console.log(Math.max(1, 9, 3), Math.min(), Math.sqrt(16), Math.pow(2, 8), Math.PI.toFixed(4), Math.hypot(3, 4));
console.log(Number.isInteger(5.0), Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53), Number.EPSILON > 0, (1234.5678).toFixed(2), (0.000001234).toExponential(2));
console.log(Math.random() < 1, Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1 <= 6);   // random: NOT for security (use crypto, Unit 3)

const cents = (price) => Math.round(price * 100);          // 19.99 -> 1999
const itemsInCents = [cents(19.99), cents(5.01)];
const total = itemsInCents.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
console.log(total, (total / 100).toFixed(2), 19.99 + 5.01);

console.log(BigInt(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) + 2n, 10n ** 20n, typeof 1n, 7n / 2n);   // integer division; mixing with numbers throws
3 -2 -3 3 -2 3 9 Infinity 4 256 3.1416 5 true false true 1234.57 1.23e-6 true true 2500 25.00 25 9007199254740993n 100000000000000000000n bigint 3n

TypeScript is JavaScript plus a type system. You describe the shape of your data, and the compiler (tsc) finds mistakes before the code runs. Types are erased: the program that runs is plain JavaScript, so TypeScript adds no runtime cost and no runtime checks (untrusted input still needs validation, Unit 5).

Since Node 22.18 you can run .ts files directly: Node strips the type annotations and runs the rest. It does not check types, so keep tsc --noEmit in your workflow. Only "erasable" syntax is supported (no enum, no parameter properties; the erasableSyntaxOnly compiler option enforces this). Import with the real extension (./user.ts).

// Primitives and inference: TypeScript works out most types by itself
const port = 3000;                           // type: number (inferred)
let title: string = "API";                   // explicit annotation
const ids: number[] = [1, 2, 3];
const pair: [string, number] = ["age", 30];  // tuple: fixed length and types

// Object shapes: interface or type alias
interface User { id: number; name: string; email?: string }
type Role = "admin" | "editor" | "viewer";   // union of literal values: only these three are allowed
type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string };   // generic, discriminated union

// Functions: type the parameters and (optionally) the return value
function parsePort(raw: string | undefined): Result<number> {
  if (raw === undefined) return { ok: false, error: "missing" };       // narrowing: after this, raw is a string
  const n = Number(raw);
  return Number.isInteger(n) ? { ok: true, value: n } : { ok: false, error: "not an integer" };
}

const r = parsePort("8080");
if (r.ok) console.log("port", r.value);       // narrowing on the 'ok' field: value exists only in this branch
else console.log("error", r.error);

// Generics: one function, many types
function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined { return items[0]; }
const firstId = first(ids);                  // number | undefined
const u: User = { id: 1, name: "Ana" };
const roles: Record<Role, number> = { admin: 3, editor: 2, viewer: 1 };   // an object whose keys must be exactly the Role values
console.log(port, title, pair, firstId, u, roles, parsePort(undefined));
port 8080 3000 API [ 'age', 30 ] 1 { id: 1, name: 'Ana' } { admin: 3, editor: 2, viewer: 1 } { ok: false, error: 'missing' }

The same ideas in a real two-file project, run by Node and checked by tsc:

// Types describe the shape of data. They exist only while you write code: Node erases them before running.
export interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email?: string; // optional property
}

export type Role = "admin" | "editor" | "viewer"; // a union of exact strings

export function describe(user: User, role: Role = "viewer"): string {
  return `${user.name} (#${user.id}) has the role ${role}`;
}

console.log(describe({ id: 1, name: "Ana" }, "admin"));
import { describe } from "./user.ts";

describe({ id: "7", name: "Raj" }); // id must be a number
describe({ id: 8, name: "Lee" }, "owner"); // "owner" is not a Role
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2023",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "types": ["node"]
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
$ node src/user.ts
Ana (#1) has the role admin
$ npx tsc --noEmit
src/bad.ts(3,12): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
src/bad.ts(4,34): error TS2345: Argument of type '"owner"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Role | undefined'.
ToolCommandRole
Nodenode file.tsRuns TypeScript by erasing types. No checking.
tscnpx tsc --noEmitType-checks the project. Run in CI and in your editor.
tsxnpx tsx watch src/server.tsRuns TypeScript with restart-on-change and full syntax support (enums, decorators). Popular in development.
@types/node, @types/expressnpm i -D @types/node @types/expressType definitions for libraries written in plain JavaScript.
How this guide uses itThe main text teaches in plain JavaScript so every concept is visible. Unit 4 shows how to type Express handlers, and the capstone project in Unit 11 adds a TypeScript version of the key files.
03

Unit 3: Node.js Core

The runtime itself and its built-in modules: the event loop, process, path, fs, os, url, util, events, buffers, streams, http, fetch, crypto, timers, child processes, workers, npm and the command line. No packages needed; everything here ships with Node.

Node.js is a program that runs JavaScript outside the browser. It combines the V8 engine (Chrome's JavaScript engine, which compiles your code to machine code) with libuv (a C library that handles the event loop, files, sockets and a thread pool) and a set of built-in modules written on top of them (fs, http, crypto and more).

Browser hasNode has instead
window, document, DOM, localStorageglobalThis, process, Buffer, node:fs, node:http
Sandboxed from the machineFull access to files, network, processes (so be careful with what you run)
One user, one pageMany users hitting one long-running process
Shared globals: fetch, URL, AbortController, setTimeout, structuredClone, TextEncoder, crypto, performance, consoleSame, so a lot of browser code just works
 
console.log(typeof window, typeof document, typeof localStorage);          // browser-only things: undefined
console.log(typeof process, typeof Buffer, typeof fetch, typeof URL, typeof AbortController, typeof structuredClone);
console.log(globalThis === global, typeof require, typeof module, typeof __dirname);   // CommonJS helpers are missing in ES modules
const { node, v8, uv } = process.versions;
console.log("node", node.split(".")[0], "| v8 and libuv are bundled:", typeof v8, typeof uv);
console.log(process.release.name, process.release.lts ?? "(not an LTS build)");
undefined undefined undefined object function function function function function true undefined undefined undefined node 22 | v8 and libuv are bundled: string string node Jod

The REPL and handy command line modes

Running node with no file opens the REPL (read, evaluate, print, loop). Inside it: _ is the last result, .help lists commands, .exit or Ctrl+D leaves, and built-in modules are available without import (type os.cpus().length). Tab completes names.

$ printf '2 + 2\n_ * 10\nconst s = "node"\ns.toUpperCase()\n' | node -i
Welcome to Node.js v22.22.0.
Type ".help" for more information.
> 4
> 40
> undefined
> 'NODE'
>
Release linesEven-numbered versions become LTS (long-term support) and are the ones to run in production. Node 22 is in maintenance (end of life 2027-04-30), Node 24 is the active LTS (end of life 2028-04-30), and Node 26 is Current with LTS planned for 2026-10-28. This guide was verified on Node 22.22 and Express 5.3, and everything shown also works on 24.

The event loop is the reason one Node process can serve thousands of connections: it is a loop that keeps picking the next piece of ready work. Your JavaScript is one thread; waiting (for disk, network, timers) costs nothing because the OS does it and tells libuv when it is done.

PhaseRuns
timersCallbacks of setTimeout/setInterval whose time has come (a delay is a minimum, not a promise).
pollMost I/O callbacks: a file was read, a request arrived, a database answered. If nothing is ready it waits here (up to the next timer).
checksetImmediate callbacks: "run this right after the I/O phase".
closeCleanup callbacks such as a socket closing.
between every callbackprocess.nextTick queue, then promise microtasks, until both are empty.
 
import fs from "node:fs";

// From the main script the order of these two is NOT guaranteed (it depends on process start-up speed)...
// ...but inside an I/O callback setImmediate always wins, because the check phase comes right after poll.
fs.readFile(import.meta.filename, () => {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("timeout"), 0);
  setImmediate(() => console.log("immediate"));
  process.nextTick(() => console.log("nextTick (before both)"));
});
nextTick (before both) immediate timeout

Never block the loop

While your synchronous code runs, nothing else can: no other request, no timer. A 2-second loop in one handler makes every user wait 2 seconds. The measure below counts how often a 10 ms timer fires while we do the same work three ways.

import { pbkdf2Sync, pbkdf2 } from "node:crypto";
import { promisify } from "node:util";

async function measure(label, work) {
  let ticks = 0;
  const timer = setInterval(() => ticks++, 10);         // a heartbeat: proves the loop is alive
  await work();
  clearInterval(timer);
  console.log(label.padEnd(34), ticks > 3 ? "loop stayed responsive" : `loop was FROZEN (ticks: ${ticks})`);
}

const hashSync = () => { for (let i = 0; i < 6; i++) pbkdf2Sync("pw", "salt", 120_000, 64, "sha512"); };
const hashAsync = promisify(pbkdf2);

await measure("pbkdf2Sync (blocks the thread)", async () => hashSync());
await measure("pbkdf2 async (thread pool)", () => Promise.all(Array.from({ length: 6 }, () => hashAsync("pw", "salt", 120_000, 64, "sha512"))));
pbkdf2Sync (blocks the thread) loop was FROZEN (ticks: 0) pbkdf2 async (thread pool) loop stayed responsive
  • Async I/O (fs.promises, fetch, database drivers) is non-blocking by design.
  • Some library work (crypto.pbkdf2, scrypt, zlib, dns.lookup, many fs calls) runs on libuv's thread pool, 4 threads by default. Raise it with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 if you saturate it.
  • CPU-heavy JavaScript (image processing, huge JSON, big loops) blocks. Move it to a worker thread, a separate process, or a queue (later in this unit and Unit 8).
  • Synchronous APIs (readFileSync, JSON.parse of huge input) are fine at start-up and in scripts, and a bug inside request handlers.
Server ruleInside a request handler: no *Sync functions, no long loops, no catastrophic regexes. Measure event-loop delay in production (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay, Unit 10).

process is a global that represents this running program: its arguments, environment, working directory and lifecycle.

console.log(process.argv.length, process.argv0 === "node");     // [0] node path, [1] script path, then your own arguments
console.log(process.env.HOME !== undefined, typeof process.env.NOPE, process.env.NOPE ?? "default");   // env values are strings or undefined
console.log(typeof process.cwd(), typeof process.pid, process.platform, process.arch);   // platform here is the Linux machine that built this guide: yours may say win32 or darwin
console.log(typeof process.uptime(), process.memoryUsage().heapUsed > 0, typeof process.hrtime.bigint());
console.log(process.exitCode, process.version.startsWith("v22"), process.title);

process.env.MY_FLAG = "on";                                     // changes this process (and its children) only
console.log(process.env.MY_FLAG, process.env.NUM = 42, typeof process.env.NUM);   // everything is turned into a string
2 true true undefined default string number linux x64 number true bigint undefined true node on 42 string

Command line arguments

The built-in util.parseArgs handles flags without a library:

import { parseArgs } from "node:util";
const argv = ["--port", "8080", "-v", "--name=api", "input.txt", "--no-color"];     // normally process.argv.slice(2)
const { values, positionals } = parseArgs({
  args: argv,
  options: {
    port: { type: "string", short: "p", default: "3000" },
    verbose: { type: "boolean", short: "v" },
    name: { type: "string" },
    "no-color": { type: "boolean" },
  },
  allowPositionals: true,
});
console.log(values, positionals, Number(values.port));
[Object: null prototype] { port: '8080', verbose: true, name: 'api', 'no-color': true } [ 'input.txt' ] 8080

Exit codes, signals and shutdown

CodeMeaning
0Success
1Uncaught exception or unhandled rejection (also the usual "generic failure")
130 / 143Terminated by SIGINT (Ctrl+C) / SIGTERM (convention: 128 + signal number)
  • Set process.exitCode = 1 and let the program finish naturally (cleanup runs). process.exit(1) stops immediately and can cut off pending writes and logs.
  • A server should listen for SIGTERM (sent by Docker, Kubernetes, kill, and process managers) and SIGINT and shut down gracefully: stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close the database, then exit.
  • SIGKILL (kill -9) cannot be caught.
import http from "node:http";

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => res.end("ok"));
await new Promise((resolve) => server.listen(0, resolve));

let closing = false;
function shutdown(signal) {
  if (closing) return;                                  // a second signal must not start a second shutdown
  closing = true;
  console.log(`${signal} received: stop accepting connections`);
  server.close(() => console.log("all requests finished, server closed"));   // waits for in-flight requests
  server.closeIdleConnections();                        // drop idle keep-alive sockets so close() can finish
  // here you would also close the database pool, flush logs, and so on
}
process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM"));
process.on("SIGINT", () => shutdown("SIGINT"));
response: ok SIGTERM received: stop accepting connections all requests finished, server closed

Lifecycle events

process.on("beforeExit", () => console.log("beforeExit: the loop is empty (async work may still be scheduled here)"));
process.on("exit", (code) => console.log("exit: code", code, "(only synchronous code can run now)"));

setTimeout(() => console.log("last piece of work"), 10);
process.exitCode = 3;                                   // finish normally, but report failure
last piece of work beforeExit: the loop is empty (async work may still be scheduled here) exit: code 3 (only synchronous code can run now) [process exited with code 3]
process.on("uncaughtException", (err, origin) => {
  console.error("fatal:", err.message, `(${origin})`);  // log it, then exit: the process may be in a broken state
  process.exit(1);
});
process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason) => { throw reason; });   // turn rejections into the same path

setTimeout(() => { throw new Error("boom"); }, 5);
fatal: boom (uncaughtException) [process exited with code 1]
Do not resumeAn uncaughtException handler is for logging and exiting, never for carrying on. The program state is unknown after a bug. Let a process manager (Unit 10) start a fresh process.

stdin, stdout and pipes

Node programs fit into shell pipelines: process.stdin is a readable stream, process.stdout a writable one, and console.error writes to stderr, so errors do not pollute piped output.

$ echo "hello pipes" | node -e "process.stdin.on('data', (d) => process.stdout.write(d.toString().toUpperCase()))"
HELLO PIPES
$ node -e "console.log('to stdout'); console.error('to stderr')" 2>/dev/null
to stdout
$ printf 'b\na\nc\n' | node -e "const l = require('fs').readFileSync(0, 'utf8').trim().split('\n'); console.log(l.sort().join(','))"
a,b,c

Never build file paths by gluing strings with /: Windows uses \. node:path builds and takes apart paths correctly for the current OS. It only manipulates strings; it never touches the disk.

FunctionDoes
path.join(a, b, ...)Joins segments with the right separator and cleans up .. and //. Result may stay relative.
path.resolve(a, b, ...)Builds an absolute path, processing right to left until one is absolute, starting from the current working directory.
basename / dirname / extnameFile name, folder, extension (with the dot).
parse / formatSplit into {root, dir, base, name, ext} and back.
relative(from, to)How to get from one path to another.
normalize, isAbsolute, sepTidy a path, test it, the OS separator.
path.posix / path.win32Force one flavour (for URLs, or for testing Windows logic anywhere).
 
import path from "node:path";

console.log(path.join("uploads", "2026", "..", "10", "photo.png"));          // uploads/10/photo.png
console.log(path.resolve("/srv", "app", "../data", "db.json"));               // always absolute
console.log(path.resolve("/srv", "/etc", "hosts"));                           // a later absolute path wins

const file = "/var/www/site/index.min.js";
console.log(path.basename(file), path.basename(file, ".js"), path.dirname(file), path.extname(file));
console.log(path.parse(file));
console.log(path.format({ dir: "/tmp", name: "report", ext: ".pdf" }), path.relative("/a/b/c", "/a/d"));
console.log(path.isAbsolute("/x"), path.isAbsolute("x"), path.sep, path.normalize("/a//b/./c/../d"));

console.log(path.win32.join("C:\\Users", "ana", "docs"), path.win32.basename("C:\\Users\\ana\\a.txt"));   // Windows rules, on any OS
console.log(import.meta.dirname === path.dirname(import.meta.filename));     // the folder of the current file (ES modules)
uploads/10/photo.png /srv/data/db.json /etc/hosts index.min.js index.min /var/www/site .js { root: '/', dir: '/var/www/site', base: 'index.min.js', ext: '.js', name: 'index.min' } /tmp/report.pdf ../../d true false / /a/b/d C:\Users\ana\docs a.txt true
Path traversalIf a path includes user input (/files/:name), a request for ../../etc/passwd escapes your folder. Resolve it, then check it still starts with your base folder. Unit 7 shows the exact guard and attacks it with a real request.

node:fs reads and writes the file system. Every operation comes in three styles. Use the promise style in new code.

StyleImportExampleUse
Promisesimport fs from "node:fs/promises"await fs.readFile(p, "utf8")Servers and almost everything
Callbacksimport fs from "node:fs"fs.readFile(p, "utf8", (err, text) => {})Old code
Synchronousimport fs from "node:fs"fs.readFileSync(p, "utf8")Scripts, start-up config. Never in request handlers.
 
import fs from "node:fs/promises";
import path from "node:path";

await fs.mkdir("data/logs", { recursive: true });             // creates parents, no error if it already exists
await fs.writeFile("data/hello.txt", "Hello\n");               // creates or REPLACES the file
await fs.appendFile("data/hello.txt", "second line\n");        // adds to the end

const text = await fs.readFile("data/hello.txt", "utf8");      // with an encoding you get a string...
const raw = await fs.readFile("data/hello.txt");               // ...without one you get a Buffer (bytes)
console.log(JSON.stringify(text), raw.length, raw instanceof Buffer);

const info = await fs.stat("data/hello.txt");
console.log(info.size, info.isFile(), info.isDirectory(), info.mtime instanceof Date);

await fs.writeFile("data/logs/app.log", "");
await fs.copyFile("data/hello.txt", "data/copy.txt");
await fs.rename("data/copy.txt", "data/renamed.txt");          // also how you move a file

const names = (await fs.readdir("data")).sort();               // order is not guaranteed by the OS: sort when it matters
console.log(names);
for (const entry of await fs.readdir("data", { withFileTypes: true })) {
  console.log(entry.isDirectory() ? "dir " : "file", path.join(entry.parentPath, entry.name));
}
console.log((await fs.readdir("data", { recursive: true })).sort());

await fs.cp("data", "backup", { recursive: true });            // copy a whole folder
await fs.rm("data/renamed.txt");
await fs.rm("backup", { recursive: true, force: true });      // like rm -rf: force means "no error if missing"
console.log((await fs.readdir("data")).sort());
"Hello\nsecond line\n" 18 true 18 true false true [ 'hello.txt', 'logs', 'renamed.txt' ] file data/hello.txt dir data/logs file data/renamed.txt [ 'hello.txt', 'logs', 'logs/app.log', 'renamed.txt' ] [ 'hello.txt', 'logs' ]

Errors: always check the code

File errors have a stable error.code. Test the code, never the message text.

CodeMeaningTypical response
ENOENTNo such file or directory404, or create it
EEXISTAlready exists409, or reuse it
EACCES / EPERMPermission deniedFix permissions; 500 for the user
EISDIR / ENOTDIRExpected a file / a folder400
EMFILEToo many open filesClose handles; use streams; raise ulimit -n
ENOSPCDisk fullAlert someone
 
import fs from "node:fs/promises";

try {
  await fs.readFile("does-not-exist.txt", "utf8");
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.code, err.syscall, err.path, "|", err.message);
}

await fs.writeFile("once.txt", "first");
try {
  await fs.writeFile("once.txt", "second", { flag: "wx" });        // 'wx': write, but FAIL if it already exists
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.code);
}

const exists = (p) => fs.access(p).then(() => true, () => false);  // no fs.exists: just try the real operation when you can
console.log(await exists("once.txt"), await exists("nope.txt"));

// JSON files: read, change, write back
await fs.writeFile("db.json", JSON.stringify({ users: [] }, null, 2));
const db = JSON.parse(await fs.readFile("db.json", "utf8"));
db.users.push({ id: 1, name: "Ana" });
await fs.writeFile("db.json", JSON.stringify(db, null, 2) + "\n");
console.log(await fs.readFile("db.json", "utf8"));
ENOENT open does-not-exist.txt | ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'does-not-exist.txt' EEXIST true false { "users": [ { "id": 1, "name": "Ana" } ] }

Safe writing, big files and file handles

  • Atomic writes. If the process dies halfway through writeFile, the file is left half-written. Write to a temporary file in the same folder, then rename it over the target: a rename is atomic, so readers see either the old or the new content, never a mix.
  • Large files. readFile loads the whole file in memory. For anything big or unbounded (uploads, logs, exports) use streams (below) so memory stays flat.
  • Concurrent writers. Two requests appending or rewriting the same file will corrupt it. For shared state use a database (Unit 6).
  • A file handle (fs.open) gives positioned reads and line-by-line iteration. Always close it (await using in newer Node, or try/finally).
import fs from "node:fs/promises";
import path from "node:path";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

async function writeFileAtomic(file, data) {
  const tmp = path.join(path.dirname(file), `.${path.basename(file)}.${randomUUID()}.tmp`);
  await fs.writeFile(tmp, data);
  await fs.rename(tmp, file);                                  // swap in one step
}
await writeFileAtomic("settings.json", JSON.stringify({ theme: "dark" }));
console.log(await fs.readFile("settings.json", "utf8"), (await fs.readdir(".")).filter((n) => n.endsWith(".tmp")).length, "temp files left");

await fs.writeFile("lines.txt", "alpha\nbeta\ngamma\n");
const handle = await fs.open("lines.txt", "r");
try {
  for await (const line of handle.readLines()) console.log("line:", line);   // reads line by line without loading it all
} finally {
  await handle.close();
}

const fh = await fs.open("lines.txt", "r");
const { bytesRead, buffer } = await fh.read(Buffer.alloc(5), 0, 5, 6);      // read 5 bytes starting at byte 6
console.log(bytesRead, buffer.toString());
await fh.close();
{"theme":"dark"} 0 temp files left line: alpha line: beta line: gamma 5 beta
Also in fsfs.watch(dir) and fs.watchFile report changes (used by node --watch); fs.createReadStream/createWriteStream stream files; fs.mkdtemp makes a unique temporary folder; fs.chmod, fs.symlink, fs.utimes, fs.truncate do what their names say; fs.constants holds flag values. Permissions on Windows are limited compared with Linux and macOS.

os: information about the machine

import os from "node:os";
console.log(os.platform(), os.arch(), JSON.stringify(os.EOL), os.cpus().length > 0, os.totalmem() > os.freemem());
console.log(typeof os.hostname(), typeof os.homedir(), os.tmpdir(), os.availableParallelism() >= 1, typeof os.uptime());
// os.cpus().length (or availableParallelism) is how many worker processes or threads make sense on this machine
linux x64 "\n" true true string string /tmp true number

URL and URLSearchParams

Do not take URLs apart with regexes or string splitting. The global URL class parses them following the web standard, and URLSearchParams reads and builds query strings with correct escaping.

const u = new URL("https://ana:secret@api.example.com:8443/v1/users/42?role=admin&tag=a&tag=b#top");
console.log(u.protocol, u.username, u.hostname, u.port, u.host, u.pathname, u.search, u.hash, u.origin);

console.log(u.searchParams.get("role"), u.searchParams.getAll("tag"), u.searchParams.has("x"), [...u.searchParams.keys()]);
u.searchParams.set("page", "2");                              // edits the URL itself
u.searchParams.append("q", "node & express");                 // escaping is automatic
u.hash = "";
console.log(u.href);

const params = new URLSearchParams({ a: "1", b: "hello world" });
console.log(params.toString(), Object.fromEntries(new URLSearchParams("x=1&y=2")));

console.log(new URL("../v2/items", "https://api.example.com/v1/users/").href);   // resolve a relative URL against a base
console.log(URL.canParse("not a url"), URL.canParse("http://ok.test"));
console.log(encodeURIComponent("a b&c=d/é"), decodeURIComponent("%E2%9C%93"));

import { fileURLToPath, pathToFileURL } from "node:url";
console.log(fileURLToPath("file:///srv/app/index.js"), pathToFileURL("/srv/app/index.js").href);
https: ana api.example.com 8443 api.example.com:8443 /v1/users/42 ?role=admin&tag=a&tag=b #top https://api.example.com:8443 admin [ 'a', 'b' ] false [ 'role', 'tag', 'tag' ] https://ana:secret@api.example.com:8443/v1/users/42?role=admin&tag=a&tag=b&page=2&q=node+%26+express a=1&b=hello+world { x: '1', y: '2' } https://api.example.com/v1/v2/items false true a%20b%26c%3Dd%2F%C3%A9 ✓ /srv/app/index.js file:///srv/app/index.js
Constructor throwsnew URL("bad") throws a TypeError. When the string comes from a user, test with URL.canParse or wrap in try/catch. And when you accept a URL to fetch (webhooks, avatars), validate it first: an attacker can point it at internal addresses (SSRF, Unit 7).

util: the toolbox

import util, { promisify, callbackify, inspect, format, isDeepStrictEqual } from "node:util";
import { readFile } from "node:fs";

const readFileAsync = promisify(readFile);                      // turn an (err, result) callback API into promises
console.log((await readFileAsync(import.meta.filename, "utf8")).length > 0);

const sleepCb = callbackify(async () => "done");                // and the other way round, for old APIs
sleepCb((err, value) => console.log(err, value));

console.log(format("%s is %d years old, %j, 100%%", "Ana", 30, { a: 1 }));    // printf-style
const deep = { a: { b: { c: { d: { e: 1 } } } }, list: Array.from({ length: 120 }, (_, i) => i) };
console.log(inspect(deep, { depth: null, maxArrayLength: 3, breakLength: Infinity }));   // console.log truncates deep structures: inspect shows more
console.log(isDeepStrictEqual({ a: [1, 2] }, { a: [1, 2] }), util.types.isPromise(Promise.resolve()), util.types.isDate(new Date()));
// styleText("red", "error") wraps text in terminal colour codes; they are skipped when output is not a terminal

const bytes = new TextEncoder().encode("héllo");                 // string -> UTF-8 bytes
console.log(bytes, new TextDecoder().decode(bytes), bytes.length);
true Ana is 30 years old, {"a":1}, 100% { a: { b: { c: { d: { e: 1 } } } }, list: [ 0, 1, 2, ... 117 more items ] } true true true Uint8Array(6) [ 104, 195, 169, 108, 108, 111 ] héllo 6 null done

console is more than log

console.log("plain %s and %d", "text", 5);
console.info("info"); console.debug("debug");               // go to stdout, like log
console.error("error goes to stderr"); console.warn("warn too");
console.table([{ id: 1, name: "Ana" }, { id: 2, name: "Raj" }]);
console.dir({ a: { b: { c: { d: 1 } } } }, { depth: 0 });
console.group("group"); console.log("indented"); console.groupEnd();
console.count(); console.count(); console.count("other");
console.assert(1 === 2, "assertion failed (only prints when false)");
// console.time("label") then console.timeEnd("label") prints the elapsed milliseconds (the number changes on every run)
plain text and 5 info debug ┌─────────┬────┬───────┐ │ (index) │ id │ name │ ├─────────┼────┼───────┤ │ 0 │ 1 │ 'Ana' │ │ 1 │ 2 │ 'Raj' │ └─────────┴────┴───────┘ { a: [Object] } group indented default: 1 default: 2 other: 1 [stderr] error goes to stderr warn too Assertion failed: assertion failed (only prints when false)
In productionuse a structured logger (pino, Unit 10) rather than console.log: JSON lines, levels, timestamps, redaction, and much faster.

Many Node objects (HTTP servers, sockets, streams, processes) announce things by emitting events. You attach listeners with .on(name, fn); code elsewhere calls .emit(name, ...args). This is the observer pattern, and you can use it in your own code to decouple parts of an app ("when a user signs up, send an email and record an audit entry").

import { EventEmitter, once, on } from "node:events";

const bus = new EventEmitter();
bus.on("signup", (user) => console.log("send welcome email to", user.email));
bus.on("signup", (user) => console.log("audit log: created", user.id));      // many listeners, called in the order added
bus.once("signup", () => console.log("runs only for the first signup"));

console.log("emit returned:", bus.emit("signup", { id: 1, email: "ana@example.com" }));   // true: somebody was listening
console.log("emit returned:", bus.emit("signup", { id: 2, email: "raj@example.com" }));
console.log(bus.emit("nobody-listens"), bus.listenerCount("signup"), bus.eventNames());

const handler = () => console.log("temporary");
bus.on("tick", handler); bus.off("tick", handler);                 // remove with off (removeListener)
console.log(bus.listenerCount("tick"));

// Listeners are called synchronously, in order, before emit() returns.
bus.on("sync", () => console.log("  listener ran"));
console.log("before emit"); bus.emit("sync"); console.log("after emit");

// Waiting for an event with promises
setTimeout(() => bus.emit("ready", "payload", 42), 10);
console.log(await once(bus, "ready"));                              // resolves with an array of the emitted args

// Consuming events as an async stream
const ac = new AbortController();
setTimeout(() => { bus.emit("msg", "one"); bus.emit("msg", "two"); ac.abort(); }, 10);
try { for await (const [m] of on(bus, "msg", { signal: ac.signal })) console.log("msg", m); }
catch (e) { if (e.name !== "AbortError") throw e; console.log("stopped"); }
send welcome email to ana@example.com audit log: created 1 runs only for the first signup emit returned: true send welcome email to raj@example.com audit log: created 2 emit returned: true false 2 [ 'signup' ] 0 before emit listener ran after emit [ 'payload', 42 ] msg one msg two stopped

Rules that save you from bugs

import { EventEmitter } from "node:events";

class Downloader extends EventEmitter {                   // your own class can emit events
  start() {
    this.emit("progress", 50);
    this.emit("progress", 100);
    this.emit("done");
  }
}
const d = new Downloader();
d.on("progress", (pct) => console.log(pct + "%"));
d.on("done", () => console.log("finished"));
d.start();

// The special name "error": emitting it with NO listener throws and crashes the process.
// Always attach an error listener to emitters that can fail (sockets, streams, servers).
d.emit("error", new Error("network lost"));
50% 100% finished file:///app/app.mjs:17 d.emit("error", new Error("network lost")); ^ Error: network lost at file:///app/app.mjs:17:17 Emitted 'error' event on Downloader instance at: at file:///app/app.mjs:17:3 Node.js v22.22.0 [process exited with code 1]
  • Listeners run synchronously. A slow listener delays emit and everything after it. Do slow work with await inside the listener (but then errors are not caught by emit: add your own try/catch).
  • More than 10 listeners for one event prints a MaxListenersExceededWarning: usually a leak (adding a listener per request and never removing it). Fix the leak; only raise setMaxListeners when many listeners are intended.
  • Use once() for one-shot events and off() to clean up, especially on long-lived emitters.

Text is easy; files, network packets, images and encrypted data are bytes. A Buffer is Node's fixed-size array of bytes (a subclass of Uint8Array). When you read a file without an encoding or receive a request body chunk, you get a Buffer.

const a = Buffer.from("héllo wörld", "utf8");
console.log(a, a.length, "héllo wörld".length);                     // bytes versus characters: é and ö use 2 bytes each
console.log(Buffer.byteLength("日本語"), "日本語".length);

console.log(a.toString("hex"), a.toString("base64"), a.toString("utf8", 0, 6));
console.log(Buffer.from("68656c6c6f", "hex").toString(), Buffer.from("aGk=", "base64").toString());
console.log(Buffer.from("subjects?id=1&x=ü").toString("base64url"));   // URL-safe base64 (used in JWTs)

const zeros = Buffer.alloc(4);                                       // zero-filled (safe)
const b = Buffer.from([0x48, 0x69, 33]);                              // from an array of bytes
console.log(zeros, b.toString(), b[0], b.at(-1));

const joined = Buffer.concat([Buffer.from("ab"), Buffer.from("cd")]);
console.log(joined.toString(), joined.equals(Buffer.from("abcd")), Buffer.compare(Buffer.from("a"), Buffer.from("b")));

const copy = Buffer.from(joined);                                    // a real copy
const view = joined.subarray(1, 3);                                  // a VIEW of the same memory, not a copy
view[0] = 0x58;                                                      // 0x58 is "X"
console.log(joined.toString(), copy.toString());                     // joined changed through the view, the copy did not

// reading and writing numbers: a binary protocol header with a 2-byte id and a 4-byte length
const header = Buffer.alloc(6);
header.writeUInt16BE(0xcafe, 0);
header.writeUInt32BE(1_000_000, 2);
console.log(header, header.readUInt16BE(0).toString(16), header.readUInt32BE(2));

console.log(JSON.stringify(Buffer.from("hi")), Buffer.isBuffer(b), b instanceof Uint8Array);
<Buffer 68 c3 a9 6c 6c 6f 20 77 c3 b6 72 6c 64> 13 11 9 3 68c3a96c6c6f2077c3b6726c64 aMOpbGxvIHfDtnJsZA== héllo hello hi c3ViamVjdHM_aWQ9MSZ4PcO8 <Buffer 00 00 00 00> Hi! 72 33 abcd true -1 aXcd abcd <Buffer ca fe 00 0f 42 40> cafe 1000000 {"type":"Buffer","data":[104,105]} true true
Common bugs(1) Joining chunks with + turns them into strings and can split a multi-byte character in two. Collect chunks in an array and Buffer.concat them, or use a stream decoder. (2) Never use Buffer.allocUnsafe for data you will send: it may expose old memory contents. (3) subarray shares memory, Buffer.from(buf) copies.

A stream processes data in small chunks instead of all at once. Reading a 5 GB file into memory fails; streaming it uses a few kilobytes. Streams are everywhere in Node: file reads, HTTP requests and responses, sockets, compression, process.stdin.

TypeYouExamples
Readableread chunks out of itfs.createReadStream, HTTP request (server side), HTTP response (client side), process.stdin
Writablewrite chunks into itfs.createWriteStream, HTTP response (server side), process.stdout
Duplexboth, independentTCP socket
Transformwrite in, read changed data outzlib.createGzip(), crypto.createHash(), your own parser
 
import fs from "node:fs";
import zlib from "node:zlib";
import readline from "node:readline";
import { once } from "node:events";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";
import { Transform } from "node:stream";

// 1. build a 50,000 line file by writing with a stream (and respecting backpressure)
const out = fs.createWriteStream("big.txt");
for (let i = 1; i <= 50_000; i++) {
  if (!out.write(`line ${i}\n`)) await once(out, "drain");       // write() returned false: wait until the buffer empties
}
out.end();
await once(out, "finish");
console.log("file size:", fs.statSync("big.txt").size, "bytes");

// 2. pipeline connects streams, forwards errors and cleans everything up. Prefer it over .pipe()
const upper = new Transform({
  transform(chunk, encoding, callback) { callback(null, chunk.toString().toUpperCase()); },   // (error, outputChunk)
});
await pipeline(fs.createReadStream("big.txt"), upper, zlib.createGzip(), fs.createWriteStream("big.txt.gz"));
console.log("gzipped smaller:", fs.statSync("big.txt.gz").size < fs.statSync("big.txt").size / 3);

// 3. read it back: gunzip and count lines, never holding the file in memory
const rl = readline.createInterface({ input: fs.createReadStream("big.txt.gz").pipe(zlib.createGunzip()) });
let lines = 0, last = "";
for await (const line of rl) { lines++; last = line; }
console.log(lines, last);
file size: 538894 bytes gzipped smaller: true 50000 LINE 50000

Backpressure and building your own

A fast source can overwhelm a slow destination. Every writable has an internal buffer limited by highWaterMark. When write() returns false the buffer is full: stop writing until the drain event. pipeline does this for you automatically; ignoring it is how servers run out of memory.

import { Readable, Writable, Transform } from "node:stream";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";

const slow = new Writable({
  highWaterMark: 16,                                            // tiny buffer, to see the effect
  write(chunk, encoding, callback) { setTimeout(callback, 5); },   // pretend each write takes 5 ms
});
console.log("first write ok?", slow.write("12345678"));          // true: 8 of 16 bytes buffered
console.log("second write ok?", slow.write("12345678"));         // false: buffer full, please wait
slow.once("drain", () => console.log("drain: safe to write again"));
await new Promise((resolve) => slow.once("drain", resolve));

// Object mode: chunks are JavaScript values instead of bytes. Great for data processing pipelines.
async function* numbers() { for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) yield i; }
const results = [];
await pipeline(
  Readable.from(numbers()),                                     // any iterable or async generator becomes a Readable
  new Transform({ objectMode: true, transform(n, enc, cb) { cb(null, n % 2 ? { odd: n } : null); } }),   // null = drop this chunk
  new Writable({ objectMode: true, write(obj, enc, cb) { results.push(obj); cb(); } }),
);
console.log(results);

// Async iteration works on any Readable, and pipeline accepts async generators as transforms
const doubled = [];
await pipeline(Readable.from([1, 2, 3]), async function* (source) { for await (const n of source) yield n * 2; }, async function (source) { for await (const n of source) doubled.push(n); });
console.log(doubled);
first write ok? true second write ok? false drain: safe to write again [ { odd: 1 }, { odd: 3 }, { odd: 5 } ] [ 2, 4, 6 ]
Web StreamsNode also supports the browser's ReadableStream/WritableStream API (used by fetch response bodies). Convert with Readable.fromWeb() and Readable.toWeb(). Express itself uses classic Node streams (Unit 4 pipes files to responses).
Always handle stream errorsA stream without an error listener crashes the process when something fails (a missing file, a dropped connection). Use pipeline, which forwards errors to the returned promise, instead of chaining .pipe().

Express is a thin layer over Node's own http module, so learn the raw version once and Express stops being magic. http.createServer(handler) calls handler(req, res) for every request. req is a readable stream (method, URL, headers, body); res is a writable stream (status, headers, body).

This is a small notes API with no framework. The lines under // ::run are the requests; the transcript shows each request and response.

import http from "node:http";

const notes = [{ id: 1, text: "first" }];

async function readJson(req) {
  const chunks = [];
  for await (const chunk of req) chunks.push(chunk);       // the body arrives in pieces: collect them all
  const text = Buffer.concat(chunks).toString();
  return text ? JSON.parse(text) : undefined;
}

function send(res, status, data) {
  const body = JSON.stringify(data);
  res.writeHead(status, { "content-type": "application/json; charset=utf-8", "content-length": Buffer.byteLength(body) });
  res.end(body);
}

const app = async (req, res) => {
  const url = new URL(req.url, `http://${req.headers.host}`);   // req.url is only the path and query
  try {
    if (req.method === "GET" && url.pathname === "/notes") return send(res, 200, notes);

    if (req.method === "POST" && url.pathname === "/notes") {
      const body = await readJson(req);
      if (!body?.text) return send(res, 400, { error: "text is required" });
      const note = { id: notes.length + 1, text: body.text };
      notes.push(note);
      res.setHeader("location", `/notes/${note.id}`);
      return send(res, 201, note);
    }

    const m = url.pathname.match(/^\/notes\/(\d+)$/);        // routing by hand: a regex per route
    if (req.method === "GET" && m) {
      const note = notes.find((n) => n.id === Number(m[1]));
      return note ? send(res, 200, note) : send(res, 404, { error: "not found" });
    }

    send(res, 404, { error: "no such route" });
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof SyntaxError) return send(res, 400, { error: "invalid JSON" });
    console.error(err);
    send(res, 500, { error: "internal error" });
  }
};
> GET /notes < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < [{"id":1,"text":"first"}] > POST /notes {"text":"second"} < 201 Created < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < location: /notes/2 < {"id":2,"text":"second"} > POST /notes {oops > content-type: application/json < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"invalid JSON"} > POST /notes {} < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"text is required"} > GET /notes/2 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":2,"text":"second"} > GET /notes/99 < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"not found"} > DELETE /anything < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"no such route"}

It works, and the pain points are exactly what Express removes: parsing the URL and the body by hand, one regex per route, repeating send() and error handling everywhere, no shared middleware (logging, auth, CORS, compression), no route parameters. Unit 4 rebuilds this same API in a dozen lines.

Streams, server settings and constants

import http from "node:http";
import fs from "node:fs";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";

fs.writeFileSync("report.txt", "row\n".repeat(25_000));            // a 100 KB file

const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "text/plain" });
  try {
    await pipeline(fs.createReadStream("report.txt"), res);       // memory stays flat however big the file is
  } catch {
    res.destroy();                                                 // client went away mid-download: nothing to send
  }
});
await new Promise((r) => server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", r));
const { port } = server.address();                                // port 0 asks the OS for any free port

const res = await fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}/`);
const text = await res.text();
console.log(res.status, res.headers.get("transfer-encoding"), text.length);   // no content-length: sent in chunks

console.log("timeouts (ms):", { headers: server.headersTimeout, request: server.requestTimeout, keepAlive: server.keepAliveTimeout });
console.log(http.STATUS_CODES[418], http.METHODS.includes("PATCH"), http.METHODS.length > 20);
server.close();
server.closeAllConnections();
200 chunked 100000 timeouts (ms): { headers: 60000, request: 300000, keepAlive: 5000 } I'm a Teapot true true
  • server.listen(port, host): use 0.0.0.0 inside Docker so the container accepts outside traffic; 127.0.0.1 accepts only local traffic. Port 0 picks a free port (great for tests).
  • Timeouts protect you from slow or hostile clients: headersTimeout (time to send headers), requestTimeout (whole request), keepAliveTimeout (idle connection life, set it higher than your load balancer's).
  • res.writeHead + res.end versus res.statusCode = + res.setHeader + res.write + res.end: the same thing; headers must be sent before the body.
  • Calling res.end() twice, or setting headers after the body started, throws ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT: a classic bug in Express handlers that respond twice.
  • node:https is the same API with TLS certificates; in practice a reverse proxy (nginx, a load balancer) terminates TLS (Unit 10).

Backends constantly call other services: payment providers, email APIs, other microservices. Node 18+ includes the browser's fetch (built on the undici HTTP client). It returns a promise of a Response.

fetch does not reject on 404 or 500It rejects only when the network fails (DNS, refused connection, timeout, abort). A server answering 500 is a successful fetch. Always check res.ok (status 200 to 299) or res.status.
import http from "node:http";
import net from "node:net";

// a small server to call (stands in for "some other service")
const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  const url = new URL(req.url, "http://x");
  if (url.pathname === "/json") { res.setHeader("content-type", "application/json"); return res.end(JSON.stringify({ hello: "world", n: Number(url.searchParams.get("n") ?? 0) })); }
  if (url.pathname === "/echo") {
    let body = ""; for await (const c of req) body += c;
    res.setHeader("content-type", "application/json");
    return res.end(JSON.stringify({ method: req.method, type: req.headers["content-type"], auth: req.headers.authorization, body }));
  }
  if (url.pathname === "/slow") return setTimeout(() => res.end("late"), 500);
  if (url.pathname === "/redirect") { res.writeHead(302, { location: "/json?n=7" }); return res.end(); }
  res.writeHead(404).end("nope");
});
await new Promise((r) => server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", r));
const base = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`;

// GET + JSON
let res = await fetch(`${base}/json?n=${encodeURIComponent(5)}`);
console.log(res.status, res.ok, res.headers.get("content-type"), await res.json());

// POST with a JSON body and headers
res = await fetch(`${base}/echo`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json", authorization: "Bearer abc123" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: "Ana" }),
});
console.log(await res.json());

// a 404 is NOT an exception
res = await fetch(`${base}/missing`);
console.log(res.status, res.ok, await res.text());

// redirects are followed by default
res = await fetch(`${base}/redirect`);
console.log(res.redirected, res.url.endsWith("/json?n=7"), (await res.json()).n);
console.log((await fetch(`${base}/redirect`, { redirect: "manual" })).status);

// a form upload: FormData sets the multipart headers for you
const form = new FormData();
form.append("title", "hello");
form.append("file", new Blob(["file contents"], { type: "text/plain" }), "a.txt");
const up = await (await fetch(`${base}/echo`, { method: "POST", body: form })).json();
console.log(up.type.startsWith("multipart/form-data; boundary="), up.body.includes('filename="a.txt"'));

// timeouts and cancellation with AbortSignal
try { await fetch(`${base}/slow`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(50) }); }
catch (err) { console.log(err.name, "-", err.message); }

// network failure: nothing is listening on that port any more
server.close(); server.closeAllConnections();
const probe = net.createServer();
await new Promise((r) => probe.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", r));
const deadPort = probe.address().port;
probe.close();
try { await fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${deadPort}/json`); }
catch (err) { console.log(err.name, "-", err.message, "| cause:", err.cause.code); }
200 true application/json { hello: 'world', n: 5 } { method: 'POST', type: 'application/json', auth: 'Bearer abc123', body: '{"name":"Ana"}' } 404 false nope true true 7 302 true true TimeoutError - The operation was aborted due to timeout TypeError - fetch failed | cause: ECONNREFUSED

A resilient client: check, time out, retry

Other servers are slow, flaky and sometimes down. Always set a timeout, treat 5xx and network errors as retryable, never retry non-idempotent requests blindly, and back off exponentially (wait 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms...) with a little randomness (jitter) so a crowd of clients does not retry in lockstep.

import http from "node:http";
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

let calls = 0;
const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {           // fails twice, then works
  calls++;
  if (calls < 3) { res.writeHead(503); return res.end("busy"); }
  res.end("finally ok");
});
await new Promise((r) => server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", r));
const url = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}/`;

async function fetchWithRetry(url, { retries = 3, timeoutMs = 1000, baseMs = 20 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      const res = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs) });
      if (res.status < 500) return res;                    // success or a client error: do not retry
      throw new Error(`server answered ${res.status}`);
    } catch (err) {
      if (attempt >= retries) throw err;                   // out of attempts: give up with the last error
      const delay = baseMs * 2 ** attempt + Math.random() * baseMs;
      console.log(`attempt ${attempt + 1} failed (${err.message}), retrying`);
      await sleep(delay);
    }
  }
}
const res = await fetchWithRetry(url);
console.log(res.status, await res.text(), "after", calls, "calls");
server.close(); server.closeAllConnections();
attempt 1 failed (server answered 503), retrying attempt 2 failed (server answered 503), retrying 200 finally ok after 3 calls
DetailsThe body can be read once: res.json(), res.text(), res.arrayBuffer(), res.blob() or stream it with res.body. Unread bodies keep connections busy, so always consume or cancel them (await res.body?.cancel()). For heavy use, the undici package exposes connection pools, Agent and a faster request(); axios and got are popular wrappers.

node:crypto wraps OpenSSL. Rule one: never invent your own cryptography. Use these building blocks for what they are meant for.

NeedUseNot
Fingerprint data (cache keys, checksums, ETags)createHash("sha256")md5/sha1 for security
Prove a message came from someone with a shared secret (webhooks, signed cookies)createHmac("sha256", secret)A plain hash of secret + message
Store passwordsscrypt, or argon2/bcrypt (Unit 7)Any fast hash, encryption
Unpredictable tokens, IDs, saltsrandomBytes, randomUUID, randomIntMath.random()
Keep data secret and tamper-proofaes-256-gcmECB mode, home-made XOR
Digital signature (public/private key)sign/verify with Ed25519 or RSA
 
import crypto from "node:crypto";

console.log(crypto.createHash("sha256").update("hello").digest("hex"));      // same input, same output, always
console.log(crypto.createHash("sha256").update("hello").update(" world").digest("base64url"));   // update() can be called in pieces
console.log(crypto.createHmac("sha256", "my-secret").update("payload").digest("hex"));      // a hash that needs the key

console.log(crypto.randomBytes(16).toString("hex").length, crypto.randomUUID().length, crypto.randomInt(1, 7) <= 6);
console.log(crypto.randomUUID().replace(/[0-9a-f]/g, "x"));                  // the shape of a v4 UUID
console.log(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(4)).length);               // the same API browsers have

// timing-safe comparison: === leaks, through response time, how many leading characters were right
const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", "k").update("m").digest();
const given = crypto.createHmac("sha256", "k").update("m").digest();
console.log(crypto.timingSafeEqual(expected, given), expected.length);      // buffers must have equal length or it throws

// the web crypto API is available too
const digest = await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", new TextEncoder().encode("hello"));
console.log(Buffer.from(digest).toString("hex").slice(0, 16));
