Passwords, encryption and signatures

import crypto from "node:crypto";
import { promisify } from "node:util";
const scrypt = promisify(crypto.scrypt);

// 1. Password hashing: slow on purpose, unique random salt per password
async function hashPassword(password) {
  const salt = crypto.randomBytes(16);
  const key = await scrypt(password, salt, 64);
  return `${salt.toString("hex")}:${key.toString("hex")}`;       // store this single string
}
async function verifyPassword(password, stored) {
  const [salt, key] = stored.split(":");
  const candidate = await scrypt(password, Buffer.from(salt, "hex"), 64);
  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(candidate, Buffer.from(key, "hex"));
}
const stored = await hashPassword("correct horse");
console.log(stored.length, await verifyPassword("correct horse", stored), await verifyPassword("wrong", stored));
console.log((await hashPassword("correct horse")) !== stored, "(same password, different salt, different hash)");

// 2. Authenticated encryption: confidentiality AND tamper detection
const key = crypto.randomBytes(32);                             // 256-bit key, keep it in a secret store
function encrypt(text) {
  const iv = crypto.randomBytes(12);                            // never reuse an IV with the same key
  const cipher = crypto.createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, iv);
  const data = Buffer.concat([cipher.update(text, "utf8"), cipher.final()]);
  return Buffer.concat([iv, cipher.getAuthTag(), data]).toString("base64");
}
function decrypt(token) {
  const raw = Buffer.from(token, "base64");
  const decipher = crypto.createDecipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, raw.subarray(0, 12));
  decipher.setAuthTag(raw.subarray(12, 28));
  return Buffer.concat([decipher.update(raw.subarray(28)), decipher.final()]).toString("utf8");
}
const token = encrypt("card ending 4242");
console.log(decrypt(token));
const tampered = Buffer.from(token, "base64"); tampered[tampered.length - 1] ^= 1;      // flip one bit
try { decrypt(tampered.toString("base64")); } catch (e) { console.log("tamper detected:", e.message); }

// 3. Signatures: sign with the private key, anyone with the public key can verify
const { publicKey, privateKey } = crypto.generateKeyPairSync("ed25519");
const message = Buffer.from("order #1001: 3 items");
const signature = crypto.sign(null, message, privateKey);
console.log(signature.length, crypto.verify(null, message, publicKey, signature), crypto.verify(null, Buffer.from("order #1001: 30 items"), publicKey, signature));
161 true false true (same password, different salt, different hash) card ending 4242 tamper detected: Unsupported state or unable to authenticate data 64 true false
Encryption is not hashingHashes cannot be reversed (use for passwords, with a slow algorithm); encryption can (use for data you must read back). Never store passwords encrypted. Never put a secret key in source code or a Git repository (Unit 10 covers configuration).
import { setTimeout as sleep, setInterval as every } from "node:timers/promises";

const t = setTimeout(() => console.log("never runs"), 1000);
clearTimeout(t);                                             // cancel before it fires

let n = 0;
const iv = setInterval(() => { n++; console.log("tick", n); if (n === 3) clearInterval(iv); }, 10);   // always clear intervals, or the process never exits
await sleep(60);

console.log(await sleep(5, "sleep returns a value"));       // timers/promises: await-able, no callbacks
for await (const _ of every(10)) { console.log("async interval"); if (++n >= 5) break; }

const bg = setInterval(() => {}, 1000);
bg.unref();                                                   // do not keep the process alive just for this timer
console.log("hasRef:", bg.hasRef());

queueMicrotask(() => console.log("microtask"));              // runs right after the current code, before timers
setImmediate(() => console.log("setImmediate"));
console.log("sync done");
tick 1 tick 2 tick 3 sleep returns a value async interval async interval hasRef: false sync done microtask setImmediate
RememberA timer delay is a minimum; if the loop is busy it fires late. Maximum delay is about 24.8 days (231-1 ms): longer waits need a real scheduler (cron, a job queue, Unit 8). Timers are not persistent: a restart forgets them.

AbortController: one way to cancel anything

An AbortController has a signal you hand to cancellable operations (fetch, timers, streams, fs.readFile, events.on, child processes, your own functions) and an abort() method that cancels them all. Use it for client disconnects, request timeouts and shutdown.

import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const ac = new AbortController();
setTimeout(() => ac.abort(new Error("user cancelled")), 20);
try { await sleep(1000, null, { signal: ac.signal }); }
catch (err) { console.log(err.name, "| reason:", err.cause?.message); }

try { await sleep(1000, null, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(20) }); }          // a signal that aborts itself after 20 ms
catch (err) { console.log(err.name, "| cause:", err.cause?.name); }

const either = AbortSignal.any([AbortSignal.timeout(5000), ac.signal]);          // abort on whichever comes first
console.log("combined aborted?", either.aborted, either.reason?.message);

// your own functions can honour a signal too
async function work(signal) {
  for (let step = 1; step <= 5; step++) {
    signal.throwIfAborted();                                    // checkpoint: throws if cancelled
    await sleep(10);
  }
  return "finished";
}
console.log(await work(new AbortController().signal));
try { await work(AbortSignal.timeout(25)); } catch (e) { console.log("work stopped:", e.name); }

try { await readFile(import.meta.filename, { signal: AbortSignal.abort() }); } catch (e) { console.log("readFile:", e.name); }

// measuring time: performance.now() is monotonic (never jumps backwards like Date.now() can)
const start = performance.now();
performance.mark("a");
await sleep(25);
performance.mark("b");
const m = performance.measure("sleep", "a", "b");
console.log(performance.now() - start >= 25, Math.round(m.duration) >= 24, typeof performance.timeOrigin);
console.log(process.hrtime.bigint() > 0n);                      // nanosecond clock for micro-benchmarks
AbortError | reason: user cancelled AbortError | cause: TimeoutError combined aborted? true user cancelled finished work stopped: TimeoutError readFile: AbortError true true number true

A backend sometimes has to run another program: ffmpeg to convert a video, git, a Python script, or another Node process. Pick the function by what you need:

FunctionShell?OutputUse for
exec(cmd)YesBuffered string (limited size)Quick shell one-liners with fixed text only
execFile(file, args)NoBufferedRun a program with arguments. The safe default.
spawn(file, args)NoStreamsLong-running or large-output programs (ffmpeg, tail)
fork(module)NoStreams + message channelAnother Node script that you talk to with send()/on("message")
 
import { exec, execFile, spawn } from "node:child_process";
import { promisify } from "node:util";
const execP = promisify(exec), execFileP = promisify(execFile);

// shell injection: user text pasted into a shell command can add commands of its own
const userInput = "hello; echo INJECTED";
console.log("exec     :", JSON.stringify((await execP(`echo ${userInput}`)).stdout));            // BOTH commands ran!
console.log("execFile :", JSON.stringify((await execFileP("echo", [userInput])).stdout));        // one harmless argument

// a failing program: non-zero exit code makes the promise reject
try { await execFileP("node", ["-e", "console.error('bad things'); process.exit(3)"]); }
catch (err) { console.log("exit code", err.code, "| stderr:", err.stderr.trim()); }

// spawn: stream the output while the program runs
const child = spawn("node", ["-e", "for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) console.log('line', i)"]);
child.stdout.on("data", (chunk) => process.stdout.write("child said: " + chunk));
const code = await new Promise((resolve) => child.on("close", resolve));
console.log("child exited with", code);

// feed stdin and set a timeout
const sorter = spawn("sort");
let sorted = ""; sorter.stdout.on("data", (c) => (sorted += c));
sorter.stdin.end("pear\napple\nfig\n");
await new Promise((r) => sorter.on("close", r));
console.log(JSON.stringify(sorted));
try { await execFileP("node", ["-e", "setTimeout(() => {}, 5000)"], { timeout: 100 }); } catch (e) { console.log("killed by timeout:", e.killed); }
exec : "hello\nINJECTED\n" execFile : "hello; echo INJECTED\n" exit code 3 | stderr: bad things child said: line 1 child said: line 2 child said: line 3 child exited with 0 "apple\nfig\npear\n" killed by timeout: true
Command injectionNever build a shell string from user input. Use execFile or spawn with an array of arguments, so the user text can only ever be one argument. Even then, validate it (a value starting with - can be read as an option: pass -- before it where the program supports that).

fork: a second Node process you can message

import { fork } from "node:child_process";

if (process.send) {
  // ---- child side ----
  process.on("message", (job) => {
    let total = 0;
    for (let i = 1; i <= job.upTo; i++) total += i;               // pretend this is heavy work
    process.send({ id: job.id, total });
    process.disconnect();                                           // close the channel so the child can exit
  });
} else {
  // ---- parent side ----
  const child = fork(import.meta.filename);
  child.send({ id: 1, upTo: 1_000_000 });
  child.on("message", (result) => console.log("parent received", result));
  await new Promise((resolve) => child.on("exit", resolve));
  console.log("child finished");
}
parent received { id: 1, total: 500000500000 } child finished

One Node process uses one core for JavaScript. Two tools go beyond it:

worker_threadscluster
WhatExtra threads inside one processExtra processes sharing one listening port
MemorySeparate heaps; can share SharedArrayBufferFully separate
Best forCPU-heavy jobs (image resize, hashing, parsing) inside a requestUsing every core for an HTTP server
If one crashesThe thread dies, the process may liveOnly that worker dies, the primary restarts it
AlternativesA job queue and separate worker service (Unit 8)Run several containers/PM2 instances behind a load balancer (Unit 10)
 
import { Worker, isMainThread, parentPort, workerData } from "node:worker_threads";

function fib(n) { return n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); }      // deliberately slow CPU work

if (isMainThread) {
  // ---- main thread: keep the loop free and hand the heavy work to a worker ----
  let ticks = 0;
  const heartbeat = setInterval(() => ticks++, 5);

  const run = (n) => new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const worker = new Worker(import.meta.filename, { workerData: { n } });   // the same file, running as a worker
    worker.once("message", resolve);
    worker.once("error", reject);
  });
  const [a, b] = await Promise.all([run(32), run(33)]);            // two workers at the same time
  clearInterval(heartbeat);
  console.log("results:", a, b);
  console.log(ticks > 5 ? "main thread stayed responsive while workers computed" : "main thread was blocked");
} else {
  // ---- worker thread ----
  parentPort.postMessage(fib(workerData.n));
}
results: 2178309 3524578 main thread stayed responsive while workers computed

The thread-creation cost is real (tens of milliseconds), so for many small jobs keep a pool of workers (libraries: piscina, workerpool) instead of starting one per request.

cluster: a pool of server processes

import cluster from "node:cluster";
import http from "node:http";
import os from "node:os";

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const workers = 2;                                       // in production: os.availableParallelism()

if (cluster.isPrimary) {
  console.log(`primary: starting ${workers} workers (this machine has ${os.availableParallelism() > 0 ? "some" : "no"} CPUs)`);
  for (let i = 0; i < workers; i++) cluster.fork();

  let listening = 0;
  cluster.on("listening", (worker) => console.log(`primary: worker ${worker.id} is listening on port ${port} (${++listening}/${workers})`));
  cluster.on("exit", (worker, code, signal) => {
    if (signal === "SIGTERM") return;                    // we asked it to stop
    console.log(`primary: worker ${worker.id} died, starting a replacement`);
    cluster.fork();                                      // keep the pool full
  });
  process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
    for (const id in cluster.workers) cluster.workers[id].kill("SIGTERM");
    process.exit(0);
  });
} else {
  http.createServer((req, res) => res.end(`handled by worker ${cluster.worker.id}\n`)).listen(port);   // all workers share one port
}

The operating system hands each new connection to the primary, which distributes them round-robin. Six requests, two workers:

$ for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl localhost:3000/; done
handled by worker 2
handled by worker 1
handled by worker 2
handled by worker 1
handled by worker 2
handled by worker 1
primary: starting 2 workers (this machine has some CPUs) primary: worker 1 is listening on port 3000 (1/2) primary: worker 2 is listening on port 3000 (2/2)
In practiceMany teams skip cluster and run one process per container with an orchestrator (Docker, Kubernetes) or let PM2 manage processes (pm2 start app.js -i max). The rules for any multi-process design are the same: no state kept in process memory (sessions, caches, counters live in Redis or a database, Unit 6), because the next request may land on a different process.

npm (Node Package Manager) installs libraries from the public registry and runs your project scripts. package.json is the manifest that describes your project; package-lock.json pins the exact versions that were installed.

$ npm init -y

    "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1"
  },
  "keywords": [],
  "author": "",
  "license": "ISC"
}
$ npm pkg set type=module scripts.start="node index.js" scripts.hello="echo hello from a script"
$ echo 'import ms from "ms"; console.log(ms("2 days"), ms(90000));' > index.js
$ npm install ms@2.1.3

found 0 vulnerabilities
$ cat package.json

hello from a script
FieldPurpose
name, versionIdentity. Lowercase, no spaces. version follows semver.
type"module" (ES modules) or "commonjs" (default).
main / exportsEntry point when others import your package. exports is the modern, stricter form.
scriptsNamed commands: npm run name. start and test can omit run. prestart/postinstall style hooks run around them.
dependenciesNeeded at runtime in production.
devDependenciesNeeded only to develop and test (nodemon, test tools, TypeScript, linters).
enginesWhich Node versions you support: { "node": ">=22" }.
bin, files, privateCommand-line entry points, what gets published, and true to block accidental publishing.
workspacesSeveral packages in one repository (monorepo).

Versions and the lockfile

Versions look like MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (semver): a patch fixes bugs, a minor adds features without breaking, a major may break your code.

RangeAccepts
"^4.18.2" (npm's default)4.18.2 up to, but excluding, 5.0.0 (minor and patch updates)
"~4.18.2"4.18.2 up to, but excluding, 4.19.0 (patch updates only)
"4.18.2"Exactly this version
">=4 <6", "*", "latest"Ranges and wildcards (avoid */latest in apps)
"^0.2.3"For 0.x versions only the patch moves: 0.2.3 up to, but excluding, 0.3.0
  • Commit package-lock.json. It records the exact version of every package (including nested ones), so a teammate and your server install the same tree.
  • npm install may update the lockfile; npm ci installs exactly the lockfile (and fails if it disagrees with package.json). Use npm ci in CI and Docker builds.
  • Never commit node_modules/; put it in .gitignore.

Everyday commands

CommandDoes
npm init -yCreate a package.json with defaults
npm install express / npm i expressAdd a dependency (saves ^version)
npm i -D nodemonAdd a dev dependency
npm iInstall everything in package.json
npm ciClean, exact install from the lockfile (CI, Docker)
npm uninstall pkgRemove
npm update / npm outdatedUpdate within ranges / show newer versions
npm ls / npm ls --allShow the dependency tree
npm view pkg versionsRegistry information
npm run script / npm test / npm startRun a script
npx toolRun a package's command without installing it globally (npx tsc --noEmit)
npm audit / npm audit fixCheck for known vulnerabilities
npm pack / npm publishBuild the tarball / publish to the registry
npm config get registry, npm cache lsConfiguration and cache
Supply chainEvery dependency is code you run with your server's permissions. Prefer popular, maintained packages; check for look-alike names (typosquatting); keep the tree small; commit the lockfile; run npm audit in CI; consider npm ci --ignore-scripts for untrusted installs, since packages can run install scripts. pnpm and yarn are alternatives with the same package.json; bun and deno are different runtimes that can run much of the same code.
FlagEffect
--watchRestart when imported files change. Replaces nodemon in most cases. --watch-path=./src narrows it.
--env-file=.envLoad variables from a file into process.env (no dotenv needed). Repeatable.
--check / -cParse a file for syntax errors without running it.
--import ./setup.js, --requirePreload a module (instrumentation, polyfills) before your app.
--testRun the built-in test runner (Unit 9).
--inspect, --inspect-brkOpen a debugger port (break on first line with -brk).
--max-old-space-size=2048Heap limit in MB (default depends on system memory).
--trace-warnings, --trace-uncaughtShow where warnings or errors originated.
--permission + --allow-fs-read= ...Permission model: deny file, process and worker access unless allowed.
NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=1024"Environment variable carrying flags into every Node process (including those started by npm scripts).
NODE_ENV=productionA convention, not a Node setting: Express and many libraries switch to faster, quieter behaviour.
 
$ printf 'GREETING=hello\nPORT=9000\n# comments are ignored\nQUOTED="a b c"\n' > .env
$ node --env-file=.env -p "process.env.GREETING + ' on port ' + process.env.PORT + ' / ' + process.env.QUOTED"
hello on port 9000 / a b c
$ echo 'const x = ;' > bad.js
$ node --check bad.js 2>&1 | grep -E "SyntaxError|const x"
const x = ;
SyntaxError: Unexpected token ';'
$ node --permission -p "require('fs').readFileSync('/etc/hostname', 'utf8')" 2>&1 | grep "Error:"
Error: Access to this API has been restricted. Use --allow-fs-read to manage permissions.
$ node --permission --allow-fs-read=/etc/hostname -p "require('fs').readFileSync('/etc/hostname', 'utf8').length > 0"
true
$ NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=512" node -p "Math.round(require('v8').getHeapStatistics().heap_size_limit / 1048576) + ' MB heap limit'"
560 MB heap limit

The heap limit printed above is a little over the 512 you asked for because V8 also counts its young generation. Without the flag the default is derived from the machine's memory.

.env filesKeep them out of Git (.gitignore), ship a .env.example with fake values, and in production prefer real environment variables or a secret manager. Values are always strings: convert and validate them at start-up (Unit 10).

Debugging

  1. Read the stack trace. The first line is the message; the first frame in your file is usually the culprit.
  2. console.log / console.table / console.dir(obj, { depth: null }) for quick looks; remove them afterwards or move to a logger.
  3. A real debugger. Run node --inspect-brk app.js and open chrome://inspect, or press F5 in VS Code (it attaches automatically, "JavaScript Debug Terminal"). Set breakpoints, step, inspect variables, and use conditional breakpoints and logpoints.
  4. The debugger; statement pauses when a debugger is attached and is ignored otherwise.
  5. Narrow it down: reproduce with the smallest request (a curl command), then bisect the code path.
  6. Source maps (--enable-source-maps) make stack traces point at your TypeScript instead of compiled output.
04

Unit 4: Express.js

The most widely used Node web framework (version 5): routing, requests and responses, middleware, body parsing, error handling, static files, templates, project structure, TypeScript and the move from Express 4. Every transcript is a real request to a real running app.

Express is a small framework on top of Node's http module. It gives you three things: routing (which function handles which URL and method), middleware (reusable steps that run for requests) and nicer request/response helpers (res.json(), req.params). Everything else (databases, validation, authentication) you add with libraries. This guide uses Express 5 (the current version); a table in this unit lists what changed from Express 4, which most older tutorials still show.

Set up a project

$ npm init -y
Wrote to ~/demo/my-api/package.json:

{
  "name": "my-api",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1"
  },
  "keywords": [],
  "author": "",
  "license": "ISC"
}
$ npm pkg set type=module
$ npm install express

added 65 packages, and audited 66 packages in 1s

29 packages are looking for funding
  run `npm fund` for details

found 0 vulnerabilities
$ npm ls --depth=0
my-api@1.0.0 ~/demo/my-api
`-- express@5.3.0

Express 5 needs Node 18 or newer. "type": "module" lets you write import instead of require. Now the smallest useful server:

import express from "express";

const app = express();
const port = process.env.PORT ?? 3000;

// A route: when a GET request for "/" arrives, run this function
app.get("/", (req, res) => {
  res.send("Hello from Express!");
});

// :name is a route parameter. Whatever is in that part of the URL ends up in req.params.name
app.get("/hello/:name", (req, res) => {
  res.json({ message: `Hello, ${req.params.name}!` });
});

// Start accepting connections. In Express 5 the callback also receives start-up errors (for example, port already in use)
app.listen(port, (error) => {
  if (error) throw error;
  console.log(`Listening on http://localhost:${port}`);
});
$ curl localhost:3000/
Hello from Express!
$ curl localhost:3000/hello/Ana
{"message":"Hello, Ana!"}
$ curl -i localhost:3000/missing
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 146
Date: Fri, 23 Oct 2026 09:30:00 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>Error</title>
</head>
<body>
<pre>Cannot GET /missing</pre>
</body>
</html>
Listening on http://localhost:3000

Line by line: express() creates the app. app.get(path, handler) registers a route. The handler receives req (the request) and res (the response) and must send something. app.listen opens the port. The unknown URL got a ready-made 404 page: Express answers that itself when no route matches.

Development workflow

  • node --watch server.js restarts the server on every save (nodemon is no longer required). Add it as a script: "dev": "node --watch server.js".
  • Test with curl (shown throughout this guide), a REST client (Postman, Insomnia, Bruno, the VS Code "REST Client" extension) or the browser for GET requests.
  • Use an environment variable for the port (process.env.PORT ?? 3000) so the same code runs on your laptop, in Docker and on a host that assigns the port.
  • If the port is taken you get EADDRINUSE. In Express 5 the listen callback receives that error (in Express 4 it was an unhandled event). Check what is using it: lsof -i :3000 (macOS/Linux) or netstat -ano | findstr :3000 (Windows).
import express from "express";

const first = express().listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => {             // port 0: any free port
  const { port } = first.address();
  express().listen(port, "127.0.0.1", (error) => {                 // same port again
    console.log("second server error:", error?.code, "-", error?.message);
    first.close();
  });
});
second server error: EADDRINUSE - listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000

A route is app.METHOD(path, ...handlers). Express checks routes in the order you wrote them and runs the first one that matches both method and path; that handler ends the request by responding (or passes on with next()).

import express from "express";
const app = express();

app.get("/", (req, res) => res.send("home"));
app.post("/items", (req, res) => res.status(201).send("created"));
app.put("/items/:id", (req, res) => res.send(`replace item ${req.params.id}`));
app.patch("/items/:id", (req, res) => res.send(`update item ${req.params.id}`));
app.delete("/items/:id", (req, res) => res.sendStatus(204));
app.all("/secret", (req, res) => res.send(`all methods land here, this was a ${req.method}`));

app.get("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", (req, res) => res.json(req.params));    // several parameters
app.get("/flights/:from-:to", (req, res) => res.json(req.params));              // - and . are separators between parameters
app.get("/search", (req, res) => res.json({ q: req.query.q, tags: req.query.tag }));   // ?q=...&tag=...
> GET / < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < home > POST /items < 201 Created < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < created > PUT /items/7 < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < replace item 7 > DELETE /items/7 < 204 No Content > PATCH /secret < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < all methods land here, this was a PATCH > GET /users/3/posts/9 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"userId":"3","postId":"9"} > GET /flights/LAX-SFO < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"from":"LAX","to":"SFO"} > GET /search?q=node%20js&tag=a&tag=b < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"q":"node js","tags":["a","b"]} > HEAD / < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
  • Route parameters (:id) are always strings in req.params. Convert and validate them (Number(req.params.id), Number.isInteger).
  • Query string values are in req.query; repeating a key (tag=a&tag=b) gives an array. They are strings too, and a missing key is undefined.
  • HEAD requests are answered by the matching GET route automatically (headers only, no body).

Path syntax in Express 5

Express 5 uses a newer path matcher (path-to-regexp 8). Old patterns from Express 4 articles (*, :id?, /:id(\d+)) now throw an error at start-up. The new forms:

You wantExpress 5 pathExpress 4 spelling
Named parameter/users/:idsame
Wildcard, one or more segments/files/*splat (value in req.params.splat, an array)/files/*
Wildcard, zero or more/files{/*splat}/files/*?
Optional segment/users{/:id}/users/:id?
Optional piece inside a segment/book{-:edition}/book-:edition?
Digits onlyvalidate in the handler, or use a RegExp route /^\/users\/(\d+)$//users/:id(\d+)
A literal reserved characterescape it: /price/\\$:amount-
Several paths, one handler["/a", "/b"]same
 
import express from "express";
const app = express();

app.get("/files/*splat", (req, res) => res.json({ route: "files", splat: req.params.splat }));
app.get("/docs{/:section}", (req, res) => res.json({ route: "docs", section: req.params.section ?? null }));
app.get(/^\/ids\/(\d+)$/, (req, res) => res.json({ route: "regex", id: Number(req.params[0]) }));   // regex captures land in req.params[0]
app.get(["/ping", "/health"], (req, res) => res.send("pong"));
> GET /files/img/logo/small.png < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"route":"files","splat":["img","logo","small.png"]} > GET /docs < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"route":"docs","section":null} > GET /docs/install < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"route":"docs","section":"install"} > GET /ids/42 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"route":"regex","id":42} > GET /ids/abc < 404 Not Found < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < <!DOCTYPE html> < <html lang="en"> < <head> < <meta charset="utf-8 ... > GET /health < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < pong
import express from "express";

for (const path of ["/users/:id(\\d+)", "/files/*", "/users/:id?"]) {
  try {
    express().get(path, () => {});
    console.log("accepted:", path);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(`${path.padEnd(18)} ${error.name}: ${error.message.split(";")[0]}`);
  }
}
/users/:id(\d+) TypeError: Unexpected ( at index 10: /users/:id(\d+) /files/* TypeError: Missing parameter name at index 8: /files/* /users/:id? TypeError: Unexpected ? at index 10: /users/:id?

Routers: split routes into modules

An express.Router() is a mini-app with its own routes and middleware. You mount it under a prefix with app.use(prefix, router), so each feature (users, orders, admin) lives in its own file. Inside a router, paths are relative to the mount point.

import express from "express";
const app = express();

const users = express.Router();
users.param("id", (req, res, next, value) => {                  // runs for every route with :id in this router
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(value)) return res.status(400).json({ error: `id must be digits, got "${value}"` });
  req.userId = Number(value);                                     // convert once, use as a number afterwards
  next();
});
users.get("/", (req, res) => res.json({ list: ["ana", "raj"], baseUrl: req.baseUrl }));
users.get("/:id", (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.userId, path: req.path, originalUrl: req.originalUrl }));

const admin = express.Router();
admin.use((req, res, next) => (req.get("x-admin") === "yes" ? next() : res.status(403).json({ error: "admins only" })));   // protects every route below
admin.get("/stats", (req, res) => res.json({ users: 2 }));

app.use("/api/users", users);                                     // mounted under a prefix
app.use("/admin", admin);

app.route("/book")                                                // one path, several methods
  .get((req, res) => res.send("read the book"))
  .post((req, res) => res.status(201).send("write the book"));
> GET /api/users < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"list":["ana","raj"],"baseUrl":"/api/users"} > GET /api/users/7 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":7,"path":"/7","originalUrl":"/api/users/7"} > GET /api/users/abc < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"id must be digits, got \"abc\""} > GET /admin/stats < 403 Forbidden < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"admins only"} > GET /admin/stats > x-admin: yes < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"users":2} > POST /book < 201 Created < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < write the book
Three names for the URLInside a mounted router, req.originalUrl is the full URL as received (/api/users/7), req.baseUrl is the mount prefix (/api/users) and req.path is the rest (/7).

Order, 404, 405 and the routing options

  • Order matters. Put specific routes before general ones: /users/me must come before /users/:id, or "me" is captured as an id.
  • 404: a final app.use(...) with no path, after all routes, catches everything that matched nothing.
  • 405: Express answers 404 for a known path with the wrong method. If you prefer an accurate 405 Method Not Allowed, add a catch-all on the route and send an Allow header.
  • OPTIONS: when a request reaches the end of the stack without an answer, Express replies to OPTIONS itself with an Allow header. A catch-all 404 (or .all()) handler answers first, so that automatic reply is only seen on apps without one. Browsers send OPTIONS as CORS preflight requests, which the cors middleware answers (Unit 7).
  • Matching is case-insensitive and ignores a trailing slash by default. Change with app.set("case sensitive routing", true) and app.set("strict routing", true).
import express from "express";
const app = express();

app.get("/users/me", (req, res) => res.send("the current user"));    // specific first...
app.get("/users/:id", (req, res) => res.send(`user ${req.params.id}`));  // ...general second

app.route("/thing")
  .get((req, res) => res.send("a thing"))
  .all((req, res) => res.set("Allow", "GET, HEAD").status(405).json({ error: `${req.method} not allowed here` }));

app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: `Cannot ${req.method} ${req.path}` }));   // last: nothing matched
> GET /users/me < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < the current user > GET /users/42 < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < user 42 > GET /USERS/42/ < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < user 42 > DELETE /thing < 405 Method Not Allowed < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < allow: GET, HEAD < {"error":"DELETE not allowed here"} > GET /nowhere < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"Cannot GET /nowhere"}
import express from "express";
const app = express();
app.get("/users/:id", (req, res) => res.send("a user"));
app.put("/users/:id", (req, res) => res.send("updated"));      // no catch-all 404 in this app
> OPTIONS /users/42 < 200 OK < content-type: text/plain < allow: GET, HEAD, PUT < GET, HEAD, PUT
Handlers must answer onceEvery request must end with exactly one response. Forgetting to respond leaves the client hanging until it times out. Responding twice throws ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT. After res.json(...) in an if, return so the code below does not also run: return res.status(400).json(...).

req extends Node's IncomingMessage. Everything the client sent is on it.

PropertyHolds
req.method"GET", "POST"...
req.paramsRoute parameters (strings)
req.queryParsed query string (strings and arrays). Read-only in Express 5.
req.bodyThe parsed body, but only after a body-parsing middleware ran. undefined otherwise.
req.headers / req.get(name)Headers. Names are lower case in req.headers; req.get() is case-insensitive.
req.path, req.originalUrl, req.baseUrlURL pieces (see Routing)
req.hostname, req.hostHost without / with the port (from the Host header or X-Forwarded-Host behind a trusted proxy)
req.protocol, req.secure"http"/"https"; secure is true for https
req.ip, req.ipsClient address. Behind a proxy this is the proxy until you set trust proxy.
req.cookies, req.signedCookiesOnly with the cookie-parser middleware (Unit 7)
req.is("json")Does the Content-Type match?
req.accepts(types)Content negotiation: which of these can the client take (from the Accept header)?
req.fresh / req.staleConditional-request (ETag/304) state
req.app, req.res, req.routeReferences to the app, the response and the matched route
 
import express from "express";
const app = express();

app.post("/inspect/:topic", (req, res) => {
  res.json({
    method: req.method,
    url: { originalUrl: req.originalUrl, path: req.path, baseUrl: req.baseUrl },
    params: req.params,
    query: req.query,
    body: req.body ?? null,                                 // undefined: we installed no body parser
    host: { hostname: req.hostname, protocol: req.protocol, secure: req.secure },
    ip: { ip: req.ip, ips: req.ips },
    agent: req.get("User-Agent"),
    isJson: Boolean(req.is("json")),
    wants: req.accepts(["html", "json"]),                   // the best match, in YOUR order of preference when the client has none
    cookies: req.cookies ?? null,                           // undefined: no cookie-parser
  });
});
> POST /inspect/express?page=2&sort=name&sort=age {"name":"Ana"} > user-agent: demo-client/1.0 > accept: application/json < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"method":"POST","url":{"originalUrl":"/inspect/express?page=2&sort=name&sort=age","path":"/inspect/express","baseUrl":""},"params":{"topic":"express"},"query":{"page":"2","sort":["name","age"]},"body":null,"host":{"hostname":"127.0.0.1","protocol":"http","secure":false},"ip":{"ip":"127.0.0.1","ips":[]},"agent":"demo-client/1.0","isJson":true,"wants":"json","cookies":null}

The query string parser (changed in Express 5)

Express 5 parses queries with Node's simple querystring rules: flat keys, repeated keys become arrays, and a[b]=1 is just a key named a[b]. If you want nested objects, opt in with app.set("query parser", "extended"). Whatever you choose, validate it: a query value may be a string, an array, or (with the extended parser) an object, and code that assumes a string breaks.

import express from "express";
const app = express();
app.get("/q", (req, res) => res.json(req.query));
> GET /q?name=Ana&tag=a&tag=b&filter[age]=30&ids[]=1&ids[]=2 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"name":"Ana","tag":["a","b"],"filter[age]":"30","ids[]":["1","2"]} > GET /q?name=Ana&tag=a&tag=b&filter[age]=30&ids[]=1&ids[]=2 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"name":"Ana","tag":["a","b"],"filter":{"age":"30"},"ids":["1","2"]}

Behind a proxy: trust proxy

In production a load balancer or nginx usually sits in front of Node. Then the TCP connection comes from the proxy, and the real client address, protocol and host arrive in X-Forwarded-For, -Proto and -Host headers. Express ignores those headers unless you say how many proxies to trust, because any client can forge them.

import express from "express";
const app = express();
app.get("/me", (req, res) => res.json({ ip: req.ip, ips: req.ips, protocol: req.protocol, secure: req.secure }));
--- no trust proxy: forwarded headers are ignored (they could be forged) > GET /me > x-forwarded-for: 1.2.3.4, 203.0.113.9 > x-forwarded-proto: https < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"ip":"127.0.0.1","ips":[],"protocol":"http","secure":false} --- trust proxy = 1: only the entry added by OUR proxy is believed, the forged 1.2.3.4 is ignored > GET /me > x-forwarded-for: 1.2.3.4, 203.0.113.9 > x-forwarded-proto: https < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"ip":"203.0.113.9","ips":["203.0.113.9"],"protocol":"https","secure":true}
Get this right before using req.ipRate limiting, audit logs and "secure" cookies all depend on req.ip/req.secure. Set trust proxy to the number of proxy hops you actually have (1 for one load balancer), never to true on an internet-facing app without a proxy, since anyone can then spoof their address with a header.

You can also attach your own data to req in middleware (req.user = ..., req.requestId = ...) so later handlers can use it, or better, to res.locals (below). With TypeScript, declare the extra properties (see the TypeScript entry).

res extends Node's ServerResponse. Most methods return res so you can chain them: res.status(201).location("/x").json(obj).

MethodDoes
res.send(body)Send a string (HTML), Buffer (binary), object/array/number/boolean (as JSON). Sets Content-Type and Content-Length, handles ETag.
res.json(obj)Send JSON. Use this for APIs: it is explicit and also handles null and strings correctly.
res.status(code)Set the status (not yet sent). Chainable. Throws for numbers outside 100-999.
res.sendStatus(code)Set status and send its standard text as the body (204, 404 Not Found).
res.redirect([status,] url)Redirect (default 302). Use 301/308 for permanent, 303 after a POST form, 307/308 to keep the method.
res.set(name, value) / res.append / res.getHeaders. res.type("json") sets Content-Type, res.location(url), res.vary(h), res.links({...}) for pagination.
res.cookie(name, value, opts) / res.clearCookie(name)Set or remove a cookie (options in Unit 7).
res.format({...})Respond differently depending on the Accept header (JSON for APIs, HTML for browsers).
res.sendFile(path, {root}) / res.download(path, name)Stream a file (with caching headers, ranges) / as an attachment.
res.render(view, data)Render a template (below).
res.end()End with no body (Node's own method).
res.localsAn object that lives for this request only: pass data from middleware to later handlers and to templates.
res.headersSentTrue once headers went out: too late to change status or headers.
 
import express from "express";
const app = express();

app.get("/text", (req, res) => res.send("plain string"));                      // string becomes text/html
app.get("/html", (req, res) => res.send("<h1>Hello</h1>"));
app.get("/object", (req, res) => res.send({ shortcut: true }));                 // object becomes JSON
app.get("/json", (req, res) => res.status(200).json({ ok: true, items: [1, 2] }));
app.get("/binary", (req, res) => res.send(Buffer.from("abc")));                  // Buffer becomes application/octet-stream
app.get("/empty", (req, res) => res.status(204).end());                          // success with no body
app.get("/created", (req, res) => res.status(201).location("/things/9").json({ id: 9 }));
app.get("/gone", (req, res) => res.sendStatus(410));
app.get("/typed", (req, res) => res.type("text/csv").send("id,name\n1,Ana\n"));
app.get("/custom", (req, res) => res.set({ "X-Request-Id": "abc-123", "Cache-Control": "no-store" }).json({ headers: "set" }));
> GET /text < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < plain string > GET /html < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < <h1>Hello</h1> > GET /object < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"shortcut":true} > GET /json < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"ok":true,"items":[1,2]} > GET /binary < 200 OK < content-type: application/octet-stream < abc > GET /empty < 204 No Content > GET /created < 201 Created < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < location: /things/9 < {"id":9} > GET /gone < 410 Gone < content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 < Gone > GET /typed < 200 OK < content-type: text/csv; charset=utf-8 < id,name < 1,Ana < > GET /custom < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < x-request-id: abc-123 < cache-control: no-store < {"headers":"set"}

Redirects, content negotiation, files and cookies

import express from "express";
import { writeFileSync, mkdirSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

mkdirSync("files", { recursive: true });
writeFileSync("files/report.txt", "Quarterly report\n");
const root = path.resolve("files");                                  // sendFile needs an absolute path or a root option

const app = express();
app.get("/old", (req, res) => res.redirect(301, "/new"));            // permanent
app.get("/login-success", (req, res) => res.redirect("/dashboard")); // 302 by default
app.get("/back", (req, res) => res.redirect(req.get("Referrer") ?? "/"));   // the old "back" keyword was removed in Express 5

app.get("/profile", (req, res) =>                                    // one URL, the format the client asked for
  res.format({
    "text/html": () => res.send("<h1>Ana</h1>"),
    "application/json": () => res.json({ name: "Ana" }),
    default: () => res.status(406).send("Not Acceptable"),
  }));

app.get("/report", (req, res) => res.sendFile("report.txt", { root }));
app.get("/report/download", (req, res) => res.download(path.join(root, "report.txt"), "q3-report.txt"));

app.get("/cookie", (req, res) => {
  res.cookie("theme", "dark", { httpOnly: true, sameSite: "lax", expires: new Date("2030-01-01T00:00:00Z") });
  res.send("cookie set");
});

app.get("/page/:n", (req, res) => {                                  // pagination links in a header
  const n = Number(req.params.n);
  res.links({ prev: `/page/${n - 1}`, next: `/page/${n + 1}` });
  res.json({ page: n });
});
> GET /old < 301 Moved Permanently < content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 < location: /new < Moved Permanently. Redirecting to /new > GET /login-success < 302 Found < content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 < location: /dashboard < Found. Redirecting to /dashboard > GET /back > referer: /products < 302 Found < content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 < location: /products < Found. Redirecting to /products > GET /profile > accept: application/json < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < vary: Accept < {"name":"Ana"} > GET /profile > accept: text/html < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < <h1>Ana</h1> > GET /profile > accept: image/png < 406 Not Acceptable < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < Not Acceptable > GET /report < 200 OK < content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 < Quarterly report < > GET /report/download < 200 OK < content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 < content-disposition: attachment; filename=q3-report.txt < Quarterly report < > GET /cookie < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < set-cookie: theme=dark; Path=/; Expires=Tue, 01 Jan 2030 00:00:00 GMT; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax < cookie set > GET /page/3 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < link: </page/2>; rel="prev", </page/4>; rel="next" < {"page":3}

res.locals and checking headersSent

import express from "express";
const app = express();

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.locals.requestId = "req-001";                         // visible to later middleware, handlers and templates
  res.locals.startedAt = Date.now();
  next();
});
app.get("/who", (req, res) => {
  const before = res.headersSent;                           // false: nothing has been written yet
  res.json({ id: res.locals.requestId, sentBefore: before });
  // from here on res.headersSent is true: it is too late to change the status or any header
});
> GET /who < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":"req-001","sentBefore":false}
Common response mistakes(1) res.send() or res.json() called twice. (2) Sending a body with 204 or 304 (it is dropped). (3) res.json(undefined) sends nothing useful: send null or an object. (4) Redirecting to a URL taken from user input without checking it (an open redirect, Unit 7). (5) Returning raw error objects: their messages can reveal internals.

Middleware is the heart of Express. A middleware is a function (req, res, next) that sits in the request's path. It can read or change req and res, end the request by responding, or pass it on by calling next(). Logging, parsing bodies, authentication, CORS and compression are all middleware, and even your route handlers are just the last middleware in the chain.

  • app.use(fn): runs for every request (all methods, all paths) that reaches it.
  • app.use("/api", fn): only for URLs starting with /api.
  • app.get("/x", fn1, fn2, handler): middleware only for that route; pass several functions or an array.
  • Middleware runs in the order registered. If a middleware neither responds nor calls next(), the request hangs.
  • next(err) skips to error-handling middleware (next entry). next("route") skips the remaining handlers of the current route and tries the next matching route.
import express from "express";
const app = express();

const mark = (label) => (req, res, next) => {          // a factory: returns a middleware that records its label
  (req.trace ??= []).push(label);
  next();                                              // forget this line and the request hangs forever
};

app.use(mark("1 app.use: every request"));
app.use("/api", mark("2 app.use('/api'): only /api and below"));

app.get("/api/items", mark("3 route-level middleware"), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ trace: [...req.trace, "4 handler responds"] });
});
app.get("/plain", (req, res) => res.json({ trace: req.trace }));

app.get("/user/:id", (req, res, next) => {            // next("route"): skip to the next route that matches
  if (req.params.id === "0") return next("route");
  res.send("regular user");
});
app.get("/user/:id", (req, res) => res.send("special case for id 0"));

app.use(mark("5 registered after the routes"));       // only requests that matched no route get here
app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ trace: req.trace }));
> GET /api/items < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"trace":["1 app.use: every request","2 app.use('/api'): only /api and below","3 route-level middleware","4 handler responds"]} > GET /plain < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"trace":["1 app.use: every request"]} > GET /user/7 < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < regular user > GET /user/0 < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < special case for id 0 > GET /missing < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"trace":["1 app.use: every request","5 registered after the routes"]}

Middleware you will actually write

import express from "express";
const app = express();
const accessLog = [];
let counter = 0;

// 1. request id + access log. Real code uses crypto.randomUUID() and a logger such as pino
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  req.id = req.get("x-request-id") ?? `req-${String(++counter).padStart(3, "0")}`;   // keep the caller's id if it sent one
  res.setHeader("X-Request-Id", req.id);               // clients can quote it in bug reports
  const start = process.hrtime.bigint();
  res.on("finish", () => {                             // fires after the response has been sent
    const ms = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / 1e6;
    accessLog.push(`${req.id} ${req.method} ${req.originalUrl} ${res.statusCode} ${ms < 100 ? "fast" : "slow"}`);   // log the real ms in practice
  });
  next();
});

// 2. a middleware FACTORY: configure it once per route
const sessions = { "token-ana": { name: "Ana", role: "admin" }, "token-raj": { name: "Raj", role: "viewer" } };
const requireRole = (role) => (req, res, next) => {
  const user = sessions[req.get("authorization")?.replace("Bearer ", "")];
  if (!user) return res.status(401).json({ error: "login required" });
  if (user.role !== role) return res.status(403).json({ error: `requires the ${role} role` });
  req.user = user;                                     // later handlers can rely on req.user
  next();
};

app.get("/public", (req, res) => res.send("anyone can read this"));
app.get("/admin", requireRole("admin"), (req, res) => res.json({ hello: req.user.name }));
app.get("/_log", (req, res) => res.json(accessLog));
> GET /public < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < x-request-id: req-001 < anyone can read this > GET /admin < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"login required"} > GET /admin > authorization: Bearer token-raj < 403 Forbidden < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"requires the admin role"} > GET /admin > authorization: Bearer token-ana < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"hello":"Ana"} > GET /public > x-request-id: from-the-client < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < x-request-id: from-the-client < anyone can read this > GET /_log < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < ["req-001 GET /public 200 fast","req-002 GET /admin 401 fast","req-003 GET /admin 403 fast","req-004 GET /admin 200 fast","from-the-client GET /public 200 fast"]
MiddlewareWhat it doesCovered in
express.json(), express.urlencoded(), express.text(), express.raw()Parse request bodies (built in)next entry
express.static(dir)Serve files (built in)Static files
express.Router()Modular routes (built in)Routing
corsCross-origin permissionsUnit 7
helmetSecurity headersUnit 7
express-rate-limitThrottle abusive clientsUnit 7
cookie-parser, express-sessionCookies and server sessionsUnit 7
morgan, pino-httpHTTP request loggingUnit 10
compressiongzip/brotli responsesUnit 10
multerFile uploads (multipart)Unit 5
passportAuthentication strategiesUnit 7
Order is behaviourPut helmet, cors, the logger and body parsers before your routes and the error handler after them. A parser registered after the route that needs req.body does nothing for it. Each middleware also costs time on every request: keep them cheap.

Node delivers a request body as a raw stream. Express's body parsers read the stream, turn it into a value and store it in req.body. Which parser runs depends on the request's Content-Type:

ParserHandlesreq.body becomes
express.json()application/jsonObject or array
express.urlencoded({ extended: false })application/x-www-form-urlencoded (HTML forms)Object of strings. extended: true allows nested a[b]=1.
express.text()text/plainString
express.raw()application/octet-stream (or your type)Buffer (needed to verify webhook signatures)
multer (separate package)multipart/form-data (file uploads)Unit 5
 
import express from "express";
const app = express();

app.post("/none", (req, res) => res.json({ body: req.body ?? "undefined" }));            // no parser installed
app.post("/json", express.json(), (req, res) => res.json({ body: req.body ?? "undefined" }));   // a parser used on one route
app.post("/small", express.json({ limit: "20b" }), (req, res) => res.json({ ok: true }));       // custom size limit
app.post("/form", express.urlencoded({ extended: false }), (req, res) => res.json(req.body));
app.post("/form-extended", express.urlencoded({ extended: true }), (req, res) => res.json(req.body));
app.post("/text", express.text(), (req, res) => res.json({ length: req.body.length, body: req.body }));
app.post("/raw", express.raw({ type: "application/octet-stream" }), (req, res) => res.json({ isBuffer: Buffer.isBuffer(req.body), bytes: req.body.length }));

// a JSON error handler so the failures below are readable (the next entry explains error handlers)
app.use((err, req, res, next) => res.status(err.status ?? 500).json({ error: err.type ?? "error", message: err.message }));
> POST /none {"a":1} < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"body":"undefined"} > POST /json {"name":"Ana","tags":["a","b"]} < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"body":{"name":"Ana","tags":["a","b"]}} > POST /json {"a":1} > content-type: text/plain < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"body":"undefined"} > POST /json {broken json > content-type: application/json < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"entity.parse.failed","message":"Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2)"} > POST /json "just a string" > content-type: application/json < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"entity.parse.failed","message":"Unexpected token '\"', \"\"just a string\"\" is not valid JSON"} > POST /small {"message":"this body is longer than twenty bytes"} < 413 Payload Too Large < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"entity.too.large","message":"request entity too large"} > POST /form name=Ana&langs[]=js&langs[]=py > content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"name":"Ana","langs[]":["js","py"]} > POST /form-extended name=Ana&langs[]=js&langs[]=py&addr[city]=Pune > content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"name":"Ana","langs":["js","py"],"addr":{"city":"Pune"}} > POST /text plain words > content-type: text/plain < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"length":11,"body":"plain words"} > POST /raw binary-ish > content-type: application/octet-stream < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"isBuffer":true,"bytes":10}
  • In Express 5 req.body is undefined when no parser ran or the content type did not match (Express 4 gave {}). Always check before reading properties, and validate the shape (Unit 5).
  • Install the parsers globally with app.use(express.json()) for an API, or per route as above. The default size limit is 100 kB; raise it only where you need to ({ limit: "5mb" }), because large JSON bodies cost memory and CPU.
  • Parser errors carry status and type: entity.parse.failed (400), entity.too.large (413), charset.unsupported (415).
  • Behind an HTTP client that sends the wrong header you get "empty body" bugs: check Content-Type first (curl -H "Content-Type: application/json").

Things go wrong: bad input, missing records, a database that is down, a bug. A good API turns each into the right status and a useful, safe message, logs the details for you, and never leaks internals to the client.

  • Synchronous throw inside a handler or middleware is caught by Express and forwarded to the error handler.
  • Express 5: a rejected promise (any async handler that throws or awaits something that rejects) is also forwarded automatically. In Express 4 you needed try/catch + next(err) or a wrapper library in every async handler.
  • An error-handling middleware has four parameters (err, req, res, next) (Express recognises it by the count) and is registered after all routes.
  • You can also pass errors yourself: next(err).
import express from "express";
const app = express();
const serverLog = [];                                        // stands in for your logger

// Errors you expect have a status and a message that is safe to show
class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(status, message, details) { super(message); this.status = status; this.details = details; }
}
const notFound = (what) => new HttpError(404, `${what} not found`);

const items = new Map([[1, { id: 1, name: "Keyboard" }]]);

app.get("/ok", (req, res) => res.json({ ok: true }));
app.get("/items/:id", async (req, res) => {                 // async handler: a throw becomes a rejection, Express 5 forwards it
  const item = items.get(Number(req.params.id));
  if (!item) throw notFound("Item");
  res.json(item);
});
app.get("/bad-input", (req, res) => { throw new HttpError(400, "Validation failed", [{ field: "email", problem: "must be an email address" }]); });
app.get("/bug", async () => { const user = undefined; return user.name; });     // a programmer error: TypeError
app.get("/manual", (req, res, next) => next(new HttpError(409, "Already exists")));   // passing an error yourself

// 404 for everything that matched no route: a normal middleware placed after the routes
app.use((req, res, next) => next(new HttpError(404, `Cannot ${req.method} ${req.path}`)));

// The error handler: four parameters, registered last
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  if (res.headersSent) return next(err);                    // the response already started: let Express close the connection
  const expected = err instanceof HttpError || err.status < 500;   // body-parser errors carry a status too
  if (!expected) serverLog.push(`${req.method} ${req.path}: ${err.stack.split("\n")[0]}`);   // log bugs with full details, privately
  res.status(expected ? err.status ?? 400 : 500).json({
    error: { message: expected ? err.message : "Something went wrong on our side", details: err.details },   // never send err.message of a bug
  });
});
> GET /ok < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"ok":true} > GET /items/1 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"name":"Keyboard"} > GET /items/99 < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":{"message":"Item not found"}} > GET /bad-input < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":{"message":"Validation failed","details":[{"field":"email","problem":"must be an email address"}]}} > GET /manual < 409 Conflict < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":{"message":"Already exists"}} > GET /bug < 500 Internal Server Error < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":{"message":"Something went wrong on our side"}} > GET /no/such/route < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":{"message":"Cannot GET /no/such/route"}} server log (only the bug was logged): [ "GET /bug: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')" ]
Default handlerIf you register no error middleware, Express answers errors with an HTML page. In development (NODE_ENV unset) that page contains the stack trace, in production just the status text. Either way the stack goes to stderr. Always set NODE_ENV=production when deploying, and write your own handler so API clients always get JSON.

What Express cannot catch

Express only catches errors raised while a handler is running or returned as a promise. An error thrown later, from a timer or an event callback that no promise is waiting on, escapes to the process level and crashes the server:

import express from "express";
const app = express();

app.get("/crash", (req, res) => {
  setTimeout(() => { throw new Error("thrown inside a timer callback"); }, 0);   // runs later, outside Express
  res.send("responded fine");
});
app.use((err, req, res, next) => res.status(500).json({ error: "never reached for the timer error" }));
file:///app/app.mjs:6 setTimeout(() => { throw new Error("thrown inside a timer callback"); }, 0); // runs later, outside Express ^ Error: thrown inside a timer callback at Timeout._onTimeout (file:///app/app.mjs:6:28) Node.js v22.22.0 [process exited with code 1]
  • Wrap callback-style APIs in promises (util.promisify) and await them in the handler.
  • Add an error listener to every emitter and stream you create.
  • As a last line of defence log in process.on("uncaughtException") and ("unhandledRejection") then exit; a process manager restarts you (Unit 3, Unit 10). Do not keep running after one.
Error response checklistRight status code. A stable machine-readable shape ({ error: { code, message, details } }, Unit 5). A request id so you can find the log line. No stack traces, SQL, file paths, or "user does not exist" versus "wrong password" differences on login. Log 5xx at error level, 4xx at info or warn.

express.static(folder) serves the files in a folder as-is (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, a built React app). It sets Content-Type, ETag, Last-Modified and Cache-Control, supports conditional and range requests, and refuses to leave the folder.

import express from "express";
import http from "node:http";
import path from "node:path";
import { mkdirSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

mkdirSync("public/css", { recursive: true });
writeFileSync("public/index.html", "<h1>Home</h1>");
writeFileSync("public/about.html", "<h1>About</h1>");
writeFileSync("public/css/site.css", "body { margin: 0 }");
writeFileSync("public/.env", "SECRET=do-not-serve-me");

const publicDir = path.resolve("public");                       // relative paths depend on where node was started: use an absolute one
const app = express();
app.use(express.static(publicDir, {
  maxAge: "1d",                                                  // Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400
  extensions: ["html"],                                          // /about also serves about.html
  // dotfiles: "ignore" is the default: .env is never served
}));
app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).send("no such file"));
> GET / < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < <h1>Home</h1> > GET /about < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < <h1>About</h1> > GET /css/site.css < 200 OK < content-type: text/css; charset=utf-8 < cache-control: public, max-age=86400 < content-length: 18 < body { margin: 0 } > GET /.env < 404 Not Found < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < no such file > GET /nothing.png < 404 Not Found < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < no such file If-None-Match sent back -> 304 same, plus Cache-Control: no-cache -> 200
  • Caching strategy. Files with a hash in the name (app.3f9a1c.js, what Vite and webpack produce) can be cached for a year with immutable; index.html should be revalidated so users get new releases. A common split: maxAge: "1y", immutable: true for the assets folder and no max-age for HTML.
  • 304 and hard refresh. A normal reload sends the stored ETag back as If-None-Match and gets an empty 304. A hard refresh also sends Cache-Control: no-cache, which forces a full 200. Node's own fetch adds that header itself whenever you pass a conditional header, so use curl or node:http to observe 304s.
  • Mount path. app.use("/assets", express.static(dir)) serves dir/logo.png at /assets/logo.png.
  • Other options: index (default file), fallthrough (false answers 404 itself), redirect (add a slash for directories), setHeaders(res, file) for custom headers, etag, lastModified.
  • In production put a CDN or nginx in front for static files: they are faster and take load off Node (Unit 10).

Single-page apps (React, Vue, Angular)

A single-page app handles URLs like /dashboard/settings in the browser. When someone opens or refreshes that URL the server must return index.html instead of a 404. Register the API first, then the static files, then a catch-all:

import express from "express";
import path from "node:path";
import { mkdirSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

mkdirSync("dist", { recursive: true });
writeFileSync("dist/index.html", "<div id='root'></div><script src='/app.js'></script>");
writeFileSync("dist/app.js", "console.log('client app')");
const dist = path.resolve("dist");

const app = express();
app.get("/api/health", (req, res) => res.json({ status: "up" }));
app.all("/api/{*splat}", (req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: "unknown API route" }));   // API typos must not return HTML
app.use(express.static(dist));
app.get("/{*splat}", (req, res) => res.sendFile("index.html", { root: dist }));                 // everything else: the client router decides
> GET /api/health < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"status":"up"} > GET /api/nope < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"unknown API route"} > GET /app.js < 200 OK < content-type: text/javascript; charset=utf-8 < console.log('client app') > GET /dashboard/settings < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < <div id='root'></div><script src='/app.js'></script>

An API returns JSON and lets a front-end app draw the page. A server-rendered site returns finished HTML. Express renders HTML with a view engine (EJS, Pug, Handlebars, Nunjucks): you write a template with placeholders, call res.render("name", data), and the engine fills it in. Server rendering is great for content sites, admin pages, e-mails and anything that needs fast first paint and good SEO, with no client-side framework.

EJS tagMeaning
<%= value %>Output the value HTML-escaped (safe default)
<%- value %>Output raw HTML (only for markup you trust)
<% code %>Run JavaScript (loops, conditions), prints nothing
<%- include("partials/header") %>Insert another template (shared header, footer, layout)
 
import express from "express";
import path from "node:path";
import { mkdirSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

mkdirSync("views/partials", { recursive: true });
writeFileSync("views/partials/header.ejs", `<header>My Shop - <%= title %></header>\n`);
writeFileSync("views/products.ejs", [
  `<%- include("partials/header") %>`,
  `<h1><%= title %></h1>`,
  `<% if (products.length === 0) { %><p>Nothing here yet.</p><% } else { %>`,
  `<ul>`,
  `<% for (const p of products) { %>  <li><%= p.name %> - $<%= p.price.toFixed(2) %></li>`,
  `<% } %></ul>`,
  `<% } %>`,
  `<p>Safe: <%= note %></p>`,
  `<p>Raw:  <%- note %></p>`,
].join("\n"));

const app = express();
app.set("view engine", "ejs");                                // so res.render("products") finds products.ejs
app.set("views", path.resolve("views"));                      // folder of templates (default: ./views)

app.get("/products", (req, res) => {
  res.render("products", {
    title: "Catalogue",
    products: [{ name: "Keyboard", price: 49.5 }, { name: "Mouse <wireless>", price: 19 }],
    note: "<script>alert('xss')</script>",                    // user-supplied text must never become markup
  });
});
app.get("/empty", (req, res) => res.render("products", { title: "Empty", products: [], note: "-" }));
> GET /products < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < <header>My Shop - Catalogue</header> < < <h1>Catalogue</h1> < < <ul> < <li>Keyboard - $49.50</li> < <li>Mouse &lt;wireless&gt; - $19.00</li> < </ul> < < <p>Safe: &lt;script&gt;alert(&#39;xss&#39;)&lt;/script&gt;</p> < <p>Raw: <script>alert('xss')</script></p> > GET /empty < 200 OK < content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 < <header>My Shop - Empty</header> < < <h1>Empty</h1> < <p>Nothing here yet.</p> < <p>Safe: -</p> < <p>Raw: -</p>
Cross-site scripting (XSS)The escaped line turned <script> into harmless &lt;script&gt; text; the raw line would have run the attacker's script in every visitor's browser. Use <%= %> by default and reserve <%- %> for HTML you generated. Unit 7 covers XSS and Content-Security-Policy in depth.
  • res.render(view, data, callback); res.locals and app.locals are merged into every template's data (handy for the current user or the site name).
  • Set app.set("view cache", true) in production (it is on automatically when NODE_ENV=production).
  • Install an engine with npm install ejs (Pug: pug, Handlebars: hbs, Nunjucks: nunjucks); Express loads it by the file extension.
  • Forms: <form method="post" action="/login"> posts urlencoded data (use express.urlencoded), and the usual pattern is Post / Redirect / Get: handle the POST, then res.redirect(303, "/thanks") so a refresh does not resubmit.

Express does not impose a structure, so every project invents one, and a messy one is the main reason Express apps become hard to change. The pattern that scales is simple: separate the concerns and let each layer know only about the one below it.

LayerResponsibilityKnows aboutNever contains
Routes / controllersHTTP: read req, call the service, send res, choose status codesExpress, the serviceBusiness rules, SQL
ServiceBusiness rules: what is allowed, validation of meaning, orchestration of several repositoriesThe repositories, domain errorsreq/res, SQL
RepositoryData access: queries, mapping rows to objectsThe database driverHTTP, business decisions
Composition root (server.js)Reads configuration, creates the pieces, wires them together, starts listening, handles shutdownEverythingAnything else
 
notes-api/
├── src/
│   ├── server.js            composition root: config, wiring, listen, shutdown
│   ├── app.js               createApp({ services }): middleware, routers, error handling (no listen!)
│   ├── config.js            read and validate environment variables once
│   ├── errors.js            HttpError and friends
│   ├── middleware/          auth.js, request-id.js, error-handler.js
│   └── notes/               one folder per feature
│       ├── notes.routes.js
│       ├── notes.service.js
│       ├── notes.repository.js
│       └── notes.schemas.js
├── test/                    notes.test.js ...
├── .env.example
└── package.json

The key trick is splitting app.js (builds the app from the pieces it is given, never calls listen) from server.js (decides the real pieces and opens the port). Tests then build the app with a fake repository and send requests without a network port (Unit 9). Here is a small but complete example, one file at a time:

// Errors the app raises on purpose. The error handler turns them into HTTP responses.
export class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(status, message, details) {
    super(message);
    this.status = status;
    this.details = details;
  }
}
export const badRequest = (message, details) => new HttpError(400, message, details);
export const notFound = (what) => new HttpError(404, `${what} not found`);
export const conflict = (message) => new HttpError(409, message);
// Data access only: knows how notes are stored, knows nothing about HTTP or business rules.
// This version keeps them in memory. A Postgres version would expose the same functions.
export function createNotesRepository() {
  const rows = new Map();
  let nextId = 1;

  return {
    async list() {
      return [...rows.values()];
    },
    async get(id) {
      return rows.get(id) ?? null;
    },
    async findByTitle(title) {
      return [...rows.values()].find((n) => n.title.toLowerCase() === title.toLowerCase()) ?? null;
    },
    async create({ title }) {
      const note = { id: nextId++, title, done: false };
      rows.set(note.id, note);
      return note;
    },
    async update(id, patch) {
      const note = rows.get(id);
      if (!note) return null;
      Object.assign(note, patch);
      return note;
    },
    async remove(id) {
      return rows.delete(id);
    },
  };
}
import { badRequest, conflict, notFound } from "./errors.js";

// Business rules only: what is allowed and what it means. No req, no res, no SQL.
export function createNotesService(repo) {
  return {
    list: () => repo.list(),

    async get(id) {
      const note = await repo.get(id);
      if (!note) throw notFound("Note");
      return note;
    },

    async create(input) {
      const title = typeof input?.title === "string" ? input.title.trim() : "";
      if (!title) throw badRequest("title is required");
      if (title.length > 40) throw badRequest("title must be at most 40 characters");
      if (await repo.findByTitle(title)) throw conflict("a note with this title already exists");
      return repo.create({ title });
    },

    async setDone(id, done) {
      if (typeof done !== "boolean") throw badRequest("done must be true or false");
      const note = await repo.update(id, { done });
      if (!note) throw notFound("Note");
      return note;
    },

    async remove(id) {
      if (!(await repo.remove(id))) throw notFound("Note");
    },
  };
}
import express from "express";
import { badRequest } from "./errors.js";

// HTTP only: translate requests into service calls and results into responses.
export function createNotesRouter(notesService) {
  const router = express.Router();

  router.param("id", (req, res, next, value) => {
    const id = Number(value);
    if (!Number.isInteger(id) || id < 1) return next(badRequest("id must be a positive integer"));
    req.noteId = id;
    next();
  });

  router.get("/", async (req, res) => {
    res.json(await notesService.list());
  });

  router.post("/", async (req, res) => {
    const note = await notesService.create(req.body);
    res.status(201).location(`/notes/${note.id}`).json(note);
  });

  router.get("/:id", async (req, res) => {
    res.json(await notesService.get(req.noteId));
  });

  router.patch("/:id", async (req, res) => {
    res.json(await notesService.setDone(req.noteId, req.body?.done));
  });

  router.delete("/:id", async (req, res) => {
    await notesService.remove(req.noteId);
    res.status(204).end();
  });

  return router;
}
import express from "express";
import { createNotesRouter } from "./notes.routes.js";
import { HttpError, notFound } from "./errors.js";

// Builds the app from the pieces it is given. It never calls listen(), so tests can use it without opening a port.
export function createApp({ notesService }) {
  const app = express();
  app.disable("x-powered-by");
  app.use(express.json({ limit: "100kb" }));

  app.get("/health", (req, res) => res.json({ status: "ok" }));
  app.use("/notes", createNotesRouter(notesService));

  app.use((req, res, next) => next(notFound(`Route ${req.method} ${req.path}`)));

  app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
    if (res.headersSent) return next(err);
    const expected = err instanceof HttpError || (err.status >= 400 && err.status < 500);
    if (!expected) console.error(err);
    res.status(expected ? err.status : 500).json({
      error: { message: expected ? err.message : "Internal server error", details: err.details },
    });
  });

  return app;
}
import { createApp } from "./app.js";
import { createNotesRepository } from "./notes.repository.js";
import { createNotesService } from "./notes.service.js";

// The composition root: the only place that decides which concrete pieces are used.
const notesRepository = createNotesRepository();
const notesService = createNotesService(notesRepository);
const app = createApp({ notesService });

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const server = app.listen(port, () => console.log(`Notes API listening on http://localhost:${port}`));

process.on("SIGTERM", () => server.close(() => process.exit(0)));
