Why the effort pays off: swapping a layer

Because the service receives its repository as an argument (dependency injection), you can give it a different one without touching the service. A database in production, an in-memory fake in tests, a failing one to test error handling:

// a copy of the service's idea, reduced: it depends on "something with get()", not on any particular database
function createGreeter(userRepo) {
  return {
    async greet(id) {
      const user = await userRepo.get(id);
      if (!user) throw new Error(`user ${id} not found`);
      return `Hello, ${user.name}!`;
    },
  };
}

const inMemory = { get: async (id) => ({ 1: { name: "Ana" } })[id] ?? null };           // for tests
const broken = { get: async () => { throw new Error("database is down"); } };            // to test failure handling
// const postgres = { get: (id) => pool.query("select * from users where id = $1", [id]).then((r) => r.rows[0]) };   // for production

console.log(await createGreeter(inMemory).greet(1));
for (const [label, repo] of [["missing user", inMemory], ["database down", broken]]) {
  try { await createGreeter(repo).greet(2); } catch (error) { console.log(`${label}: ${error.message}`); }
}
Hello, Ana! missing user: user 2 not found database down: database is down
  • Feature folders (notes/, users/, billing/) beat technical folders (controllers/, models/) once the app has more than a handful of routes: everything that changes together lives together.
  • Thin controllers, fat services. If a route handler is longer than about 15 lines, logic probably belongs in a service.
  • No globals and no circular imports. Pass dependencies in; if two modules import each other, extract the shared part.
  • One place for configuration (config.js): read process.env once at start-up, validate it, and export a frozen object. Unit 10 builds this.
  • You do not need every layer for a tiny app. Start with routes plus a service, add a repository when you add a database, and split into features as it grows.

TypeScript catches a whole class of mistakes (req.params.id is a string, a missing field in a response, a typo in req.query) while you type. Install the types for libraries that ship without them: npm i -D typescript @types/node @types/express. Types are erased, so they do not validate real requests (use a runtime validator, Unit 5).

RequestHandler<Params, ResBody, ReqBody, Query> describes everything about a handler: the route parameters, the response body, the request body and the query string.

// Shapes shared by the whole app. They exist only for the compiler: Node erases them before running.
export interface Note {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  done: boolean;
}

export interface CreateNoteBody {
  title: string;
}

export interface ErrorBody {
  error: { message: string };
}

// Teach TypeScript about the extra property our auth middleware adds to every request
declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request {
      requestId?: string;
    }
  }
}
import express from "express";
import type { ErrorRequestHandler, RequestHandler } from "express";
import type { CreateNoteBody, ErrorBody, Note } from "./types.ts";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const notes: Note[] = [{ id: 1, title: "Learn Express", done: false }];

// RequestHandler<Params, ResponseBody, RequestBody, Query>: the four type arguments describe what goes in and out
const listNotes: RequestHandler<{}, Note[], undefined, { done?: string }> = (req, res) => {
  const onlyDone = req.query.done === "true";
  res.json(onlyDone ? notes.filter((n) => n.done) : notes);
};

const getNote: RequestHandler<{ id: string }, Note | ErrorBody> = (req, res) => {
  const note = notes.find((n) => n.id === Number(req.params.id));   // req.params.id is a string: the compiler reminds us to convert
  if (!note) {
    res.status(404).json({ error: { message: "Note not found" } });
    return;
  }
  res.json(note);
};

const createNote: RequestHandler<{}, Note | ErrorBody, CreateNoteBody> = (req, res) => {
  const title = req.body?.title;                                     // the body type is a promise from us, not a check: validate at runtime
  if (typeof title !== "string" || title.trim() === "") {
    res.status(400).json({ error: { message: "title is required" } });
    return;
  }
  const note: Note = { id: notes.length + 1, title: title.trim(), done: false };
  notes.push(note);
  res.status(201).json(note);
};

app.get("/notes", listNotes);
app.get("/notes/:id", getNote);
app.post("/notes", createNote);

const onError: ErrorRequestHandler = (err, req, res, _next) => {
  res.status(500).json({ error: { message: "Something went wrong" } } satisfies ErrorBody);
};
app.use(onError);

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
app.listen(port, () => console.log(`Typed Express app on http://localhost:${port}`));
{

    "target": "es2023",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "types": ["node"]
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

[{"id":1,"title":"Learn Express","done":false}]
$ curl -X POST localhost:3000/notes -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Ship it"}'
{"id":2,"title":"Ship it","done":false}

{"error":{"message":"title is required"}}

The compiler is a second pair of eyes. This file has three typical mistakes:

import express from "express";
import type { RequestHandler } from "express";
import type { Note } from "./types.ts";

const app = express();

// Mistake 1: params are strings, not numbers
const byId: RequestHandler<{ id: string }, Note> = (req, res) => {
  const id: number = req.params.id;
  res.json({ id, title: "x", done: false });
};

// Mistake 2: the response shape does not match the declared type
const wrong: RequestHandler<{}, Note> = (req, res) => {
  res.json({ id: 1, title: "x" });
};

// Mistake 3: a typo in a property name
app.get("/typo", (req, res) => {
  res.send(req.querry);
});
$ npx tsc --noEmit
src/mistakes.ts(9,9): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
src/mistakes.ts(15,12): error TS2741: Property 'done' is missing in type '{ id: number; title: string; }' but required in type 'Note'.
src/mistakes.ts(20,16): error TS2551: Property 'querry' does not exist on type 'Request<{}, any, any, ParsedQs, Record<string, any>>'. Did you mean 'query'?
TaskHow
Run during developmentnode --watch src/server.ts (Node 22.18+ strips types), or npx tsx watch src/server.ts for full TypeScript syntax
Check types (CI and editor)npx tsc --noEmit
Production buildCompile with tsc (set outDir, remove noEmit) or a bundler such as tsup/esbuild, then run the JavaScript in dist/ with node dist/server.js
Add a property to reqDeclaration merging: declare global { namespace Express { interface Request { user?: User } } } as in types.ts
Type the error handlerErrorRequestHandler
Shared request/response typesInfer types from your validation schemas (z.infer<typeof schema>) so the type and the runtime check can never disagree (Unit 5)

app.set(name, value) and app.get(name) store settings; app.enable/disable are shortcuts for booleans.

SettingDefaultMeaning
envprocess.env.NODE_ENV or "development"Drives error pages and view caching. Set NODE_ENV=production in production.
x-powered-bytrueAdds X-Powered-By: Express. Disable it: it advertises your stack to attackers.
etag"weak"ETag generation for res.send/json (enables 304 responses). false turns off.
json spacesnoneIndentation for res.json (pretty-print in development only).
query parser"simple""extended", false or a custom function.
trust proxyfalseHow many proxy hops to believe (earlier entry).
case sensitive routing, strict routingfalseWhether /A differs from /a, and /a/ from /a.
views, view engine, view cache./views, none, on in productionTemplates (earlier entry).
subdomain offset2For req.subdomains.
 
import express from "express";
const app = express();
console.log("defaults:", { env: app.get("env"), poweredBy: app.get("x-powered-by"), etag: app.get("etag"), query: app.get("query parser"), trustProxy: app.get("trust proxy"), jsonSpaces: app.get("json spaces") ?? null });

app.locals.siteName = "Notebox";                         // data shared by the whole app (and its templates)
app.get("/info", (req, res) => res.json({ site: req.app.locals.siteName, items: [1, 2] }));

const admin = express();                                 // a whole app can be mounted inside another one
admin.on("mount", (parent) => console.log("admin mounted at", admin.mountpath, "inside an app that has locals:", Boolean(parent.locals.siteName)));
admin.get("/", (req, res) => res.send(`admin home (mountpath ${admin.mountpath})`));
app.use("/admin", admin);

listen, http.createServer and a graceful shutdown

app.listen(...) is shorthand for http.createServer(app).listen(...) and returns the Node http.Server, which you need for shutdown, timeouts and WebSockets (Unit 8). To serve HTTPS yourself use https.createServer({ key, cert }, app), though normally a proxy or load balancer terminates TLS.

When a deploy or an orchestrator stops your process it sends SIGTERM. A graceful shutdown stops accepting new connections, lets requests already running finish, closes the database, and then exits. Without it every deploy drops live requests.

import express from "express";
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

const app = express();
app.get("/slow", async (req, res) => { await sleep(150); res.send("slow request finished"); });
const server = app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await new Promise((resolve) => server.once("listening", resolve));

let shuttingDown = false;
app.use((req, res, next) => {                            // while draining, tell clients to use another connection
  if (shuttingDown) res.set("Connection", "close");
  next();
});

function shutdown(signal) {
  if (shuttingDown) return;
  shuttingDown = true;
  console.log(`${signal}: no new connections, waiting for running requests`);
  server.close(async () => {                             // called when the last connection has ended
    console.log("server closed");                        // here: await pool.end(), await redis.quit(), flush logs
    clearTimeout(forceExit);
  });
  server.closeIdleConnections();                         // idle keep-alive sockets would otherwise block close()
  const forceExit = setTimeout(() => { console.error("forced exit after timeout"); process.exit(1); }, 10_000);   // never wait forever
  forceExit.unref();
}
process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM"));
SIGTERM: no new connections, waiting for running requests the running request still got its answer: slow request finished server closed

Most blog posts and Stack Overflow answers still show Express 4. Express 5 is the default from npm install express, needs Node 18+, and keeps the same style. These are the differences you will actually hit. Each row was run in this guide's lab (the entry that shows it is named).

AreaExpress 4Express 5
Async handler errorsNeeded try/catch + next(err) or a wrapperRejections and throws are forwarded to the error handler (Error Handling)
Wildcards/files/*/files/*splat, and /{*splat} to include the root (Routing)
Optional parts/:id?{/:id} (Routing)
Regex in a path/:id(\d+), /[a|b]Not allowed in strings: validate in the handler, or pass a RegExp or an array of paths
req.body without a parser{}undefined (Body Parsing)
req.queryWritable; extended parser by default (nested objects)Read-only getter; simple parser by default (Request)
express.urlencoded()extended: true by defaultextended: false by default (Body Parsing)
app.listen errorsUnhandled error eventPassed to the callback (Your First Server)
req.hostWithout the portWith the port (req.hostname is without)
req.paramsUnmatched optional params were undefined/""Omitted; wildcard values are arrays; prototype-less object
res.status(n)AnythingThrows unless an integer 100 to 999
res.clearCookieHonoured maxAge/expiresIgnores them (always expires the cookie)
express.static dotfilesServed unless hidden"ignore" by default: /.well-known returns 404 unless you allow it
MIME typesapplication/javascripttext/javascript (from newer mime-db)
Debug namespaceDEBUG=express:routerDEBUG=router,router:*
 
import express from "express";

const removed = {
  "app.del()  -> app.delete()": typeof express.application.del,
  "req.param(name)  -> req.params/query/body": typeof express.request.param,
  "res.sendfile()  -> res.sendFile()": typeof express.response.sendfile,
  "req.acceptsCharset()  -> acceptsCharsets()": typeof express.request.acceptsCharset,
};
for (const [name, type] of Object.entries(removed)) console.log(name.padEnd(46), type === "undefined" ? "gone" : type);
console.log("req.acceptsCharsets()".padEnd(46), typeof express.request.acceptsCharsets, "(the plural name is the new one)");
app.del() -> app.delete() gone req.param(name) -> req.params/query/body gone res.sendfile() -> res.sendFile() gone req.acceptsCharset() -> acceptsCharsets() gone req.acceptsCharsets() function (the plural name is the new one)

Argument orders and number handling changed for the response helpers. The old forms do not error cleanly, they quietly do something else, which is why they need a hunt through your code:

import express from "express";
const app = express();

app.get("/json-with-status", (req, res) => res.json(201, { created: true }));      // Express 4: status first, body second
app.get("/send-number", (req, res) => res.send(404));                                // Express 4: a number meant "status"
app.get("/redirect-old-order", (req, res) => res.redirect("/target", 301));          // Express 4: (url, status)
app.get("/redirect-back", (req, res) => res.redirect("back"));                       // Express 4: the "back" keyword
app.get("/status-as-string", (req, res) => res.status("404").send("x"));
app.use((err, req, res, next) => res.status(500).json({ error: err.message }));
> GET /json-with-status < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < 201 > GET /send-number < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < 404 > GET /redirect-old-order < 500 Internal Server Error < content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"Invalid status code: \"/target\". Status code must be an integer."} > GET /redirect-back < 302 Found < content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 < location: back < Found. Redirecting to back > GET /status-as-string < 500 Internal Server Error < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"Invalid status code: \"404\". Status code must be an integer."} --- the Express 5 spellings: res.status(201).json(body), res.sendStatus(404), res.redirect(301, url), res.redirect(req.get('Referrer') ?? '/') [stderr] Fri, 23 Oct 2026 09:30:00 GMT express deprecated Url must be a string at file:///app/app.mjs:7:50 Fri, 23 Oct 2026 09:30:00 GMT express deprecated Status must be a number at file:///app/app.mjs:7:50
Migrating an app(1) Upgrade to Node 18+ and run your tests on Express 4's latest. (2) npm install express@5. (3) Search your code for the removed methods above and for every route path containing *, ? or (. (4) Remove your try/catch + next(err) boilerplate and any async-wrapper library. (5) Check anything that relied on req.body being {}, on the extended query parser, or on req.host without a port. The official guide at expressjs.com/en/guide/migrating-5.html lists everything, and it documents a codemod recipe, npx codemod@latest @expressjs/v5-migration-recipe, that rewrites many of the mechanical changes (not run in this guide's lab).
05

Unit 5: REST API Engineering

Designing an API other people can use without reading your code: resources and verbs, validation, error format, pagination and filtering, file uploads, caching, concurrency, idempotency and documentation. Every pattern is built and exercised with real requests.

REST is a style for web APIs: you expose resources (things: books, orders, users) at URLs, and clients use the standard HTTP methods to act on them. If you follow the conventions, a developer can guess your API. Most "REST APIs" really mean "JSON over HTTP with sensible URLs", and that is the target.

URLs name things, methods say what to do

DoDon't
GET /books, GET /books/42GET /getBooks, /getBookById?id=42
POST /books (create)POST /createBook
DELETE /books/42GET /books/42/delete (GET must never change data)
Plural nouns, lower case, hyphens: /order-itemsVerbs, camelCase or underscores in paths, trailing file extensions
Nesting for ownership, one or two levels: /authors/7/booksDeep chains: /a/1/b/2/c/3/d/4. Use /books/9 once you know the id.
Filters in the query string: /books?author=7&year=1965Filters in the path

What each method promises

MethodUseSafe (no changes)Idempotent (repeat = same result)Typical success
GETReadYesYes200
HEADHeaders onlyYesYes200
POSTCreate in a collection; trigger an actionNoNo201 + Location (or 200/202)
PUTReplace the whole resourceNoYes200 or 204
PATCHPartially updateNoUsually, if written as "set these fields"200 (with the new resource) or 204
DELETERemoveNoYes204 (a repeat may be 404; both are fine)

Idempotent matters because networks fail: a client that did not get an answer wants to retry. Retrying a PUT or DELETE is harmless; retrying a POST can create a duplicate (the Idempotency-Key pattern later in this unit fixes that).

import express from "express";
const app = express();
app.disable("x-powered-by");

const books = new Map([[1, { id: 1, title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965 }]]);
let nextId = 2;

// bodies must be JSON: say so clearly instead of failing mysteriously
app.use((req, res, next) => (["POST", "PUT", "PATCH"].includes(req.method) && !req.is("application/json")
  ? res.status(415).json({ error: "Content-Type must be application/json" }) : next()));
app.use(express.json());

function problems(body, { partial = false } = {}) {                 // tiny hand-written validation (the next entry uses Zod)
  const errors = [];
  const need = (ok, msg, key) => { if (!partial || key in (body ?? {})) if (!ok) errors.push(msg); };
  need(typeof body?.title === "string" && body.title.trim() !== "", "title must be a non-empty string", "title");
  need(typeof body?.author === "string" && body.author.trim() !== "", "author must be a non-empty string", "author");
  need(Number.isInteger(body?.year), "year must be an integer", "year");
  return errors;
}
const pick = ({ title, author, year }) => ({ title: title?.trim(), author: author?.trim(), year });
const find = (req, res) => {
  const book = books.get(Number(req.params.id));
  if (!book) res.status(404).json({ error: "book not found" });
  return book;
};

app.get("/v1/books", (req, res) => res.json({ data: [...books.values()] }));
app.get("/v1/books/:id", (req, res) => { const b = find(req, res); if (b) res.json(b); });

app.post("/v1/books", (req, res) => {
  const errors = problems(req.body);
  if (errors.length) return res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid book", details: errors });
  const book = { id: nextId++, ...pick(req.body) };
  books.set(book.id, book);
  res.status(201).location(`/v1/books/${book.id}`).json(book);        // 201 + where the new resource lives
});

app.put("/v1/books/:id", (req, res) => {                              // REPLACE: every field is required
  const old = find(req, res); if (!old) return;
  const errors = problems(req.body);
  if (errors.length) return res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid book", details: errors });
  const book = { id: old.id, ...pick(req.body) };
  books.set(book.id, book);
  res.json(book);
});

app.patch("/v1/books/:id", (req, res) => {                            // UPDATE: only the fields that were sent
  const old = find(req, res); if (!old) return;
  const errors = problems(req.body, { partial: true });
  if (errors.length) return res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid book", details: errors });
  const changes = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(pick(req.body)).filter(([k]) => k in req.body));   // ignore fields we do not know
  const book = Object.assign(old, changes);
  res.json(book);
});

app.delete("/v1/books/:id", (req, res) => { const b = find(req, res); if (b) { books.delete(b.id); res.status(204).end(); } });
> GET /v1/books < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"data":[{"id":1,"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert","year":1965}]} > POST /v1/books {"title":"Neuromancer","author":"William Gibson","year":1984} < 201 Created < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < location: /v1/books/2 < {"id":2,"title":"Neuromancer","author":"William Gibson","year":1984} > POST /v1/books {"title":"Neuromancer","author":"William Gibson","year":1984} < 201 Created < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":3,"title":"Neuromancer","author":"William Gibson","year":1984} > POST /v1/books {"title":"","year":"soon"} < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"invalid book","details":["title must be a non-empty string","author must be a non-empty string","year must be an integer"]} > POST /v1/books title=Dune > content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded < 415 Unsupported Media Type < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"Content-Type must be application/json"} > PUT /v1/books/1 {"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert","year":1966} < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert","year":1966} > PUT /v1/books/1 {"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert","year":1966} < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert","year":1966} > PATCH /v1/books/1 {"year":1965,"publisher":"ignored"} < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert","year":1965} > PUT /v1/books/1 {"year":1965} < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"invalid book","details":["title must be a non-empty string","author must be a non-empty string"]} > DELETE /v1/books/3 < 204 No Content > DELETE /v1/books/3 < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"book not found"} > GET /v1/books/3 < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"book not found"}

Status codes for every operation

SituationStatus
Read OK / update OK with body200 OK
Created201 Created with Location
Accepted for later processing (jobs)202 Accepted and a status URL
Success, nothing to return204 No Content
Not changed (conditional GET)304 Not Modified
Malformed JSON, failed validation400 Bad Request (some APIs use 422 for "well-formed but invalid"; pick one and keep it)
No or bad credentials / lacks permission401 Unauthorized / 403 Forbidden
No such resource (or hidden for security)404 Not Found
Wrong method for that URL405 Method Not Allowed + Allow
Wrong Content-Type415 Unsupported Media Type
Conflict (duplicate email, edit clash)409 Conflict
Precondition failed (If-Match mismatch)412 (or 428 if the header is missing)
Body too big413 Payload Too Large
Rate limited429 Too Many Requests + Retry-After
Server bug / dependency down500 / 503 Service Unavailable

PUT versus PATCH

  • PUT sends the complete new representation; fields you omit are removed or reset. Predictable, idempotent, but clients must send everything.
  • PATCH sends only what changes. The simple, popular form is JSON Merge Patch (what the example uses: send the fields to change; null clears a field). The more precise JSON Patch (RFC 6902, a list of { "op": "replace", "path": "/year", "value": 1965 } operations) suits arrays and atomic multi-step edits.

Shapes and conventions that save arguments later

  • Pick one naming style for JSON keys (camelCase is the JavaScript norm) and never mix.
  • Dates as ISO 8601 UTC strings (2026-10-23T09:30:00Z). Money as integer minor units plus currency ({ "amount": 1999, "currency": "USD" }). IDs as strings so you can move to UUIDs without breaking clients.
  • Collections return an object, not a bare array: { "data": [...] , "meta": {...} }, so you can add pagination and totals without a breaking change.
  • Never expose internal fields (password hashes, internal flags). Return an explicit response shape, not the database row.
  • Unknown fields in requests: ignore (lenient) or reject (strict). Choose deliberately; strict catches typos.
  • Actions that are not CRUD: model them as a sub-resource or a state change: POST /orders/42/cancellation, POST /users/7/password-reset, or PATCH /orders/42 { "status": "cancelled" } with rules in the service. Avoid verbs scattered everywhere.
  • Long jobs: answer 202 Accepted with Location: /jobs/123; clients poll that resource (or you call a webhook, Unit 8).
  • Versioning: put a major version in the path (/v1/...) and keep it for years. Adding fields and endpoints is backward compatible; removing or renaming fields, changing types or meanings is breaking and needs /v2. Announce retirement with Deprecation and Sunset response headers.
  • Be liberal in what you accept, strict in what you send, and document every field.

Everything a client sends (body, query, params, headers) is untrusted text until you check it. TypeScript types vanish at run time and cannot protect you. Validate at the edge, turn the input into a trusted, correctly typed object, and let the rest of the code assume it is valid ("parse, don't validate"). Zod (v4 here) is the most popular schema library: one definition gives you validation, coercion, defaults, error messages and (in TypeScript) the type.

import { z } from "zod";

const CreateUser = z.object({
  name: z.string().trim().min(2, "name is too short"),          // trim first, then check the length
  email: z.email(),                                              // built-in format checks (also z.url(), z.uuid(), z.iso.datetime())
  age: z.coerce.number().int().min(0).max(130).optional(),       // "30" from a query/form becomes 30
  role: z.enum(["admin", "editor", "viewer"]).default("viewer"), // missing value gets a default
  tags: z.array(z.string()).max(3).default([]),
});

// success: clean, converted data. Unknown keys are dropped by default
const good = CreateUser.safeParse({ name: "  Ana ", email: "ana@example.com", age: "30", isAdmin: true });
console.log(good.success, good.data);

// failure: every problem at once, with the path to each
const bad = CreateUser.safeParse({ name: "A", email: "nope", age: "abc", role: "boss", tags: [1] });
console.log(bad.success);
console.log(bad.error.issues.map((i) => `${i.path.join(".")}: ${i.message}`));
console.log(z.flattenError(bad.error).fieldErrors);              // { field: [messages] }: handy for forms
console.log(z.prettifyError(bad.error));                         // human readable, for logs
true { name: 'Ana', email: 'ana@example.com', age: 30, role: 'viewer', tags: [] } false [ 'name: name is too short', 'email: Invalid email address', 'age: Invalid input: expected number, received NaN', 'role: Invalid option: expected one of "admin"|"editor"|"viewer"', 'tags.0: Invalid input: expected string, received number' ] { name: [ 'name is too short' ], email: [ 'Invalid email address' ], age: [ 'Invalid input: expected number, received NaN' ], role: [ 'Invalid option: expected one of "admin"|"editor"|"viewer"' ], tags: [ 'Invalid input: expected string, received number' ] } ✖ name is too short → at name ✖ Invalid email address → at email ✖ Invalid input: expected number, received NaN → at age ✖ Invalid option: expected one of "admin"|"editor"|"viewer" → at role ✖ Invalid input: expected string, received number → at tags[0]

The pieces you will use daily

import { z } from "zod";
const show = (label, result) => console.log(label.padEnd(22), result.success ? JSON.stringify(result.data) : "ERROR " + result.error.issues[0].message);

// query strings are strings: coerce, bound and default them
const Query = z.object({
  page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1),
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20),
  sort: z.enum(["name", "-name", "created"]).default("created"),
});
show("query {limit:'50'}", Query.safeParse({ limit: "50" }));
show("query {limit:'500'}", Query.safeParse({ limit: "500" }));

// strictObject rejects unknown keys instead of silently dropping them
show("strict + extra key", z.strictObject({ a: z.string() }).safeParse({ a: "x", b: 1 }));

// a field that depends on another: refine
const Signup = z.object({ password: z.string().min(8), confirm: z.string() })
  .refine((d) => d.password === d.confirm, { path: ["confirm"], error: "passwords do not match" });
show("password mismatch", Signup.safeParse({ password: "12345678", confirm: "x" }));

// a union decided by a field: discriminatedUnion gives precise errors
const Shape = z.discriminatedUnion("type", [
  z.object({ type: z.literal("circle"), r: z.number().positive() }),
  z.object({ type: z.literal("rect"), w: z.number(), h: z.number() }),
]);
show("rect ok", Shape.safeParse({ type: "rect", w: 2, h: 3 }));
show("rect missing h", Shape.safeParse({ type: "rect", w: 2 }));

// transform: change the value while validating (normalise)
show("transform", z.string().transform((s) => s.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, "-")).safeParse("Hello Big World"));

// reuse: derive new schemas instead of repeating fields
const User = z.object({ id: z.number(), name: z.string(), email: z.email() });
show("partial (PATCH)", User.omit({ id: true }).partial().safeParse({ name: "New" }));
console.log("pick keys:", Object.keys(User.pick({ name: true }).shape));

// the classic coercion trap: any non-empty string is truthy
console.log("coerce.boolean('false') =", z.coerce.boolean().parse("false"), "| stringbool('false') =", z.stringbool().parse("false"));
query {limit:'50'} {"page":1,"limit":50,"sort":"created"} query {limit:'500'} ERROR Too big: expected number to be <=100 strict + extra key ERROR Unrecognized key: "b" password mismatch ERROR passwords do not match rect ok {"type":"rect","w":2,"h":3} rect missing h ERROR Invalid input: expected number, received undefined transform "hello-big-world" partial (PATCH) {"name":"New"} pick keys: [ 'name' ] coerce.boolean('false') = true | stringbool('false') = false
z.coerce.boolean() is a trapIt uses JavaScript truthiness, so the string "false" becomes true. For flags from query strings or environment variables use z.stringbool() (accepts "true/false/1/0/yes/no/on/off"). Likewise z.coerce.number() turns "" into 0: use a refinement if an empty field must be rejected.

A validate middleware for Express

Write the checking code once as middleware. Because req.query is read-only in Express 5, put the parsed values somewhere new (req.valid) and have handlers read only from there.

import express from "express";
import { z } from "zod";
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

// validate({ body, query, params }) -> middleware. On failure: 400 with every problem listed
const validate = (schemas) => (req, res, next) => {
  const valid = {};
  const problems = [];
  for (const part of ["params", "query", "body"]) {
    if (!schemas[part]) continue;
    const result = schemas[part].safeParse(req[part] ?? {});
    if (result.success) valid[part] = result.data;
    else for (const issue of result.error.issues) problems.push({ in: part, field: issue.path.join("."), message: issue.message });
  }
  if (problems.length) return res.status(400).json({ error: "validation failed", problems });
  req.valid = valid;                                       // trusted, converted values
  next();
};

const Id = z.object({ id: z.coerce.number().int().positive() });
const CreateUser = z.object({ name: z.string().trim().min(2), email: z.email(), age: z.number().int().min(13).optional() });
const ListQuery = z.object({ page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1), limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(50).default(10), q: z.string().trim().max(50).optional() });

const users = [];
app.post("/users", validate({ body: CreateUser }), (req, res) => {
  const user = { id: users.length + 1, ...req.valid.body };       // name is already trimmed, email already checked
  users.push(user);
  res.status(201).json(user);
});
app.get("/users", validate({ query: ListQuery }), (req, res) => res.json({ query: req.valid.query, total: users.length }));
app.get("/users/:id", validate({ params: Id }), (req, res) => {
  const user = users.find((u) => u.id === req.valid.params.id);   // a real number now, not a string
  user ? res.json(user) : res.status(404).json({ error: "user not found" });
});
> POST /users {"name":" Ana ","email":"ana@example.com","isAdmin":true} < 201 Created < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"name":"Ana","email":"ana@example.com"} > POST /users {"name":"A","email":"nope","age":9} < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"validation failed","problems":[{"in":"body","field":"name","message":"Too small: expected string to have >=2 characters"},{"in":"body","field":"email","message":"Invalid email address"},{"in":"body","field":"age","message":"Too small: expected number to be >=13"}]} > POST /users > content-type: application/json < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"validation failed","problems":[{"in":"body","field":"name","message":"Invalid input: expected string, received undefined"},{"in":"body","field":"email","message":"Invalid input: expected string, received undefined"}]} > GET /users?limit=500&page=0 < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"validation failed","problems":[{"in":"query","field":"page","message":"Too small: expected number to be >=1"},{"in":"query","field":"limit","message":"Too big: expected number to be <=50"}]} > GET /users?q=ana < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"query":{"page":1,"limit":10,"q":"ana"},"total":1} > GET /users/abc < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"validation failed","problems":[{"in":"params","field":"id","message":"Invalid input: expected number, received NaN"}]} > GET /users/1 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"name":"Ana","email":"ana@example.com"}
  • Validate the output too. Run responses through a schema that lists exactly the public fields (UserPublic.parse(row)), so a password hash can never leak because someone added a column.
  • One source of truth. In TypeScript, type CreateUser = z.infer<typeof CreateUser> keeps the type and the check identical. Zod 4 can also generate JSON Schema (z.toJSONSchema(schema)) for your API documentation (OpenAPI entry).
  • Business rules are not schema rules. "Email is unique" needs the database (return 409); the schema only checks the shape.
  • Alternatives: express-validator (chains of checks on fields), Joi, Yup, Valibot (smaller bundles), ajv with JSON Schema (fastest, standard format, used by Fastify). The principle is the same.
import express from "express";
import { body, query, validationResult, matchedData } from "express-validator";
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.post("/signup",
  body("email").isEmail().withMessage("must be an email").normalizeEmail(),
  body("password").isLength({ min: 8 }).withMessage("at least 8 characters"),
  query("ref").optional().isAlphanumeric(),
  (req, res) => {
    const result = validationResult(req);
    if (!result.isEmpty()) return res.status(400).json({ errors: result.array().map((e) => ({ field: e.path, message: e.msg })) });
    res.status(201).json(matchedData(req));               // only the fields that were validated
  });
> POST /signup {"email":"Ana@Example.COM","password":"long-enough-pw","extra":"dropped"} < 201 Created < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"email":"ana@example.com","password":"long-enough-pw"} > POST /signup?ref=!! {"email":"nope","password":"short"} < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"errors":[{"field":"email","message":"must be an email"},{"field":"password","message":"at least 8 characters"},{"field":"ref","message":"Invalid value"}]}

An API is only as friendly as its errors. Clients need to know three things: what class of problem it is (a stable code they can switch on), what to tell the user (a message), and which field is wrong. Invent one shape and use it for every error from every route, including 404s, parser errors and crashes.

You can use the standard: RFC 9457 Problem Details, media type application/problem+json, with these members: type (a URI naming the error kind), title (short, constant per type), status, detail (this occurrence), instance (which request) plus any extension members of your own (errors, requestId).

import express from "express";
import { z } from "zod";
const app = express();
let counter = 0;
app.use((req, res, next) => { req.id = `req-${String(++counter).padStart(4, "0")}`; next(); });   // real code: crypto.randomUUID()
app.use(express.json({ limit: "1kb" }));

class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(status, code, title, detail, extra = {}) { super(detail ?? title); Object.assign(this, { status, code, title, detail, extra }); }
}
const errors = {
  notFound: (what) => new ApiError(404, "not-found", "Resource not found", `${what} does not exist`),
  conflict: (detail) => new ApiError(409, "conflict", "Conflict", detail),
  forbidden: () => new ApiError(403, "forbidden", "Forbidden", "you may not do that"),
};

const Body = z.object({ email: z.email(), age: z.number().int().min(13) });
app.post("/users", (req, res) => {
  const parsed = Body.safeParse(req.body);
  if (!parsed.success) throw new ApiError(400, "validation-failed", "Validation failed", "one or more fields are invalid", {
    errors: parsed.error.issues.map((i) => ({ field: i.path.join("."), message: i.message })),
  });
  if (parsed.data.email === "taken@example.com") throw errors.conflict("a user with this email already exists");
  res.status(201).json({ id: 1, ...parsed.data });
});
app.get("/users/:id", () => { throw errors.notFound("user 99"); });
app.get("/crash", () => { null.boom; });                      // a bug

app.use((req, res, next) => next(errors.notFound(`${req.method} ${req.path}`)));
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {                           // THE place where every failure becomes a response
  if (res.headersSent) return next(err);
  let problem;
  if (err instanceof ApiError) problem = err;
  else if (err.type === "entity.parse.failed") problem = new ApiError(400, "invalid-json", "Invalid JSON", "the request body is not valid JSON");
  else if (err.type === "entity.too.large") problem = new ApiError(413, "payload-too-large", "Payload too large", "the request body exceeds the 1 kB limit");
  else problem = new ApiError(500, "internal", "Internal server error", "something went wrong; quote the request id when contacting support");   // never err.message
  if (problem.status >= 500) console.log(`[${req.id}] logged privately:`, err.message);
  res.status(problem.status).type("application/problem+json").json({
    type: `https://api.example.com/problems/${problem.code}`,
    title: problem.title, status: problem.status, detail: problem.detail, instance: req.originalUrl, requestId: req.id,
    ...problem.extra,
  });
});
> POST /users {"email":"nope","age":9} < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8 < {"type":"https://api.example.com/problems/validation-failed","title":"Validation failed","status":400,"detail":"one or more fields are invalid","instance":"/users","requestId":"req-0001","errors":[{"field":"email","message":"Invalid email address"},{"field":"age","message":"Too small: expected number to be >=13"}]} > POST /users {"email":"taken@example.com","age":30} < 409 Conflict < content-type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8 < {"type":"https://api.example.com/problems/conflict","title":"Conflict","status":409,"detail":"a user with this email already exists","instance":"/users","requestId":"req-0002"} > GET /users/99 < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8 < {"type":"https://api.example.com/problems/not-found","title":"Resource not found","status":404,"detail":"user 99 does not exist","instance":"/users/99","requestId":"req-0003"} > POST /users {broken > content-type: application/json < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8 < {"type":"https://api.example.com/problems/invalid-json","title":"Invalid JSON","status":400,"detail":"the request body is not valid JSON","instance":"/users","requestId":"req-0004"} > POST /users {"pad":"xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx ... < 413 Payload Too Large < content-type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8 < {"type":"https://api.example.com/problems/payload-too-large","title":"Payload too large","status":413,"detail":"the request body exceeds the 1 kB limit","instance":"/users","requestId":"req-0005"} [req-0006] logged privately: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'boom') > GET /crash < 500 Internal Server Error < content-type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8 < {"type":"https://api.example.com/problems/internal","title":"Internal server error","status":500,"detail":"something went wrong; quote the request id when contacting support","instance":"/crash","requestId":"req-0006"} > PUT /nowhere < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/problem+json; charset=utf-8 < {"type":"https://api.example.com/problems/not-found","title":"Resource not found","status":404,"detail":"PUT /nowhere does not exist","instance":"/nowhere","requestId":"req-0007"}
  • Stable codes. Clients write if (err.code === "validation-failed"); they should never parse human text. Keep codes in your docs as a catalogue and never reuse one for a different meaning.
  • Machine part and human part. title/detail may be translated or reworded; type/status are the contract.
  • Request id. Return the id you also write to the log (requestId, or an X-Request-Id header). A support ticket with an id takes minutes, without one hours.
  • Security. Do not reveal whether an account exists on login ("invalid email or password" for both), do not echo secrets or SQL, and keep stack traces in logs only.
  • Map known infrastructure errors at the boundary: a Postgres unique violation (23505) becomes 409, a foreign-key violation (23503) becomes 409 or 400, a timeout becomes 503 (Unit 6 does this).

A list endpoint that returns "everything" works with ten rows and kills the server with a million. Every collection endpoint needs a maximum page size, a deterministic order and a way to ask for the next page.

Offset (?page=3&limit=20)Cursor (?after=abc123&limit=20)
How it worksSkip (page-1)*limit rows"Rows after this one in the sort order". The cursor is an opaque token encoding the last row's sort key.
Jump to page 50YesNo (next/previous only)
Total count / page numbersEasy (count(*))Awkward
Rows inserted or deleted while pagingItems shift: you see duplicates or miss rowsStable
Speed on page 10,000Slow: the database still walks every skipped rowFast: an index seek
Best forAdmin tables, small data, "page 3 of 10" UIsFeeds, infinite scroll, big or fast-changing data, public APIs
 
import express from "express";
import { z } from "zod";
const app = express();

let nextId = 1;
const products = Array.from({ length: 23 }, (_, i) => ({ id: nextId++, name: `Product ${String(i + 1).padStart(2, "0")}`, price: 5 + (i % 7) * 10, inStock: i % 3 !== 0 }));

const ListQuery = z.object({
  page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1),
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(10).default(5),            // the cap protects the server
  sort: z.enum(["id", "-id", "price", "-price", "name"]).default("id"),  // a WHITELIST: never pass user text into ORDER BY
  maxPrice: z.coerce.number().optional(),
  inStock: z.stringbool().optional(),
  q: z.string().trim().toLowerCase().optional(),
});

function applyFilters(query) {
  let rows = products.filter((p) =>
    (query.maxPrice === undefined || p.price <= query.maxPrice) &&
    (query.inStock === undefined || p.inStock === query.inStock) &&
    (!query.q || p.name.toLowerCase().includes(query.q)));
  const desc = query.sort.startsWith("-"), key = query.sort.replace("-", "");
  rows = rows.toSorted((a, b) => (a[key] < b[key] ? -1 : a[key] > b[key] ? 1 : a.id - b.id) * (desc ? -1 : 1));   // id as tie-breaker: stable order
  return rows;
}

app.get("/products", (req, res) => {
  const parsed = ListQuery.safeParse(req.query);
  if (!parsed.success) return res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid query", fields: z.flattenError(parsed.error).fieldErrors });
  const q = parsed.data;
  const rows = applyFilters(q);
  const start = (q.page - 1) * q.limit;
  const pages = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(rows.length / q.limit));
  const link = (page) => `</products?${new URLSearchParams({ ...req.query, page, limit: q.limit })}>`;
  res.set("Link", [q.page > 1 && `${link(q.page - 1)}; rel="prev"`, q.page < pages && `${link(q.page + 1)}; rel="next"`].filter(Boolean).join(", "));
  res.json({ data: rows.slice(start, start + q.limit).map((p) => p.id), meta: { total: rows.length, page: q.page, pages, limit: q.limit } });
});

// cursor pagination: the cursor says "continue after this id". Opaque to clients (base64url of JSON)
const encode = (obj) => Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(obj)).toString("base64url");
const decode = (s) => JSON.parse(Buffer.from(s, "base64url").toString());
app.get("/feed", (req, res) => {
  const limit = Math.min(Number(req.query.limit) || 5, 10);
  const afterId = req.query.after ? decode(req.query.after).id : 0;
  const rows = products.filter((p) => p.id > afterId).slice(0, limit + 1);       // fetch one extra to know if there is more
  const hasMore = rows.length > limit;
  const page = rows.slice(0, limit);
  res.json({ data: page.map((p) => p.id), next: hasMore ? encode({ id: page.at(-1).id }) : null });
});
> GET /products?limit=5&page=2 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < link: </products?limit=5&page=1>; rel="prev", </products?limit=5&page=3>; rel="next" < {"data":[6,7,8,9,10],"meta":{"total":23,"page":2,"pages":5,"limit":5}} > GET /products?limit=5&page=5 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < link: </products?limit=5&page=4>; rel="prev" < {"data":[21,22,23],"meta":{"total":23,"page":5,"pages":5,"limit":5}} > GET /products?sort=-price&maxPrice=35&inStock=true&limit=4 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"data":[18,11,17,3],"meta":{"total":9,"page":1,"pages":3,"limit":4}} > GET /products?q=product 2&limit=10 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"data":[20,21,22,23],"meta":{"total":4,"page":1,"pages":1,"limit":10}} > GET /products?limit=100&sort=password < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"invalid query","fields":{"limit":["Too big: expected number to be <=10"],"sort":["Invalid option: expected one of \"id\"|\"-id\"|\"price\"|\"-price\"|\"name\""]}} --- a row is added while a client reads pages of 5 offset page 1: [ 23, 22, 21, 20, 19 ] page 2: [ 19, 18, 17, 16, 15 ] <- id 19 appears twice cursor walk saw 25 rows, duplicates: 0
  • Always cap limit and give it a default. Return the cap in the docs.
  • Always sort deterministically: add a unique tie-breaker (id) to the sort, or pages may overlap when many rows share the same value.
  • Whitelist sort and filter fields. Passing a user string into ORDER BY is SQL injection (Unit 7); map allowed names to real columns instead.
  • For cursor pagination in SQL use keyset conditions, WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 21; Unit 6 shows it with an index and EXPLAIN.
  • Expose navigation in both the body (meta, next) and the Link header (RFC 8288); some clients prefer one, some the other.
  • Search with ?q= starts simple (ILIKE) and graduates to Postgres full-text search or a search engine (Elasticsearch, Meilisearch, Typesense) when relevance and speed matter.

Browsers upload files as multipart/form-data, which express.json() does not read. Multer parses it: text fields go to req.body, files to req.file (one) or req.files (several). An upload is user-controlled bytes on your server, so the rules matter more than the code:

  • Limit file size, file count and field count (limits) so one request cannot fill memory or disk.
  • Never trust the file name or the declared type. Both come from the client. Check the real content (the first bytes, "magic numbers"), and pick your own stored name.
  • Store outside the public folder and serve files through a route you control, with X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so an uploaded .html file can never run as a page on your site.
  • Check that the user is allowed to upload, and to read the file later.
import express from "express";
import multer from "multer";
import path from "node:path";
import fs from "node:fs/promises";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const uploadDir = path.resolve("uploads");                        // not inside any public/static folder
await fs.mkdir(uploadDir, { recursive: true });

// The first bytes of a file identify its real format, whatever it is called
const signatures = [
  { type: "image/png", ext: ".png", bytes: [0x89, 0x50, 0x4e, 0x47, 0x0d, 0x0a, 0x1a, 0x0a] },
  { type: "image/jpeg", ext: ".jpg", bytes: [0xff, 0xd8, 0xff] },
  { type: "application/pdf", ext: ".pdf", bytes: [0x25, 0x50, 0x44, 0x46] },
];
const sniff = (buffer) => signatures.find((s) => s.bytes.every((byte, i) => buffer[i] === byte));

const upload = multer({
  storage: multer.memoryStorage(),                                // kept in RAM: fine for small files. Use diskStorage or a stream for big ones
  limits: { fileSize: 5_000, files: 1, fields: 5 },               // 5 kB for the demo; real limits: a few MB
  fileFilter: (req, file, cb) => cb(null, ["image/png", "image/jpeg", "application/pdf"].includes(file.mimetype)),   // cheap first filter on the DECLARED type
});

const app = express();
app.post("/files", upload.single("file"), async (req, res) => {
  if (!req.file) return res.status(400).json({ error: "send a PNG, JPEG or PDF in the 'file' field" });
  const kind = sniff(req.file.buffer);                            // the real check
  if (!kind) return res.status(415).json({ error: "the content is not a PNG, JPEG or PDF" });
  const id = `${randomUUID()}${kind.ext}`;                        // OUR name: the client's name could be "../../app.js"
  await fs.writeFile(path.join(uploadDir, id), req.file.buffer);
  res.status(201).json({ id, type: kind.type, bytes: req.file.size, originalName: path.basename(req.file.originalname), note: req.body.note });
});

app.get("/files/:id", (req, res) => {
  if (!/^[0-9a-f-]{36}\.(png|jpg|pdf)$/.test(req.params.id)) return res.status(400).json({ error: "bad file id" });   // an allow-list pattern
  res.set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff");                   // the browser must believe our Content-Type
  res.sendFile(req.params.id, { root: uploadDir, dotfiles: "deny" }, (err) => { if (err && !res.headersSent) res.status(404).json({ error: "no such file" }); });
});

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {                                // Multer's own errors have codes
  if (err instanceof multer.MulterError) {
    const status = err.code === "LIMIT_FILE_SIZE" ? 413 : 400;
    return res.status(status).json({ error: err.code, field: err.field });
  }
  next(err);
});
a real PNG 201 {"id":"<uuid>.png","type":"image/png","bytes":108,"originalName":"evil name.png","note":"my avatar"} text renamed to .png 415 {"error":"the content is not a PNG, JPEG or PDF"} declared as text/plain 400 {"error":"send a PNG, JPEG or PDF in the 'file' field"} 6 kB (limit is 5 kB) 413 {"error":"LIMIT_FILE_SIZE","field":"file"} wrong field name 400 {"error":"LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE","field":"document"} download: 200 image/png nosniff 108 bytes path trick: 400 | unknown id: 404
Multer optionUse
upload.single("field"), .array("photos", 5), .fields([...]), .none()Which file fields to accept (anything else raises LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE)
memoryStorage() / diskStorage({ destination, filename })Buffer in RAM (req.file.buffer) / write to disk (req.file.path)
limitsfileSize, files, fields, fieldSize, parts, headerPairs
fileFilter(req, file, cb)cb(null, true) accept, cb(null, false) skip silently, cb(error) abort
Beyond the basicsFor large files do not pass them through your server at all: your API hands the browser a short-lived pre-signed URL for object storage (S3, Google Cloud Storage, R2) and the browser uploads straight there; your server stores only the key and metadata. That needs cloud credentials, so it is described here but not run in this guide. Also consider re-encoding images (the sharp library) to strip metadata and neutralise malformed files, virus scanning (ClamAV) for documents you redistribute, per-user quotas, resumable uploads (the tus protocol), and deleting orphaned files.

Caching headers

HTTP has caching built in; using it makes APIs faster and cheaper with a few headers.

Header or valueMeaning
Cache-Control: no-storeNever store (private or sensitive responses: account pages, tokens)
no-cacheMay store, but must revalidate with the server before each reuse (cheap with ETag: 304)
max-age=60Fresh for 60 s without asking the server
public / privateShared caches (CDN, proxy) may store / only the user's own browser may
s-maxage=300Like max-age but for shared caches only
stale-while-revalidate=30Serve the stale copy while refreshing in the background
immutableWill never change (hashed asset file names)
ETag / If-None-MatchA version fingerprint, and the question "do you still have this version?" answered with 304 Not Modified and no body
Last-Modified / If-Modified-SinceThe time-based alternative to ETags
Vary: Accept-LanguageThe response differs by this request header: caches must key on it

Rules of thumb: public reference data (a country list) gets public, max-age=3600; per-user data gets private, no-cache (revalidate) or no-store; anything with credentials in the URL or a response containing secrets gets no-store. Express adds weak ETags to res.send/json automatically and answers conditional requests with 304 for you.

import express from "express";
import http from "node:http";
const app = express();

const rates = { USD: 1, EUR: 0.92, INR: 83.2 };
app.get("/rates", (req, res) => {
  res.set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=60");               // browsers and CDNs may reuse it for a minute
  res.json(rates);                                              // Express adds an ETag and handles If-None-Match for us
});
app.get("/me", (req, res) => {
  res.set("Cache-Control", "private, no-store");                // personal data: never keep a copy anywhere shared
  res.json({ name: "Ana" });
});
> GET /rates < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < cache-control: public, max-age=60 < {"USD":1,"EUR":0.92,"INR":83.2} > GET /me < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < cache-control: private, no-store < {"name":"Ana"} first request : 200 body 31 bytes, etag present: true revalidation : 304 body 0 bytes (nothing re-sent)

The lost update problem and If-Match

Two people open the same record, both edit, both save. Whoever saves last silently erases the other's change. Optimistic concurrency control prevents this without locks: every version has an identifier (an ETag, or a version number), and a write must say which version it was based on with If-Match. If the record has changed since, the server answers 412 Precondition Failed and the client re-reads and retries. If the header is missing on an endpoint that requires it, answer 428 Precondition Required.

import express from "express";
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const doc = { id: 1, title: "Plan", body: "v1 text", version: 1 };
const etag = () => `"${doc.version}"`;

app.get("/docs/1", (req, res) => res.set("ETag", etag()).json(doc));

app.put("/unsafe/docs/1", (req, res) => {                        // last write wins: someone's work is lost
  Object.assign(doc, { body: req.body.body, version: doc.version + 1 });
  res.set("ETag", etag()).json(doc);
});

app.put("/docs/1", (req, res) => {                               // safe: the write names the version it was based on
  const ifMatch = req.get("If-Match");
  if (!ifMatch) return res.status(428).json({ error: "send If-Match with the ETag you read" });
  if (ifMatch !== etag()) return res.status(412).json({ error: "the document changed, reload and merge", current: doc.version });
  Object.assign(doc, { body: req.body.body, version: doc.version + 1 });
  res.set("ETag", etag()).json(doc);
});
--- unsafe: Ana and Raj both read version 1 > PUT /unsafe/docs/1 {"body":"Ana's careful edit"} < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"title":"Plan","body":"Ana's careful edit","version":2} > PUT /unsafe/docs/1 {"body":"Raj's edit (silently erases Ana's)"} < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"title":"Plan","body":"Raj's edit (silently erases Ana's)","version":3} --- safe: both read, both try to save both hold ETag "3" > PUT /docs/1 {"body":"Ana saves first"} > if-match: "3" < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < etag: "4" < {"id":1,"title":"Plan","body":"Ana saves first","version":4} > PUT /docs/1 {"body":"Raj tries with the old tag"} > if-match: "3" < 412 Precondition Failed < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"the document changed, reload and merge","current":4} > PUT /docs/1 {"body":"no header at all"} < 428 Precondition Required < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"send If-Match with the ETag you read"}

In SQL the same idea is a version column: UPDATE docs SET body = $1, version = version + 1 WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3, and if zero rows changed, return 409/412 (Unit 6).

Idempotency keys: making POST safe to retry

A phone on a bad network posts "pay 50", the connection drops, and the app cannot know whether the server processed it. If it retries and the server runs it twice, the customer is charged twice. The fix (used by Stripe and most payment APIs): the client sends a unique Idempotency-Key header, and the server remembers the first outcome for that key and replays it for any repeat instead of doing the work again.

import express from "express";
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const seen = new Map();            // key -> { fingerprint, state: "processing" | "done", status, body }   (use Redis with a TTL in production)
function idempotent(req, res, next) {
  const key = req.get("Idempotency-Key");
  if (!key) return res.status(400).json({ error: "Idempotency-Key header is required" });
  const fingerprint = JSON.stringify(req.body);                     // same key must mean the same request
  const entry = seen.get(key);
  if (entry) {
    if (entry.fingerprint !== fingerprint) return res.status(422).json({ error: "this key was used with a different request" });
    if (entry.state === "processing") return res.status(409).set("Retry-After", "1").json({ error: "the first request is still running" });
    return res.status(entry.status).set("Idempotency-Replayed", "true").json(entry.body);   // replay the stored answer
  }
  seen.set(key, { fingerprint, state: "processing" });              // claim the key BEFORE doing any work
  const send = res.json.bind(res);
  res.json = (body) => { seen.set(key, { fingerprint, state: "done", status: res.statusCode, body }); return send(body); };
  next();
}

const orders = [];
app.post("/orders", idempotent, async (req, res) => {
  await sleep(30);                                                   // pretend to charge a card and write to the database
  const order = { id: orders.length + 1, item: req.body.item };
  orders.push(order);
  res.status(201).json(order);
});
app.get("/orders", (req, res) => res.json(orders));
> POST /orders {"item":"keyboard"} < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"Idempotency-Key header is required"} > POST /orders {"item":"keyboard"} > idempotency-key: order-2026-10-23-ana-0001 < 201 Created < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"item":"keyboard"} > POST /orders {"item":"keyboard"} > idempotency-key: order-2026-10-23-ana-0001 < 201 Created < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < idempotency-replayed: true < {"id":1,"item":"keyboard"} > POST /orders {"item":"mouse"} > idempotency-key: order-2026-10-23-ana-0001 < 422 Unprocessable Entity < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"this key was used with a different request"} > GET /orders < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < [{"id":1,"item":"keyboard"}] two simultaneous requests with one key -> [ 201, 409 ] (one processed, one told to wait) orders in total: 2
  • Keys are chosen by the client (a UUID per user action). Store them with an expiry (24 hours is typical) in Redis or the database, scoped per user.
  • Store the key atomically before the work starts (a unique constraint or Redis SET NX), otherwise two parallel requests both pass the check.
  • Also design operations to be naturally idempotent where you can ("set status to paid" rather than "add a payment"), and make consumers of events (Unit 8) idempotent too.

An API nobody can learn is an API nobody uses. OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) is the standard machine-readable description of a REST API: a JSON or YAML document listing every path, method, parameter, request body, response and security scheme. From one document you get interactive docs (Swagger UI, Redoc), client SDKs and type definitions (openapi-typescript, orval), mock servers, linters (Spectral) and contract tests.

Top-level keyContents
openapiThe spec version ("3.1.0", which uses full JSON Schema)
infoTitle, version, description, contact, license
serversBase URLs (production, staging)
pathsEach path with its operations (get, post...): parameters, requestBody, responses, security, tags
componentsReusable schemas, responses, parameters, securitySchemes referenced with $ref
security, tagsDefault auth requirements and grouping

Hand-written specs drift from the code. The best defence is a single source of truth: define each schema once in Zod, use it for validation and generate the OpenAPI schema from it with z.toJSONSchema().

import { z } from "zod";

const CreateNote = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(1).max(100).describe("Short title shown in lists"),
  done: z.boolean().default(false),
  tags: z.array(z.string()).max(5).optional(),
});
const strip = ({ $schema, ...rest }) => rest;                       // OpenAPI 3.1 does not want the $schema key
console.log("as a REQUEST body (io: input) :", JSON.stringify(strip(z.toJSONSchema(CreateNote, { io: "input" }))));
console.log("as a RESPONSE body (io: output):", JSON.stringify(strip(z.toJSONSchema(CreateNote, { io: "output" }))));
console.log("differences: 'done' is optional to send but required in what you return, and the output form adds additionalProperties:false");
as a REQUEST body (io: input) : {"type":"object","properties":{"title":{"type":"string","minLength":1,"maxLength":100,"description":"Short title shown in lists"},"done":{"default":false,"type":"boolean"},"tags":{"maxItems":5,"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}},"required":["title"]} as a RESPONSE body (io: output): {"type":"object","properties":{"title":{"type":"string","minLength":1,"maxLength":100,"description":"Short title shown in lists"},"done":{"default":false,"type":"boolean"},"tags":{"maxItems":5,"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}},"required":["title","done"],"additionalProperties":false} differences: 'done' is optional to send but required in what you return, and the output form adds additionalProperties:false
import express from "express";
import swaggerUi from "swagger-ui-express";
import { z } from "zod";

const CreateNote = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(100), done: z.boolean().default(false) });
const Note = CreateNote.extend({ id: z.number().int() });
const ApiError = z.object({ type: z.string(), title: z.string(), status: z.number().int(), detail: z.string().optional() });
const schema = (zodSchema, io) => { const { $schema, ...rest } = z.toJSONSchema(zodSchema, { io, target: "draft-2020-12" }); return rest; };

const spec = {
  openapi: "3.1.0",
  info: { title: "Notebox API", version: "1.0.0", description: "Notes for everyone. All errors use application/problem+json." },
  servers: [{ url: "https://api.example.com/v1", description: "Production" }],
  tags: [{ name: "notes" }],
  components: {
    securitySchemes: { bearerAuth: { type: "http", scheme: "bearer", bearerFormat: "JWT" } },
    schemas: { CreateNote: schema(CreateNote, "input"), Note: schema(Note, "output"), Error: schema(ApiError, "output") },
    responses: { Problem: { description: "Error", content: { "application/problem+json": { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Error" } } } } },
  },
  security: [{ bearerAuth: [] }],
  paths: {
    "/notes": {
      get: {
        tags: ["notes"], summary: "List notes",
        parameters: [
          { name: "limit", in: "query", schema: { type: "integer", minimum: 1, maximum: 50, default: 10 } },
          { name: "done", in: "query", schema: { type: "boolean" } },
        ],
        responses: { 200: { description: "A page of notes", content: { "application/json": { schema: { type: "array", items: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Note" } } } } }, 401: { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } },
      },
      post: {
        tags: ["notes"], summary: "Create a note",
        requestBody: { required: true, content: { "application/json": { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/CreateNote" } } } },
        responses: { 201: { description: "Created", headers: { Location: { schema: { type: "string" } } }, content: { "application/json": { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Note" } } } }, 400: { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } },
      },
    },
    "/notes/{id}": {
      get: {
        tags: ["notes"], summary: "Get one note",
        parameters: [{ name: "id", in: "path", required: true, schema: { type: "integer" } }],
        responses: { 200: { description: "The note", content: { "application/json": { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Note" } } } }, 404: { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } },
      },
    },
  },
};

const app = express();
app.get("/openapi.json", (req, res) => res.json(spec));                          // for tools and code generators
app.use("/docs", swaggerUi.serve, swaggerUi.setup(spec));                          // interactive documentation for people
3.1.0 | Notebox API 1.0.0 GET,POST /notes GET /notes/{id} schemas: [ 'CreateNote', 'Note', 'Error' ] Note schema: {"type":"object","properties":{"title":{"type":"string","minLength":1,"maxLength":100},"done":{"default":false,"type":"boolean"},"id":{"type":"integer","minimum":-9007199254740991,"maximum":9007199254740991}},"required":["title","done","id"],"additionalProperties":false} $refs checked: 8 | dangling: 0 GET /docs/ -> 200 text/html; charset=utf-8 | contains Swagger UI: true
  • Frameworks that build the spec from code save effort: @asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi, zod-openapi, tsoa, routing-controllers, or Fastify and NestJS which generate it from route schemas. swagger-jsdoc reads comments above routes.
  • Document the errors (every status each endpoint can return, with an example) and the auth scheme; most integration time is lost on those, not on the happy path.
  • Keep the spec honest with tests: validate real responses against the schemas in your test suite (Unit 9) and lint the document in CI.
  • Do not expose interactive docs on a production API that holds sensitive operations without thinking: they reveal your whole surface. Often docs are public, the "Try it out" button is limited to a sandbox.
06

Unit 6: Databases

Where your data lives when the process stops. SQL on a real PostgreSQL 16 server (queries, joins, indexes, transactions), SQLite, the pg driver, migrations, query builders and ORMs, Redis for caching and counters, MongoDB concepts, and the data-access patterns that keep an Express app correct under load.

Variables in your Node process vanish when it restarts, and a second process (or a second server) cannot see them. A database is a separate program that stores data durably, lets many processes share it, and answers questions about it quickly. Your Express app talks to it over a network connection using a driver (pg for PostgreSQL, mysql2, better-sqlite3, mongodb, ioredis).

KindExamplesGood atWatch out for
Relational (SQL)PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLiteStructured data with relationships, transactions, flexible queries, reportingSchema changes need migrations; scaling writes across machines is harder
DocumentMongoDB, FirestoreNested records read as a whole, flexible shape, easy horizontal scalingJoins and cross-document consistency are weaker; "schemaless" still needs discipline
Key-value / in-memoryRedis, MemcachedVery fast lookups, caching, sessions, counters, rate limits, queuesMemory is limited; data may be lost unless persistence is configured
Wide-column, time seriesCassandra, TimescaleDB, InfluxDBHuge write volumes, metrics, logsNarrow query patterns
SearchElasticsearch, OpenSearch, MeilisearchFull-text search, ranking, filtersA copy of the data, not the source of truth
GraphNeo4jRelationship-heavy queries (social graphs, recommendations)A niche; Postgres handles many cases
The default choiceWhen you are unsure, start with PostgreSQL. It handles relational data, JSON documents (jsonb), full-text search, queues (SKIP LOCKED) and even simple caching, so one system covers most early needs. Add Redis when you have a measured need for speed or shared counters. Reach for the others when a specific requirement demands it.

ACID: what a transaction promises

LetterMeaningExample
AtomicityAll the steps happen, or none doMoving money: debit and credit both commit or both roll back
ConsistencyEvery committed state obeys the rules (constraints, foreign keys)A negative balance is refused by a CHECK
IsolationConcurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished workTwo buyers cannot both take the last item
DurabilityOnce committed, it survives a crashThe write is on disk (the write-ahead log) before "OK" is returned

Words you will meet

TermMeaning
Table, row, columnA table is a set of rows; each row has the same typed columns
Primary keyThe column that identifies a row uniquely
Foreign keyA column that must match a primary key in another table (the relationship)
IndexA sorted lookup structure that makes searches fast and costs a little on every write
MigrationA versioned script that changes the schema, applied in order on every environment
Connection poolA small set of reusable open connections shared by all requests
ORM / query builderA library that builds SQL from JavaScript objects and calls
ReplicaA read-only copy that takes read traffic off the main server
ShardingSplitting data across servers by a key (a late-stage scaling step)

The rest of this unit works from the bottom up: SQL itself first (it outlives every framework), then the Node drivers, then the tools that sit on top.

SQL is a language for asking a database questions about sets of rows. These examples run against a real PostgreSQL 16 server using psql; the same statements work through any Node driver. We build a tiny shop that the next entries keep using.

TypeUseNotes
integer, bigint, smallintWhole numbersbigint for ids that may pass 2 billion
numeric(10,2)Exact decimals (money)Never use real/double precision for money
text, varchar(n)StringsIn Postgres text is fine; add a CHECK for length
booleantrue / false / NULL
timestamptzA moment in time (stored as UTC)Prefer it over timestamp (no zone)
date, time, intervalCalendar date, clock time, duration
uuidRandom or time-ordered identifiersgen_random_uuid() is built in
jsonbJSON documents, indexableUse json only to keep exact text
integer[], text[]ArraysHandy, but a join table is usually better
GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITYAuto-incrementing idModern replacement for serial
 
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id         integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name       text NOT NULL,
  email      text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  city       text,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE products (
  id    integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name  text NOT NULL,
  price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
  stock integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  status      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new',
  placed_on   date NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id   integer NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  qty        integer NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city) VALUES
  ('Ana',  'ana@example.com',  'Lisbon'),
  ('Raj',  'raj@example.com',  'Pune'),
  ('Mei',  'mei@example.com',  'Pune'),
  ('Omar', 'omar@example.com', NULL);

INSERT INTO products (name, price, stock) VALUES
  ('Keyboard', 49.90, 12),
  ('Mouse',    19.50, 40),
  ('Monitor', 189.00,  5),
  ('Cable',     4.25,  0);

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, status, placed_on) VALUES
  (1, 'paid',    '2026-10-01'),
  (1, 'new',     '2026-10-12'),
  (2, 'paid',    '2026-10-05'),
  (3, 'shipped', '2026-10-09');

INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES
  (1, 1, 1), (1, 2, 2),
  (2, 3, 1),
  (3, 2, 1), (3, 4, 10),
  (4, 1, 2), (4, 3, 1);

SELECT id, name, city FROM customers;
CREATE TABLE customers ( id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, email text NOT NULL UNIQUE, city text, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); CREATE TABLE products ( id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0), stock integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 ); CREATE TABLE orders ( id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id), status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new', placed_on date NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE order_items ( order_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, product_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id), qty integer NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0), PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id) ); INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city) VALUES ('Ana', 'ana@example.com', 'Lisbon'), ('Raj', 'raj@example.com', 'Pune'), ('Mei', 'mei@example.com', 'Pune'), ('Omar', 'omar@example.com', NULL); INSERT INTO products (name, price, stock) VALUES ('Keyboard', 49.90, 12), ('Mouse', 19.50, 40), ('Monitor', 189.00, 5), ('Cable', 4.25, 0); INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, status, placed_on) VALUES (1, 'paid', '2026-10-01'), (1, 'new', '2026-10-12'), (2, 'paid', '2026-10-05'), (3, 'shipped', '2026-10-09'); INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES (1, 1, 1), (1, 2, 2), (2, 3, 1), (3, 2, 1), (3, 4, 10), (4, 1, 2), (4, 3, 1); SELECT id, name, city FROM customers; id | name | city ----+------+-------- 1 | Ana | Lisbon 2 | Raj | Pune 3 | Mei | Pune 4 | Omar | (4 rows)
-- filtering and sorting
SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > 10 ORDER BY price DESC;

-- LIMIT and OFFSET (take the 2nd and 3rd cheapest)
SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1;

-- pattern and list matching (ILIKE ignores case)
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE email ILIKE 'A%' OR name IN ('Raj', 'Omar');

-- NULL is "unknown": = NULL never matches, IS NULL does
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = NULL;
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city IS NULL;
SELECT name, COALESCE(city, 'unknown') AS city FROM customers ORDER BY name;

-- ranges, expressions and aliases
SELECT name, price, price * stock AS stock_value FROM products WHERE stock BETWEEN 1 AND 20;

-- text and date functions
SELECT upper(name) AS shout, length(email) AS email_len, left(email, 3) AS prefix FROM customers WHERE id = 1;
SELECT placed_on, to_char(placed_on, 'DD Mon YYYY') AS pretty, placed_on + 30 AS due FROM orders WHERE id = 1;
-- filtering and sorting SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > 10 ORDER BY price DESC; name | price ----------+-------- Monitor | 189.00 Keyboard | 49.90 Mouse | 19.50 (3 rows) -- LIMIT and OFFSET (take the 2nd and 3rd cheapest) SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1; name | price ----------+------- Mouse | 19.50 Keyboard | 49.90 (2 rows) -- pattern and list matching (ILIKE ignores case) SELECT name FROM customers WHERE email ILIKE 'A%' OR name IN ('Raj', 'Omar'); name ------ Ana Raj Omar (3 rows) -- NULL is "unknown": = NULL never matches, IS NULL does SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = NULL; name ------ (0 rows) SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city IS NULL; name ------ Omar (1 row) SELECT name, COALESCE(city, 'unknown') AS city FROM customers ORDER BY name; name | city ------+--------- Ana | Lisbon Mei | Pune Omar | unknown Raj | Pune (4 rows) -- ranges, expressions and aliases SELECT name, price, price * stock AS stock_value FROM products WHERE stock BETWEEN 1 AND 20; name | price | stock_value ----------+--------+------------- Keyboard | 49.90 | 598.80 Monitor | 189.00 | 945.00 (2 rows) -- text and date functions SELECT upper(name) AS shout, length(email) AS email_len, left(email, 3) AS prefix FROM customers WHERE id = 1; shout | email_len | prefix -------+-----------+-------- ANA | 15 | ana (1 row) SELECT placed_on, to_char(placed_on, 'DD Mon YYYY') AS pretty, placed_on + 30 AS due FROM orders WHERE id = 1; placed_on | pretty | due ------------+-------------+------------ 2026-10-01 | 01 Oct 2026 | 2026-10-31 (1 row)
-- UPDATE changes rows that match WHERE (no WHERE changes every row!)
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE name = 'Keyboard' RETURNING id, name, stock;

-- INSERT ... RETURNING gives you the generated id without a second query
INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Zed', 'zed@example.com') RETURNING id, created_at IS NOT NULL AS has_timestamp;

-- DELETE with a condition
DELETE FROM customers WHERE email = 'zed@example.com' RETURNING name;

-- the database enforces your rules, so bad data is refused
INSERT INTO products (name, price) VALUES ('Broken', -5);
INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Dup', 'ana@example.com');
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, placed_on) VALUES (999, '2026-10-20');
DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1;

-- ON DELETE CASCADE removes the children together with the parent
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, placed_on) VALUES (4, '2026-10-20') RETURNING id AS new_order \gset
INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES (:new_order, 2, 1), (:new_order, 4, 3);
SELECT count(*) AS items_before FROM order_items WHERE order_id = :new_order;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = :new_order;
SELECT count(*) AS items_after FROM order_items WHERE order_id = :new_order;
-- UPDATE changes rows that match WHERE (no WHERE changes every row!) UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE name = 'Keyboard' RETURNING id, name, stock; id | name | stock ----+----------+------- 1 | Keyboard | 11 (1 row) -- INSERT ...
