RETURNING gives you the generated id without a second query INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Zed', 'zed@example.com') RETURNING id, created_at IS NOT NULL AS has_timestamp; id | has_timestamp ----+--------------- 5 | t (1 row) -- DELETE with a condition DELETE FROM customers WHERE email = 'zed@example.com' RETURNING name; name ------ Zed (1 row) -- the database enforces your rules, so bad data is refused INSERT INTO products (name, price) VALUES ('Broken', -5); ERROR: new row for relation "products" violates check constraint "products_price_check" DETAIL: Failing row contains (5, Broken, -5.00, 0). INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Dup', 'ana@example.com'); ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "customers_email_key" DETAIL: Key (email)=(ana@example.com) already exists. INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, placed_on) VALUES (999, '2026-10-20'); ERROR: insert or update on table "orders" violates foreign key constraint "orders_customer_id_fkey" DETAIL: Key (customer_id)=(999) is not present in table "customers". DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1; ERROR: update or delete on table "customers" violates foreign key constraint "orders_customer_id_fkey" on table "orders" DETAIL: Key (id)=(1) is still referenced from table "orders". -- ON DELETE CASCADE removes the children together with the parent INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, placed_on) VALUES (4, '2026-10-20') RETURNING id AS new_order \gset INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty) VALUES (:new_order, 2, 1), (:new_order, 4, 3); SELECT count(*) AS items_before FROM order_items WHERE order_id = :new_order; items_before -------------- 2 (1 row) DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = :new_order; SELECT count(*) AS items_after FROM order_items WHERE order_id = :new_order; items_after ------------- 0 (1 row)

Look at the id of the order created above: it is not 5. The refused inserts earlier still used up identity numbers, so generated ids can have gaps. Never rely on ids being continuous, and never reuse one by hand. (\gset is a psql feature that stores a result in a variable; from Node you simply read the returned row.)

An UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE touches every row. Run the WHERE as a SELECT first, work inside a transaction in production consoles, and never build SQL by gluing user input into a string (the pg entry shows the injection and the fix).

Data is split into tables to avoid repeating it; a join puts the pieces back together for one query. INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills the right side with NULL when nothing matches (the way to find "customers with no orders").

-- who bought what (INNER JOIN: only rows that match everywhere)
SELECT c.name AS customer, o.id AS order_id, p.name AS product, i.qty, p.price * i.qty AS line_total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers   c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products    p ON p.id = i.product_id
ORDER BY o.id, p.name;

-- LEFT JOIN: keep customers even when they have no orders
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY orders DESC, c.name;

-- anti-join: customers that never ordered
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.name;
-- who bought what (INNER JOIN: only rows that match everywhere) SELECT c.name AS customer, o.id AS order_id, p.name AS product, i.qty, p.price * i.qty AS line_total FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id ORDER BY o.id, p.name; customer | order_id | product | qty | line_total ----------+----------+----------+-----+------------ Ana | 1 | Keyboard | 1 | 49.90 Ana | 1 | Mouse | 2 | 39.00 Ana | 2 | Monitor | 1 | 189.00 Raj | 3 | Cable | 10 | 42.50 Raj | 3 | Mouse | 1 | 19.50 Mei | 4 | Keyboard | 2 | 99.80 Mei | 4 | Monitor | 1 | 189.00 (7 rows) -- LEFT JOIN: keep customers even when they have no orders SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY orders DESC, c.name; name | orders ------+-------- Ana | 2 Mei | 1 Raj | 1 Omar | 0 (4 rows) -- anti-join: customers that never ordered SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.name; name ------ Omar (1 row)
-- one summary row for the whole table
SELECT COUNT(*) AS products, MIN(price) AS cheapest, MAX(price) AS dearest, ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS average, SUM(stock) AS units FROM products;

-- one summary row per group
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

-- WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping, HAVING filters groups AFTER
SELECT c.city, COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) AS customers, SUM(i.qty) AS items
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status <> 'new'
GROUP BY c.city
HAVING SUM(i.qty) > 3
ORDER BY items DESC;

-- revenue per customer, biggest first
SELECT c.name, SUM(p.price * i.qty) AS revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

-- the COUNT variants
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(city) AS non_null_cities, COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS distinct_cities FROM customers;
-- one summary row for the whole table SELECT COUNT(*) AS products, MIN(price) AS cheapest, MAX(price) AS dearest, ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS average, SUM(stock) AS units FROM products; products | cheapest | dearest | average | units ----------+----------+---------+---------+------- 4 | 4.25 | 189.00 | 65.66 | 56 (1 row) -- one summary row per group SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status; status | orders ---------+-------- new | 1 paid | 2 shipped | 1 (3 rows) -- WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping, HAVING filters groups AFTER SELECT c.city, COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) AS customers, SUM(i.qty) AS items FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status <> 'new' GROUP BY c.city HAVING SUM(i.qty) > 3 ORDER BY items DESC; city | customers | items ------+-----------+------- Pune | 2 | 14 (1 row) -- revenue per customer, biggest first SELECT c.name, SUM(p.price * i.qty) AS revenue FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY revenue DESC; name | revenue ------+--------- Mei | 288.80 Ana | 277.90 Raj | 62.00 (3 rows) -- the COUNT variants SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(city) AS non_null_cities, COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS distinct_cities FROM customers; all_rows | non_null_cities | distinct_cities ----------+-----------------+----------------- 4 | 3 | 2 (1 row)
-- scalar subquery: products dearer than the average
SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products) ORDER BY price;

-- IN with a subquery: customers who ordered a Monitor
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (
  SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id WHERE p.name = 'Monitor'
);

-- EXISTS stops at the first match: good for "has at least one"
SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid');

-- NOT IN returns nothing at all when the list contains a NULL; NOT EXISTS behaves as you expect
CREATE TEMP TABLE blocked (customer_id integer);
INSERT INTO blocked VALUES (2), (NULL);
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM blocked) ORDER BY name;
SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked b WHERE b.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY name;

-- UNION combines result sets (UNION ALL keeps duplicates and is faster)
SELECT name AS label, 'customer' AS kind FROM customers WHERE city = 'Pune'
UNION ALL
SELECT name, 'product' FROM products WHERE price < 20
ORDER BY kind, label;
-- scalar subquery: products dearer than the average SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products) ORDER BY price; name | price ---------+-------- Monitor | 189.00 (1 row) -- IN with a subquery: customers who ordered a Monitor SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN ( SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id WHERE p.name = 'Monitor' ); name ------ Ana Mei (2 rows) -- EXISTS stops at the first match: good for "has at least one" SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'); name ------ Ana Raj (2 rows) -- NOT IN returns nothing at all when the list contains a NULL; NOT EXISTS behaves as you expect CREATE TEMP TABLE blocked (customer_id integer); INSERT INTO blocked VALUES (2), (NULL); SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM blocked) ORDER BY name; name ------ (0 rows) SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked b WHERE b.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY name; name ------ Ana Mei Omar (3 rows) -- UNION combines result sets (UNION ALL keeps duplicates and is faster) SELECT name AS label, 'customer' AS kind FROM customers WHERE city = 'Pune' UNION ALL SELECT name, 'product' FROM products WHERE price < 20 ORDER BY kind, label; label | kind -------+---------- Mei | customer Raj | customer Cable | product Mouse | product (4 rows)
JoinKeeps
INNER JOIN (or JOIN)Only matching pairs
LEFT JOINAll left rows; right columns are NULL if no match
RIGHT JOINThe mirror image (rarely needed: swap the tables)
FULL JOINAll rows from both sides
CROSS JOINEvery combination (a cartesian product)
Join mistakes to avoidForgetting the ON condition multiplies rows (every row matches every row). Putting a filter on the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE silently turns it into an inner join; put it in the ON clause instead. Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must be in GROUP BY.
-- a CTE (WITH) names a sub-result so the main query reads top to bottom
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.placed_on, SUM(p.price * i.qty) AS total
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
  GROUP BY o.id
)
SELECT c.name, t.id AS order_id, t.total
FROM order_totals t JOIN customers c ON c.id = t.customer_id
WHERE t.total > 50
ORDER BY t.total DESC;

-- window functions calculate across related rows WITHOUT collapsing them
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.placed_on, SUM(p.price * i.qty) AS total
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
  GROUP BY o.id
)
SELECT id, customer_id, placed_on, total,
       SUM(total) OVER (ORDER BY placed_on)                                     AS running_total,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_on)          AS nth_order_of_customer,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total DESC)                                        AS rank_by_total,
       total - LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY placed_on)                             AS change_from_previous
FROM order_totals
ORDER BY placed_on;

-- "top 1 per group": the newest order of each customer
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id, id, placed_on FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, placed_on DESC;
-- a CTE (WITH) names a sub-result so the main query reads top to bottom WITH order_totals AS ( SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.placed_on, SUM(p.price * i.qty) AS total FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id GROUP BY o.id ) SELECT c.name, t.id AS order_id, t.total FROM order_totals t JOIN customers c ON c.id = t.customer_id WHERE t.total > 50 ORDER BY t.total DESC; name | order_id | total ------+----------+-------- Mei | 4 | 288.80 Ana | 2 | 189.00 Ana | 1 | 88.90 Raj | 3 | 62.00 (4 rows) -- window functions calculate across related rows WITHOUT collapsing them WITH order_totals AS ( SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.placed_on, SUM(p.price * i.qty) AS total FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id GROUP BY o.id ) SELECT id, customer_id, placed_on, total, SUM(total) OVER (ORDER BY placed_on) AS running_total, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_on) AS nth_order_of_customer, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total DESC) AS rank_by_total, total - LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY placed_on) AS change_from_previous FROM order_totals ORDER BY placed_on; id | customer_id | placed_on | total | running_total | nth_order_of_customer | rank_by_total | change_from_previous ----+-------------+------------+--------+---------------+-----------------------+---------------+---------------------- 1 | 1 | 2026-10-01 | 88.90 | 88.90 | 1 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2026-10-05 | 62.00 | 150.90 | 1 | 4 | -26.90 4 | 3 | 2026-10-09 | 288.80 | 439.70 | 1 | 1 | 226.80 2 | 1 | 2026-10-12 | 189.00 | 628.70 | 2 | 2 | -99.80 (4 rows) -- "top 1 per group": the newest order of each customer SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id, id, placed_on FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, placed_on DESC; customer_id | id | placed_on -------------+----+------------ 1 | 2 | 2026-10-12 2 | 3 | 2026-10-05 3 | 4 | 2026-10-09 (3 rows)
-- jsonb stores documents; -> returns json, ->> returns text, @> tests containment
CREATE TABLE events (id serial PRIMARY KEY, payload jsonb NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO events (payload) VALUES
  ('{"type":"signup","user":{"name":"Ana","plan":"free"},"tags":["web","promo"]}'),
  ('{"type":"login","user":{"name":"Raj","plan":"pro"},"tags":["mobile"]}');

SELECT payload->>'type' AS type, payload->'user'->>'name' AS name, payload #>> '{user,plan}' AS plan FROM events;
SELECT id FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"user":{"plan":"pro"}}';
SELECT id FROM events WHERE payload->'tags' ? 'promo';
UPDATE events SET payload = jsonb_set(payload, '{user,plan}', '"team"') WHERE id = 1 RETURNING payload->'user' AS user;
CREATE INDEX events_payload_gin ON events USING gin (payload);   -- makes @> and ? fast on big tables

-- generate_series builds rows from nothing (test data, calendars)
SELECT d::date AS day, to_char(d, 'Dy') AS weekday FROM generate_series('2026-10-23'::date, '2026-10-26'::date, '1 day') AS d;

-- date maths
SELECT date '2026-10-23' + 7 AS next_week, date_trunc('month', timestamp '2026-10-23 15:30') AS month_start,
       age(date '2026-10-23', date '2000-01-15') AS age, extract(dow FROM date '2026-10-23') AS day_of_week;

-- arrays and string_agg
SELECT string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name) AS names, array_agg(id ORDER BY id) AS ids FROM customers;
-- jsonb stores documents; -> returns json, ->> returns text, @> tests containment CREATE TABLE events (id serial PRIMARY KEY, payload jsonb NOT NULL); INSERT INTO events (payload) VALUES ('{"type":"signup","user":{"name":"Ana","plan":"free"},"tags":["web","promo"]}'), ('{"type":"login","user":{"name":"Raj","plan":"pro"},"tags":["mobile"]}'); SELECT payload->>'type' AS type, payload->'user'->>'name' AS name, payload #>> '{user,plan}' AS plan FROM events; type | name | plan --------+------+------ signup | Ana | free login | Raj | pro (2 rows) SELECT id FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"user":{"plan":"pro"}}'; id ---- 2 (1 row) SELECT id FROM events WHERE payload->'tags' ? 'promo'; id ---- 1 (1 row) UPDATE events SET payload = jsonb_set(payload, '{user,plan}', '"team"') WHERE id = 1 RETURNING payload->'user' AS user; user --------------------------------- {"name": "Ana", "plan": "team"} (1 row) CREATE INDEX events_payload_gin ON events USING gin (payload); -- makes @> and ? fast on big tables -- generate_series builds rows from nothing (test data, calendars) SELECT d::date AS day, to_char(d, 'Dy') AS weekday FROM generate_series('2026-10-23'::date, '2026-10-26'::date, '1 day') AS d; day | weekday ------------+--------- 2026-10-23 | Fri 2026-10-24 | Sat 2026-10-25 | Sun 2026-10-26 | Mon (4 rows) -- date maths SELECT date '2026-10-23' + 7 AS next_week, date_trunc('month', timestamp '2026-10-23 15:30') AS month_start, age(date '2026-10-23', date '2000-01-15') AS age, extract(dow FROM date '2026-10-23') AS day_of_week; next_week | month_start | age | day_of_week ------------+---------------------+------------------------+------------- 2026-10-30 | 2026-10-01 00:00:00 | 26 years 9 mons 8 days | 5 (1 row) -- arrays and string_agg SELECT string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name) AS names, array_agg(id ORDER BY id) AS ids FROM customers; names | ids ---------------------+----------- Ana, Mei, Omar, Raj | {1,2,3,4} (1 row)
-- upsert: insert, or update if the unique key already exists (atomic, race-free)
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city) VALUES ('Ana Silva', 'ana@example.com', 'Porto')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name, city = EXCLUDED.city
RETURNING id, name, city;

-- ignore duplicates silently
INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Raj again', 'raj@example.com') ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers FROM customers;

-- counters without a read-modify-write race
CREATE TABLE page_hits (page text PRIMARY KEY, hits integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0);
INSERT INTO page_hits VALUES ('/home', 1) ON CONFLICT (page) DO UPDATE SET hits = page_hits.hits + 1;
INSERT INTO page_hits VALUES ('/home', 1) ON CONFLICT (page) DO UPDATE SET hits = page_hits.hits + 1;
SELECT * FROM page_hits;

-- the single most useful statement for queues: claim a row nobody else has claimed
CREATE TABLE jobs (id serial PRIMARY KEY, task text, state text DEFAULT 'queued');
INSERT INTO jobs (task) VALUES ('send email'), ('resize image');
UPDATE jobs SET state = 'running'
WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE state = 'queued' ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1)
RETURNING id, task, state;
-- upsert: insert, or update if the unique key already exists (atomic, race-free) INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city) VALUES ('Ana Silva', 'ana@example.com', 'Porto') ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name, city = EXCLUDED.city RETURNING id, name, city; id | name | city ----+-----------+------- 1 | Ana Silva | Porto (1 row) -- ignore duplicates silently INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Raj again', 'raj@example.com') ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING; SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers FROM customers; customers ----------- 4 (1 row) -- counters without a read-modify-write race CREATE TABLE page_hits (page text PRIMARY KEY, hits integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0); INSERT INTO page_hits VALUES ('/home', 1) ON CONFLICT (page) DO UPDATE SET hits = page_hits.hits + 1; INSERT INTO page_hits VALUES ('/home', 1) ON CONFLICT (page) DO UPDATE SET hits = page_hits.hits + 1; SELECT * FROM page_hits; page | hits -------+------ /home | 2 (1 row) -- the single most useful statement for queues: claim a row nobody else has claimed CREATE TABLE jobs (id serial PRIMARY KEY, task text, state text DEFAULT 'queued'); INSERT INTO jobs (task) VALUES ('send email'), ('resize image'); UPDATE jobs SET state = 'running' WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE state = 'queued' ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1) RETURNING id, task, state; id | task | state ----+------------+--------- 1 | send email | running (1 row)

Designing tables

  • One fact in one place (normalization). If a customer's city is copied onto every order, changing it means updating thousands of rows, and some will be missed. Put it in customers and reference it by id.
  • One-to-many: the "many" side holds a foreign key to the "one" (orders.customer_id). Many-to-many: a join table with two foreign keys (order_items: orders and products). One-to-one: a foreign key that is also UNIQUE.
  • Let the database enforce rules: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, REFERENCES. Application checks can be bypassed (a second service, a script, a bug); constraints cannot.
  • Normal forms in one breath: 1NF no repeating groups or lists in a column; 2NF every column depends on the whole key; 3NF columns depend on the key and nothing but the key. Denormalize on purpose, later, for a measured speed reason.
  • Use timestamptz, numeric for money (or integer cents), text for strings, identity or UUID primary keys, and created_at/updated_at on most tables.

Indexes

Without an index the database reads every row to answer a filter (a sequential scan). A B-tree index is a sorted structure that finds a row in a handful of steps, like a book index. The price: extra disk and slower writes, since each index must be updated. Primary keys and UNIQUE constraints get one automatically; foreign key columns do not, and joins on them need one.

CREATE TABLE users (id serial PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL, country text NOT NULL, created_at date NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO users (email, country, created_at)
SELECT 'user' || n || '@example.com', (ARRAY['PT','IN','US','BR','JP'])[1 + n % 5], date '2024-01-01' + (n % 700)
FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS n;
ANALYZE users;

-- no index on email yet: Postgres must read the whole table
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user77777@example.com';

CREATE INDEX users_email_idx ON users (email);
ANALYZE users;

-- now it jumps straight to the row
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user77777@example.com';

-- the index is not used when you wrap the column in a function...
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'user77777@example.com';
-- ...unless you index the same expression
CREATE INDEX users_lower_email_idx ON users (lower(email));
ANALYZE users;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'user77777@example.com';

-- a column with only 5 distinct values matches a fifth of the table (see rows=...), so an index helps far less
CREATE INDEX users_country_idx ON users (country);
ANALYZE users;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE country = 'PT';
CREATE TABLE users (id serial PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL, country text NOT NULL, created_at date NOT NULL); INSERT INTO users (email, country, created_at) SELECT 'user' || n || '@example.com', (ARRAY['PT','IN','US','BR','JP'])[1 + n % 5], date '2024-01-01' + (n % 700) FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS n; ANALYZE users; -- no index on email yet: Postgres must read the whole table EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user77777@example.com'; QUERY PLAN --------------------------------------------------------- Seq Scan on users (cost=0.00..2074.00 rows=1 width=32) Filter: (email = 'user77777@example.com'::text) (2 rows) CREATE INDEX users_email_idx ON users (email); ANALYZE users; -- now it jumps straight to the row EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user77777@example.com'; QUERY PLAN ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Index Scan using users_email_idx on users (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=32) Index Cond: (email = 'user77777@example.com'::text) (2 rows) -- the index is not used when you wrap the column in a function... EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'user77777@example.com'; QUERY PLAN ----------------------------------------------------------- Seq Scan on users (cost=0.00..2324.00 rows=500 width=32) Filter: (lower(email) = 'user77777@example.com'::text) (2 rows) -- ...unless you index the same expression CREATE INDEX users_lower_email_idx ON users (lower(email)); ANALYZE users; EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'user77777@example.com'; QUERY PLAN ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Index Scan using users_lower_email_idx on users (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=32) Index Cond: (lower(email) = 'user77777@example.com'::text) (2 rows) -- a column with only 5 distinct values matches a fifth of the table (see rows=...), so an index helps far less CREATE INDEX users_country_idx ON users (country); ANALYZE users; EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE country = 'PT'; QUERY PLAN -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Bitmap Heap Scan on users (cost=225.51..1296.63 rows=19770 width=32) Recheck Cond: (country = 'PT'::text) -> Bitmap Index Scan on users_country_idx (cost=0.00..220.57 rows=19770 width=0) Index Cond: (country = 'PT'::text) (4 rows)
Index ideaUse
CREATE INDEX ON t (col)Equality, range and sort on one column
Composite (a, b)Filters on a, or on a and b. Column order matters: it does not help a filter on b alone
UNIQUE indexEnforces uniqueness (and speeds lookups)
Partial WHERE status = 'new'Small index over only the rows you query
Expression (lower(email))Case-insensitive search
GINjsonb, arrays, full-text search
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLYBuild on a live table without blocking writes

Reading EXPLAIN and fixing pagination

EXPLAIN shows the plan the database chose; EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and shows real times (it really executes, so wrap writes in a transaction you roll back). Look for Seq Scan on big tables, estimated versus actual row counts that differ wildly (run ANALYZE), and sorts that spill to disk. Entry rest-pagination showed why offset pages get slower and unstable; the fix is keyset pagination, which an index on the sort columns makes cheap.

CREATE INDEX users_created_id_idx ON users (created_at, id);
ANALYZE users;

-- page 2000 by OFFSET: the database walks and throws away 99,980 rows first
EXPLAIN SELECT id, created_at FROM users ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 99980;

-- keyset: "give me 20 rows after the last one I saw", answered straight from the index
EXPLAIN SELECT id, created_at FROM users WHERE (created_at, id) > ('2025-11-20', 99000) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 20;

-- the rows of that keyset page (the client sends back the last created_at and id it saw)
SELECT id, created_at FROM users WHERE (created_at, id) > ('2025-11-20', 99000) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 3;
CREATE INDEX users_created_id_idx ON users (created_at, id); ANALYZE users; -- page 2000 by OFFSET: the database walks and throws away 99,980 rows first EXPLAIN SELECT id, created_at FROM users ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 99980; QUERY PLAN ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Limit (cost=5899.10..5900.28 rows=20 width=8) -> Index Only Scan using users_created_id_idx on users (cost=0.29..5900.28 rows=100000 width=8) (2 rows) -- keyset: "give me 20 rows after the last one I saw", answered straight from the index EXPLAIN SELECT id, created_at FROM users WHERE (created_at, id) > ('2025-11-20', 99000) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 20; QUERY PLAN --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Limit (cost=0.29..43.42 rows=20 width=8) -> Index Only Scan using users_created_id_idx on users (cost=0.29..3141.77 rows=1457 width=8) Index Cond: (ROW(created_at, id) > ROW('2025-11-20'::date, 99000)) (3 rows) -- the rows of that keyset page (the client sends back the last created_at and id it saw) SELECT id, created_at FROM users WHERE (created_at, id) > ('2025-11-20', 99000) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 3; id | created_at -------+------------ 99389 | 2025-11-20 690 | 2025-11-21 1390 | 2025-11-21 (3 rows)
Index habitsIndex the columns you filter, join and sort on, then measure with EXPLAIN instead of guessing. Drop indexes nobody uses (pg_stat_user_indexes shows scans). Do not index everything: every index slows every insert, update and delete.

A transaction groups statements into one all-or-nothing unit. Every statement already runs in one implicitly; you write BEGIN ... COMMIT when several statements must succeed together (order plus items plus stock change, a money transfer). If anything fails, ROLLBACK undoes the lot.

CREATE TABLE accounts (id int PRIMARY KEY, owner text, balance numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0));
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'Ana', 100), (2, 'Raj', 50);

-- a transfer: both updates happen or neither
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 30 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY id;

-- you changed your mind: ROLLBACK discards everything since BEGIN
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT balance AS inside_the_transaction FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT balance AS after_rollback FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;

-- an error inside a transaction poisons it: the CHECK refuses the debit,
-- the next statement is rejected, and only ROLLBACK is accepted
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT 1;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY id;
CREATE TABLE accounts (id int PRIMARY KEY, owner text, balance numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0)); INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'Ana', 100), (2, 'Raj', 50); -- a transfer: both updates happen or neither BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 30 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT; SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY id; id | owner | balance ----+-------+--------- 1 | Ana | 70.00 2 | Raj | 80.00 (2 rows) -- you changed your mind: ROLLBACK discards everything since BEGIN BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0 WHERE id = 1; SELECT balance AS inside_the_transaction FROM accounts WHERE id = 1; inside_the_transaction ------------------------ 0.00 (1 row) ROLLBACK; SELECT balance AS after_rollback FROM accounts WHERE id = 1; after_rollback ---------------- 70.00 (1 row) -- an error inside a transaction poisons it: the CHECK refuses the debit, -- the next statement is rejected, and only ROLLBACK is accepted BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1; ERROR: new row for relation "accounts" violates check constraint "accounts_balance_check" DETAIL: Failing row contains (1, Ana, -430.00). SELECT 1; ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block ROLLBACK; SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY id; id | owner | balance ----+-------+--------- 1 | Ana | 70.00 2 | Raj | 80.00 (2 rows)
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 5 WHERE id = 1;      -- step 1: keep this
SAVEPOINT before_risky_step;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE id = 2;   -- step 2: fails the CHECK
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_risky_step;                     -- undo only step 2; the transaction is usable again
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1 WHERE id = 2;      -- step 3
COMMIT;
SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY id;
BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 5 WHERE id = 1; -- step 1: keep this SAVEPOINT before_risky_step; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE id = 2; -- step 2: fails the CHECK ERROR: new row for relation "accounts" violates check constraint "accounts_balance_check" DETAIL: Failing row contains (2, Raj, -920.00). ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_risky_step; -- undo only step 2; the transaction is usable again UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1 WHERE id = 2; -- step 3 COMMIT; SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY id; id | owner | balance ----+-------+--------- 1 | Ana | 75.00 2 | Raj | 81.00 (2 rows)

Isolation and locks

When transactions overlap, the isolation level decides what one may see of the other. Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED: each statement sees only data committed before it started.

LevelWhat you getCost
READ COMMITTED (default)No dirty reads; two reads in one transaction can differCheapest; use row locks or atomic updates for read-then-write logic
REPEATABLE READOne consistent snapshot for the whole transaction; conflicting updates fail with a serialization errorYour code must retry on error 40001
SERIALIZABLEBehaves as if transactions ran one after anotherMore retries; the safest for tricky invariants
  • Atomic updates beat read-modify-write: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 30 checks and changes in one step, and the row count tells you whether it worked.
  • Row locks: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the rows you read until the transaction ends, so a second transaction waits. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED skips rows others hold (queues). NOWAIT fails instead of waiting.
  • Deadlock: A waits for B while B waits for A. Postgres detects it and aborts one with error 40P01. Prevent it by always locking rows in the same order, and keep transactions short (no HTTP calls inside one).
  • Optimistic locking with a version column (the same idea as If-Match in Unit 5) avoids holding locks while a user thinks. Two overlapping transactions, a real lock wait, a deadlock and the retry pattern are run for real in the pg entry next.
-- choose the level when the transaction starts
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SHOW transaction_isolation;
COMMIT;

-- check and change in ONE statement; no row returned means "not enough money"
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 70 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 70 RETURNING id, balance;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 70 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 70 RETURNING id, balance;
-- choose the level when the transaction starts BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SHOW transaction_isolation; transaction_isolation ----------------------- repeatable read (1 row) COMMIT; -- check and change in ONE statement; no row returned means "not enough money" UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 70 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 70 RETURNING id, balance; id | balance ----+--------- 1 | 5.00 (1 row) UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 70 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 70 RETURNING id, balance; id | balance ----+--------- (0 rows)

SQLite is a complete SQL database that lives in a single file and runs inside your process: no server, no network, no password. It is perfect for tests, command-line tools, prototypes, desktop and mobile apps, and surprisingly many small production sites. It allows one writer at a time (many readers), so it is a poor fit once many app servers need to write to the same data. Everything you learned in SQL applies, with a few differences: types are flexible (a column's declared type is only a hint unless the table is STRICT), there is no real boolean or date type (use INTEGER 0/1 and ISO text), and foreign keys are off until you turn them on.

Two ways to use it from Node: the popular better-sqlite3 package (a fast, synchronous API, which is fine here because the database is in-process), and the built-in node:sqlite module (DatabaseSync) that ships with Node 22.

import Database from "better-sqlite3";

const db = new Database("notes.db");                      // a file; use ":memory:" for tests
db.pragma("journal_mode = WAL");                          // readers do not block the writer
db.pragma("foreign_keys = ON");                           // off by default in SQLite!

db.exec(`
  CREATE TABLE notes (
    id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    title   TEXT NOT NULL,
    done    INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (done IN (0, 1)),
    created TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
  ) STRICT
`);

// prepare once, run many times. ? and :name are placeholders: never glue values into the SQL
const insert = db.prepare("INSERT INTO notes (title) VALUES (:title)");
console.log("run:", insert.run({ title: "buy milk" }));          // { changes, lastInsertRowid }
insert.run({ title: "write guide" });

console.log("get:", db.prepare("SELECT id, title, done FROM notes WHERE id = ?").get(1));       // one row or undefined
console.log("all:", db.prepare("SELECT id, title FROM notes ORDER BY id").all());              // array of rows
console.log("pluck:", db.prepare("SELECT title FROM notes WHERE id = ?").pluck().get(2));       // just the value
console.log("missing:", db.prepare("SELECT * FROM notes WHERE id = ?").get(99));

for (const row of db.prepare("SELECT id, title FROM notes").iterate()) console.log("iterate:", row.id, row.title);   // row by row, no big array

console.log("journal_mode:", db.pragma("journal_mode", { simple: true }));
run: { changes: 1, lastInsertRowid: 1 } get: { id: 1, title: 'buy milk', done: 0 } all: [ { id: 1, title: 'buy milk' }, { id: 2, title: 'write guide' } ] pluck: write guide missing: undefined iterate: 1 buy milk iterate: 2 write guide journal_mode: wal
import Database from "better-sqlite3";
const db = new Database(":memory:");
db.pragma("foreign_keys = ON");
db.exec(`
  CREATE TABLE authors (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE) STRICT;
  CREATE TABLE books (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, author_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES authors(id), pages INTEGER) STRICT;
`);
const addAuthor = db.prepare("INSERT INTO authors (name) VALUES (?)");
const addBook = db.prepare("INSERT INTO books (title, author_id, pages) VALUES (?, ?, ?)");

// db.transaction wraps a function: it commits when the function returns, rolls back if it throws
const addAuthorWithBooks = db.transaction((name, titles) => {
  const { lastInsertRowid } = addAuthor.run(name);
  for (const title of titles) addBook.run(title, lastInsertRowid, 200);
  return titles.length;
});
console.log("added books:", addAuthorWithBooks("Ursula", ["Earthsea", "The Dispossessed"]));

try { addAuthorWithBooks("Octavia", ["Kindred", null]); }                 // the null title violates NOT NULL, so the author is rolled back too
catch (e) { console.log("rolled back because:", e.code); }
console.log("authors now:", db.prepare("SELECT name FROM authors").all());

for (const [label, fn] of [
  ["duplicate name      ", () => addAuthor.run("Ursula")],
  ["unknown author id   ", () => addBook.run("Ghost", 999, 1)],
  ["text in INTEGER col ", () => addBook.run("Bad", 1, "many")],
]) { try { fn(); } catch (e) { console.log(label, e.code, "|", e.message); } }

// a join works exactly like Postgres
console.log(db.prepare("SELECT a.name, count(*) AS books FROM authors a JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id GROUP BY a.id").all());
added books: 2 rolled back because: SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_NOTNULL authors now: [ { name: 'Ursula' } ] duplicate name SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE | UNIQUE constraint failed: authors.name unknown author id SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_FOREIGNKEY | FOREIGN KEY constraint failed text in INTEGER col SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_DATATYPE | cannot store TEXT value in INTEGER column books.pages [ { name: 'Ursula', books: 2 } ]
import { DatabaseSync } from "node:sqlite";

const db = new DatabaseSync(":memory:");
db.exec("CREATE TABLE kv (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT) STRICT");
const set = db.prepare("INSERT INTO kv VALUES (?, ?) ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET value = excluded.value");
set.run("theme", "dark");
set.run("theme", "light");                                       // upsert, same SQL as Postgres
console.log(db.prepare("SELECT * FROM kv").all());               // all() returns an array of rows (objects with no prototype)
console.log(db.prepare("SELECT value FROM kv WHERE key = ?").get("theme"));
[ [Object: null prototype] { key: 'theme', value: 'light' } ] [Object: null prototype] { value: 'light' }
Choose SQLite whenChoose Postgres when
One process or one server owns the dataSeveral app servers share the data
Tests, scripts, local tools, edge or embeddedMany concurrent writers, heavy write load
You want zero setup and a single-file backupYou need roles, replicas, rich types, extensions (PostGIS, pgvector)
Practical notesBecause better-sqlite3 is synchronous, a very slow query blocks the event loop, so keep queries short and indexed. Put the database file on a persistent volume (a container's own disk is wiped on redeploy) and back it up with VACUUM INTO 'backup.db' or the backup API, not by copying the file while it is being written. SQLite also has full-text search (FTS5) and JSON functions built in.

pg (node-postgres) is the standard driver. You create one Pool per process at startup and share it everywhere. pool.query(sql, params) borrows a connection, runs the statement and returns it. The connection string below points at the local database created for this guide; in a real app it comes from process.env.DATABASE_URL (Unit 10).

import pg from "pg";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb", max: 5 });

await pool.query("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS pg_people");
await pool.query(`CREATE TABLE pg_people (
  id serial PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, balance numeric(10,2) NOT NULL, visits bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  born date, meta jsonb, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now())`);

// $1, $2 are placeholders: the values travel separately from the SQL text, so they can never become SQL
const inserted = await pool.query(
  "INSERT INTO pg_people (name, balance, born, meta) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4) RETURNING id, name",
  ["Ana", "19.99", "1990-05-17", { langs: ["pt", "en"] }],          // objects are sent as JSON
);
console.log("rows:", inserted.rows, "| rowCount:", inserted.rowCount, "| command:", inserted.command);

const { rows, fields } = await pool.query("SELECT * FROM pg_people WHERE id = $1", [1]);
console.log("columns:", fields.map((f) => f.name).join(", "));
const p = rows[0];
console.log("numeric  ->", typeof p.balance, JSON.stringify(p.balance), "(a string, so no rounding surprises)");
console.log("bigint   ->", typeof p.visits, JSON.stringify(p.visits), "(a string: it may not fit in a double)");
console.log("date     ->", p.born instanceof Date ? "a Date object" : typeof p.born);
console.log("timestamptz ->", p.created_at instanceof Date ? "a Date object" : typeof p.created_at);
console.log("jsonb    ->", typeof p.meta, JSON.stringify(p.meta));

// you can change how types arrive. Parsers are global, so set them once at startup
pg.types.setTypeParser(pg.types.builtins.DATE, (text) => text);                    // keep "1990-05-17" as text: no time zone surprises
pg.types.setTypeParser(pg.types.builtins.INT8, (text) => Number(text));            // fine while counts stay below 9 quadrillion
const again = (await pool.query("SELECT born, visits FROM pg_people")).rows[0];
console.log("after custom parsers:", again);

await pool.query("DROP TABLE pg_people");
await pool.end();                                                                  // close every connection (needed or the script never exits)
rows: [ { id: 1, name: 'Ana' } ] | rowCount: 1 | command: INSERT columns: id, name, balance, visits, born, meta, created_at numeric -> string "19.99" (a string, so no rounding surprises) bigint -> string "0" (a string: it may not fit in a double) date -> a Date object timestamptz -> a Date object jsonb -> object {"langs":["pt","en"]} after custom parsers: { born: '1990-05-17', visits: 0 }
Never build SQL by joining strings with user input. That is SQL injection, still one of the most common ways sites are breached. Placeholders ($1) are the cure, because the database receives the query and the values separately. Two limits to remember: placeholders cannot stand in for table or column names (check those against an allow-list in your code) and they are not interpolated into LIKE patterns for you (put the % in the value).
import pg from "pg";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb" });
await pool.query("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS pg_users");
await pool.query("CREATE TABLE pg_users (id serial PRIMARY KEY, name text, secret text)");
await pool.query("INSERT INTO pg_users (name, secret) VALUES ('ana', 'ana-secret'), ('raj', 'raj-secret')");

// VULNERABLE: the input becomes part of the SQL
async function findUnsafe(name) {
  const sql = `SELECT name, secret FROM pg_users WHERE name = '${name}'`;
  console.log("  sql sent:", sql);
  return (await pool.query(sql)).rows;
}
// SAFE: the same input is only ever a value
async function findSafe(name) {
  return (await pool.query("SELECT name, secret FROM pg_users WHERE name = $1", [name])).rows;
}

const attack = "nobody' OR '1'='1";
console.log("unsafe, honest input:", await findUnsafe("ana"));
console.log("unsafe, attacker input:");
console.log("  returns", (await findUnsafe(attack)).length, "rows: every user's secret leaked");
console.log("safe, attacker input:", await findSafe(attack));

// stacked statements: without values the server runs every statement it is sent; with placeholders it refuses more than one
const stacked = await pool.query("SELECT 1; SELECT 2");
console.log("no placeholders: ran", stacked.length, "statements in one call");
try { await pool.query("SELECT $1; SELECT 2", ["x"]); }
catch (e) { console.log("with placeholders:", e.message); }

await pool.query("DROP TABLE pg_users");
await pool.end();
sql sent: SELECT name, secret FROM pg_users WHERE name = 'ana' unsafe, honest input: [ { name: 'ana', secret: 'ana-secret' } ] unsafe, attacker input: sql sent: SELECT name, secret FROM pg_users WHERE name = 'nobody' OR '1'='1' returns 2 rows: every user's secret leaked safe, attacker input: [] no placeholders: ran 2 statements in one call with placeholders: cannot insert multiple commands into a prepared statement

Transactions with a dedicated client

A transaction must run on one connection. pool.query may use a different connection for each call, so pool.query("BEGIN") followed by more pool.query calls is a bug. Instead check a client out with pool.connect(), run BEGIN ... COMMIT on it, and always release it in finally. Wrap that once in a helper and reuse it.

import pg from "pg";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb" });

async function withTransaction(work) {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");
    const result = await work(client);            // use `client`, never `pool`, inside
    await client.query("COMMIT");
    return result;
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();                             // forgetting this slowly empties the pool
  }
}

await pool.query("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS pg_accounts");
await pool.query("CREATE TABLE pg_accounts (id int PRIMARY KEY, owner text, balance int NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0))");
await pool.query("INSERT INTO pg_accounts VALUES (1, 'Ana', 100), (2, 'Raj', 20)");
const balances = async () => (await pool.query("SELECT owner, balance FROM pg_accounts ORDER BY id")).rows.map((r) => `${r.owner}=${r.balance}`).join(" ");

async function transfer(from, to, amount) {
  return withTransaction(async (client) => {
    const debit = await client.query("UPDATE pg_accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1", [amount, from]);
    if (debit.rowCount === 0) throw new Error("insufficient funds");      // thrown after BEGIN: everything rolls back
    await client.query("UPDATE pg_accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2", [amount, to]);
    return "ok";
  });
}

console.log("start:           ", await balances());
console.log("transfer 30:     ", await transfer(1, 2, 30), "->", await balances());
console.log("transfer 500:    ", await transfer(1, 2, 500).catch((e) => e.message), "->", await balances());

// a failure in the middle undoes the first half as well
try {
  await withTransaction(async (client) => {
    await client.query("UPDATE pg_accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1");
    throw new Error("something else broke");
  });
} catch (e) {
  console.log("mid-way failure: ", e.message, "->", await balances());
}

await pool.query("DROP TABLE pg_accounts");
await pool.end();
start: Ana=100 Raj=20 transfer 30: ok -> Ana=70 Raj=50 transfer 500: insufficient funds -> Ana=70 Raj=50 mid-way failure: something else broke -> Ana=70 Raj=50

Concurrency for real: lost updates, locks, deadlocks and retries

Everything above works on a quiet database. Under load, many requests overlap, and these are the failures that appear. All of them are run below with real concurrent connections.

import pg from "pg";
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb", max: 12 });
await pool.query("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS pg_counter");
await pool.query("CREATE TABLE pg_counter (id int PRIMARY KEY, n int NOT NULL)");
await pool.query("INSERT INTO pg_counter VALUES (1, 0)");
const clients = await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => pool.connect()));   // ten requests in flight at once

// 1. read-modify-write in JavaScript: every request reads 0, adds one, writes 1
const seen = await Promise.all(clients.map((c) => c.query("SELECT n FROM pg_counter WHERE id = 1")));
await Promise.all(clients.map((c, i) => c.query("UPDATE pg_counter SET n = $1 WHERE id = 1", [seen[i].rows[0].n + 1])));
console.log("10 increments with read-then-write ->", (await pool.query("SELECT n FROM pg_counter")).rows[0].n, "(nine updates were lost)");

// 2. let the database do the arithmetic atomically
await pool.query("UPDATE pg_counter SET n = 0 WHERE id = 1");
await Promise.all(clients.map((c) => c.query("UPDATE pg_counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = 1")));
console.log("10 increments with n = n + 1       ->", (await pool.query("SELECT n FROM pg_counter")).rows[0].n);
clients.forEach((c) => c.release());

// 3. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE: the second transaction waits for the first to finish
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([pool.connect(), pool.connect()]);
await a.query("BEGIN");
await a.query("SELECT * FROM pg_counter WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE");                 // A holds the row lock
setTimeout(() => a.query("COMMIT"), 300);                                           // ...for 300 ms
const started = Date.now();
await b.query("BEGIN");
await b.query("SELECT * FROM pg_counter WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE");                 // B blocks until A commits
console.log("B waited for A's lock for about 300 ms:", Date.now() - started >= 250);
await b.query("COMMIT");

// 4. NOWAIT: fail immediately instead of waiting
await a.query("BEGIN");
await a.query("SELECT * FROM pg_counter WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE");
await b.query("BEGIN");
await b.query("SELECT * FROM pg_counter WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT").catch((e) => console.log("NOWAIT ->", e.code, e.message));
await b.query("ROLLBACK"); await a.query("ROLLBACK");
a.release(); b.release();

await pool.query("DROP TABLE pg_counter");
await pool.end();
10 increments with read-then-write -> 1 (nine updates were lost) 10 increments with n = n + 1 -> 10 B waited for A's lock for about 300 ms: true NOWAIT -> 55P03 could not obtain lock on row in relation "pg_counter"
import pg from "pg";
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb", max: 6 });
await pool.query("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS pg_dead");
await pool.query("CREATE TABLE pg_dead (id int PRIMARY KEY, n int NOT NULL)");
await pool.query("INSERT INTO pg_dead VALUES (1, 100), (2, 100)");

// Run a whole transaction again if Postgres says it was a victim of concurrency (40P01 deadlock, 40001 serialization)
async function retrying(label, work, log) {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= 5; attempt++) {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    try {
      await client.query("BEGIN");
      await work(client);
      await client.query("COMMIT");
      return attempt;
    } catch (err) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");
      if (!["40P01", "40001"].includes(err.code)) throw err;           // a real bug: do not retry
      log.push(`${label} attempt ${attempt}: ${err.code} ${err.message}`);
      await sleep(20 * attempt + Math.random() * 20);                    // back off, with jitter
    } finally { client.release(); }
  }
  throw new Error(`${label} gave up`);
}

// two transfers lock the same two rows in OPPOSITE order: the classic deadlock
const lockInOrder = (first, second) => async (c) => {
  await c.query("UPDATE pg_dead SET n = n - 1 WHERE id = $1", [first]);
  await sleep(100);                                                      // both now hold one row and want the other
  await c.query("UPDATE pg_dead SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = $1", [second]);
};
const log = [];
await Promise.all([retrying("A", lockInOrder(1, 2), log), retrying("B", lockInOrder(2, 1), log)]);
console.log("deadlock victims retried:", log.length, "| error codes:", [...new Set(log.map((l) => l.split(" ")[3]))].join(","));
console.log("both transfers eventually committed:", JSON.stringify((await pool.query("SELECT id, n FROM pg_dead ORDER BY id")).rows));

// the cure for deadlocks: every code path locks rows in the SAME order (lowest id first)
const ordered = (a, b) => lockInOrder(Math.min(a, b), Math.max(a, b));
const log2 = [];
await Promise.all([retrying("A", ordered(1, 2), log2), retrying("B", ordered(2, 1), log2)]);
console.log("same lock order -> deadlocks:", log2.length);

// REPEATABLE READ: two transactions read, then both update the same row: one gets 40001
const log3 = [];
const bump = async (c) => {
  await c.query("SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ");
  const { rows } = await c.query("SELECT n FROM pg_dead WHERE id = 1");
  await sleep(100);
  await c.query("UPDATE pg_dead SET n = $1 WHERE id = 1", [rows[0].n + 10]);
};
await Promise.all([retrying("S1", bump, log3), retrying("S2", bump, log3)]);
console.log("serialization failures retried:", log3.length, "| code:", log3[0]?.split(" ")[3]);
console.log("id 1 after both bumps (98 + 10 + 10, nothing lost):", (await pool.query("SELECT n FROM pg_dead WHERE id = 1")).rows[0].n);

await pool.query("DROP TABLE pg_dead");
await pool.end();
deadlock victims retried: 1 | error codes: 40P01 both transfers eventually committed: [{"id":1,"n":100},{"id":2,"n":100}] same lock order -> deadlocks: 0 serialization failures retried: 1 | code: 40001 id 1 after both bumps (98 + 10 + 10, nothing lost): 118

Errors have codes: turn them into HTTP answers

A failed query throws an error with a five-character SQLSTATE code plus constraint, table and detail. Map the ones you expect to proper status codes; let everything else become a generic 500 (Unit 4's error middleware).

CodeMeaningTypical HTTP answer
23505unique_violation409 Conflict ("email already registered")
23503foreign_key_violation409 or 422 (the referenced row is missing, or still referenced)
23502 / 23514not_null / check violation400 or 422 (validation should have caught it)
22P02invalid_text_representation ('abc' as an integer)400
40001 / 40P01serialization failure / deadlockRetry the transaction; 503 if it keeps failing
55P03lock_not_available (NOWAIT)409 or 423
57014query canceled (statement timeout)503 or 504
53300 / 08xxxtoo many connections / connection trouble503, and alert someone
42P01 / 42703undefined table / column500: a bug or a missed migration
 
import pg from "pg";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb" });
await pool.query("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS pg_member, pg_team");
await pool.query("CREATE TABLE pg_team (id int PRIMARY KEY)");
await pool.query("CREATE TABLE pg_member (id serial PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL UNIQUE, team_id int REFERENCES pg_team(id))");
await pool.query("INSERT INTO pg_team VALUES (1)");
await pool.query("INSERT INTO pg_member (email, team_id) VALUES ('ana@example.com', 1)");

const toHttp = (err) => ({ "23505": 409, "23503": 409, "23502": 422, "22P02": 400, "40001": 503, "40P01": 503 })[err.code] ?? 500;

const attempts = {
  "duplicate email": () => pool.query("INSERT INTO pg_member (email) VALUES ('ana@example.com')"),
  "unknown team   ": () => pool.query("INSERT INTO pg_member (email, team_id) VALUES ('raj@example.com', 99)"),
  "missing email  ": () => pool.query("INSERT INTO pg_member (email) VALUES (NULL)"),
  "bad integer    ": () => pool.query("SELECT $1::int", ["abc"]),
  "typo in table  ": () => pool.query("SELECT * FROM pg_memberz"),
};
for (const [label, run] of Object.entries(attempts)) {
  try { await run(); } catch (e) {
    console.log(label, e.code, `-> HTTP ${toHttp(e)}`, "|", e.constraint ?? e.table ?? "-", "|", e.message);
  }
}
// the driver's error is a normal Error subclass with extra fields
const err = await pool.query("SELECT * FROM pg_memberz").catch((e) => e);
console.log("instanceof Error:", err instanceof Error, "| class:", err.constructor.name);

await pool.query("DROP TABLE pg_member, pg_team");
await pool.end();
duplicate email 23505 -> HTTP 409 | pg_member_email_key | duplicate key value violates unique constraint "pg_member_email_key" unknown team 23503 -> HTTP 409 | pg_member_team_id_fkey | insert or update on table "pg_member" violates foreign key constraint "pg_member_team_id_fkey" missing email 23502 -> HTTP 422 | pg_member | null value in column "email" of relation "pg_member" violates not-null constraint bad integer 22P02 -> HTTP 400 | - | invalid input syntax for type integer: "abc" typo in table 42P01 -> HTTP 500 | - | relation "pg_memberz" does not exist instanceof Error: true | class: DatabaseError
Do not leak database messages to clients. e.message and e.detail contain table names, constraint names and sometimes the data itself (Key (email)=(ana@example.com) already exists). Log them, and send the client your own sentence.

The pool: sizing, limits and shutdown

OptionMeaning and advice
max (default 10)Most connections this process opens. A request that needs one when all are busy waits in a queue. Total across all processes must stay under the server's max_connections (100 by default): 4 app instances with max: 10 already use 40.
connectionTimeoutMillisHow long a request may wait for a free connection before failing (default: forever, so set it, for example 2000)
idleTimeoutMillisClose connections unused for this long (default 10 s)
statement_timeout, query_timeoutCancel queries that run too long, so one bad query cannot hold a connection forever
pool.on("error", fn)Idle clients can fail (the database restarts). Without a handler this crashes your process.
await pool.end()On shutdown, after the HTTP server stops accepting requests
 
import pg from "pg";
const pool = new pg.Pool({
  connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb",
  max: 2,                                   // tiny on purpose
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 300,             // give up waiting after 300 ms
});
pool.on("error", (err) => console.error("idle client error", err.message));      // always register this

const one = await pool.connect();
const two = await pool.connect();           // both connections are now checked out
console.log("total:", pool.totalCount, "idle:", pool.idleCount, "waiting:", pool.waitingCount);

try { await pool.query("SELECT 1"); }       // needs a third connection: queues, then times out
catch (e) { console.log("third request ->", e.message); }

one.release();                               // give one back and the next request goes through
console.log("after release:", (await pool.query("SELECT 'served' AS result")).rows[0].result);
two.release();
await pool.end();
total: 2 idle: 0 waiting: 0 third request -> timeout exceeded when trying to connect after release: served

If requests time out waiting for a connection, the usual causes are a leaked client (a missing release() on an error path), transactions held open while calling slow external services, or one slow query. Raising max hides these until the database itself runs out of connections. For many instances, put PgBouncer in front of Postgres.

Your schema changes over time, and it must change identically on your laptop, in CI, in staging and in production. A migration is a numbered, version-controlled script describing one change. A tool records which migrations have run (in a table of its own) and applies only the new ones, in order. Rules: never edit a migration that has been applied elsewhere (write a new one), commit migrations with the code that needs them, and run them as a deploy step, not on application start in every instance.

The idea is small enough to build in a few lines. This runner keeps a schema_migrations table and runs each pending migration inside a transaction, so a failing one leaves nothing half-applied.

import pg from "pg";
const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb" });
await pool.query("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS schema_migrations, mg_notes");

const migrations = [                                          // normally one .sql file each, named 001_create_notes.sql ...
  { id: "001_create_notes", up: "CREATE TABLE mg_notes (id serial PRIMARY KEY, title text NOT NULL)" },
  { id: "002_add_done",     up: "ALTER TABLE mg_notes ADD COLUMN done boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false" },
  { id: "003_broken",       up: "ALTER TABLE mg_notes ADD COLUMN oops nonexistent_type" },
  { id: "004_index_title",  up: "CREATE INDEX mg_notes_title_idx ON mg_notes (title)" },
];

async function migrate() {
  await pool.query("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (id text PRIMARY KEY, applied_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now())");
  const done = new Set((await pool.query("SELECT id FROM schema_migrations")).rows.map((r) => r.id));
  for (const m of migrations) {
    if (done.has(m.id)) continue;                            // already applied: skip
    const client = await pool.connect();
    try {
      await client.query("BEGIN");
      await client.query(m.up);
      await client.query("INSERT INTO schema_migrations (id) VALUES ($1)", [m.id]);
      await client.query("COMMIT");
      console.log("applied", m.id);
    } catch (err) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");
      console.log("FAILED ", m.id, "->", err.message);
      return false;                                          // stop: later migrations depend on this one
    } finally { client.release(); }
  }
  return true;
}

console.log("run 1:", await migrate());
migrations.splice(2, 1);                                     // we fix the problem by removing the broken one (in real life: a new migration)
console.log("run 2:", await migrate());
console.log("run 3 (nothing to do):", await migrate());
console.log("recorded:", (await pool.query("SELECT id FROM schema_migrations ORDER BY id")).rows.map((r) => r.id));

await pool.query("DROP TABLE schema_migrations, mg_notes");
await pool.end();
applied 001_create_notes applied 002_add_done FAILED 003_broken -> type "nonexistent_type" does not exist run 1: false applied 004_index_title run 2: true run 3 (nothing to do): true recorded: [ '001_create_notes', '002_add_done', '004_index_title' ]

In practice you use a tool. knex migrations are JavaScript files with up and down functions; node-pg-migrate, Drizzle Kit, Prisma Migrate, Sequelize CLI and plain-SQL tools like Flyway, dbmate and golang-migrate work the same way. A knex project:

// Where knex finds the database and the migration files
export default {
  client: "pg",
  connection: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb",   // local development database
  migrations: { directory: "./migrations" },
};
// up: apply the change. down: undo it exactly.
export async function up(knex) {
  await knex.schema.createTable("kx_notes", (t) => {
    t.increments("id");
    t.text("title").notNullable();
    t.timestamp("created_at").notNullable().defaultTo(knex.fn.now());
  });
}

export async function down(knex) {
  await knex.schema.dropTable("kx_notes");
}
export async function up(knex) {
  await knex.schema.alterTable("kx_notes", (t) => {
    t.boolean("done").notNullable().defaultTo(false);
    t.index("done");
  });
}

export async function down(knex) {
  await knex.schema.alterTable("kx_notes", (t) => {
    t.dropIndex("done");
    t.dropColumn("done");
  });
}
$ npx knex migrate:status
No Completed Migration files Found.

20261002100000_add_done_flag.js
$ npx knex migrate:up

$ npx knex migrate:up

$ npx knex migrate:list

No Pending Migration files Found.
$ npx knex migrate:down

Create a new migration file with npx knex migrate:make add_tags (it writes a timestamped file with empty up/down functions).

ChangeSafe way on a live table
Add a columnAdd it nullable or with a constant default (fast in modern Postgres), deploy code that writes it, backfill in batches, then add NOT NULL
Rename or remove a columnExpand and contract: add the new column, write to both, switch reads, stop writing the old one, drop it in a later release. Never rename in one step while old code is still running.
Add an indexCREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (cannot run inside a transaction block, so give that migration its own file or disable the transaction)
Add a foreign key or constraintADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately, so you do not lock the table while it scans
Change a column typeUsually a new column, a backfill and a switch; a direct ALTER TYPE can rewrite and lock the whole table
Big data fixUpdate in batches of a few thousand rows, never one statement over millions
HabitsTest migrations on a copy of production data. Keep schema migrations and data migrations separate. Make each down truthful, or state that the change is irreversible. Take a backup before risky changes, and give migrations a short lock_timeout so a stuck lock fails fast instead of queueing every request behind it.
LevelExamplesYou writeTrade-off
Raw driverpg, mysql2, better-sqlite3SQL stringsFull power and clarity; you map rows to objects and keep SQL and code in sync yourself
Query builderknex, kyselyChained JavaScript that produces SQLComposable (conditional filters), still close to SQL; little magic
Type-safe SQL layerDrizzle, kyselyTable definitions in TypeScript, queries that mirror SQLTypes flow from the schema into results; thin and fast
Full ORMSequelize, TypeORM, Prisma, Mongoose (MongoDB)Models and relations; the tool writes the SQLFast for CRUD and relations; hides queries, so slow ones (N+1) hide too

No choice is wrong; a mistake is using an ORM without knowing the SQL it emits. Learn SQL first (you did), turn on query logging while developing, and drop to raw SQL for reports and hot paths.

knex: a query builder

import knex from "knex";
const db = knex({ client: "pg", connection: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb", pool: { min: 0, max: 5 } });

await db.schema.dropTableIfExists("kb_posts");
await db.schema.dropTableIfExists("kb_users");
await db.schema.createTable("kb_users", (t) => {
  t.increments("id");
  t.text("name").notNullable();
  t.text("email").notNullable().unique();
});
await db.schema.createTable("kb_posts", (t) => {
  t.increments("id");
  t.integer("user_id").notNullable().references("id").inTable("kb_users").onDelete("CASCADE");
  t.text("title").notNullable();
  t.integer("views").notNullable().defaultTo(0);
  t.index("user_id");
});

await db("kb_users").insert([{ name: "Ana", email: "ana@example.com" }, { name: "Raj", email: "raj@example.com" }]);
await db("kb_posts").insert([
  { user_id: 1, title: "Hello", views: 40 },
  { user_id: 1, title: "Second", views: 5 },
  { user_id: 2, title: "Raj writes", views: 25 },
]);

// a query is an object until you await it, so you can print the SQL it will send
const query = db("kb_posts as p")
  .join("kb_users as u", "u.id", "p.user_id")
  .where("p.views", ">", 10)
  .andWhere((b) => b.where("u.name", "Ana").orWhere("u.name", "Raj"))     // grouped conditions: (a OR b)
  .select("p.id", "p.title", "u.name as author")
  .orderBy("p.views", "desc")
  .limit(5);
console.log(query.toSQL().toNative());                                    // the SQL with $1 placeholders, and the values
console.log(await query);

// composable filters: add conditions only when the input is present
const search = ({ author, minViews }) => db("kb_posts as p").join("kb_users as u", "u.id", "p.user_id")
  .select("p.title").orderBy("p.id")
  .modify((qb) => { if (author) qb.where("u.name", author); if (minViews) qb.where("p.views", ">=", minViews); });
console.log("author=Ana         ->", (await search({ author: "Ana" })).map((r) => r.title));
console.log("minViews=20        ->", (await search({ minViews: 20 })).map((r) => r.title));
console.log("no filters         ->", (await search({})).length, "rows");

// update, increment, upsert, delete, aggregate, raw
await db("kb_posts").where({ id: 2 }).increment("views", 100);
await db("kb_users").insert({ name: "Ana Silva", email: "ana@example.com" }).onConflict("email").merge();
console.log("after upsert   ->", await db("kb_users").where({ email: "ana@example.com" }).first("id", "name"));
console.log("aggregate      ->", await db("kb_posts").sum({ total: "views" }).count({ posts: "*" }).first(), "(Postgres returns sums and counts as strings)");
console.log("raw with value ->", (await db.raw("select count(*)::int as n from kb_posts where views > ?", [10])).rows[0]);

// transactions: the callback gets a trx object that you use instead of db
try {
  await db.transaction(async (trx) => {
    await trx("kb_posts").insert({ user_id: 2, title: "Draft", views: 0 });
    throw new Error("changed my mind");                                    // throwing rolls everything back
  });
} catch (e) { console.log("transaction ->", e.message, "| posts still:", (await db("kb_posts").count({ n: "*" }).first()).n); }

await db.schema.dropTable("kb_posts");
await db.schema.dropTable("kb_users");
await db.destroy();
{ sql: 'select "p"."id", "p"."title", "u"."name" as "author" from "kb_posts" as "p" inner join "kb_users" as "u" on "u"."id" = "p"."user_id" where "p"."views" > $1 and ("u"."name" = $2 or "u"."name" = $3) order by "p"."views" desc limit $4', bindings: [ 10, 'Ana', 'Raj', 5 ] } [ { id: 1, title: 'Hello', author: 'Ana' }, { id: 3, title: 'Raj writes', author: 'Raj' } ] author=Ana -> [ 'Hello', 'Second' ] minViews=20 -> [ 'Hello', 'Raj writes' ] no filters -> 3 rows after upsert -> { id: 1, name: 'Ana Silva' } aggregate -> { total: '170', posts: '3' } (Postgres returns sums and counts as strings) raw with value -> { n: 3 } transaction -> changed my mind | posts still: 3

Drizzle: type-safe and close to SQL

With Drizzle you describe tables in code (in TypeScript, the column types flow into every query result) and write queries that read like SQL. There is no hidden loading: what you write is what runs.

import pg from "pg";
import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/node-postgres";
import { pgTable, serial, text, integer } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";
import { eq, gt, and, sql, desc, count } from "drizzle-orm";

// the schema in code (in a real project this lives in src/db/schema.ts)
const users = pgTable("dz_users", { id: serial().primaryKey(), name: text().notNull() });
const posts = pgTable("dz_posts", { id: serial().primaryKey(), userId: integer("user_id").notNull().references(() => users.id), title: text().notNull(), views: integer().notNull().default(0) });

const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb" });
const db = drizzle(pool);
await db.execute(sql`DROP TABLE IF EXISTS dz_posts, dz_users`);
await db.execute(sql`CREATE TABLE dz_users (id serial PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL)`);
await db.execute(sql`CREATE TABLE dz_posts (id serial PRIMARY KEY, user_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES dz_users(id), title text NOT NULL, views int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)`);

const [ana, raj] = await db.insert(users).values([{ name: "Ana" }, { name: "Raj" }]).returning();
await db.insert(posts).values([{ userId: ana.id, title: "Hello", views: 40 }, { userId: ana.id, title: "Second", views: 5 }, { userId: raj.id, title: "Raj writes", views: 25 }]);

const popular = db.select({ title: posts.title, author: users.name, views: posts.views })
  .from(posts).innerJoin(users, eq(posts.userId, users.id))
  .where(and(gt(posts.views, 10), eq(users.name, "Ana")))
  .orderBy(desc(posts.views));
console.log(popular.toSQL());                                   // the exact SQL and parameters
console.log(await popular);

console.log(await db.select({ author: users.name, posts: count() }).from(users).leftJoin(posts, eq(posts.userId, users.id)).groupBy(users.name).orderBy(users.name));
console.log(await db.update(posts).set({ views: sql`${posts.views} + 1` }).where(eq(posts.title, "Second")).returning({ title: posts.title, views: posts.views }));

await db.execute(sql`DROP TABLE dz_posts, dz_users`);
await pool.end();
{ sql: 'select "dz_posts"."title", "dz_users"."name", "dz_posts"."views" from "dz_posts" inner join "dz_users" on "dz_posts"."user_id" = "dz_users"."id" where ("dz_posts"."views" > $1 and "dz_users"."name" = $2) order by "dz_posts"."views" desc', params: [ 10, 'Ana' ] } [ { title: 'Hello', author: 'Ana', views: 40 } ] [ { author: 'Ana', posts: 2 }, { author: 'Raj', posts: 1 } ] [ { title: 'Second', views: 6 } ]

Sequelize: a classic ORM, and the N+1 problem

An ORM maps tables to models and rows to objects, and lets you load related rows through associations. Convenience has a famous trap. Load 5 authors, then loop over them asking for each author's books, and you send 1 query for the list plus 5 more, one per author: the N+1 problem. At 5 rows nobody notices; at 500 rows per page the endpoint crawls. The fix is to load related rows together (eager loading, a join, or one extra WHERE author_id IN (...) query).

import { Sequelize, DataTypes } from "sequelize";

let queries = 0;                                                   // count every statement Sequelize sends
const sequelize = new Sequelize("postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb", { logging: () => queries++ });

const Author = sequelize.define("Author", { name: { type: DataTypes.STRING, allowNull: false } }, { tableName: "sq_authors", timestamps: false });
const Book = sequelize.define("Book", { title: DataTypes.STRING }, { tableName: "sq_books", timestamps: false });
Author.hasMany(Book, { foreignKey: "authorId" });                  // an author has many books
Book.belongsTo(Author, { foreignKey: "authorId" });                // a book belongs to one author

await sequelize.query("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sq_books, sq_authors");
await sequelize.sync();                                            // creates the tables from the models (use migrations in real projects)
for (const name of ["Ursula", "Octavia", "Chinua", "Toni", "Jorge"]) {
  const author = await Author.create({ name });
  await Book.bulkCreate([{ title: `${name}: one`, authorId: author.id }, { title: `${name}: two`, authorId: author.id }]);
}

queries = 0;
const authors = await Author.findAll();
const lazy = [];
for (const a of authors) lazy.push({ author: a.name, books: (await a.getBooks()).length });   // one query PER author
console.log("N+1 version  : queries =", queries, "(1 for the authors + 5 for their books)");

queries = 0;
const eager = await Author.findAll({ include: Book });             // ONE query with a LEFT JOIN
console.log("eager version: queries =", queries, "->", eager.map((a) => `${a.name}:${a.Books.length}`).join(" "));

queries = 0;
const titles = await Book.findAll({ include: { model: Author, where: { name: "Toni" } }, attributes: ["title"] });
console.log("filter by related row: queries =", queries, "->", titles.map((b) => b.title));

await sequelize.query("DROP TABLE sq_books, sq_authors");
await sequelize.close();
N+1 version : queries = 6 (1 for the authors + 5 for their books) eager version: queries = 1 -> Ursula:2 Octavia:2 Chinua:2 Toni:2 Jorge:2 filter by related row: queries = 1 -> [ 'Toni: one', 'Toni: two' ]

Prisma

Prisma is the most popular schema-first ORM: you describe the data in a schema.prisma file, prisma migrate creates and applies migrations, and prisma generate produces a fully typed client. It is not run in this guide because generating the client downloads engine files from Prisma's servers, which the build environment cannot reach. This is the shape of a project; follow the current Prisma documentation for exact setup, since it changed between major versions.

generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client"
  output   = "../generated/prisma"
}

datasource db {
  provider = "postgresql"
}

model Author {
  id    Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
  name  String
  books Book[]
}

model Book {
  id       Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
  title    String
  author   Author @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id])
  authorId Int
  @@index([authorId])
}
import { PrismaClient } from "../generated/prisma/client.js";
import { PrismaPg } from "@prisma/adapter-pg";

const prisma = new PrismaClient({ adapter: new PrismaPg({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL }) });

const ana = await prisma.author.create({ data: { name: "Ana", books: { create: [{ title: "One" }, { title: "Two" }] } } });
const withBooks = await prisma.author.findMany({ include: { books: true }, where: { name: { startsWith: "A" } }, orderBy: { id: "asc" }, take: 10 });
await prisma.$transaction([prisma.book.deleteMany({ where: { authorId: ana.id } }), prisma.author.delete({ where: { id: ana.id } })]);
ChoosingWant to stay close to SQL, with types: Drizzle or kysely. Want the friendliest schema, migrations and client with a bigger runtime: Prisma. Existing codebase or Active-Record style: Sequelize or TypeORM. Just need dynamic queries on top of a driver: knex. Whatever you pick: log the SQL in development, watch for N+1, put an index on every foreign key, and keep one escape hatch for raw SQL.

Redis is an in-memory data store that answers in microseconds. It is not a replacement for your main database; it is the speed and coordination layer beside it. Typical jobs: caching expensive results, sessions, rate-limit counters, distributed locks, leaderboards, queues (BullMQ, Unit 8) and pub/sub between server instances. Keys are strings; values can be strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets and more. Every command is atomic, which is what makes counters and locks safe across many servers.

127.0.0.1:6379> SET greeting "hello world"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET greeting
"hello world"

OK
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL session:42
(integer) 60
127.0.0.1:6379> SET temp "short lived" PX 300
OK
...
127.0.0.1:6379> GET temp
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR page:hits
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> INCRBY page:hits 9
(integer) 10
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET user:1 name Ana plan pro
(integer) 2

"Ana"

(integer) 2

1) "web"
2) "promo"

From Node the best client is ioredis (the official redis package works too). Create one client per purpose and reuse it. The first two patterns, cache-aside and the thundering herd, are the ones you will use most.

import { Redis } from "ioredis";
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";
const redis = new Redis(6399);                                     // the default port is 6379; real apps pass a URL: new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL)
await redis.flushall();

let dbCalls = 0;
const loadUserFromDb = async (id) => { dbCalls++; await sleep(50); return { id, name: `user ${id}` }; };    // pretend this is a slow query

// cache-aside: look in Redis first; on a miss, load from the database, then store it with a time limit
async function getUser(id) {
  const key = `user:${id}`;
  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached) return { ...JSON.parse(cached), from: "cache" };
  const user = await loadUserFromDb(id);
  await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(user), "EX", 60);            // always set a TTL: stale data must eventually disappear
  return { ...user, from: "database" };
}
console.log(await getUser(1));
console.log(await getUser(1));
console.log("database calls so far:", dbCalls);

// when the data changes, delete the cached copy (invalidation) so the next read refreshes it
await redis.del("user:1");
console.log(await getUser(1));
console.log("database calls so far:", dbCalls);

// the thundering herd: a popular key expires and 20 requests miss at the same moment
dbCalls = 0;
await redis.del("user:7");
await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: 20 }, () => getUser(7)));
console.log("20 simultaneous misses -> database calls:", dbCalls);

// fix: share one in-flight load between the requests of this process (single flight)
const inflight = new Map();
function getUserOnce(id) {
