  if (!inflight.has(id)) inflight.set(id, getUser(id).finally(() => inflight.delete(id)));
  return inflight.get(id);
}
dbCalls = 0;
await redis.del("user:7");
await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: 20 }, () => getUserOnce(7)));
console.log("20 simultaneous misses with single flight -> database calls:", dbCalls);

await redis.quit();
{ id: 1, name: 'user 1', from: 'database' } { id: 1, name: 'user 1', from: 'cache' } database calls so far: 1 { id: 1, name: 'user 1', from: 'database' } database calls so far: 2 20 simultaneous misses -> database calls: 20 20 simultaneous misses with single flight -> database calls: 1
import { Redis } from "ioredis";
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";
const redis = new Redis(6399);
await redis.flushall();

// fixed-window rate limit: INCR is atomic, so many servers share one counter. The Lua script makes
// "increment, and set the expiry on the first hit" a single indivisible step
const hit = (key, windowSeconds) => redis.eval(
  "local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]); if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end; return n",
  1, key, windowSeconds);
const limit = 5;
const results = [];
for (let i = 1; i <= 7; i++) results.push(`#${i}:${(await hit("rl:ip:203.0.113.9", 10)) <= limit ? "allowed" : "BLOCKED"}`);
console.log(results.join(" "));
const left = await redis.ttl("rl:ip:203.0.113.9");
console.log("the counter expires by itself within the window:", left > 0 && left <= 10);

// a lock: SET NX only succeeds for the first caller; EX makes it expire if the holder crashes
const token = "worker-1";
console.log("worker-1 gets the lock :", (await redis.set("lock:invoice-run", token, "EX", 10, "NX")) === "OK");
console.log("worker-2 gets the lock :", (await redis.set("lock:invoice-run", "worker-2", "EX", 10, "NX")) === "OK");
// release safely: delete the key only if it still holds MY token (it may have expired and been taken by someone else)
const release = (key, who) => redis.eval("if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end", 1, key, who);
console.log("worker-2 releases (not its lock):", await release("lock:invoice-run", "worker-2"));
console.log("worker-1 releases              :", await release("lock:invoice-run", "worker-1"));

// pub/sub: a subscribing connection can only subscribe, so use a second connection to publish
const subscriber = new Redis(6399);
const received = [];
subscriber.on("message", (channel, message) => received.push(`${channel}: ${message}`));
await subscriber.subscribe("orders");
console.log("subscribers that got the message:", await redis.publish("orders", "order 17 paid"));
await sleep(50);
console.log("received:", received);
console.log("messages are not stored: a late subscriber sees nothing from before it subscribed");

subscriber.disconnect();
await redis.quit();
#1:allowed #2:allowed #3:allowed #4:allowed #5:allowed #6:BLOCKED #7:BLOCKED the counter expires by itself within the window: true worker-1 gets the lock : true worker-2 gets the lock : false worker-2 releases (not its lock): 0 worker-1 releases : 1 subscribers that got the message: 1 received: [ 'orders: order 17 paid' ] messages are not stored: a late subscriber sees nothing from before it subscribed

An Express cache middleware

import express from "express";
import { Redis } from "ioredis";
const redis = new Redis(6399);
await redis.flushall();

// cache GET responses for `seconds`; X-Cache tells you (and your monitoring) what happened
const cache = (seconds) => async (req, res, next) => {
  const key = `http:${req.originalUrl}`;
  const hit = await redis.get(key);
  if (hit) return res.set("X-Cache", "HIT").type("json").send(hit);
  const send = res.json.bind(res);
  res.json = (body) => {
    if (res.statusCode === 200) redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(body), "EX", seconds);   // only cache successes
    return send(body);
  };
  res.set("X-Cache", "MISS");
  next();
};

let computed = 0;
const app = express();
app.get("/report/:month", cache(30), (req, res) => {
  computed++;                                                       // an expensive aggregation in real life
  res.json({ month: req.params.month, computedTimes: computed });
});
> GET /report/2026-10 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < x-cache: MISS < {"month":"2026-10","computedTimes":1} > GET /report/2026-10 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < x-cache: HIT < {"month":"2026-10","computedTimes":1} > GET /report/2026-09 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < x-cache: MISS < {"month":"2026-09","computedTimes":2} expensive work ran 2 times for 3 requests
  • Always set a TTL on cache keys, and decide how stale is acceptable. "There are only two hard things: cache invalidation and naming things."
  • Use a key convention (user:42, rl:ip:1.2.3.4) with a version or prefix per app. Never use KEYS * on a real server (it blocks everything); use SCAN.
  • Cache public data per URL, but include the user id in the key for per-user data, or you will show one person another's page.
  • Redis memory is finite: set maxmemory and an eviction policy (allkeys-lru for a cache). By default, data is lost on restart unless you enable persistence (RDB snapshots or AOF), so treat it as disposable unless you configured otherwise.
  • Handle Redis being down: a cache failure should slow your API, not break it. Catch errors and fall back to the database.
What was and was not run. This guide's build environment has no MongoDB server, so nothing below that talks to a database was executed. What was run for real: the Mongo query operator semantics (with the mingo library, which implements MongoDB's query and aggregation language in JavaScript) and Mongoose schema validation (which works without a connection). Server code is shown as "not run here".

MongoDB stores documents (JSON-like objects, stored as BSON) in collections instead of rows in tables. A document can nest objects and arrays, so data that is read together is stored together. There is no required schema, no joins by default and every document gets a unique _id (an ObjectId).

SQLMongoDB
database, table, row, columndatabase, collection, document, field
SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 25db.users.find({ age: { $gt: 25 } })
INSERTinsertOne, insertMany
UPDATE ... SETupdateOne(filter, { $set: {...} })
DELETEdeleteOne, deleteMany
JOIN$lookup in an aggregation pipeline, or embed the data
GROUP BY$group stage
CREATE INDEXcreateIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true })
transactionmulti-document transactions (replica set required); single-document writes are atomic already
 
import { MongoClient, ObjectId } from "mongodb";

const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI);          // one client per process, like a pool
await client.connect();
const users = client.db("app").collection("users");
await users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true });

const { insertedId } = await users.insertOne({ name: "Ana", email: "ana@example.com", tags: ["web"], createdAt: new Date() });
const ana = await users.findOne({ _id: insertedId });
const page = await users.find({ tags: "web" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(10).toArray();
await users.updateOne({ _id: insertedId }, { $set: { name: "Ana Silva" }, $addToSet: { tags: "pro" }, $inc: { logins: 1 } });
await users.deleteOne({ _id: new ObjectId(req.params.id) });      // ids from URLs are strings: convert, and validate them first

// duplicate key errors have code 11000, the counterpart of Postgres 23505
try { await users.insertOne({ email: "ana@example.com" }); } catch (e) { if (e.code === 11000) { /* answer 409 */ } }

The query and update language, run with mingo

import { Query, Aggregator } from "mingo";

const orders = [
  { _id: 1, customer: "Ana", status: "paid",    total: 88.9, items: [{ sku: "kb", qty: 1 }, { sku: "ms", qty: 2 }], shipTo: { city: "Lisbon" } },
  { _id: 2, customer: "Ana", status: "new",     total: 189,  items: [{ sku: "mon", qty: 1 }],                       shipTo: { city: "Lisbon" } },
  { _id: 3, customer: "Raj", status: "paid",    total: 62,   items: [{ sku: "ms", qty: 1 }, { sku: "cb", qty: 10 }], shipTo: { city: "Pune" } },
  { _id: 4, customer: "Mei", status: "shipped", total: 29.5, items: [],                                             shipTo: { city: "Pune" } },
];
const find = (filter) => new Query(filter).find(orders).all().map((o) => o._id);

console.log("total > 60               ->", find({ total: { $gt: 60 } }));
console.log("status in (paid, new)    ->", find({ status: { $in: ["paid", "new"] } }));
console.log("paid AND total < 80      ->", find({ status: "paid", total: { $lt: 80 } }));
console.log("OR                       ->", find({ $or: [{ customer: "Mei" }, { total: { $gte: 189 } }] }));
console.log("dot notation shipTo.city ->", find({ "shipTo.city": "Pune" }));
console.log("array contains sku ms    ->", find({ "items.sku": "ms" }));
console.log("$elemMatch (same item!)  ->", find({ items: { $elemMatch: { sku: "ms", qty: { $gte: 2 } } } }));
console.log("empty array              ->", find({ items: { $size: 0 } }));
console.log("field is missing         ->", find({ coupon: { $exists: false } }));
console.log("regex on customer        ->", find({ customer: { $regex: "^A" } }));

// an aggregation pipeline: stages that each transform the stream of documents
const report = new Aggregator([
  { $match: { status: { $in: ["paid", "shipped"] } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$shipTo.city", orders: { $sum: 1 }, revenue: { $sum: "$total" } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } },
]).run(orders);
console.log("revenue by city:", report);
total > 60 -> [ 1, 2, 3 ] status in (paid, new) -> [ 1, 2, 3 ] paid AND total < 80 -> [ 3 ] OR -> [ 2, 4 ] dot notation shipTo.city -> [ 3, 4 ] array contains sku ms -> [ 1, 3 ] $elemMatch (same item!) -> [ 1 ] empty array -> [ 4 ] field is missing -> [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] regex on customer -> [ 1, 2 ] revenue by city: [ { _id: 'Pune', orders: 2, revenue: 91.5 }, { _id: 'Lisbon', orders: 1, revenue: 88.9 } ]

Mongoose: schemas on top of the driver

Mongoose adds what "schemaless" lacks: a schema with types, defaults and validation, models with methods and virtual fields, middleware hooks, and population (a join-like lookup). Validation runs in your Node process before the data is sent, so it works even without a database connection:

import mongoose from "mongoose";

const userSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  name:  { type: String, required: [true, "name is required"], minlength: [2, "name is too short"], trim: true },
  email: { type: String, required: true, lowercase: true, trim: true, match: [/^\S+@\S+\.\S+$/, "email looks wrong"] },
  age:   { type: Number, min: [0, "age cannot be negative"], max: 130 },
  role:  { type: String, enum: ["user", "admin"], default: "user" },
}, { timestamps: true });                                          // adds createdAt and updatedAt

userSchema.virtual("domain").get(function () { return this.email.split("@")[1]; });   // computed, never stored
userSchema.set("toJSON", { virtuals: true, transform: (doc, out) => { delete out._id; delete out.__v; return out; } });

const User = mongoose.model("User", userSchema);

const good = new User({ name: "  Ana ", email: "  ANA@Example.COM ", extra: "not in the schema" });
await good.validate();                                             // sanitizers ran: trim, lowercase, default
const { createdAt, updatedAt, id, ...shown } = good.toJSON();      // leave out the generated values here
console.log("valid document:", shown, "| unknown field kept:", "extra" in good.toObject());

const bad = new User({ name: "A", email: "nope", age: -5, role: "root" });
try { await bad.validate(); }
catch (err) { for (const [field, e] of Object.entries(err.errors)) console.log("invalid", field.padEnd(5), "->", e.message); }

const type = new User({ name: "Bo", email: "bo@example.com", age: "forty" });
try { await type.validate(); } catch (err) { console.log("wrong type age ->", err.errors.age.name, "|", err.errors.age.message); }
valid document: { name: 'Ana', email: 'ana@example.com', role: 'user', domain: 'example.com' } | unknown field kept: false invalid name -> name is too short invalid email -> email looks wrong invalid age -> age cannot be negative invalid role -> `root` is not a valid enum value for path `role`. wrong type age -> CastError | Cast to Number failed for value "forty" (type string) at path "age" for model "User"
When MongoDB fits, and when notIt fits data that is naturally a nested document read as a whole (a product catalog with varying attributes, a CMS page, event payloads), rapid prototyping, and horizontal scaling by shard key. It is a weaker fit for data with many relationships and reporting across them, where SQL joins, constraints and transactions do more work for you. Mongo's flexibility does not remove the need for a design: embed what you read together, reference what grows without bound, index what you query, and validate with a schema (Mongoose, or JSON Schema validation inside MongoDB).

These are the habits that keep database code correct as an app grows. All of them run below against real Postgres.

  • One pool per process, created at startup, shared by every request, closed on shutdown. Never create a pool per request.
  • A repository layer: all SQL for a table lives in one module with functions like find, create and update. Routes call it, and never see SQL. That keeps queries testable and swappable (the layering from Unit 4).
  • Optimistic locking: a version column and WHERE version = $n turns lost updates into a clear 409.
  • Soft delete: deleted_at instead of DELETE, when you need undo or an audit trail. Every read must then filter deleted_at IS NULL (put it in the repository, once). Remember legal requirements to really delete personal data.
  • Keyset pagination for lists that grow.
  • Readiness checks that run SELECT 1 so a load balancer stops sending traffic to an instance whose database is unreachable. A liveness check should not touch the database, or a database outage would make orchestrators restart healthy processes.
import express from "express";
import pg from "pg";

const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb", max: 5, connectionTimeoutMillis: 1000 });
await pool.query("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS rp_notes");
await pool.query(`CREATE TABLE rp_notes (
  id serial PRIMARY KEY,
  title text NOT NULL CHECK (length(title) BETWEEN 1 AND 100),
  body text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  version integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  deleted_at timestamptz,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now())`);

// ---- repository: the only place that knows SQL ----
const columns = "id, title, body, version";                                         // name columns instead of SELECT *
const notes = {
  async create({ title, body = "" }) {
    return (await pool.query(`INSERT INTO rp_notes (title, body) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING ${columns}`, [title, body])).rows[0];
  },
  async find(id) {
    return (await pool.query(`SELECT ${columns} FROM rp_notes WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL`, [id])).rows[0] ?? null;
  },
  async list({ after = 0, limit = 3 }) {                                           // keyset: "rows after the last id I saw"
    const { rows } = await pool.query("SELECT id, title, version FROM rp_notes WHERE id > $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT $2", [after, limit + 1]);
    return { items: rows.slice(0, limit), nextAfter: rows.length > limit ? rows[limit - 1].id : null };
  },
  async update(id, expectedVersion, { title, body }) {                              // optimistic locking
    const { rows } = await pool.query(
      `UPDATE rp_notes SET title = COALESCE($3, title), body = COALESCE($4, body), version = version + 1
       WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2 AND deleted_at IS NULL RETURNING ${columns}`, [id, expectedVersion, title ?? null, body ?? null]);
    if (rows[0]) return { note: rows[0] };
    return { conflict: (await this.find(id)) !== null };                            // exists but the version differed, or does not exist
  },
  async softDelete(id) {
    return (await pool.query("UPDATE rp_notes SET deleted_at = now() WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL", [id])).rowCount === 1;
  },
  async restore(id) {
    return (await pool.query("UPDATE rp_notes SET deleted_at = NULL WHERE id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NOT NULL", [id])).rowCount === 1;
  },
};

// ---- routes: HTTP only ----
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
const badId = (req, res) => { const id = Number(req.params.id); if (Number.isInteger(id) && id > 0) return id; res.status(400).json({ error: "id must be a positive integer" }); };

app.post("/notes", async (req, res) => res.status(201).json(await notes.create(req.body)));
app.get("/notes", async (req, res) => res.json(await notes.list({ after: Number(req.query.after) || 0 })));
app.get("/notes/:id", async (req, res) => {
  const id = badId(req, res); if (!id) return;
  const note = await notes.find(id);
  if (!note) return res.status(404).json({ error: "not found" });
  res.set("ETag", `"${note.version}"`).json(note);
});
app.put("/notes/:id", async (req, res) => {
  const id = badId(req, res); if (!id) return;
  const version = Number((req.get("If-Match") ?? "").replaceAll('"', ""));
  if (!version) return res.status(428).json({ error: "send If-Match with the version you read" });
  const result = await notes.update(id, version, req.body);
  if (result.note) return res.set("ETag", `"${result.note.version}"`).json(result.note);
  res.status(result.conflict ? 412 : 404).json({ error: result.conflict ? "someone changed this note, reload it" : "not found" });
});
app.delete("/notes/:id", async (req, res) => { const id = badId(req, res); if (id) res.sendStatus(await notes.softDelete(id) ? 204 : 404); });
app.post("/notes/:id/restore", async (req, res) => { const id = badId(req, res); if (id) res.sendStatus(await notes.restore(id) ? 204 : 404); });

// liveness: "is the process up". readiness: "can it serve traffic", which includes the database
app.get("/health/live", (req, res) => res.json({ status: "up" }));
app.get("/health/ready", async (req, res) => {
  try { await pool.query("SELECT 1"); res.json({ status: "ready" }); }
  catch (err) { res.status(503).json({ status: "database unavailable" }); }
});

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {                                                  // database check violations become 400s, the rest 500
  if (err.code === "23514" || err.code === "23502") return res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid note", constraint: err.constraint });
  console.error("unexpected:", err.message);
  res.status(500).json({ error: "internal error" });
});
> GET /notes < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"items":[{"id":1,"title":"one","version":1},{"id":2,"title":"two","version":1},{"id":3,"title":"three","version":1}],"nextAfter":3} > GET /notes?after=3 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"items":[{"id":4,"title":"four","version":1},{"id":5,"title":"five","version":1}],"nextAfter":null} > POST /notes {"title":""} < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"invalid note","constraint":"rp_notes_title_check"} --- two editors, one version > GET /notes/1 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < etag: "1" < {"id":1,"title":"one","body":"","version":1} > PUT /notes/1 {"title":"Ana's edit"} > if-match: "1" < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"title":"Ana's edit","body":"","version":2} > PUT /notes/1 {"title":"Raj's edit"} > if-match: "1" < 412 Precondition Failed < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"someone changed this note, reload it"} > PUT /notes/999 {"title":"x"} > if-match: "1" < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"not found"} --- soft delete > DELETE /notes/2 < 204 No Content > GET /notes/2 < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"not found"} rows still in the table: 5 > POST /notes/2/restore < 204 No Content after restore: 200 --- health > GET /health/live < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"status":"up"} > GET /health/ready < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"status":"ready"} > GET /health/ready < 503 Service Unavailable < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"status":"database unavailable"}

On shutdown, order matters: stop accepting new requests first, let in-flight ones finish, then close the pool. (Unit 10 covers this fully with signals.)

const server = app.listen(3000);

async function shutdown(signal) {
  console.log(`${signal}: closing`);
  server.close(async () => {          // 1. stop taking new connections, wait for running requests
    await pool.end();                 // 2. then close the database connections
    process.exit(0);
  });
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10_000).unref();   // 3. never hang forever
}
process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM"));      // sent by Docker, Kubernetes and most platforms
process.on("SIGINT", () => shutdown("SIGINT"));        // Ctrl+C
07

Unit 7: Authentication and Security

Who is calling, what are they allowed to do, and how attackers try to abuse your server. Password storage, sessions and cookies, JWT, OAuth, authorization, CSRF, CORS, security headers, rate limiting, and the injection family of attacks, each shown as a real attack followed by the fix.

Everything a client sends is untrusted: the body, the URL, headers, cookies, file names, even the Content-Type. Security work is mostly one habit applied everywhere: decide what is allowed, check it on the server, and refuse everything else. Hiding a button in the browser protects nothing, because attackers do not use your browser.

  • Defense in depth: assume each layer will fail someday, and add another (validation and parameterized queries and a least-privilege database user).
  • Least privilege: give users, services and database accounts only the permissions they need.
  • Fail closed: when a check errors or is missing, deny.
  • Do not invent cryptography: use node:crypto, well-known libraries and standard protocols.
  • Say little: generic error messages to clients, detailed logs for you, no secrets in either.

The OWASP Top 10 is the industry's list of the most common web application risks. The 2025 edition, mapped to what you do in a Node and Express backend (and where this guide shows it):

2025 categoryTypical Express causeDefense
A01 Broken Access ControlAnyone can read /orders/17 by changing the number (IDOR); missing role checksCheck ownership and role on every request, on the server (authorization entry)
A02 Security MisconfigurationDebug mode, default passwords, verbose errors, open CORS, missing headersHelmet, strict config per environment, production checklist (Unit 10)
A03 Software Supply Chain FailuresA malicious or vulnerable npm package; unpinned installsLockfile, npm ci, npm audit, few dependencies, review updates
A04 Cryptographic FailuresPlain-text or MD5 passwords, HTTP instead of HTTPS, hard-coded keysPassword hashing, TLS, secrets in the environment
A05 InjectionSQL built from strings, exec(userInput), NoSQL operators in JSON, XSSParameterized queries, execFile, validation, output escaping
A06 Insecure DesignNo limits on password tries, coupons, refunds, uploadsThreat-model features; rate limits; business-rule checks
A07 Authentication FailuresWeak passwords, no lockout, session ids that never change, tokens that never expireStrong hashing, regenerate sessions, short-lived tokens, MFA
A08 Software or Data Integrity FailuresTrusting unsigned data, unsafe deserialization, unverified updates and webhooksVerify signatures (webhook entry), never eval input
A09 Security Logging and Alerting FailuresNo record of failed logins; logs that contain passwordsStructured logs and alerts, redaction (Unit 10)
A10 Mishandling of Exceptional ConditionsUnhandled rejections crash the process; errors that fail open or leak detailsCentral error middleware, fail closed, tests for failure paths
How to use this unitRead each entry in this order: passwords, sessions, JWT, authorization (the most common real-world bug), OAuth, then the web-attack entries. Every attack in them is executed against a small server, and the fix is shown beside it.

Never store passwords, and never store them encrypted (encryption can be reversed, and the key will leak with the data). Store a hash: a one-way fingerprint. When someone logs in, hash what they typed and compare. If your database leaks, the attacker gets hashes, and the only way to use them is to guess passwords one at a time, so the hash must make each guess expensive.

  • SHA-256, MD5, SHA-1 are the wrong tool: designed to be fast, so a graphics card can try billions of guesses per second.
  • A salt (random bytes stored with the hash) makes every hash unique, so identical passwords look different and precomputed "rainbow tables" are useless.
  • A password hashing function adds a tunable cost: Argon2id (the modern first choice, memory-hard), scrypt (built into Node), bcrypt (old and widely supported), PBKDF2 (when you must follow FIPS rules).
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import { promisify } from "node:util";
import argon2 from "argon2";
import bcrypt from "bcryptjs";
const scrypt = promisify(crypto.scrypt);
const timed = async (fn) => { const t = performance.now(); const value = await fn(); return [value, performance.now() - t]; };

// 1. plain SHA-256: same input, same output, and very fast
const sha = (pw) => crypto.createHash("sha256").update(pw).digest("hex");
const [shaHash, shaMs] = await timed(() => sha("hunter2"));
console.log("sha256 twice identical      :", sha("hunter2") === sha("hunter2"), "(a rainbow table of common passwords works)");

// 2. Argon2id: random salt inside, so the same password gives a different hash every time
const [a1, argonMs] = await timed(() => argon2.hash("hunter2"));
const a2 = await argon2.hash("hunter2");
console.log("argon2 twice identical      :", a1 === a2);
console.log("argon2 hash looks like      :", a1.replace(/\$[^$]{22}\$[^$]{43}$/, "$<salt>$<hash>"));
console.log("argon2 verify right / wrong :", await argon2.verify(a1, "hunter2"), await argon2.verify(a1, "hunter3"));

// 3. bcrypt: cost 12 means 2^12 rounds
const [b1, bcryptMs] = await timed(() => bcrypt.hash("hunter2", 12));
console.log("bcrypt hash looks like      :", b1.replace(/[^$]{53}$/, "<salt+hash>"), "| verify:", await bcrypt.compare("hunter2", b1));

// 4. scrypt from node:crypto
const [, scryptMs] = await timed(() => scrypt("hunter2", crypto.randomBytes(16), 64));

console.log("sha256 is at least 20x faster than every password hash:", [argonMs, bcryptMs, scryptMs].every((ms) => ms > shaMs * 20));
console.log("each password hash takes tens of milliseconds or more :", [argonMs, bcryptMs, scryptMs].every((ms) => ms > 10));

// a bcrypt trap: only the first 72 bytes count
const long = "a".repeat(72);
const hashed = await bcrypt.hash(long + "FIRST", 10);
console.log("bcrypt accepts a different tail after 72 bytes:", await bcrypt.compare(long + "SECOND", hashed));
sha256 twice identical : true (a rainbow table of common passwords works) argon2 twice identical : false argon2 hash looks like : $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,p=4,t=3$<salt>$<hash> argon2 verify right / wrong : true false bcrypt hash looks like : $2b$12$<salt+hash> | verify: true sha256 is at least 20x faster than every password hash: true each password hash takes tens of milliseconds or more : true bcrypt accepts a different tail after 72 bytes: true
AlgorithmStarting parameters (OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet at time of writing)Notes
Argon2idmemory 19 MiB, 2 iterations, 1 lane (or 46 MiB, 1 iteration)Best default. argon2 npm package (native code)
scryptN = 2^17, r = 8, p = 1 (about 128 MiB)Built in: crypto.scrypt, no dependency
bcryptcost 10 or more (12 is common)Ignores bytes beyond 72, so do not pre-hash long input naively. bcryptjs is pure JavaScript
PBKDF2-SHA256600,000 iterationsOnly if a standard requires it. crypto.pbkdf2

Tune the cost so one hash takes roughly 100 to 300 ms on your production hardware, and store the parameters inside the hash string (all of the formats above do), so you can raise the cost later and re-hash each user's password on their next successful login. Below is a complete module using only node:crypto, then a login API that uses it.

import express from "express";
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import { promisify } from "node:util";
const scrypt = promisify(crypto.scrypt);

// ---- password module: format "scrypt$N$r$p$salt$hash" so parameters travel with each hash ----
const PARAMS = { N: 2 ** 15, r: 8, p: 1 };                                   // about 32 MiB; raise N as hardware improves
const derive = (password, salt, length, { N, r, p }) =>
  scrypt(password.normalize("NFKC"), salt, length, { N, r, p, maxmem: 128 * N * r * 2 });   // NFKC: the same text typed two ways hashes the same

async function hashPassword(password) {
  const salt = crypto.randomBytes(16);                                       // unique per password
  const key = await derive(password, salt, 64, PARAMS);
  return ["scrypt", PARAMS.N, PARAMS.r, PARAMS.p, salt.toString("base64"), key.toString("base64")].join("$");
}
async function verifyPassword(password, stored) {
  const [scheme, N, r, p, saltB64, keyB64] = stored.split("$");
  if (scheme !== "scrypt") return false;
  const expected = Buffer.from(keyB64, "base64");
  const actual = await derive(password, Buffer.from(saltB64, "base64"), expected.length, { N: +N, r: +r, p: +p });
  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(actual, expected);                           // constant-time compare: no timing leak of how many bytes matched
}
const needsRehash = (stored) => Number(stored.split("$")[1]) < PARAMS.N;      // stored with weaker settings than today's

// ---- the API ----
const users = new Map();                                                      // email -> { id, email, passwordHash }
const DUMMY_HASH = await hashPassword("a password nobody has");               // used to spend the same time for unknown users
const COMMON = new Set(["password123", "1234567890", "qwertyuiop", "letmein123"]);

const app = express();
app.use(express.json({ limit: "10kb" }));

app.post("/register", async (req, res) => {
  const { email, password } = req.body ?? {};
  if (typeof email !== "string" || !/^\S+@\S+\.\S+$/.test(email)) return res.status(400).json({ error: "a valid email is required" });
  if (typeof password !== "string" || password.length < 10 || password.length > 128) return res.status(400).json({ error: "password must be 10 to 128 characters" });   // length matters more than symbols; the upper limit stops giant-input abuse
  if (COMMON.has(password.toLowerCase())) return res.status(400).json({ error: "that password is too common" });
  if (users.has(email.toLowerCase())) return res.status(409).json({ error: "that email is already registered" });
  const user = { id: users.size + 1, email: email.toLowerCase(), passwordHash: await hashPassword(password) };
  users.set(user.email, user);
  res.status(201).json({ id: user.id, email: user.email });                    // never send the hash back
});

app.post("/login", async (req, res) => {
  const { email, password } = req.body ?? {};
  const user = typeof email === "string" ? users.get(email.toLowerCase()) : undefined;
  const ok = await verifyPassword(String(password ?? ""), user ? user.passwordHash : DUMMY_HASH);   // always do the expensive work
  if (!user || !ok) return res.status(401).json({ error: "invalid email or password" });          // the same sentence for both cases
  res.json({ id: user.id, email: user.email, rehashNeeded: needsRehash(user.passwordHash) });
});
> POST /register {"email":"ana@example.com","password":"short"} < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"password must be 10 to 128 characters"} > POST /register {"email":"ana@example.com","password":"Password123"} < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"that password is too common"} > POST /register {"email":"Ana@Example.com","password":"correct horse battery"} < 201 Created < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"email":"ana@example.com"} > POST /register {"email":"Ana@Example.com","password":"correct horse battery"} < 409 Conflict < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"that email is already registered"} > POST /login {"email":"ana@example.com","password":"correct horse battery"} < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"email":"ana@example.com","rehashNeeded":false} wrong password : 401 {"error":"invalid email or password"} unknown user : 401 {"error":"invalid email or password"} identical answers, so the endpoint does not reveal which emails exist: true stored value : scrypt$32768$8$1$<salt>$<hash> unknown user takes a similar time to a wrong password (no timing leak): true

Rules for a login system

  • Same message, same time for "no such user" and "wrong password" (shown above). The register and reset flows can still reveal whether an email exists, so rate-limit them and weigh the trade-off.
  • Length over complexity: require at least 8 characters (10 or more is better), allow long passphrases and every character, and reject passwords from breached-password lists (the Have I Been Pwned range API checks without sending the password). Do not force symbols or periodic changes.
  • Rate-limit and lock out gently (the rate limiting entry), and offer multi-factor authentication (TOTP apps, passkeys/WebAuthn).
  • Never log passwords, including in request logging of bodies. Never email them.
  • Hashing is CPU-heavy: crypto.scrypt and argon2 run on the libuv thread pool (not the main thread), but a flood of logins can still saturate it, which is another reason for rate limits.

Reset tokens

A password-reset link carries a secret token. Make it random (not guessable from a user id or time), short-lived, single-use, and store only its hash, so a database leak does not hand out working reset links.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

const sha256 = (text) => crypto.createHash("sha256").update(text).digest("hex");

// 1. create: 32 random bytes is 256 bits of unguessable secret
const token = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString("base64url");               // goes into the email link, then is forgotten
const record = { userId: 7, tokenHash: sha256(token), expiresAt: Date.now() + 30 * 60 * 1000, usedAt: null };   // this is what you store
console.log("token length in the link:", token.length, "characters | stored hash length:", record.tokenHash.length);
console.log("the stored record cannot be turned back into the token:", !JSON.stringify(record).includes(token));

// 2. use: hash what the user presents, find the record by that hash, check expiry and single use
function redeem(presented, rec, now = Date.now()) {
  if (!rec || sha256(presented) !== rec.tokenHash) return "invalid token";
  if (rec.usedAt) return "already used";
  if (now > rec.expiresAt) return "expired";
  rec.usedAt = now;                                                        // single use: mark it spent in the same step as changing the password
  return "ok: set the new password, then end all of this user's sessions";
}
console.log("wrong token     :", redeem("not-the-token", record));
console.log("right token     :", redeem(token, record));
console.log("same token again:", redeem(token, record));

const old = { ...record, usedAt: null, expiresAt: Date.now() - 1 };
console.log("after 30 minutes:", redeem(token, old));
token length in the link: 43 characters | stored hash length: 64 the stored record cannot be turned back into the token: true wrong token : invalid token right token : ok: set the new password, then end all of this user's sessions same token again: already used after 30 minutes: expired
After a password reset or change, end every existing session and revoke refresh tokens: whoever stole the old password may still be logged in. Notify the user by email whenever their password changes.

HTTP has no memory: every request arrives alone. A cookie is a small value the server asks the browser to send back on every later request to the same site. Authentication on classic web apps uses it like this: after login the server creates a session (a record on the server holding who you are), sends the browser only a random session id in a cookie, and looks the record up on each request. The cookie is a coat-check ticket; the data stays on the server.

Cookie attributeEffectSet it for sessions?
HttpOnlyJavaScript on the page cannot read it (document.cookie), so XSS cannot steal itAlways
SecureSent only over HTTPSAlways in production
SameSite=LaxNot sent on cross-site POSTs or subrequests, only on top-level navigations (the default in modern browsers); blocks most CSRFLax or Strict
SameSite=StrictNever sent on cross-site requests, even when following a link to youFor sensitive apps
SameSite=NoneSent everywhere (requires Secure)Only for deliberate cross-site embedding
Max-Age / ExpiresLifetime; without it the cookie ends when the browser closesSet a sensible limit
Path, DomainWhere it is sent. Without Domain it stays on the exact host (safer)Leave Domain unset
__Host- name prefixThe browser enforces Secure, Path=/ and no DomainGood hardening
 
import express from "express";
import cookieParser from "cookie-parser";
const app = express();
app.use(cookieParser("a-long-random-secret-from-the-environment"));         // the secret enables signed cookies

app.get("/set", (req, res) => {
  res.cookie("theme", "dark", { maxAge: 7 * 24 * 3600 * 1000, sameSite: "lax", path: "/" });                   // a harmless preference
  res.cookie("prefs", "compact", { signed: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: "lax", secure: true });            // signed: tampering is detected
  res.json({ ok: true });
});
app.get("/read", (req, res) => res.json({ plain: req.cookies, signed: req.signedCookies }));
Set-Cookie: theme=dark; Max-Age=604800; Path=/; Expires=<date>; SameSite=Lax Set-Cookie: prefs=<value>.<signature>; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax > GET /read < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"plain":{"theme":"dark"},"signed":{"prefs":"compact"}} > GET /read > cookie: prefs=s%3Aadmin.ZmFrZXNpZ25hdHVyZQ < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"plain":{},"signed":{"prefs":false}}

The plain cookie reaches the server as a string the user could have edited; the signed one is only accepted if the signature matches, otherwise it appears as false. A signature proves who made a value, not that it is secret: signed cookies are still readable. Never put anything sensitive in a cookie value. A session id is the right pattern: the cookie holds a random identifier and the data lives on the server.

express-session with Redis

express-session creates the session id, signs the cookie and loads req.session on every request. Its default MemoryStore leaks memory and cannot be shared between processes, so use a real store (Redis via connect-redis) outside of tests.

import express from "express";
import session from "express-session";
import { RedisStore } from "connect-redis";
import { createClient } from "redis";                              // the official client, which connect-redis is written for

const redis = createClient({ url: "redis://127.0.0.1:6399" });
await redis.connect();
await redis.flushAll();

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.use(session({
  name: "sid",                                                    // do not advertise "connect.sid"
  secret: ["current-secret-from-env", "previous-secret-for-rotation"],   // first signs, all verify: rotate without logging everyone out
  store: new RedisStore({ client: redis, prefix: "sess:", ttl: 3600 }),   // sessions live in Redis, shared by every server
  resave: false,                                                  // do not rewrite unchanged sessions
  saveUninitialized: false,                                       // no session (and no cookie) until you store something
  cookie: { httpOnly: true, sameSite: "lax", maxAge: 60 * 60 * 1000 },      // add secure: true behind HTTPS
}));

const accounts = { ana: "pw-ana", raj: "pw-raj" };                // demo only: real code verifies a password hash (previous entry)

app.post("/login", (req, res, next) => {
  if (accounts[req.body.user] !== req.body.password) return res.status(401).json({ error: "invalid credentials" });
  req.session.regenerate((err) => {                               // NEW session id on login: defeats session fixation
    if (err) return next(err);
    req.session.userId = req.body.user;
    req.session.save((err2) => (err2 ? next(err2) : res.json({ loggedInAs: req.session.userId })));
  });
});

const requireLogin = (req, res, next) => (req.session.userId ? next() : res.status(401).json({ error: "log in first" }));
app.get("/me", requireLogin, (req, res) => res.json({ user: req.session.userId }));

app.post("/logout", (req, res, next) => {
  req.session.destroy((err) => {                                  // remove it on the SERVER, then clear the cookie
    if (err) return next(err);
    res.clearCookie("sid").json({ loggedOut: true });
  });
});
> GET /me < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"log in first"} sessions in Redis before login: 0 (no cookie was set for an anonymous visitor) > POST /login {"user":"ana","password":"nope"} < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"invalid credentials"} login set-cookie flags: [ 'sid=<id>; Path=/; Expires=<date>; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax' ] sessions in Redis after login: 1 > GET /me < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"user":"ana"} planted id became a real session: false sessions in Redis now: 2 (ana's and raj's, each under a freshly generated id) > POST /logout < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"loggedOut":true} > GET /me < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"log in first"} sessions in Redis after ana logs out: 1 (raj's remains)

The Secure cookie gotcha

With cookie.secure: true, express-session refuses to send the cookie over a plain-HTTP connection, which looks like "login works but I am never logged in". Behind a proxy or load balancer that terminates HTTPS, Express itself sees HTTP, so you must tell it to trust the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto header.

import express from "express";
import session from "express-session";

function build({ trustProxy }) {
  const app = express();
  if (trustProxy) app.set("trust proxy", 1);                        // believe the FIRST proxy hop's X-Forwarded-* headers
  app.use(session({ secret: "demo", resave: false, saveUninitialized: false, cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true } }));
  app.get("/start", (req, res) => { req.session.visited = true; res.json({ secureConnection: req.secure }); });
  return app;
}


for (const trustProxy of [false, true]) {
  const app2 = build({ trustProxy });
  const server = app2.listen(0);
  const base2 = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`;
  const asHttp = await fetch(`${base2}/start`);
  const behindTls = await fetch(`${base2}/start`, { headers: { "x-forwarded-proto": "https" } });
  console.log(`trust proxy ${String(trustProxy).padEnd(5)} | direct http: cookie sent = ${asHttp.headers.has("set-cookie")} | via proxy header: cookie sent = ${behindTls.headers.has("set-cookie")} (req.secure = ${(await behindTls.json()).secureConnection})`);
  server.close();
}
trust proxy false | direct http: cookie sent = false | via proxy header: cookie sent = false (req.secure = false) trust proxy true | direct http: cookie sent = false | via proxy header: cookie sent = true (req.secure = true)
Only set trust proxy when a proxy really sits in front. Otherwise any client can forge X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For, defeating secure-cookie logic and IP-based rate limiting. Use the exact number of hops (1), not true.
  • Regenerate the session id on login (and on privilege changes) to prevent fixation, and destroy it on logout on the server.
  • Set an idle and absolute lifetime (maxAge, rolling: true for a sliding window) and store only the user id in the session, not the whole user.
  • State-changing requests authenticated by cookies also need CSRF protection (the CSRF entry).
  • Many servers means a shared store (Redis) or sticky sessions; the cookie is useless if the next server cannot find the record.

A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed, self-contained note: header.payload.signature, three base64url pieces joined by dots. The payload holds claims (sub the subject, exp expiry, iat issued-at, iss issuer, aud audience, plus your own like role). The server signs it at login; later it checks the signature instead of looking anything up. That makes JWTs handy for APIs consumed by mobile apps and other services, and for passing identity between services. The price: you cannot easily revoke one before it expires, so access tokens must be short-lived.

The payload is encoded, not encrypted. Anyone holding the token can read it. Never put passwords, personal data you would not show the user, or secrets inside.

import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";
import crypto from "node:crypto";

const secret = "a-long-random-secret-from-the-environment";
const token = jwt.sign({ sub: "42", role: "user" }, secret, { algorithm: "HS256", expiresIn: "15m", issuer: "notebox-api", audience: "notebox-web" });

const [h, p, sig] = token.split(".");
const decode = (part) => JSON.parse(Buffer.from(part, "base64url").toString());
console.log("header :", decode(h));
const payload = decode(p);
console.log("payload:", { ...payload, iat: "<now>", exp: "<now + 15 min>" }, "| lifetime seconds:", payload.exp - payload.iat);

// what "signed" means: HMAC-SHA256 over "header.payload" with the secret. Anyone with the secret can recompute it
const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${h}.${p}`).digest("base64url");
console.log("signature recomputed by hand matches:", expected === sig);

// tamper: change role to admin, keep the old signature
const forgedPayload = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ ...payload, role: "admin" })).toString("base64url");
const tampered = `${h}.${forgedPayload}.${sig}`;
try { jwt.verify(tampered, secret); } catch (e) { console.log("tampered token ->", e.name + ":", e.message); }

// verify properly: pin the algorithm, issuer and audience
console.log("valid token    ->", jwt.verify(token, secret, { algorithms: ["HS256"], issuer: "notebox-api", audience: "notebox-web" }).sub);
try { jwt.verify(token, secret, { algorithms: ["HS256"], audience: "some-other-service" }); } catch (e) { console.log("wrong audience ->", e.message); }
try { jwt.verify(jwt.sign({ sub: "42" }, secret, { expiresIn: -10 }), secret); } catch (e) { console.log("expired token  ->", e.name + ":", e.message); }
try { jwt.verify(token, "the-wrong-secret"); } catch (e) { console.log("wrong secret   ->", e.message); }
header : { alg: 'HS256', typ: 'JWT' } payload: { sub: '42', role: 'user', iat: '<now>', exp: '<now + 15 min>', aud: 'notebox-web', iss: 'notebox-api' } | lifetime seconds: 900 signature recomputed by hand matches: true tampered token -> JsonWebTokenError: invalid signature valid token -> 42 wrong audience -> jwt audience invalid. expected: some-other-service expired token -> TokenExpiredError: jwt expired wrong secret -> invalid signature
AlgorithmKeysUse when
HS256One shared secret signs and verifies (32 or more random bytes)One service issues and checks its own tokens
RS256RSA private key signs, public key verifiesMany services verify tokens issued by one; widely supported
ES256 / EdDSAElliptic-curve private key signs, public key verifiesSame as RS256 with smaller, faster tokens and keys

With an asymmetric algorithm the verifying services never hold anything that can create tokens. They fetch the public keys from a JWKS URL (/.well-known/jwks.json), and the token header's kid says which key signed it, which makes key rotation painless. jose is a modern library for all of this:

import * as jose from "jose";
import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";
import crypto from "node:crypto";

// issuer side: an elliptic-curve key pair
const { publicKey, privateKey } = await jose.generateKeyPair("ES256");
const token = await new jose.SignJWT({ role: "user" })
  .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "ES256", kid: "key-2026-10" })
  .setSubject("42").setIssuer("notebox-api").setAudience("notebox-web").setIssuedAt().setExpirationTime("15m")
  .sign(privateKey);

// verifier side: only the PUBLIC key (in real life fetched from the JWKS URL)
const { payload, protectedHeader } = await jose.jwtVerify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ["ES256"], issuer: "notebox-api", audience: "notebox-web" });
console.log("verified:", payload.sub, payload.role, "| header:", protectedHeader);
console.log("the JWKS entry other services download:", { ...(await jose.exportJWK(publicKey)), kid: "key-2026-10", use: "sig", alg: "ES256" });

// ATTACK 1: "alg": "none". A token with no signature at all, claiming admin
const b64 = (o) => Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(o)).toString("base64url");
const noneToken = `${b64({ alg: "none", typ: "JWT" })}.${b64({ sub: "1", role: "admin" })}.`;
const naiveVerify = (t) => { const [hh, pp] = t.split("."); return JSON.parse(Buffer.from(hh, "base64url")).alg === "none" ? JSON.parse(Buffer.from(pp, "base64url")) : null; };   // a careless hand-written verifier
console.log("careless verifier accepts alg none     :", naiveVerify(noneToken)?.role);
try { jwt.verify(noneToken, "secret", { algorithms: ["HS256"] }); } catch (e) { console.log("jsonwebtoken with algorithms pinned    ->", e.message); }
await jose.jwtVerify(noneToken, publicKey, { algorithms: ["ES256"] }).catch((e) => console.log("jose                                   ->", e.code));

// ATTACK 2: algorithm confusion. The attacker knows the PUBLIC key, signs an HS256 token using it as the HMAC secret,
// hoping a verifier that trusts the token's own "alg" feeds the public key to HMAC
const rsa = crypto.generateKeyPairSync("rsa", { modulusLength: 2048 });
const publicPem = rsa.publicKey.export({ type: "spki", format: "pem" });
const hs = (t) => crypto.createHmac("sha256", publicPem).update(t).digest("base64url");
const signingInput = `${b64({ alg: "HS256", typ: "JWT" })}.${b64({ sub: "1", role: "admin" })}`;
const confusion = `${signingInput}.${hs(signingInput)}`;
try { jwt.verify(confusion, publicPem); console.log("confusion accepted"); } catch (e) { console.log("algorithm confusion rejected         ->", e.message); }
try { jwt.verify(confusion, publicPem, { algorithms: ["RS256"] }); } catch (e) { console.log("with algorithms: [\"RS256\"] pinned       ->", e.message); }
verified: 42 user | header: { alg: 'ES256', kid: 'key-2026-10' } the JWKS entry other services download: { kty: 'EC', x: '1kUFib2x6kzv_ArBMRMuc5H2swWhZ_ptR6h7mtPtkgk', y: 'xxtG2j8SA-ZzuLiI_xWPWDOV1xI7wPytrAByI4rDMAE', crv: 'P-256', kid: 'key-2026-10', use: 'sig', alg: 'ES256' } careless verifier accepts alg none : admin jsonwebtoken with algorithms pinned -> jwt signature is required jose -> ERR_JOSE_ALG_NOT_ALLOWED algorithm confusion rejected -> invalid algorithm with algorithms: ["RS256"] pinned -> invalid algorithm
Always pass the algorithms you accept (algorithms: ["HS256"]) and check iss and aud. Never let the token's own header decide how it is verified, never accept none, and keep HMAC secrets long and random (32 or more bytes), not words.

Access token plus rotating refresh token

The standard design for APIs: a short-lived access token (5 to 15 minutes) travels in the Authorization: Bearer header, and a long-lived refresh token (days) is an opaque random string kept in an httpOnly cookie, used only to get new access tokens. Each use of a refresh token rotates it (issues a new one and retires the old). If a retired token is ever presented again, someone has stolen it, so the whole family is revoked and the user must log in again. Refresh tokens live in your database, which gives you the revocation JWTs alone cannot.

import express from "express";
import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import cookieParser from "cookie-parser";

const ACCESS_SECRET = "access-secret-from-env-at-least-32-bytes-long";
const sha256 = (t) => crypto.createHash("sha256").update(t).digest("hex");
const refreshTokens = new Map();                                      // sha256(token) -> { userId, family, used }   (a database table in real life)
const revokedFamilies = new Set();

const signAccess = (userId) => jwt.sign({ sub: String(userId) }, ACCESS_SECRET, { algorithm: "HS256", expiresIn: "1s", issuer: "notebox-api" });   // 1 s only so the demo can show expiry; use 5 to 15 minutes
function issueRefresh(res, userId, family = crypto.randomUUID()) {
  const token = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString("base64url");
  refreshTokens.set(sha256(token), { userId, family, used: false });  // store only the hash
  res.cookie("refresh", token, { httpOnly: true, sameSite: "strict", path: "/auth", maxAge: 7 * 24 * 3600 * 1000 });   // path: only sent to /auth/*
}

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.use(cookieParser());

app.post("/auth/login", (req, res) => {
  if (req.body.password !== "pw-ana") return res.status(401).json({ error: "invalid credentials" });   // demo check; real code verifies a hash
  issueRefresh(res, 1);
  res.json({ accessToken: signAccess(1), expiresInSeconds: 1 });
});

app.post("/auth/refresh", (req, res) => {
  const record = refreshTokens.get(sha256(req.cookies.refresh ?? ""));
  if (!record) return res.status(401).json({ error: "unknown refresh token" });
  if (revokedFamilies.has(record.family)) return res.status(401).json({ error: "session revoked" });
  if (record.used) {                                                  // a retired token came back: it was stolen or replayed
    revokedFamilies.add(record.family);
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "refresh token reuse detected: all sessions of this login revoked" });
  }
  record.used = true;                                                 // retire this one...
  issueRefresh(res, record.userId, record.family);                    // ...and hand out the next in the same family
  res.json({ accessToken: signAccess(record.userId), expiresInSeconds: 1 });
});

app.post("/auth/logout", (req, res) => {
  const record = refreshTokens.get(sha256(req.cookies.refresh ?? ""));
  if (record) revokedFamilies.add(record.family);
  res.clearCookie("refresh", { path: "/auth" }).sendStatus(204);
});

function requireAccessToken(req, res, next) {
  const [scheme, token] = (req.get("Authorization") ?? "").split(" ");
  if (scheme !== "Bearer" || !token) return res.status(401).set("WWW-Authenticate", "Bearer").json({ error: "missing bearer token" });
  try { req.userId = jwt.verify(token, ACCESS_SECRET, { algorithms: ["HS256"], issuer: "notebox-api" }).sub; next(); }
  catch (e) { res.status(401).set("WWW-Authenticate", `Bearer error="invalid_token"`).json({ error: e.name === "TokenExpiredError" ? "token expired" : "invalid token" }); }
}
app.get("/api/me", requireAccessToken, (req, res) => res.json({ userId: req.userId }));
> GET /api/me < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"missing bearer token"} login -> 200 {"accessToken":"<jwt>","expiresInSeconds":1} | cookie: refresh=<opaque>; Max-Age=604800; Path=/auth; Expires=<date>; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict > GET /api/me > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"userId":"1"} > GET /api/me > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < www-authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token" < {"error":"token expired"} refresh -> 200 {"accessToken":"<jwt>","expiresInSeconds":1} > GET /api/me > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"userId":"1"} --- an attacker replays the OLD (already rotated) refresh token replayed old token -> 401 {"error":"refresh token reuse detected: all sessions of this login revoked"} --- and now the legitimate user's newest refresh token is dead too > POST /auth/refresh < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"session revoked"}
Where the browser keeps a tokenXSS can steal it?CSRF risk?Verdict
localStorage / sessionStorageYesNoAvoid for anything long-lived
In JavaScript memory onlyOnly while the page is compromisedNoGood for the short-lived access token
HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookieNo (it cannot read it, only use it)Yes, unless SameSite and a CSRF defenseBest for the refresh token, scoped with Path
Server-side sessionsJWT access tokens
What the client holdsA random idThe signed claims
Revoke immediatelyYes: delete the recordHard: wait for expiry, or keep a deny list (which is state again)
Lookup per requestYes (Redis, fast)No, only a signature check
Best forServer-rendered sites and one backendMobile apps, several services, third-party API clients
Honest adviceIf you have one backend and a web front end, sessions are simpler and safer: instant logout, no token juggling. Choose JWTs when you actually need stateless verification across services or non-browser clients. Do not choose them because a tutorial did.

Authentication answers "who are you?"; authorization answers "may you do this to that?". The most common serious flaw in real APIs (OWASP A01) is not a broken login, it is a missing second check: the user is logged in, so the code serves whatever record id they ask for. This is IDOR (insecure direct object reference, also called BOLA).

StatusMeaningUse when
401 UnauthorizedNot authenticated (no or bad credentials)Missing, expired or invalid token or session
403 ForbiddenAuthenticated, not allowedRole is too low, and the user is allowed to know the resource exists
404 Not FoundLooks like it does not existA record the user may not see: do not confirm it exists

Three levels of check, all needed: function level (can this role call this endpoint at all?), object level (does this record belong to this user or their team?), and field level (may they change this property, such as their own role?).

import express from "express";
import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";

const SECRET = "demo-secret-demo-secret-demo-secret";
const users = new Map([[1, { id: 1, name: "Ana", role: "user" }], [2, { id: 2, name: "Raj", role: "user" }], [3, { id: 3, name: "Root", role: "admin" }]]);
const notes = [
  { id: 1, ownerId: 1, title: "Ana's diary" },
  { id: 2, ownerId: 2, title: "Raj's bank PIN" },
];

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

// authentication: who is calling? sets req.user, or answers 401
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const token = (req.get("Authorization") ?? "").replace(/^Bearer /, "");
  try { req.user = users.get(Number(jwt.verify(token, SECRET, { algorithms: ["HS256"] }).sub)); } catch { /* anonymous */ }
  next();
});
const requireLogin = (req, res, next) => (req.user ? next() : res.status(401).json({ error: "log in first" }));
const requireRole = (...roles) => (req, res, next) => (roles.includes(req.user.role) ? next() : res.status(403).json({ error: "your role may not do this" }));

// WRONG: authenticated, but any note id is served to anyone
app.get("/v1/notes/:id", requireLogin, (req, res) => {
  const note = notes.find((n) => n.id === Number(req.params.id));
  note ? res.json(note) : res.status(404).json({ error: "not found" });
});

// RIGHT: the ownership check is part of the lookup, and "not yours" looks exactly like "does not exist"
const canRead = (user, note) => user.role === "admin" || note.ownerId === user.id;      // one policy function, reused everywhere
app.get("/notes/:id", requireLogin, (req, res) => {
  const note = notes.find((n) => n.id === Number(req.params.id));
  if (!note || !canRead(req.user, note)) return res.status(404).json({ error: "not found" });
  res.json(note);
});
// lists must be scoped too: in SQL this is WHERE owner_id = $1, never "filter in JavaScript after loading everything"
app.get("/notes", requireLogin, (req, res) => res.json(notes.filter((n) => canRead(req.user, n)).map((n) => n.title)));

// function-level: only admins list users
app.get("/admin/users", requireLogin, requireRole("admin"), (req, res) => res.json([...users.values()].map((u) => u.name)));

// WRONG: mass assignment, the client chooses which fields to set, including role
app.patch("/v1/me", requireLogin, (req, res) => { Object.assign(req.user, req.body); res.json(req.user); });
// RIGHT: an allow-list of fields the user may change about themselves
app.patch("/me", requireLogin, (req, res) => {
  const { name } = req.body;
  if (typeof name === "string" && name.length > 0) req.user.name = name.slice(0, 50);
  res.json(req.user);
});
--- Ana is logged in and tries Raj's note > GET /v1/notes/2 > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":2,"ownerId":2,"title":"Raj's bank PIN"} > GET /notes/2 > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"not found"} > GET /notes/1 > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"ownerId":1,"title":"Ana's diary"} > GET /notes > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < ["Ana's diary"] --- roles > GET /admin/users > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 403 Forbidden < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"your role may not do this"} > GET /admin/users > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < ["Ana","Raj","Root"] > GET /notes > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < ["Ana's diary","Raj's bank PIN"] > GET /admin/users < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"log in first"} --- Ana tries to promote herself > PATCH /v1/me {"name":"Ana","role":"admin"} > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"name":"Ana","role":"admin"} > PATCH /me {"name":"Raj","role":"admin"} > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":2,"name":"Raj","role":"user"} > GET /admin/users > authorization: Bearer <jwt> < 403 Forbidden < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"your role may not do this"}
  • Decide on the server, per request, from trusted data: the user id comes from the verified token or session, never from the body or a header the client controls. Do not trust a role or userId sent in the request.
  • Put ownership in the query: SELECT * FROM notes WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2. Then forgetting a check later cannot leak rows, and the database returns nothing for other people's ids.
  • Sequential ids invite guessing. Random ids (UUIDs) slow enumeration but are not access control: the ownership check is.
  • Allow-list fields on every write (validate with Zod and .strict() or pick fields by name). Never spread req.body into an update.
  • Roles are fine for small apps (user, admin). Larger ones add permissions (notes:delete), teams or tenants (every query scoped by tenant_id), or libraries such as CASL and policy engines.
  • Test authorization: for each endpoint, a test as the owner, as another user, as an admin and as nobody (Unit 9).

Passport: one interface for many login methods

Passport is Express middleware that standardises login. Each method is a strategy (passport-local for username and password, passport-google-oauth20, passport-github2, passport-jwt and 500 more). A strategy's verify callback checks the credentials and hands Passport a user; with sessions, serializeUser stores a small id and deserializeUser turns it back into req.user on later requests.

import express from "express";
import session from "express-session";
import passport from "passport";
import { Strategy as LocalStrategy } from "passport-local";
import bcrypt from "bcryptjs";

const users = [{ id: 1, email: "ana@example.com", passwordHash: bcrypt.hashSync("correct horse battery", 10) }];

passport.use(new LocalStrategy({ usernameField: "email" }, async (email, password, done) => {   // the verify callback
  const user = users.find((u) => u.email === email.toLowerCase());
  if (!user || !(await bcrypt.compare(password, user.passwordHash))) return done(null, false);   // (error, user or false)
  done(null, user);
}));
passport.serializeUser((user, done) => done(null, user.id));                                     // what goes into the session
passport.deserializeUser((id, done) => done(null, users.find((u) => u.id === id) ?? false));     // what becomes req.user

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.use(session({ secret: "demo-secret", resave: false, saveUninitialized: false, cookie: { httpOnly: true, sameSite: "lax" } }));   // use a Redis store in production
app.use(passport.initialize());
app.use(passport.session());

app.post("/login", (req, res, next) => {
  passport.authenticate("local", (err, user) => {
    if (err) return next(err);
    if (!user) return res.status(401).json({ error: "invalid email or password" });
    req.logIn(user, (err2) => (err2 ? next(err2) : res.json({ id: user.id })));                  // also regenerates the session id (fixation protection)
  })(req, res, next);
});
app.get("/me", (req, res) => (req.isAuthenticated() ? res.json({ email: req.user.email }) : res.status(401).json({ error: "log in first" })));
app.post("/logout", (req, res, next) => req.logout((err) => (err ? next(err) : res.sendStatus(204))));    // logout needs a callback in passport 0.6 and newer
> GET /me < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"log in first"} > POST /login {"email":"ana@example.com","password":"wrong"} < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"invalid email or password"} > POST /login {"email":"ana@example.com","password":"correct horse battery"} < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1} > GET /me < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"email":"ana@example.com"} > POST /logout < 204 No Content > GET /me < 401 Unauthorized < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"log in first"}

OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect

"Log in with Google" and "let this app read my calendar" are both OAuth 2.0: a way for a user to let an app act for them without giving the app their password. OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a thin layer on top that adds login: an ID token (a JWT) telling the app who the user is.

RoleWho
Resource ownerThe user
ClientYour app that wants access or identity
Authorization serverGoogle, GitHub, Auth0, Keycloak: shows the login and consent screens, issues tokens
Resource serverThe API that accepts access tokens (Google Calendar API; maybe yours)
  • Authorization code flow is the right flow for web apps and mobile apps. Do not use the old implicit flow or the password grant.
  • PKCE (code verifier and challenge) proves the app that finishes the flow is the app that started it, so a stolen code is useless. Required for public clients and recommended for all.
  • state is a random value that ties the callback to the login you started: it stops CSRF on the callback. nonce ties the ID token to this login (replay protection).
  • Exact redirect_uri matching on the server stops attackers from receiving codes at their own URL.
  • An access token is for calling an API; an ID token is for the client to learn who logged in (never send it to an API as a credential); a refresh token gets new access tokens.

In real projects you let a library or service do this (openid-client, Passport strategies, Auth.js, Auth0, Keycloak, Cognito). But the protocol is only HTTP redirects, so here is a complete working implementation with a tiny authorization server and a client running on real sockets, including the attacks the parameters exist to stop.

import express from "express";
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import * as jose from "jose";

const b64url = (buf) => Buffer.from(buf).toString("base64url");
const listen = (app) => new Promise((r) => { const s = app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => r(s)); });

// =================== the authorization server (think Google) ===================
const { publicKey, privateKey } = await jose.generateKeyPair("ES256");
const jwk = { ...(await jose.exportJWK(publicKey)), kid: "k1", alg: "ES256", use: "sig" };
const codes = new Map();                                                       // code -> what was asked for
const provider = express();
provider.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false }));
let ISSUER;                                                                     // set after the server starts
const CLIENTS = { "notebox-web": { redirectUris: ["http://127.0.0.1:CLIENT/callback"] } };   // registered in advance

provider.get("/authorize", (req, res) => {
  const q = req.query;
  const client = CLIENTS[q.client_id];
  if (!client || !client.redirectUris.includes(q.redirect_uri)) return res.status(400).send("unknown client or redirect_uri");   // never redirect to an unregistered URL
  if (q.response_type !== "code" || q.code_challenge_method !== "S256" || !q.code_challenge) return res.status(400).send("PKCE with S256 is required");
  const code = crypto.randomBytes(24).toString("base64url");
  codes.set(code, { clientId: q.client_id, redirectUri: q.redirect_uri, challenge: q.code_challenge, nonce: q.nonce, user: { sub: "ana-123", email: "ana@example.com" }, expires: Date.now() + 60_000 });   // the user logged in and approved
  res.redirect(`${q.redirect_uri}?code=${code}&state=${encodeURIComponent(q.state)}`);
});

provider.post("/token", async (req, res) => {
  const { grant_type, code, redirect_uri, client_id, code_verifier } = req.body;
  const entry = codes.get(code);
  codes.delete(code);                                                          // a code works ONCE, even if the attempt fails
  if (grant_type !== "authorization_code" || !entry || entry.expires < Date.now()) return res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid_grant" });
  if (entry.clientId !== client_id || entry.redirectUri !== redirect_uri) return res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid_grant" });
  const challenge = b64url(crypto.createHash("sha256").update(String(code_verifier)).digest());
  if (challenge !== entry.challenge) return res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid_grant", detail: "PKCE verifier does not match" });
  const idToken = await new jose.SignJWT({ email: entry.user.email, nonce: entry.nonce })
    .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "ES256", kid: "k1" }).setSubject(entry.user.sub).setIssuer(ISSUER).setAudience(client_id).setIssuedAt().setExpirationTime("5m").sign(privateKey);
  res.json({ token_type: "Bearer", access_token: crypto.randomBytes(16).toString("hex"), id_token: idToken, expires_in: 300 });
});
provider.get("/jwks.json", (req, res) => res.json({ keys: [jwk] }));

// =================== the client (your app) ===================
const pending = new Map();                                                     // state -> { verifier, nonce }   (a real app keeps this in the user's session)
const client = express();
let CLIENT_URL;

client.get("/login", (req, res) => {
  const state = b64url(crypto.randomBytes(16)), nonce = b64url(crypto.randomBytes(16)), verifier = b64url(crypto.randomBytes(32));
  pending.set(state, { verifier, nonce });
  const url = new URL(`${ISSUER}/authorize`);
  Object.entries({ response_type: "code", client_id: "notebox-web", redirect_uri: `${CLIENT_URL}/callback`, scope: "openid email", state, nonce,
    code_challenge: b64url(crypto.createHash("sha256").update(verifier).digest()), code_challenge_method: "S256" }).forEach(([k, v]) => url.searchParams.set(k, v));
  res.redirect(url.toString());
});

client.get("/callback", async (req, res) => {
  const saved = pending.get(req.query.state);
  pending.delete(req.query.state);
  if (!saved) return res.status(400).json({ error: "state does not match: possible CSRF, login rejected" });
  const tokenRes = await fetch(`${ISSUER}/token`, { method: "POST", headers: { "content-type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
    body: new URLSearchParams({ grant_type: "authorization_code", code: req.query.code, redirect_uri: `${CLIENT_URL}/callback`, client_id: "notebox-web", code_verifier: saved.verifier }) });
  const tokens = await tokenRes.json();
  if (!tokenRes.ok) return res.status(400).json({ error: "token exchange failed", detail: tokens });
  const jwks = jose.createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(`${ISSUER}/jwks.json`));        // download the provider's public keys
  const { payload } = await jose.jwtVerify(tokens.id_token, jwks, { issuer: ISSUER, audience: "notebox-web", algorithms: ["ES256"] });
  if (payload.nonce !== saved.nonce) return res.status(400).json({ error: "nonce mismatch: token replay" });
  res.json({ loggedInAs: payload.email, subject: payload.sub });
});

const pServer = await listen(provider), cServer = await listen(client);
ISSUER = `http://127.0.0.1:${pServer.address().port}`;
CLIENT_URL = `http://127.0.0.1:${cServer.address().port}`;
CLIENTS["notebox-web"].redirectUris = [`${CLIENT_URL}/callback`];

// =================== the browser (we play it by following redirects by hand) ===================
const hop = async (url, label) => { const r = await fetch(url, { redirect: "manual" }); const loc = r.headers.get("location"); console.log(label.padEnd(26), r.status, loc ? "-> " + loc.replace(/\d{4,5}/g, "<port>").replace(/(code|state|nonce|code_challenge)=[^&]+/g, "$1=<random>") : await r.text()); return loc ?? r; };

const toAuthorize = await hop(`${CLIENT_URL}/login`, "1 click Log in");
const toCallback = await hop(toAuthorize, "2 provider approves");
const done = await fetch(toCallback);
console.log("3 callback exchanges code  ", done.status, JSON.stringify(await done.json()));

console.log("--- attacks");
const loc = new URL(toCallback);
console.log("replay the same callback    :", (await fetch(toCallback)).status, JSON.stringify(await (await fetch(toCallback)).json()));
const forged = await fetch(`${CLIENT_URL}/callback?code=${loc.searchParams.get("code")}&state=attacker-chosen-state`);
console.log("forged state (CSRF)         :", forged.status, JSON.stringify(await forged.json()));

const second = await hop(`${CLIENT_URL}/login`, "second login, step 1");
const stolen = new URL(await hop(second, "second login, step 2")).searchParams.get("code");
const steal = await fetch(`${ISSUER}/token`, { method: "POST", headers: { "content-type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
  body: new URLSearchParams({ grant_type: "authorization_code", code: stolen, redirect_uri: `${CLIENT_URL}/callback`, client_id: "notebox-web", code_verifier: b64url(crypto.randomBytes(32)) }) });
console.log("stolen code, wrong verifier :", steal.status, JSON.stringify(await steal.json()));

const evil = new URL(second); evil.searchParams.set("redirect_uri", "http://evil.example/callback");
console.log("authorize to unregistered URL:", (await fetch(evil, { redirect: "manual" })).status, "(refused, nothing was redirected)");

pServer.close(); cServer.close();
1 click Log in 302 -> http://127.0.0.1:<port>/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=notebox-web&redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A<port>%2Fcallback&scope=openid+email&state=<random>&nonce=<random>&code_challenge=<random>&code_challenge_method=S256 2 provider approves 302 -> http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<random>&state=<random> 3 callback exchanges code 200 {"loggedInAs":"ana@example.com","subject":"ana-123"} --- attacks replay the same callback : 400 {"error":"state does not match: possible CSRF, login rejected"} forged state (CSRF) : 400 {"error":"state does not match: possible CSRF, login rejected"} second login, step 1 302 -> http://127.0.0.1:<port>/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=notebox-web&redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A<port>%2Fcallback&scope=openid+email&state=<random>&nonce=<random>&code_challenge=<random>&code_challenge_method=S256 second login, step 2 302 -> http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<random>&state=<random> stolen code, wrong verifier : 400 {"error":"invalid_grant","detail":"PKCE verifier does not match"} authorize to unregistered URL: 400 (refused, nothing was redirected)
What the demo skipped on purposeA real authorization server shows a login page and consent screen, keeps the user's login session, supports refresh tokens and scopes, rotates signing keys, and publishes a discovery document at /.well-known/openid-configuration. When you call someone else's provider, use a maintained library and register your exact redirect_uri in their console; when you need your own, prefer Keycloak, Ory or a hosted service to writing one.

Cross-Site Request Forgery abuses one browser rule: cookies are attached to every request to their site, no matter which page triggered it. You are logged in to bank.example. You visit evil.example, whose page contains an auto-submitting form pointed at bank.example/transfer. Your browser sends the form with your bank cookie, so the bank sees a legitimate, logged-in request. The attacker cannot read the response, but does not need to: the money has moved.

It only threatens endpoints that (1) authenticate with cookies (or other credentials the browser adds automatically) and (2) change something. APIs that need an Authorization: Bearer header set by your own JavaScript are not CSRF-able, because a foreign page cannot add that header.

A real browser needs a hostile page to demonstrate this, so the demo plays both sides: the cookie jar is the victim's browser, and the forged request carries the same headers a browser would send (Origin: https://evil.example and a form content type).

import express from "express";
import session from "express-session";
import crypto from "node:crypto";

const app = express();
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false }));          // HTML forms send application/x-www-form-urlencoded
app.use(express.json());
app.use(session({ secret: "demo-secret", resave: false, saveUninitialized: false, cookie: { httpOnly: true } }));   // note: no SameSite set in this demo

const balances = { ana: 1000, mallory: 0, raj: 0 };
app.post("/login", (req, res) => { req.session.user = "ana"; res.json({ ok: true }); });
const requireLogin = (req, res, next) => (req.session.user ? next() : res.status(401).json({ error: "log in first" }));

// 1. VULNERABLE: trusts the cookie and nothing else
app.post("/v1/transfer", requireLogin, (req, res) => {
  balances[req.session.user] -= Number(req.body.amount);
  balances[req.body.to] += Number(req.body.amount);
  res.json({ balances });
});

// 2. DEFENSE: refuse state-changing requests that did not come from our own site
const OWN_ORIGINS = new Set(["https://bank.example"]);
function sameSiteOnly(req, res, next) {
  if (["GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"].includes(req.method)) return next();            // safe methods must never change data
  const fetchSite = req.get("Sec-Fetch-Site");                                    // sent by modern browsers, cannot be set by page scripts
  if (fetchSite && !["same-origin", "none"].includes(fetchSite)) return res.status(403).json({ error: "cross-site request refused", via: "Sec-Fetch-Site" });
  const origin = req.get("Origin");
  if (origin && !OWN_ORIGINS.has(origin)) return res.status(403).json({ error: "cross-site request refused", via: "Origin" });
  next();
}
