console.log("flaky job result:", await flaky.waitUntilFinished(events));
console.log("worker saw attemptsMade:", seen, "(it ran 3 times)");

const doomed = await queue.add("charge", {}, { attempts: 2, backoff: { type: "exponential", delay: 20 } });   // waits 20 ms, then gives up
try { await doomed.waitUntilFinished(events); } catch (error) { console.log("waitUntilFinished rejected:", error.message); }
const saved = await queue.getJob(doomed.id);
console.log("kept for inspection:", { state: await saved.getState(), attemptsMade: saved.attemptsMade, failedReason: saved.failedReason });

await worker.close(); await events.close(); await queue.obliterate({ force: true }); await queue.close();
flaky job result: { sent: true } worker saw attemptsMade: [ 0, 1, 2 ] (it ran 3 times) waitUntilFinished rejected: invalid card number kept for inspection: { state: 'failed', attemptsMade: 2, failedReason: 'invalid card number' }
Not every error deserves a retryRetry transient failures (timeouts, 502, 503, 429). A validation error or "card declined" will fail identically every time: throw UnrecoverableError (exported by BullMQ) to skip the remaining attempts and go straight to failed.

Concurrency, delays, deduplication and idempotency

import { Queue, Worker, QueueEvents } from "bullmq";

const connection = { host: "127.0.0.1", port: 6399 };
const name = "demo-options-" + process.pid;
const queue = new Queue(name, { connection });
const events = new QueueEvents(name, { connection });
await events.waitUntilReady();

let running = 0, maxRunning = 0;
const worker = new Worker(name, async (job) => {
  running++; maxRunning = Math.max(maxRunning, running);
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 80));
  running--;
  return job.data.n;
}, { connection, concurrency: 2 });                                            // at most 2 jobs at once in THIS worker process

// concurrency: 6 jobs, but never more than 2 running at the same moment
const jobs = await Promise.all([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].map((n) => queue.add("work", { n })));
await Promise.all(jobs.map((job) => job.waitUntilFinished(events)));
console.log("6 jobs done, most that ever ran at once:", maxRunning);

// delay: the job sits in the "delayed" set until its time comes
const startedAt = Date.now();
const later = await queue.add("work", { n: 7 }, { delay: 150 });
console.log("state right after add:", await later.getState());
await later.waitUntilFinished(events);
console.log("ran no sooner than the delay:", Date.now() - startedAt >= 140);

// deduplication: the same jobId is stored once, however many times it is added
const first = await queue.add("work", { n: 8 }, { jobId: "order-1001" });
const second = await queue.add("work", { n: 8 }, { jobId: "order-1001" });     // e.g. the user double-clicked, or the request was retried
console.log("second add returned the same job:", first.id === second.id, "| id:", first.id);

await worker.close(); await events.close(); await queue.obliterate({ force: true }); await queue.close();
6 jobs done, most that ever ran at once: 2 state right after add: delayed ran no sooner than the delay: true second add returned the same job: true | id: order-1001

Delivery is at least once: after a worker crash, a stalled job runs again, and a retry runs the job again after it may have done part of its work. So every worker must be idempotent: running it twice must have the same effect as running it once. The standard tool is an idempotency key recorded atomically with the side effect (a unique constraint in your database, or Redis SET key NX):

import { Queue, Worker, QueueEvents } from "bullmq";
import { Redis } from "ioredis";

const connection = { host: "127.0.0.1", port: 6399 };
const redis = new Redis(6399);
const name = "demo-idem-" + process.pid;
const queue = new Queue(name, { connection });
const events = new QueueEvents(name, { connection });
await events.waitUntilReady();

const charges = [];                                                            // stands in for "the payment provider"
const worker = new Worker(name, async (job) => {
  const key = `charged:${name}:${job.data.orderId}`;
  const first = await redis.set(key, "1", "EX", 3600, "NX");                  // "OK" only for the first caller: atomic claim
  if (first === "OK") charges.push(job.data.orderId);                         // the side effect happens exactly once
  if (job.attemptsMade === 0) throw new Error("crashed after charging");      // the first attempt dies AFTER the side effect
  return { charged: true };
}, { connection });

const job = await queue.add("charge", { orderId: "A-17" }, { attempts: 3, backoff: { type: "fixed", delay: 20 } });
await job.waitUntilFinished(events);
console.log("job ran", (await queue.getJob(job.id)).attemptsMade, "times (initial run, then the retry)");
console.log("customer charged:", charges.length, "time(s)");                    // without the key this would be 2

await redis.del(`charged:${name}:A-17`); redis.disconnect();
await worker.close(); await events.close(); await queue.obliterate({ force: true }); await queue.close();
job ran 2 times (initial run, then the retry) customer charged: 1 time(s)

Repeatable jobs

A job scheduler (BullMQ 5.16 and later, replacing the old "repeatable jobs") creates jobs on a schedule, stored in Redis, so the schedule survives restarts and is registered once however many instances start. every takes milliseconds, pattern takes a cron expression. upsertJobScheduler is idempotent, so calling it on every boot is safe.

import { Queue, Worker } from "bullmq";

const connection = { host: "127.0.0.1", port: 6399 };
const name = "demo-scheduler-" + process.pid;
const queue = new Queue(name, { connection });
let runs = 0;
const worker = new Worker(name, async () => { runs++; }, { connection });

// safe to call on every startup: same id means "update", not "add another"
await queue.upsertJobScheduler("heartbeat", { every: 50 }, { name: "tick", data: { source: "scheduler" } });
await queue.upsertJobScheduler("heartbeat", { every: 50 }, { name: "tick", data: { source: "scheduler" } });
console.log("schedulers registered:", (await queue.getJobSchedulers()).length);

await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 450));
console.log("worker ran at least 3 times:", runs >= 3);
await queue.removeJobScheduler("heartbeat");
console.log("schedulers after remove:", (await queue.getJobSchedulers()).length);

await worker.close(); await queue.obliterate({ force: true }); await queue.close();
schedulers registered: 1 worker ran at least 3 times: true schedulers after remove: 0
Operating queuesRun workers as their own processes (node worker.js), scaled separately from the API. On SIGTERM call await worker.close(), which waits for running jobs. Set removeOnComplete and removeOnFail (a count or an age) so Redis does not fill up. Use separate queues for different priorities or rate limits, the limiter worker option to respect a partner's rate limit, and a dashboard such as Bull Board to look inside. Small job data only: put the user id in the job, not the whole record, and re-read fresh data in the worker. The same pattern exists in other stacks (Sidekiq, Celery); alternatives for Node are pg-boss (Postgres only) and cloud queues such as SQS.

Some work is driven by the clock rather than a request: nightly cleanups, daily digests, expiring trials. The language for schedules is cron syntax, and the node-cron package runs functions on such a schedule inside your process. Two things catch beginners: a task that takes longer than its interval overlaps itself, and with several app instances every instance runs every task unless you coordinate.

minute  hour  day-of-month  month  day-of-week      (node-cron also accepts a leading seconds field)
  0      9         *          *       1-5            means 09:00 on weekdays
ExpressionMeaning
* * * * *Every minute
*/5 * * * *Every 5 minutes (*/n is "every n")
0 9 * * 1-509:00, Monday to Friday (1-5 is a range, 0 or 7 is Sunday)
30 2 1 * *02:30 on the 1st of each month
0 0,12 * * *Midnight and noon (, is a list)
*/10 * * * * *Six fields: every 10 seconds (node-cron adds a seconds field in front)
 
import cron from "node-cron";

for (const expression of ["*/5 * * * *", "0 9 * * 1-5", "0 9 * * MON", "*/2 * * * * *", "61 * * * *", "every day"])
  console.log(expression.padEnd(14), "valid:", cron.validate(expression));
console.log("why 61 fails:", cron.validateDetailed("61 * * * *").errors[0].message);     // validate user-supplied expressions before saving them

let runs = 0;
const task = cron.schedule("* * * * * *", (context) => {                       // every second
  runs++;
  if (runs === 1) console.log("the callback gets a context with:", Object.keys(context));
}, { name: "every-second", timezone: "UTC" });                                 // ALWAYS set a timezone: the server's zone is a hidden input otherwise

await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 2300));
console.log("ran at least twice in 2.3 s:", runs >= 2);

await task.stop();                                                              // stops future runs, task can be started again
const frozen = runs;
await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1200));
console.log("no more runs after stop():", runs === frozen);
await task.destroy();                                                           // free it for good (also call on shutdown)
*/5 * * * * valid: true 0 9 * * 1-5 valid: true 0 9 * * MON valid: true */2 * * * * * valid: true 61 * * * * valid: false every day valid: false why 61 fails: 61 is a invalid expression for minute the callback gets a context with: [ 'date', 'dateLocalIso', 'triggeredAt', 'task', 'execution' ] ran at least twice in 2.3 s: true no more runs after stop(): true

Overlapping runs and running once across instances

The scheduler fires on the clock whether or not the last run finished. Below, a job that takes 1.5 s is scheduled every second: without a guard two runs are active at once. And if you deploy three instances, all three run the task, which is wrong for "send the daily email". The fix is a lock that exactly one instance can take per tick (Redis SET key NX, or a Postgres advisory lock), or run schedulers in a single dedicated process, or use BullMQ's job schedulers from the previous entry (the queue guarantees one job per tick).

import cron from "node-cron";

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
let activeNaive = 0, maxNaive = 0, activeGuarded = 0, maxGuarded = 0, skipped = 0, busy = false;

const naive = cron.schedule("* * * * * *", async () => {
  activeNaive++; maxNaive = Math.max(maxNaive, activeNaive);
  await sleep(1500);                                                           // slower than the 1 s interval
  activeNaive--;
}, { name: "naive", maxExecutions: 3 });

const guarded = cron.schedule("* * * * * *", async () => {
  if (busy) { skipped++; return; }                                            // previous run still going: skip this tick
  busy = true;
  try {
    activeGuarded++; maxGuarded = Math.max(maxGuarded, activeGuarded);
    await sleep(1500);
    activeGuarded--;
  } finally { busy = false; }                                                  // release even if the job throws
}, { name: "guarded", maxExecutions: 3 });

await sleep(4200);
console.log("without a guard, runs active at once:", maxNaive);
console.log("with a guard,    runs active at once:", maxGuarded, "| ticks skipped:", skipped > 0);
await naive.destroy(); await guarded.destroy();
without a guard, runs active at once: 2 with a guard, runs active at once: 1 | ticks skipped: true
import cron from "node-cron";
import { Redis } from "ioredis";

const redis = new Redis(6399);
const prefix = "cron-demo-" + process.pid;
const executions = new Map();                                                  // tick -> which instances actually ran it
const tasks = ["A", "B", "C"].map((instance) => cron.schedule("* * * * * *", async (context) => {
  const tick = context.date.toISOString();                                    // every instance sees the same tick time
  const won = await redis.set(`${prefix}:${tick}`, instance, "EX", 60, "NX"); // atomic: only ONE instance gets "OK"
  if (!won) return;                                                            // another instance owns this tick
  executions.set(tick, [...(executions.get(tick) ?? []), instance]);
}, { name: "digest-" + instance, timezone: "UTC" }));

await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 2600));
console.log("at least 2 ticks ran:", executions.size >= 2);
console.log("every tick ran on exactly one instance:", [...executions.values()].every((who) => who.length === 1));

for (const task of tasks) await task.destroy();
for (const tick of executions.keys()) await redis.del(`${prefix}:${tick}`);
redis.disconnect();
at least 2 ticks ran: true every tick ran on exactly one instance: true

Sending email with nodemailer

nodemailer builds a correct MIME message (headers, HTML plus plain text, attachments, encoding) and hands it to a transport. In production the transport is SMTP, or better the API of a delivery service (SES, Postmark, SendGrid, Resend) which handles reputation and bounces. In tests and demos use jsonTransport, which sends nothing and returns the message as JSON:

import nodemailer from "nodemailer";

const transport = nodemailer.createTransport({ jsonTransport: true });         // swap for the SMTP config below in production

const info = await transport.sendMail({
  from: '"Acme Notes" <no-reply@example.com>',
  to: "ana@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome to Acme Notes",
  text: "Hi Ana, welcome aboard.",                                             // ALWAYS include a plain-text version
  html: "<p>Hi <b>Ana</b>, welcome aboard.</p>",
  attachments: [{ filename: "guide.txt", content: "Getting started..." }],
});

const message = JSON.parse(info.message);
console.log("from       :", message.from);
console.log("to         :", message.to);
console.log("subject    :", message.subject);
console.log("has text and html:", Boolean(message.text), Boolean(message.html));
console.log("attachments:", message.attachments.map((a) => a.filename));
console.log("envelope   :", info.envelope);
from : { address: 'no-reply@example.com', name: 'Acme Notes' } to : [ { address: 'ana@example.com', name: '' } ] subject : Welcome to Acme Notes has text and html: true true attachments: [ 'guide.txt' ] envelope : { from: 'no-reply@example.com', to: [ 'ana@example.com' ] }
import nodemailer from "nodemailer";

const transport = nodemailer.createTransport({
  host: process.env.SMTP_HOST,                 // e.g. email-smtp.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com
  port: 587,                                   // 587 + STARTTLS, or 465 with secure: true
  secure: false,                               // false means "upgrade with STARTTLS", not "insecure"
  auth: { user: process.env.SMTP_USER, pass: process.env.SMTP_PASS },
  pool: true,                                  // reuse connections when sending many messages
});

await transport.verify();                      // fails fast at startup if host or credentials are wrong
  • Send from a queue, never inside the request: SMTP is slow and flaky. The request enqueues { template, to, data }, the worker sends, BullMQ retries (previous entry). Make the job idempotent so a retry does not mail twice.
  • Never build email from user input unescaped (HTML injection), and never put user-controlled text in headers (subject, to): nodemailer rejects newlines, but validate addresses anyway.
  • Deliverability is DNS work: SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for your sending domain, a real from address, and an unsubscribe link for bulk mail.
  • Templates: render HTML with a template engine (Handlebars, MJML for responsive email) in the worker, and test with a catcher such as Mailpit or Ethereal instead of real inboxes.
  • Secrets (SMTP password, API keys) come from environment variables, as in the config entry in Unit 10.

A webhook is an HTTP request that another service sends to your URL when something happens (a payment succeeded, a repository was pushed, a form was submitted). Your URL is public, so anybody can POST to it. Three problems follow, and each has a standard answer:

ThreatDefence
Forged request: "payment succeeded" from an attackerSignature: the sender computes an HMAC of the body with a shared secret, you recompute and compare in constant time
Replay: a real request captured and re-sent laterTimestamp inside the signed data, rejected when too old (a tolerance of a few minutes)
Duplicates: senders retry, so you receive the same event twiceEvent id remembered, second delivery acknowledged but ignored (idempotency)
Slow handler: sender times out and retriesAnswer fast with 2xx, do the work in a background job
The raw body is what is signedThe signature covers the exact bytes the sender sent. If express.json() parses the body first and you re-serialize it, spacing and key order change and verification fails (or worse, you verify something different from what you act on). Use express.raw({ type: "application/json" }) on the webhook route, verify, and only then JSON.parse the Buffer. Mount the raw parser for this route before any global express.json().
import express from "express";
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import { Queue, Worker } from "bullmq";

const SECRET = "whsec_demo_shared_secret";                                      // from the provider's dashboard, kept in an env var
const TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300;

const sign = (timestamp, rawBody, secret = SECRET) =>
  crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${timestamp}.${rawBody}`).digest("hex");   // signed data = timestamp + "." + exact body

function verify(header, rawBody) {                                              // header looks like: t=1700000000,v1=<hex>
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(String(header ?? "").split(",").map((p) => p.split("=")));
  if (!parts.t || !parts.v1) return "malformed signature header";
  if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(parts.t)) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS) return "timestamp outside tolerance";   // stops replay
  const expected = Buffer.from(sign(parts.t, rawBody), "hex");
  const received = Buffer.from(parts.v1, "hex");
  if (expected.length !== received.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(expected, received)) return "bad signature";   // constant-time compare, length checked first
  return null;                                                                  // null means valid
}

const connection = { host: "127.0.0.1", port: 6399 };
const name = "demo-webhooks-" + process.pid;
const queue = new Queue(name, { connection });
const handled = [];
const worker = new Worker(name, async (job) => { handled.push(job.data.id + ":" + job.data.type); }, { connection });

const seenEvents = new Set();                                                   // production: a table with a unique constraint on event id
const app = express();
app.post("/webhooks/payments", express.raw({ type: "application/json", limit: "100kb" }), async (req, res) => {
  const problem = verify(req.get("Stripe-Style-Signature"), req.body.toString("utf8"));
  if (problem) return res.status(400).json({ error: problem });                 // 400, not 500: the sender should not retry a forgery forever
  const event = JSON.parse(req.body.toString("utf8"));                          // parse only AFTER the signature checks out
  if (seenEvents.has(event.id)) return res.json({ received: true, duplicate: true });   // already handled: still answer 2xx
  seenEvents.add(event.id);
  await queue.add(event.type, event, { jobId: event.id });                      // do the real work in the background
  res.json({ received: true });                                                 // answer fast
});

const server = app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await new Promise((resolve) => server.once("listening", resolve));
const url = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}/webhooks/payments`;

// the sender's side: sign the exact bytes it is about to send
async function deliver(event, { secret = SECRET, timestamp = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000), tamper } = {}) {
  const body = JSON.stringify(event);
  const header = `t=${timestamp},v1=${sign(timestamp, body, secret)}`;
  const res = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", headers: { "content-type": "application/json", "Stripe-Style-Signature": header }, body: tamper ? body.replace("1999", "1") : body });
  return `${res.status} ${JSON.stringify(await res.json())}`;
}
const event = { id: "evt_1", type: "payment.succeeded", amount: 1999 };

console.log("valid                 ->", await deliver(event));
console.log("same event again      ->", await deliver(event));
console.log("body changed in flight->", await deliver({ id: "evt_2", type: "payment.succeeded", amount: 1999 }, { tamper: true }));
console.log("signed with wrong key ->", await deliver({ id: "evt_3", type: "payment.succeeded", amount: 1999 }, { secret: "guess" }));
console.log("captured 20 min ago   ->", await deliver({ id: "evt_4", type: "payment.succeeded", amount: 1999 }, { timestamp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 1200 }));
const missing = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", headers: { "content-type": "application/json" }, body: "{}" });
console.log("no signature header   ->", missing.status, JSON.stringify(await missing.json()));

await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 200));
console.log("background worker handled:", handled);

server.close(); await worker.close(); await queue.obliterate({ force: true }); await queue.close();
valid -> 200 {"received":true} same event again -> 200 {"received":true,"duplicate":true} body changed in flight-> 400 {"error":"bad signature"} signed with wrong key -> 400 {"error":"bad signature"} captured 20 min ago -> 400 {"error":"timestamp outside tolerance"} no signature header -> 400 {"error":"malformed signature header"} background worker handled: [ 'evt_1:payment.succeeded' ]

Sending webhooks: retries with backoff

If you are the provider, you promise "at least once": sign every delivery, treat any non-2xx or a timeout as failure, retry with exponential backoff (and jitter), and eventually give up and show the failure in a dashboard. Put the sending in a queue (previous entries) so one slow customer never blocks anyone.

import http from "node:http";

// a customer endpoint that is down twice, then recovers
let hits = 0;
const customer = http.createServer((req, res) => { hits++; res.statusCode = hits <= 2 ? 503 : 200; res.end("ok"); });
await new Promise((resolve) => customer.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", resolve));
const url = `http://127.0.0.1:${customer.address().port}/hook`;

async function deliverWithRetries(payload, { maxAttempts = 5, baseMs = 20 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      const res = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify(payload), signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) });   // never wait forever
      if (res.ok) return { delivered: true, attempts: attempt };
      if (res.status < 500 && res.status !== 429) return { delivered: false, attempts: attempt, reason: `permanent ${res.status}` };   // 4xx: retrying will not help
      console.log(`attempt ${attempt}: ${res.status}, will retry`);
    } catch (error) {
      console.log(`attempt ${attempt}: ${error.name}, will retry`);             // timeout or connection refused
    }
    const wait = baseMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1) * (0.5 + Math.random() / 2);       // exponential backoff with jitter
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, wait));
  }
  return { delivered: false, attempts: maxAttempts, reason: "gave up" };        // surface this in a dashboard, optionally disable the endpoint
}

console.log(await deliverWithRetries({ id: "evt_9", type: "invoice.paid" }));
customer.close();
attempt 1: 503, will retry attempt 2: 503, will retry { delivered: true, attempts: 3 }
  • Receiving: verify, dedupe, queue, answer 2xx within seconds. Never do the slow work inline.
  • Rotate secrets without downtime by accepting two signatures during the changeover (providers send both).
  • Allow only the provider's published IP ranges as an extra layer, never as the only one.
  • When you call user-supplied webhook URLs, you are an SSRF target: apply the allow-list and private-IP checks from the SSRF entry in Unit 7 before every request.
  • Log the event id and your decision for every delivery: it is the first thing you need when someone says "I never got it".

GraphQL is a query language for APIs. Instead of many fixed endpoints that each return a fixed shape, there is one endpoint (POST /graphql) and the client sends a query that names exactly the fields it wants. The server describes everything it can do in a typed schema, and each field is backed by a resolver function.

GraphQL termMeaning
typeAn object with fields, e.g. type Book { id: ID! title: String! }
!Non-null. String! always has a value, String may be null. [Book!]! is a non-null list of non-null books.
Query / MutationThe entry points: read operations and write operations. (Subscription exists for push over WebSocket or SSE.)
inputA type used for arguments, such as the body of a mutation
ResolverA function (args, context, info) that produces one field's value (when written as methods on the root object, as below)
VariablesTyped values sent beside the query ($id: ID!) instead of pasted into it: this is the injection-safe way
 
import express from "express";
import { buildSchema, GraphQLError } from "graphql";
import { createHandler } from "graphql-http/lib/use/express";

// 1. THE SCHEMA: the contract, written in the schema definition language
const schema = buildSchema(`
  type Author { id: ID! name: String! books: [Book!]! }
  type Book   { id: ID! title: String! author: Author! }
  input NewBook { title: String! authorId: ID! }
  type Query {
    books(limit: Int = 10): [Book!]!
    book(id: ID!): Book
    brokenField: String
  }
  type Mutation { addBook(input: NewBook!): Book! }
`);

// 2. THE DATA (stand-in for a database) and the RESOLVERS
const authors = { 1: { id: "1", name: "Ana" }, 2: { id: "2", name: "Raj" } };
const books = Array.from({ length: 4 }, (_, i) => ({ id: String(i + 1), title: "Book " + (i + 1), authorId: String(i % 2 + 1) }));
const toBook = (row) => ({
  id: row.id, title: row.title,
  author: () => toAuthor(authors[row.authorId]),                                // a field can be a function: resolved only when the query asks for it
});
const toAuthor = (row) => ({ ...row, books: () => books.filter((b) => b.authorId === row.id).map(toBook) });

const rootValue = {
  books: ({ limit }) => books.slice(0, limit).map(toBook),                      // args arrive already validated and typed (limit is an Int)
  book: ({ id }) => { const row = books.find((b) => b.id === id); return row ? toBook(row) : null; },   // null is allowed: the field is nullable
  brokenField: () => { throw new Error("database is down"); },
  addBook: ({ input }) => {
    if (!authors[input.authorId]) throw new GraphQLError("unknown author", { extensions: { code: "BAD_USER_INPUT" } });
    const row = { id: String(books.length + 1), title: input.title, authorId: input.authorId };
    books.push(row); return toBook(row);
  },
};

// 3. DEPTH LIMIT: queries can nest forever (author -> books -> author ...), so cap it
const depthLimit = (max) => (context) => {
  let depth = 0;
  return { Field: { enter(node) { depth++; if (depth === max + 1) context.reportError(new GraphQLError(`query is too deep (maximum ${max})`)); }, leave() { depth--; } } };
};

const app = express();
app.all("/graphql", createHandler({ schema, rootValue, validationRules: [depthLimit(4)] }));   // graphql-http parses the body itself: no express.json() needed
const server = app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await new Promise((resolve) => server.once("listening", resolve));
const url = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}/graphql`;

async function gql(title, query, variables, headers = {}) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", headers: { "content-type": "application/json", ...headers }, body: JSON.stringify({ query, variables }) });
  console.log(`--- ${title} (HTTP ${res.status})`);
  console.log(JSON.stringify(await res.json()));
}

await gql("ask for exactly the fields you want", "{ book(id: \"2\") { title author { name } } }");
await gql("variables, an alias and a fragment, a directive",
  `query Shelf($n: Int, $withAuthor: Boolean!) {
     first: books(limit: $n) { ...BookInfo }
     one:   book(id: "4")   { ...BookInfo }
   }
   fragment BookInfo on Book { title author @include(if: $withAuthor) { name } }`, { n: 2, withAuthor: false });
await gql("a mutation with an input object", "mutation($input: NewBook!) { addBook(input: $input) { id title author { name } } }", { input: { title: "Book 5", authorId: "2" } });
await gql("a resolver throws: partial data plus an errors array", "{ brokenField books(limit: 1) { title } }");
await gql("custom error code in extensions", "mutation { addBook(input: { title: \"X\", authorId: \"99\" }) { id } }");
await gql("wrong variable type", "mutation($input: NewBook!) { addBook(input: $input) { id } }", { input: { title: 5 } });
await gql("unknown field (validation error)", "{ book(id: \"1\") { color } }");
await gql("same, asking for the newer media type", "{ book(id: \"1\") { color } }", undefined, { accept: "application/graphql-response+json" });
await gql("nesting deeper than the limit", "{ books { author { books { author { books { title } } } } } }");
const viaGet = await fetch(url + "?query=" + encodeURIComponent("{ book(id: \"1\") { title } }"));
console.log("--- GET with ?query= works for queries (HTTP " + viaGet.status + "):", await viaGet.text());

server.close();
--- ask for exactly the fields you want (HTTP 200) {"data":{"book":{"title":"Book 2","author":{"name":"Raj"}}}} --- variables, an alias and a fragment, a directive (HTTP 200) {"data":{"first":[{"title":"Book 1"},{"title":"Book 2"}],"one":{"title":"Book 4"}}} --- a mutation with an input object (HTTP 200) {"data":{"addBook":{"id":"5","title":"Book 5","author":{"name":"Raj"}}}} --- a resolver throws: partial data plus an errors array (HTTP 200) {"errors":[{"message":"database is down","locations":[{"line":1,"column":3}],"path":["brokenField"]}],"data":{"brokenField":null,"books":[{"title":"Book 1"}]}} --- custom error code in extensions (HTTP 200) {"errors":[{"message":"unknown author","locations":[{"line":1,"column":12}],"path":["addBook"],"extensions":{"code":"BAD_USER_INPUT"}}],"data":null} --- wrong variable type (HTTP 200) {"errors":[{"message":"Variable \"$input\" has invalid value at .title: String cannot represent a non string value: 5","locations":[{"line":1,"column":10}]},{"message":"Variable \"$input\" has invalid value: Expected value of type \"NewBook\" to include required field \"authorId\", found: { title: 5 }.","locations":[{"line":1,"column":10}]}]} --- unknown field (validation error) (HTTP 200) {"errors":[{"message":"Cannot query field \"color\" on type \"Book\".","locations":[{"line":1,"column":19}]}]} --- same, asking for the newer media type (HTTP 400) {"errors":[{"message":"Cannot query field \"color\" on type \"Book\".","locations":[{"line":1,"column":19}]}]} --- nesting deeper than the limit (HTTP 200) {"errors":[{"message":"query is too deep (maximum 4)"}]} --- GET with ?query= works for queries (HTTP 200): {"data":{"book":{"title":"Book 1"}}}

Read the results: GraphQL reports most errors inside a 200 response (errors next to partial data, with the failed field set to null and a path), so monitoring that only looks at HTTP status will miss them. Notice that even the unknown-field validation error came back as 200 by default, and as 400 only when the client asked for the newer application/graphql-response+json media type. A ! field that fails nulls its parent, up to the nearest nullable field. Never return stack traces or database messages in message; log the real error and return a safe message plus an extensions.code.

The N+1 problem and DataLoader

Resolvers run per field, per item. A list of 100 books where each resolves its author with a database query makes 1 + 100 queries. DataLoader fixes this: within one tick it collects every load(id), calls your batch function once with all ids (WHERE id = ANY($1)), caches repeats, and hands each caller its own result. Create a new loader per request (in the context), never globally, or one user's cached data leaks to another.

import { buildSchema, graphql } from "graphql";
import DataLoader from "dataloader";

const schema = buildSchema(`
  type Author { name: String! }
  type Book { title: String! author: Author! }
  type Query { books: [Book!]! }
`);
const authors = { 1: { name: "Ana" }, 2: { name: "Raj" } };
const books = Array.from({ length: 6 }, (_, i) => ({ title: "Book " + (i + 1), authorId: i % 2 + 1 }));
const query = "{ books { title author { name } } }";

// WITHOUT: each book looks up its author on its own
let dbCalls = 0;
const findAuthor = async (id) => { dbCalls++; return authors[id]; };            // one "SELECT ... WHERE id = $1" per call
const naive = { books: () => { dbCalls++; return books.map((b) => ({ title: b.title, author: () => findAuthor(b.authorId) })); } };
const first = await graphql({ schema, source: query, rootValue: naive });
console.log("without DataLoader:", dbCalls, "database calls for", first.data.books.length, "books");

// WITH: author lookups are collected and sent together, duplicates removed
dbCalls = 0;
const batches = [];
const loaderFor = () => new DataLoader(async (ids) => {                         // new loader per request
  dbCalls++; batches.push([...ids]);                                            // one "SELECT ... WHERE id = ANY($1)" for everybody
  return ids.map((id) => authors[id]);                                          // results must be in the same order as ids
});
const loader = loaderFor();
const batched = { books: () => { dbCalls++; return books.map((b) => ({ title: b.title, author: () => loader.load(b.authorId) })); } };
const second = await graphql({ schema, source: query, rootValue: batched });
console.log("with DataLoader   :", dbCalls, "database calls | the batch asked for ids", batches[0], "once");
console.log("same answer:", JSON.stringify(first.data) === JSON.stringify(second.data));
without DataLoader: 7 database calls for 6 books with DataLoader : 2 database calls | the batch asked for ids [ 1, 2 ] once same answer: true
RESTGraphQL
Shape of responseFixed by the endpoint (over- or under-fetching)Chosen by the client query
Round trips for related dataOften severalOne
CachingEasy: HTTP caches by URL, ETag, CDNHarder: one URL, POST bodies (use persisted queries and a client cache)
ErrorsHTTP status codesMostly 200 plus an errors array
Versioning/v1, /v2Evolve the schema: add fields, deprecate with @deprecated
Hard partsMany endpoints to designN+1, query cost and depth abuse, authorization on every field
Good fitPublic APIs, simple resources, file transferVaried clients (web, mobile) needing different slices of the same data
  • Authorize in resolvers (or the data layer), not at the route: one endpoint serves everything, so every field that returns private data needs its own check using the user from context.
  • Limit cost: depth (shown), the number of items per list (limit with a maximum), request size, and a timeout. Add complexity scoring for public APIs.
  • Turn introspection off in production for private APIs and never expose a schema explorer to the public internet by accident.
  • Always use variables, never string-concatenate user input into a query.
  • In real projects you will meet GraphQL Yoga, Apollo Server and Pothos or Nexus (code-first schemas); the concepts above are identical.

Once a system is split into several services, every call becomes a network call, and networks fail in ways function calls never do: slow, down, half-working, answering twice. This entry is the toolbox for calling other services without taking yourself down along with them. Start with a hard truth: you only need most of it when you really have several services. A single well-structured app (the layered design from Unit 4) is simpler, faster and easier to run, and is the right start for nearly every product.

gRPC: typed RPC over HTTP/2

gRPC lets services call each other's functions across the network. You write the contract once in a .proto file (the protobuf language), generate or load client and server from it, and messages travel as compact binary over HTTP/2, with streaming, deadlines and status codes built in. Use it between internal services; browsers and public APIs stay on REST or GraphQL.

import fs from "node:fs";
import os from "node:os";
import path from "node:path";
import grpc from "@grpc/grpc-js";
import protoLoader from "@grpc/proto-loader";

// THE CONTRACT. Numbers (= 1, = 2) identify fields on the wire and must never change once deployed.
const proto = `
syntax = "proto3";
package notes.v1;

service Notes {
  rpc GetNote   (NoteRequest) returns (Note);          // unary: one request, one response
  rpc ListNotes (ListRequest) returns (stream Note);   // server streaming: one request, many responses
  rpc Slow      (NoteRequest) returns (Note);
}
message NoteRequest { int32 id = 1; }
message ListRequest { int32 count = 1; }
message Note        { int32 id = 1; string title = 2; }
`;
const file = path.join(fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "proto-")), "notes.proto");
fs.writeFileSync(file, proto);
const definition = protoLoader.loadSync(file, { keepCase: true, defaults: true });   // reads the contract at startup, no code generation step
const { notes } = grpc.loadPackageDefinition(definition);

// SERVER: one function per rpc
const server = new grpc.Server();
server.addService(notes.v1.Notes.service, {
  GetNote: (call, callback) => {
    if (call.request.id === 0) return callback({ code: grpc.status.NOT_FOUND, message: "no such note" });   // errors are status codes, not HTTP codes
    callback(null, { id: call.request.id, title: "Note " + call.request.id });
  },
  ListNotes: (call) => {
    for (let i = 1; i <= call.request.count; i++) call.write({ id: i, title: "Note " + i });
    call.end();
  },
  Slow: (call, callback) => setTimeout(() => callback(null, { id: 1, title: "too late" }), 500),
});
const port = await new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
  server.bindAsync("127.0.0.1:0", grpc.ServerCredentials.createInsecure(), (err, p) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve(p))));   // use TLS credentials in production

// CLIENT
const client = new notes.v1.Notes(`127.0.0.1:${port}`, grpc.credentials.createInsecure());
const unary = (method, request, options = {}) => new Promise((resolve) =>
  client[method](request, options, (err, response) => resolve(err ? { failed: grpc.status[err.code] } : response)));

console.log("unary call      :", await unary("GetNote", { id: 7 }));
console.log("missing note    :", await unary("GetNote", { id: 0 }));
console.log("with a deadline :", await unary("Slow", { id: 1 }, { deadline: Date.now() + 100 }));   // the client gives up after 100 ms

const received = [];
await new Promise((resolve) => { const stream = client.ListNotes({ count: 3 }); stream.on("data", (n) => received.push(n.title)); stream.on("end", resolve); });
console.log("server stream   :", received);

client.close(); server.forceShutdown();
unary call : { id: 7, title: 'Note 7' } missing note : { failed: 'NOT_FOUND' } with a deadline : { failed: 'DEADLINE_EXCEEDED' } server stream : [ 'Note 1', 'Note 2', 'Note 3' ]
gRPC statusClosest HTTPUse it for
OK200Success
INVALID_ARGUMENT400Bad input (never retry)
NOT_FOUND404No such resource
ALREADY_EXISTS409Duplicate create
PERMISSION_DENIED / UNAUTHENTICATED403 / 401Not allowed / who are you
RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED429Rate limit or quota (retry later)
DEADLINE_EXCEEDED504Took longer than the caller allowed
UNAVAILABLE503Server down or overloaded (the classic retryable one)
INTERNAL500A bug on the server
Protobuf rules for evolving contractsAdd new fields with new numbers (old clients ignore them). Never reuse or renumber a field, and never change a field's type: mark removed ones reserved. A new service version can then be deployed before or after its callers without a coordinated release. Keep .proto files in one shared place, and run a breaking-change check in CI (the buf tool does this).

Timeouts: the single most important setting

A call without a timeout can hang forever, holding a socket, a memory buffer and the user's request. Under load, one slow dependency then makes every request slow, then exhausts your connections: a cascading failure. Put a timeout on every outbound call (AbortSignal.timeout(ms) with fetch, deadline in gRPC, statement_timeout in Postgres), and make it shorter than your own caller's timeout so the budget shrinks as you go down the chain.

import http from "node:http";

const slow = http.createServer((req, res) => setTimeout(() => res.end("finally"), 500));   // a dependency having a bad day
await new Promise((resolve) => slow.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", resolve));
const url = `http://127.0.0.1:${slow.address().port}/`;

const started = Date.now();
try {
  await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(100) });                      // give up after 100 ms
} catch (error) {
  console.log("error name:", error.name, "| message:", error.message);
  console.log("gave up long before the server answered:", Date.now() - started < 400);
}

const ok = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) });            // a generous timeout lets the slow call finish
console.log("with 2000 ms:", await ok.text());
slow.closeAllConnections(); slow.close();
error name: TimeoutError | message: The operation was aborted due to timeout gave up long before the server answered: true with 2000 ms: finally

Retries: only when they are safe

Retrying fixes brief glitches and makes outages worse when done carelessly. The rules: retry only transient failures (timeouts, connection errors, 502, 503, 504, gRPC UNAVAILABLE); never retry 4xx; retry only idempotent operations (GET, PUT, DELETE, or a POST carrying an Idempotency-Key from the REST entry); use exponential backoff with jitter; and cap attempts. A retry loop with no wait and no cap turns one sick server into a self-inflicted denial of service.

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function withRetry(operation, { attempts = 4, baseMs = 20, isRetryable = () => true } = {}) {
  let lastError;
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= attempts; attempt++) {
    try { return await operation(attempt); }
    catch (error) {
      lastError = error;
      if (!isRetryable(error) || attempt === attempts) break;                   // permanent failure, or out of attempts
      await sleep(baseMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1) * (0.5 + Math.random() / 2));      // 10-20, 20-40, 40-80 ms ... jittered
    }
  }
  throw lastError;
}
const transient = (error) => error.transient === true;                           // your own rule: timeouts and 5xx yes, 4xx no

// 1. a dependency that fails twice, then works
const result = await withRetry(async (attempt) => {
  console.log("attempt", attempt);
  if (attempt < 3) throw Object.assign(new Error("503 Service Unavailable"), { transient: true });
  return "payment service answered";
}, { isRetryable: transient });
console.log(result);

// 2. a permanent error is not retried at all
let calls = 0;
await withRetry(async () => { calls++; throw Object.assign(new Error("400 Bad Request"), { transient: false }); }, { isRetryable: transient })
  .catch((error) => console.log("gave up after", calls, "call:", error.message));

// 3. a dependency that never recovers: the cap stops us
calls = 0;
await withRetry(async () => { calls++; throw Object.assign(new Error("503"), { transient: true }); }, { attempts: 3, isRetryable: transient })
  .catch((error) => console.log("gave up after", calls, "calls:", error.message));
attempt 1 attempt 2 attempt 3 payment service answered gave up after 1 call: 400 Bad Request gave up after 3 calls: 503

The circuit breaker

Retries help against blips. Against a dependency that is really down they add load and make every caller wait for a timeout. A circuit breaker remembers recent failures and, after a threshold, stops calling for a cooldown: callers fail instantly (and can use a fallback), and the sick service gets room to recover. After the cooldown it lets one trial call through: success closes the circuit, failure reopens it.

import http from "node:http";

class CircuitBreaker {
  state = "closed"; failures = 0; openedAt = 0;
  constructor(call, { threshold = 3, cooldownMs = 150 } = {}) { this.call = call; this.threshold = threshold; this.cooldownMs = cooldownMs; }
  async fire(...args) {
    if (this.state === "open") {
      if (Date.now() - this.openedAt < this.cooldownMs) throw new Error("circuit open: failing fast");   // no network call at all
      this.state = "half-open";                                                // cooldown over: allow a trial call
    }
    try {
      const result = await this.call(...args);
      this.state = "closed"; this.failures = 0;                                // success: everything is fine again
      return result;
    } catch (error) {
      this.failures++;
      if (this.state === "half-open" || this.failures >= this.threshold) { this.state = "open"; this.openedAt = Date.now(); }
      throw error;
    }
  }
}

// the dependency: broken until we "fix" it
let healthy = false, hits = 0;
const service = http.createServer((req, res) => { hits++; res.statusCode = healthy ? 200 : 503; res.end(healthy ? "recommendations" : "overloaded"); });
await new Promise((resolve) => service.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", resolve));
const breaker = new CircuitBreaker(async () => {
  const res = await fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${service.address().port}/`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(500) });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("upstream " + res.status);
  return res.text();
});

const attempt = async (label) => {
  try { console.log(label.padEnd(24), "->", await breaker.fire(), `| state: ${breaker.state}`); }
  catch (error) { console.log(label.padEnd(24), "->", error.message.padEnd(26), `| state: ${breaker.state} | server hits so far: ${hits}`); }
};

for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) await attempt(`call ${i} (service down)`);       // real failures: the threshold is reached
for (let i = 4; i <= 5; i++) await attempt(`call ${i} (service down)`);       // rejected instantly, the server is not touched
healthy = true;                                                                // the service recovers
await attempt("call 6 (still cooling)");                                       // still inside the cooldown: still fails fast
await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 200));                      // wait out the cooldown
await attempt("call 7 (trial call)");                                          // half-open: one real call goes through and succeeds
await attempt("call 8");
service.closeAllConnections(); service.close();
call 1 (service down) -> upstream 503 | state: closed | server hits so far: 1 call 2 (service down) -> upstream 503 | state: closed | server hits so far: 2 call 3 (service down) -> upstream 503 | state: open | server hits so far: 3 call 4 (service down) -> circuit open: failing fast | state: open | server hits so far: 3 call 5 (service down) -> circuit open: failing fast | state: open | server hits so far: 3 call 6 (still cooling) -> circuit open: failing fast | state: open | server hits so far: 3 call 7 (trial call) -> recommendations | state: closed call 8 -> recommendations | state: closed
Use a fallback, and a library when it is seriousWhen the circuit is open, return something useful instead of an error: cached data, a default, or a reduced page ("recommendations unavailable"). The class above shows the idea; in production use a maintained library such as opossum, which also adds timeouts, rolling windows and metrics. Combine the pieces in this order from the inside: timeout, then retry, then circuit breaker, plus a limit on concurrent calls (a "bulkhead") so one slow dependency cannot use every connection.

Correlation ids: following one request through many services

When a user request touches five services, a log line means nothing unless you can find all five lines for the same request. Give every request an id at the edge (or accept one from the caller), keep it in AsyncLocalStorage (Unit 3) so it is available anywhere without passing it around, put it in every log line, and forward it as a header on every outgoing call.

import express from "express";
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from "node:async_hooks";

const context = new AsyncLocalStorage();
const lines = [];
const log = (service, message) => lines.push(`[${context.getStore()?.requestId ?? "-"}] ${service}: ${message}`);

// middleware shared by both services
const requestContext = (req, res, next) => {
  const requestId = req.get("x-request-id") ?? crypto.randomUUID();            // accept the caller's id, or start a new trace
  res.set("x-request-id", requestId);
  context.run({ requestId }, next);                                            // everything this request triggers can read the id
};

// downstream "pricing" service
const pricing = express();
pricing.use(requestContext);
pricing.get("/price", (req, res) => { log("pricing", "price looked up"); res.json({ cents: 1999 }); });
const pricingServer = pricing.listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await new Promise((resolve) => pricingServer.once("listening", resolve));

// outgoing calls add the header automatically
const callService = (url) => fetch(url, { headers: { "x-request-id": context.getStore().requestId } });

// the gateway
const gateway = express();
gateway.use(requestContext);
gateway.get("/checkout", async (req, res) => {
  log("gateway", "checkout started");
  const price = await (await callService(`http://127.0.0.1:${pricingServer.address().port}/price`)).json();   // note: no id passed around by hand
  log("gateway", "checkout finished, total " + price.cents);
  res.json({ total: price.cents });
});
const gatewayServer = gateway.listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await new Promise((resolve) => gatewayServer.once("listening", resolve));
const gatewayUrl = `http://127.0.0.1:${gatewayServer.address().port}/checkout`;

await fetch(gatewayUrl, { headers: { "x-request-id": "req-42" } });            // a caller that supplies its own id
const anonymous = await fetch(gatewayUrl);                                      // no id: the gateway invents one
console.log(lines.join("\n").replace(/[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f-]{27}/g, "<generated uuid>"));   // the invented id is random, so show a placeholder
console.log("generated id looks like a UUID:", /^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/.test(anonymous.headers.get("x-request-id")));
gatewayServer.close(); pricingServer.close();
[req-42] gateway: checkout started [req-42] pricing: price looked up [req-42] gateway: checkout finished, total 1999 [<generated uuid>] gateway: checkout started [<generated uuid>] pricing: price looked up [<generated uuid>] gateway: checkout finished, total 1999 generated id looks like a UUID: true

Consistency across services: the outbox and the saga

With one database, a transaction keeps data consistent. Across services there is no shared transaction. Two patterns (described here, not run, because they need several real services and a broker) cover most needs:

  • The dual-write problem: "save the order, then publish an event" can crash in between, leaving an order nobody hears about (or an event for an order that was rolled back). The outbox makes both happen or neither, because they are rows in the same local transaction. Delivery is at least once, so consumers dedupe on the event id (as in the webhook and queue entries).
  • Saga: a business operation spanning services (reserve stock, charge card, create shipment) is a sequence of local transactions. If step three fails, earlier steps are undone by compensating actions (release the stock, refund the card), run by a coordinator (orchestration) or by services reacting to each other's events (choreography). Design each step to be idempotent and compensatable.
  • Other pieces you will meet: an API gateway as the single public entry (routing, auth, rate limits), service discovery (usually the platform's DNS, such as Kubernetes service names), message brokers (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS) for asynchronous events, and distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry), the grown-up version of the correlation id above.
  • Rule of thumb: prefer asynchronous events between services for anything that need not be answered now; use synchronous calls (REST or gRPC) only when the caller truly cannot continue without the answer, and then protect them with timeouts, careful retries and a breaker.
09

Unit 9: Testing

How to know your backend works and keep knowing it after every change: Node's built-in test runner, assertions, mocks and fake timers, testing Express apps with supertest, testing against a real database, coverage, CI, and how Vitest and Jest compare.

A test is a small program that runs your code and fails loudly when the code does something you did not intend. A backend without tests can only be changed with fear: every edit might break a feature you forgot existed. With tests, you refactor, upgrade dependencies and ship on Friday afternoon knowing that hundreds of promises still hold. Tests also document behaviour better than comments, because they cannot go out of date without failing.

Node 22 includes a complete test runner (node:test) and assertion library (node:assert), so you need no dependency to start. Everything in this unit runs on the little project below, testing-demo.

LevelWhat it provesTypical backend exampleSpeed
UnitOne piece of logic is rightCart total with a coupon and taxUnder 1 ms
IntegrationPieces work together, including real I/OPOST /notes through Express into PostgreSQL10 to 100 ms
End-to-endThe deployed system serves a real user flowSign up, log in, create a note, over HTTP against a staging serverSeconds

The code under test

Business rules live in plain functions with no I/O, no clock and no globals: those are trivially testable, which is one more reason for the layered design from Unit 4.

// Pure business rules: no I/O, no clock, no globals. The easiest code to test.
export function addItem(cart, item) {
  if (!item.name) throw new TypeError("item needs a name");
  if (!Number.isInteger(item.cents) || item.cents < 0) throw new RangeError("cents must be a non-negative integer");
  const existing = cart.find((line) => line.name === item.name);
  if (existing) return cart.map((line) => (line === existing ? { ...line, qty: line.qty + 1 } : line));
  return [...cart, { name: item.name, cents: item.cents, qty: 1 }];
}

export function subtotal(cart) {
  return cart.reduce((sum, line) => sum + line.cents * line.qty, 0);
}

export function total(cart, { taxRate = 0, coupon } = {}) {
  let amount = subtotal(cart);
  if (coupon === "TENOFF") amount = Math.round(amount * 0.9);
  else if (coupon !== undefined) throw new Error(`unknown coupon: ${coupon}`);
  return Math.round(amount * (1 + taxRate));
}

The first test file

The shape of every good test is Arrange, Act, Assert: set up the situation, do the one thing under test, check the outcome. Keep each test about one behaviour, name it as a sentence ("rejects fractional cents"), and give each test its own fresh state, because a test that depends on another test running first fails mysteriously in CI.

import { describe, it, beforeEach, test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { addItem, subtotal, total } from "../src/cart.js";

describe("cart", () => {
  let cart;
  beforeEach(() => { cart = []; });                       // a fresh cart for EVERY test: tests must not share state

  it("adds a new item with quantity 1", () => {
    cart = addItem(cart, { name: "mug", cents: 800 });
    assert.deepEqual(cart, [{ name: "mug", cents: 800, qty: 1 }]);
  });

  it("increases the quantity when the same item is added again", () => {
    cart = addItem(addItem(cart, { name: "mug", cents: 800 }), { name: "mug", cents: 800 });
    assert.equal(cart[0].qty, 2);
  });

  it("does not modify the cart it was given", () => {
    const before = Object.freeze([]);                     // freezing makes accidental mutation throw
    addItem(before, { name: "mug", cents: 800 });
    assert.equal(before.length, 0);
  });

  describe("validation", () => {
    it("rejects an item without a name", () => {
      assert.throws(() => addItem(cart, { cents: 100 }), { name: "TypeError", message: "item needs a name" });
    });
    it("rejects fractional cents", () => {
      assert.throws(() => addItem(cart, { name: "x", cents: 9.99 }), RangeError);
    });
  });

  describe("total", () => {
    const full = () => addItem(addItem(cart, { name: "mug", cents: 800 }), { name: "tea", cents: 450 });

    // table-driven tests: one assertion shape, many cases, each reported separately
    const cases = [
      { options: {}, expected: 1250 },
      { options: { taxRate: 0.2 }, expected: 1500 },
      { options: { coupon: "TENOFF" }, expected: 1125 },
      { options: { coupon: "TENOFF", taxRate: 0.2 }, expected: 1350 },
    ];
    for (const { options, expected } of cases) {
      it(`total with ${JSON.stringify(options)} is ${expected}`, () => {
        assert.equal(total(full(), options), expected);
      });
    }

    it("rejects an unknown coupon", () => {
      assert.throws(() => total(full(), { coupon: "FREE" }), /unknown coupon: FREE/);
    });
    it("an empty cart costs nothing", () => assert.equal(subtotal([]), 0));
  });

  it("applies coupons case-insensitively", { todo: "decide the business rule first" }, () => {
    assert.equal(total([{ name: "a", cents: 100, qty: 1 }], { coupon: "tenoff" }), 90);
  });

  it("supports gift wrapping", { skip: "not built yet" }, () => {});
});

test("a top-level test works too, and can contain subtests", async (t) => {
  await t.test("first subtest", () => assert.ok(true));
  await t.test("second subtest", () => assert.ok(true));
});

Read the report: ▶ is a suite (describe), ✔ a pass, ﹣ a skipped test, and the comment after # is the reason you gave. The todo test fails but does not fail the run: todo means "known unfinished", so the result is reported while the exit code stays 0. That is how you record a behaviour you have decided to build without breaking the build: the summary says fail 0 and todo 1, even though the "failing tests" block at the end repeats the todo test with its error.

You writeMeaning
test(name, fn) / it(name, fn)One test. fn may be async (a rejected promise is a failure) and receives a context t
describe(name, fn) / suiteGroups tests, and hooks apply inside it
before / afterOnce per suite: start a server, create schema
beforeEach / afterEachAround every test: fresh state, rollback
{ skip: "reason" }Do not run (shown as skipped)
{ todo: "reason" }Run, report, but never fail the build
{ only: true }Run only this one (with --test-only), handy while debugging
{ timeout: 500 }Fail if the test takes longer, so a hang cannot freeze CI
await t.test(name, fn)A subtest inside a test

Assertions

Always import assert from "node:assert/strict". The strict variant makes equal use === and prints a readable diff on failure. The legacy non-strict one coerces types ("1" == 1 passes), which hides bugs.

AssertionChecks
assert.equal(a, b) / notEqualPrimitives with === (Object.is-like)
assert.deepEqual(a, b)Objects and arrays, compared structurally and strictly
assert.ok(value)Truthy (prefer a precise assertion when you can)
assert.match(string, /regex/)String matches a pattern
assert.throws(fn, expected)Sync function throws; expected may be a class, regex, or object of properties
await assert.rejects(promise, expected)Promise rejects (do not forget await, or the test passes before it is checked)
await assert.doesNotReject(promise)Promise resolves
assert.fail(message)Fail on purpose (for code paths that must not run)

node --test with no files finds every *.test.js (also .mjs and .cjs), files named test-*.js, and everything inside folders named test. Each file runs in its own process, in parallel.

The vocabulary of test doubles

A test double replaces a real collaborator (a database, an email service, the clock) so the test is fast, deterministic and safe. People use "mock" for all of them; the precise words help you choose:

DoubleWhat it doesExample from this unit
StubReturns canned answers{ list: async () => [] }
FakeA working but simplified implementationmemoryNotes(), an in-memory repository
SpyWraps a function and records its callsmock.fn() counting how often sleep ran
MockA spy with built-in expectations ("must be called once with X")assert.equal(sent.length, 1) on a recording mailer
What makes tests goodFast (the whole suite in seconds, or nobody runs it), isolated (any test passes alone and in any order), deterministic (no real clock, randomness, network or shared data unless controlled), readable (the test is the specification) and focused on behaviour, not implementation: assert what the function returns or what the API responds, not which private helper it called, or every refactor breaks tests that were not wrong.

Code that waits, retries, reads the clock or calls other systems cannot be tested by running it for real: it would be slow and flaky. You replace those parts for the test. The cleanest way is dependency injection: let the function receive the collaborator as a parameter (as retry receives sleep below, and createApp receives notes and mailer in the next entry). When the code reaches for a global (setTimeout, Date, Math.random, an imported module) the runner can mock that instead.

// Code that depends on time and on a flaky collaborator: tested with fakes, not with real waiting.
export async function retry(operation, { attempts = 3, delayMs = 1000, sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)) } = {}) {
  let lastError;
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= attempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await operation(attempt);
    } catch (error) {
      lastError = error;
      if (attempt < attempts) await sleep(delayMs * attempt);
    }
  }
  throw lastError;
}

export function debounce(fn, waitMs) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), waitMs);
  };
}
import { describe, it, mock } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { retry, debounce } from "../src/retry.js";

describe("retry", () => {
  it("returns the first success without sleeping", async () => {
    const operation = mock.fn(async () => "done");               // a spy: records every call
    const sleep = mock.fn(async () => {});
    assert.equal(await retry(operation, { sleep }), "done");
    assert.equal(operation.mock.callCount(), 1);
    assert.equal(sleep.mock.callCount(), 0);
  });

  it("retries failures with growing waits, then succeeds", async () => {
    let calls = 0;
    const operation = mock.fn(async () => { if (++calls < 3) throw new Error("flaky"); return "ok"; });
    const waits = [];
    const result = await retry(operation, { attempts: 3, delayMs: 100, sleep: async (ms) => { waits.push(ms); } });   // a fake sleep: the test never waits
    assert.equal(result, "ok");
    assert.deepEqual(waits, [100, 200]);
  });

  it("gives up with the last error", async () => {
    const operation = async (attempt) => { throw new Error("failure " + attempt); };
    await assert.rejects(retry(operation, { attempts: 2, sleep: async () => {} }), { message: "failure 2" });
  });
});

describe("debounce with fake timers", () => {
  it("calls the function once, after the quiet period", (t) => {
    t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout"] });             // time is now under the test's control
    const fn = mock.fn();
    const debounced = debounce(fn, 300);
    debounced("a"); debounced("b"); debounced("c");             // three quick calls
    t.mock.timers.tick(299);
    assert.equal(fn.mock.callCount(), 0);                       // not yet
    t.mock.timers.tick(1);
    assert.equal(fn.mock.callCount(), 1);                       // exactly once, with the LAST arguments
    assert.deepEqual(fn.mock.calls[0].arguments, ["c"]);
  });
});

describe("mocking a method on an object", () => {
  it("replaces Math.random for one test only", (t) => {
    t.mock.method(Math, "random", () => 0.5);                   // restored automatically when the test ends
    assert.equal(Math.random(), 0.5);
  });
  it("sees the real Math.random again", () => {
    assert.notEqual(Math.random(), 0.5);                        // (a real random number is 0.5 with probability about 2^-53)
  });
});

Reading the code above:

  • mock.fn(impl?) returns a function that behaves like impl and records everything in fn.mock.calls (each entry has arguments, result, error). fn.mock.callCount() is the shortcut. fn.mock.mockImplementationOnce(...) changes just the next call.
  • t.mock.method(object, "name", impl) swaps a method and restores it automatically when the test ends. Use t.mock (not the global mock) when you want that automatic cleanup.
  • t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout"] }) takes over time: tick(ms) advances it instantly, so a test of a 30-second timeout takes microseconds. Node prints an experimental warning for this API (hidden in the captured output here).

Fake timers can also control Date. Freezing the clock is how you test expiry, "created at" values and anything that mentions "today":

import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";

const isExpired = (trial, now = new Date()) => now > new Date(trial.endsAt);        // the code under test reads the real clock by default

test("a trial expires exactly when its end time passes", (t) => {
  t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["Date"], now: new Date("2026-01-15T10:00:00Z") });  // the clock is now frozen
  const trial = { endsAt: "2026-01-15T10:01:00Z" };
  assert.equal(isExpired(trial), false);

  t.mock.timers.tick(60_000);                                                        // exactly one minute passes, instantly
  assert.equal(new Date().toISOString(), "2026-01-15T10:01:00.000Z");
  assert.equal(isExpired(trial), false);                                             // equal is not greater: still valid

  t.mock.timers.tick(1);
  assert.equal(isExpired(trial), true);                                              // one millisecond later it is over
});
✔ a trial expires exactly when its end time passes ℹ tests 1 ℹ suites 0 ℹ pass 1 ℹ fail 0 ℹ cancelled 0 ℹ skipped 0 ℹ todo 0 ℹ duration_ms <varies>

Replacing a whole module

Sometimes the dependency is imported directly (import { hostname } from "node:os") and cannot be injected. Node can mock ES modules, behind an experimental flag: the mock must be installed before the module that imports it is loaded, which is why the import comes after it.

import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";

// Needs: node --test --experimental-test-module-mocks
test("replacing a whole module", async (t) => {
  t.mock.module("node:os", { namedExports: { hostname: () => "fake-host" } });   // must be set up BEFORE the importing code is loaded
  const { hostname } = await import("node:os");
  assert.equal(hostname(), "fake-host");
});
$ node --test --test-reporter=spec --experimental-test-module-mocks extras/module-mock.demo.js | head -3

ℹ tests 1
ℹ suites 0

Reading a failure

A failing test is the whole reason tests exist, so learn to read the report. This test has a deliberate mistake: the expectation says 1700 but the code returns 1600.

import { it } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { total } from "../src/cart.js";

it("a test that fails, to show the report", () => {
  const cart = [{ name: "mug", cents: 800, qty: 2 }];
  assert.deepEqual({ items: cart.length, total: total(cart) }, { items: 1, total: 1700 });
});
$ node --test --test-reporter=spec extras/failing.demo.js | sed -n '/failing tests/,$p'
✖ failing tests:

test at extras/failing.demo.js:5:1
✖ a test that fails, to show the report
  AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: Expected values to be strictly deep-equal:
  + actual - expected
  
    {
      items: 1,
  +   total: 1600
  -   total: 1700
    }
  
      at TestContext.<anonymous> (file://~/project/testing-demo/extras/failing.demo.js:7:10)
    generatedMessage: true,
    code: 'ERR_ASSERTION',
    actual: { items: 1, total: 1600 },
    expected: { items: 1, total: 1700 },
    operator: 'deepStrictEqual',
    diff: 'simple'
  }

The diff marks + actual and - expected: only the total line differs, so items is fine. The first stack frame inside your code (failing.demo.js:7) points at the assertion. The process exit code is non-zero, which is what makes CI go red.

Over-mocking is a trapA test that mocks every collaborator and then asserts that mocks were called in a certain order mostly repeats the implementation: it passes while the real system is broken (the mock was wrong) and fails when you refactor correctly. Prefer real code and fakes where cheap (pure functions, an in-memory repository), mock only the boundaries you do not control (clock, randomness, network calls to third parties, email), and test the database with a real database (next entry). Also: never mock the thing you are testing.
  • A mock restored late leaks into other tests: use t.mock or call mock.restoreAll() in afterEach.
  • Forgetting await on an async assertion makes the test pass before the assertion runs (use await assert.rejects(...)).
  • Never call the real network or send real email from a test. A fake, a local server, or a library like msw or undici's MockAgent keeps the suite offline and fast.

Testing an HTTP API means sending real requests to the real Express app and checking the response. Two design choices make that painless:

  • An app factory: createApp({ notes, mailer, now }) builds and returns the app without calling listen() and receives every dependency as a parameter. server.js calls it with the real database and then listens; tests call it with fakes.
  • supertest takes the app itself, starts it on a random free port for the duration of the request, and gives a fluent API (request(app).post("/notes").send({...})). No port conflicts, nothing left running.
import express from "express";

// An APP FACTORY: all dependencies are parameters, nothing listens on a port.
// Tests build an app with fakes; server.js builds it with the real database.
export function createApp({ notes, mailer, now = () => new Date() }) {
  const app = express();
  app.use(express.json());

  app.get("/health", (req, res) => res.json({ ok: true }));

  app.get("/notes", async (req, res) => {
    res.json(await notes.list());
  });

  app.get("/notes/:id", async (req, res) => {
    const note = await notes.get(Number(req.params.id));
    if (!note) return res.status(404).json({ error: "not found" });
    res.json(note);
  });

  app.post("/notes", async (req, res) => {
    const { title } = req.body ?? {};
    if (typeof title !== "string" || title.trim() === "") return res.status(400).json({ error: "title is required" });
    const note = await notes.create({ title: title.trim(), createdAt: now().toISOString() });
    await mailer.send({ to: "owner@example.com", subject: `New note: ${note.title}` });
    res.status(201).location(`/notes/${note.id}`).json(note);
  });

  app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
    res.status(500).json({ error: "internal error" });
  });
  return app;
}
// A tiny in-memory repository with the same interface as the real database one.
export function memoryNotes(seed = []) {
  const rows = [...seed];
  return {
    async list() { return rows; },
    async get(id) { return rows.find((n) => n.id === id) ?? null; },
    async create({ title, createdAt }) {
      const note = { id: rows.length + 1, title, createdAt };
      rows.push(note);
      return note;
    },
  };
}
import { describe, it, before, after, beforeEach } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import request from "supertest";
import { createApp } from "../src/app.js";
import { memoryNotes } from "../src/memory-notes.js";

describe("notes API", () => {
  let app, sent;
  const fixedNow = () => new Date("2026-01-15T10:00:00Z");   // a frozen clock: no flaky dates

  beforeEach(() => {
    sent = [];
    const mailer = { send: async (message) => { sent.push(message); } };   // a fake that records instead of sending
    app = createApp({ notes: memoryNotes([{ id: 1, title: "first", createdAt: "2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z" }]), mailer, now: fixedNow });
  });

  it("GET /health", async () => {
    const res = await request(app).get("/health");           // supertest starts the app on a random port by itself
    assert.equal(res.status, 200);
    assert.deepEqual(res.body, { ok: true });
  });

  it("GET /notes/:id returns the note", async () => {
    const res = await request(app).get("/notes/1");
    assert.equal(res.status, 200);
    assert.equal(res.body.title, "first");
  });

  it("GET /notes/:id returns 404 for a missing note", async () => {
    const res = await request(app).get("/notes/99");
    assert.equal(res.status, 404);
    assert.deepEqual(res.body, { error: "not found" });
  });

  it("POST /notes creates a note, sets Location and sends one email", async () => {
    const res = await request(app).post("/notes").send({ title: "  buy milk  " });
    assert.equal(res.status, 201);
    assert.equal(res.headers.location, "/notes/2");
    assert.deepEqual(res.body, { id: 2, title: "buy milk", createdAt: "2026-01-15T10:00:00.000Z" });
    assert.deepEqual(sent, [{ to: "owner@example.com", subject: "New note: buy milk" }]);
  });

  for (const [label, body] of [["no body", undefined], ["empty title", { title: "  " }], ["title is a number", { title: 5 }]]) {
    it(`POST /notes rejects ${label} with 400 and sends no email`, async () => {
      const res = await request(app).post("/notes").send(body);
      assert.equal(res.status, 400);
      assert.equal(sent.length, 0);
    });
  }

  it("turns a crashing dependency into a clean 500", async () => {
    const broken = createApp({ notes: { list: async () => { throw new Error("db exploded"); } }, mailer: {} });
    const res = await request(broken).get("/notes");
    assert.equal(res.status, 500);
    assert.deepEqual(res.body, { error: "internal error" });   // and no stack trace leaked
  });
});

describe("the same app over a real socket with fetch", () => {
  let server, base;
  before(async () => {
    server = createApp({ notes: memoryNotes(), mailer: { send: async () => {} } }).listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
    await new Promise((resolve) => server.once("listening", resolve));
    base = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`;
  });
  after(() => server.close());                               // ALWAYS close: an open server keeps the test process alive

  it("answers /health", async () => {
    const res = await fetch(base + "/health");
    assert.deepEqual(await res.json(), { ok: true });
  });
});

What the tests demonstrate, in order of importance:

  • Test the unhappy paths as carefully as the happy one: missing resource (404), invalid input (400, and no email sent), a crashing dependency (a clean 500 with no stack trace). Most production bugs live there.
  • Assert the contract: status code, the Location header, the exact body. Those are what your clients depend on.
  • Control time and side effects: the frozen now makes createdAt exact, and the recording mailer proves exactly one email was sent.
  • Both styles work: supertest for speed and convenience, and app.listen(0) plus fetch when you want a real socket. Always close the server in after, or the test process never exits.

Testing against a real database

An in-memory fake proves your routes; only a real database proves your SQL, constraints, types and transactions. The repository takes anything with a .query() method, so tests give it a single client that is inside a transaction. Every test starts a transaction and rolls it back at the end: tests see a clean database, leave nothing behind, and run quickly because nothing is ever committed.

// The real repository. It takes anything with a .query() method: a Pool in production,
// or a single client inside a transaction in tests.
export function pgNotes(db) {
  return {
    async list() {
      const { rows } = await db.query('SELECT id, title, created_at AS "createdAt" FROM test_notes ORDER BY id');
      return rows;
    },
    async get(id) {
      const { rows } = await db.query('SELECT id, title, created_at AS "createdAt" FROM test_notes WHERE id = $1', [id]);
      return rows[0] ?? null;
    },
    async create({ title, createdAt }) {
      const { rows } = await db.query('INSERT INTO test_notes (title, created_at) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id, title, created_at AS "createdAt"', [title, createdAt]);
      return rows[0];
    },
  };
}
import { describe, it, before, after, beforeEach, afterEach } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import pg from "pg";
import request from "supertest";
import { pgNotes } from "../src/pg-notes.js";
import { createApp } from "../src/app.js";

const url = process.env.DATABASE_URL;

// Tests that need a real database are skipped (not failed) when none is configured.
describe("notes on real PostgreSQL", { skip: !url && "set DATABASE_URL to run the database tests" }, () => {
  const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: url });
  let client;

  before(async () => {                                         // once: make sure the schema exists (real projects run their migrations here)
    await pool.query("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS test_notes (id serial PRIMARY KEY, title text NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL)");
  });
  after(async () => {
    await pool.query("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS test_notes");
    await pool.end();                                          // without this the test process never exits
  });

  // THE ISOLATION TRICK: every test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back, so tests leave nothing behind
  beforeEach(async () => { client = await pool.connect(); await client.query("BEGIN"); });
  afterEach(async () => { await client.query("ROLLBACK"); client.release(); });

  it("creates and reads back a note", async () => {
    const notes = pgNotes(client);
    const created = await notes.create({ title: "hello", createdAt: "2026-01-15T10:00:00Z" });
    assert.equal(typeof created.id, "number");
    assert.equal((await notes.get(created.id)).title, "hello");
    assert.equal((await notes.get(created.id + 1000)), null);
  });

  it("the database enforces NOT NULL", async () => {
    await assert.rejects(pgNotes(client).create({ title: null, createdAt: "2026-01-15T10:00:00Z" }), { code: "23502" });   // 23502 = not_null_violation
  });

  it("starts empty even though the previous test inserted a row", async () => {
    assert.deepEqual(await pgNotes(client).list(), []);        // the rollback undid it
  });

  it("works through the whole HTTP stack: route, validation, SQL", async () => {
    const app = createApp({ notes: pgNotes(client), mailer: { send: async () => {} } });
    const res = await request(app).post("/notes").send({ title: "via http" });
    assert.equal(res.status, 201);
    const { rows } = await client.query("SELECT title FROM test_notes");        // check the row with SQL, not through the code under test
    assert.deepEqual(rows, [{ title: "via http" }]);
  });
});
