  ✔ starts empty even though the previous test inserted a row
  ✔ works through the whole HTTP stack: route, validation, SQL
✔ notes on real PostgreSQL
ℹ tests 4
ℹ suites 1
ℹ pass 4
ℹ fail 0
ℹ cancelled 0
ℹ skipped 0
ℹ todo 0
ℹ duration_ms <varies>

Three details matter. The suite is skipped, not failed, when no database is configured, so a new contributor can run the unit tests immediately. The NOT NULL test asserts on the PostgreSQL error code 23502, proving the database enforces the rule and not only your validation. And the HTTP test verifies the stored row with a direct SQL query rather than through the code under test, so a bug cannot hide behind itself.

Isolation strategyHowTrade-off
Transaction per test, rolled backAs aboveFastest and simplest. Does not work for code that opens its own connections or commits (use another strategy there). Sequences (serial) are not rolled back, so never assert on generated ids.
Truncate tables before each testTRUNCATE a, b RESTART IDENTITY CASCADEWorks with any code, slower, tests must run one at a time per database
One schema or database per test workerCreate test_1, test_2, migrate eachAllows parallel test files, more setup
Disposable database per runA container started by the test run (the Testcontainers library) or a CI service containerMost realistic and reproducible. Needs Docker (not available here, so not run).
A different database for tests (SQLite in memory)Swap the driverFast, but SQL dialects, types and locking differ: tests can pass while production fails. Avoid for anything beyond trivial.

Test data: factories, not copy-paste

A factory builds a valid object with sensible defaults, and each test overrides only what it cares about. Then a test reads as "a note whose title is X", and adding a required column means changing one function instead of fifty tests.

let sequence = 0;
const makeNote = (overrides = {}) => ({
  id: ++sequence,
  title: `note ${sequence}`,
  createdAt: "2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z",
  ...overrides,                                     // each test states only what matters to it
});

console.log(makeNote());
console.log(makeNote({ title: "buy milk" }));
console.log("ten unique notes:", new Set(Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => makeNote().title)).size);
{ id: 1, title: 'note 1', createdAt: '2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z' } { id: 2, title: 'buy milk', createdAt: '2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z' } ten unique notes: 10
import jwt from "jsonwebtoken";

const TEST_SECRET = "test-secret-not-used-anywhere-else";
const app = createApp({ notes, mailer, jwtSecret: TEST_SECRET });           // inject the secret like any other dependency

const tokenFor = (user, options = {}) => jwt.sign({ sub: user.id, role: user.role }, TEST_SECRET, { expiresIn: "5m", ...options });

it("returns 401 without a token", async () => {
  assert.equal((await request(app).get("/me")).status, 401);
});
it("returns 403 for a user without the admin role", async () => {
  const res = await request(app).get("/admin/users").set("Authorization", `Bearer ${tokenFor({ id: 1, role: "user" })}`);
  assert.equal(res.status, 403);
});
it("returns 401 for an expired token", async () => {
  const res = await request(app).get("/me").set("Authorization", `Bearer ${tokenFor({ id: 1, role: "user" }, { expiresIn: -10 })}`);
  assert.equal(res.status, 401);
});

Coverage: a map of what is untested, not a score

Coverage reports which lines, branches and functions ran during the tests. Low coverage reliably tells you "nobody tests this". High coverage does not tell you the code is correct: a test that runs a line without asserting anything counts. Use it to find forgotten code, never as a target to game. Here the database tests are not running, so the report shows exactly the untested file:

$ node --test --test-reporter=spec --test-concurrency=1 --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-exclude='test/**' | sed -n '/start of coverage/,/end of coverage/p'
ℹ start of coverage report
ℹ -----------------------------------------------------------------
ℹ file             | line % | branch % | funcs % | uncovered lines
ℹ -----------------------------------------------------------------
ℹ src              |        |          |         | 
ℹ  app.js          | 100.00 |    92.31 |   85.71 | 
ℹ  cart.js         | 100.00 |    94.74 |  100.00 | 
ℹ  memory-notes.js | 100.00 |   100.00 |   80.00 | 
ℹ  pg-notes.js     |  16.67 |   100.00 |    0.00 | 4-18
ℹ  retry.js        | 100.00 |   100.00 |   80.00 | 
ℹ -----------------------------------------------------------------
ℹ all files        |  85.58 |    95.83 |   83.33 | 
ℹ -----------------------------------------------------------------
ℹ end of coverage report

pg-notes.js shows low numbers and the exact uncovered lines, because the suite that exercises it was skipped. Notice that cart.js has 100% line coverage but under 100% branch coverage: some if or ?: has a path no test takes. Branch coverage is the more honest number.

Vitest and Jest

Vitest and Jest are the popular third-party runners. They add watch mode with smart re-runs, snapshot testing, a rich mocking API (vi.fn, jest.fn), module mocking without flags, TypeScript support, and nicer failure output. Vitest is the modern choice for new projects (fast, ESM-first, Jest-compatible API). The same cart tests, written for Vitest:

import { describe, it, expect, vi } from "vitest";
import { addItem, total } from "../testing-demo/src/cart.js";
import { retry } from "../testing-demo/src/retry.js";

describe("cart (same code, Vitest syntax)", () => {
  it("adds items", () => {
    expect(addItem([], { name: "mug", cents: 800 })).toEqual([{ name: "mug", cents: 800, qty: 1 }]);
  });
  it("throws on fractional cents", () => {
    expect(() => addItem([], { name: "x", cents: 9.99 })).toThrow(RangeError);
  });
  it.each([[{}, 800], [{ taxRate: 0.5 }, 1200], [{ coupon: "TENOFF" }, 720]])("total(%j) is %i", (options, expected) => {
    expect(total([{ name: "mug", cents: 800, qty: 1 }], options)).toBe(expected);
  });
  it("retries with a spy", async () => {
    const operation = vi.fn().mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error("flaky")).mockResolvedValue("ok");
    await expect(retry(operation, { sleep: async () => {} })).resolves.toBe("ok");
    expect(operation).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
  });
});
$ npx vitest run

   Start at  09:30:00
   Duration  <varies>
node:testVitestJest
InstallNothing, built into Nodenpm i -D vitestnpm i -D jest
Assertionsnode:assertexpect(x).toEqual(y)expect(x).toEqual(y)
Mocksmock.fn, t.mock.methodvi.fn, vi.mock, vi.useFakeTimersjest.fn, jest.mock, jest.useFakeTimers
Parameterized testsLoop over cases yourselfit.eachit.each

Best forLibraries and services that want zero dependenciesNew apps, TypeScript, front and back sharing one runnerExisting Jest codebases

The concepts (arrange act assert, doubles, isolation, the pyramid) are identical in all three. If you can read node:test, you can read the others in an afternoon.

Test-driven development

TDD writes the test first. You see it fail for the right reason (the feature is missing), write the least code that passes, then clean up with the tests as a safety net. It is not a religion: it shines for logic with clear rules (pricing, validation, parsing) and for reproducing a bug (write the failing test, then fix). For exploratory work, writing tests right after is fine.

Running tests in CI

Tests that only run on your laptop protect nobody. Continuous integration runs them on every push and pull request, in a clean environment, and blocks merging when they fail. This GitHub Actions workflow uses a PostgreSQL service container so the database tests run for real. (Not run here: it needs GitHub. The commands inside are the ones you saw above.)

name: test
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env: { POSTGRES_USER: dex, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dexpass, POSTGRES_DB: dexdb }
        ports: ["5432:5432"]
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U dex" --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 10
    env:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://dex:dexpass@localhost:5432/dexdb      # a throwaway CI-only database
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }                        # also test the other Node versions you support, with a matrix
      - run: npm ci                                                   # exact versions from the lockfile, never npm install in CI
      - run: npm run lint --if-present
      - run: node --test --test-concurrency=1 --test-reporter=spec --test-reporter-destination=stdout --test-reporter=junit --test-reporter-destination=junit.xml   # readable log plus a file for CI dashboards
      - run: npm audit --audit-level=high                             # fail on serious known vulnerabilities in dependencies

Flaky tests: the suite's worst enemy

A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Once a team stops trusting red builds, tests stop protecting anyone. Almost every flaky test has one of these causes:

  • Real time: setTimeout waits, "should finish within 50 ms", dates around midnight or month ends. Use fake timers and a frozen clock.
  • Shared state: tests that depend on order, a global, or rows left by an earlier test. Fresh state per test, rollback per test.
  • Unawaited promises: the assertion runs after the test ended, or errors vanish. await everything.
  • Random data or ports: seed randomness or inject it, and listen on port 0.
  • Real network or third parties: replace them with fakes or recorded responses.
  • Parallelism: two test files using the same database tables at once. Run database files serially (--test-concurrency=1) or give each worker its own schema.

Beyond unit and integration tests

KindQuestion it answersTypical tools
End-to-endDoes the deployed system work through its real interface?Playwright (browser), a script with fetch against staging
ContractDo a consumer and a provider still agree on the API shape?Pact, or OpenAPI schema validation of real responses
Load and performanceHow many requests per second, and how does latency behave under pressure?autocannon (Unit 10), k6
MutationWould my tests notice if the code were subtly wrong?Stryker changes your code (flips > to >=) and checks that a test fails
SecurityCan common attacks succeed?The tests from Unit 7 (injection, auth bypass), npm audit, ZAP
SmokeIs the deployment alive right now?One request to /health after each deploy
What to test, and what not toTest business rules, every route's success and failure responses, authorization (each role against each protected route), validation edges, and anything that once broke. Do not test the framework, getters with no logic, or private helpers directly. A good rule: when a bug is reported, first write a test that reproduces it, watch it fail, then fix it, so the bug can never return unnoticed.
10

Unit 10: Running in Production

Writing the app is half the job. This unit is the other half: validated configuration, structured logs, metrics and health checks, graceful shutdown, performance, HTTPS, containers, reverse proxies, process managers, CI/CD and monitoring.

The same code runs on your laptop, in CI, in staging and in production. What differs is configuration: database address, secrets, log level, which features are on. The rule (from the twelve-factor app) is: config lives in the environment, never in code and never in git. Environment variables are always strings, and a missing or malformed one is the most common cause of "works locally, breaks in production". So the application should read the environment once, at startup, in one module, validate and convert it, and crash immediately with a clear message if anything is wrong, instead of failing at 3 a.m. when the first request needs the missing value.

import { z } from "zod";

const EnvSchema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(["development", "test", "production"]).default("development"),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65535).default(3000),           // env values are strings: coerce turns "8080" into 8080
  DATABASE_URL: z.url(),                                                   // required: no default for anything environment-specific
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32, "must be at least 32 characters"),
  LOG_LEVEL: z.enum(["fatal", "error", "warn", "info", "debug", "trace", "silent"]).default("info"),
  ENABLE_SIGNUP: z.stringbool().default(true),                             // "true", "1", "yes", "on" ... become real booleans (Boolean("false") would be true!)
  CORS_ORIGINS: z.string().default("").transform((value) => value.split(",").map((s) => s.trim()).filter(Boolean)),   // "a,b" becomes ["a", "b"]
});

export function loadConfig(env = process.env) {
  const parsed = EnvSchema.safeParse(env);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    // list EVERY problem at once (not one per restart) and never print the values: they may be secrets
    const message = "Invalid configuration:\n" + z.prettifyError(parsed.error);
    throw new Error(message);
  }
  return Object.freeze(parsed.data);                                       // frozen: no code can change config at runtime
}

// 1. a broken environment
try {
  loadConfig({ PORT: "99999", JWT_SECRET: "short", ENABLE_SIGNUP: "maybe" });
} catch (error) {
  console.log(error.message);
}

// 2. a good environment: defaults filled in, strings converted
const config = loadConfig({
  DATABASE_URL: "postgres://app:secret@db.internal:5432/notes",
  JWT_SECRET: "a-long-random-secret-of-at-least-32-chars",
  PORT: "8080",
  ENABLE_SIGNUP: "false",
  CORS_ORIGINS: "https://app.example.com, https://admin.example.com",
});
console.log(config.PORT, typeof config.PORT, "|", config.ENABLE_SIGNUP, "|", config.NODE_ENV, "|", config.CORS_ORIGINS);

// 3. the config object is frozen: in an ES module (always strict mode) changing it throws
try { config.PORT = 1; } catch (error) { console.log("changing a frozen config:", error.name); }
console.log("PORT is still:", config.PORT);

// 4. printing config for diagnostics: hide secrets and credentials
const printable = { ...config, JWT_SECRET: "[hidden]", DATABASE_URL: config.DATABASE_URL.replace(/\/\/[^@]*@/, "//***@") };
console.log(printable);
Invalid configuration: ✖ Too big: expected number to be <=65535 → at PORT ✖ Invalid input: expected string, received undefined → at DATABASE_URL ✖ must be at least 32 characters → at JWT_SECRET ✖ Invalid option: expected one of "true"|"1"|"yes"|"on"|"y"|"enabled"|"false"|"0"|"no"|"off"|"n"|"disabled" → at ENABLE_SIGNUP 8080 number | false | development | [ 'https://app.example.com', 'https://admin.example.com' ] changing a frozen config: TypeError PORT is still: 8080 { NODE_ENV: 'development', PORT: 8080, DATABASE_URL: 'postgres://***@db.internal:5432/notes', JWT_SECRET: '[hidden]', LOG_LEVEL: 'info', ENABLE_SIGNUP: false, CORS_ORIGINS: [ 'https://app.example.com', 'https://admin.example.com' ] }

Where the values come from

EnvironmentHow variables get in
Your laptopA .env file, loaded with node --env-file=.env or process.loadEnvFile() (Unit 7). It is git-ignored; commit a .env.example with fake values so newcomers know what to set.
CIThe CI system's secrets and variables, with throwaway test values
Containers and orchestratorsdocker run -e, env_file, Kubernetes ConfigMaps (plain values) and Secrets
Cloud platformsThe platform's environment settings, backed by a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault) for anything sensitive
  • No secrets in git, ever, not even "temporarily": history is forever. If one leaks, rotate it (issue a new one and revoke the old), do not just delete the file.
  • Environment variables are visible to anything inside the process and to people who can inspect the container. For high-value secrets prefer a secret manager that injects them at start-up and supports rotation.
  • One config module: the rest of the code imports config, and process.env appears nowhere else. That also makes tests easy: pass a different object to loadConfig.
  • Never log config wholesale, never put secrets in error messages, and never send them to the client.
  • No defaults for secrets or addresses of real systems: a default hides a missing setting and quietly points production at the wrong place. Defaults are for harmless tuning knobs (port, log level).
  • Behaviour should not branch on NODE_ENV all over the code. Use NODE_ENV=production as the switch libraries expect (Express, for example, turns on caching and hides error details), and control everything else with specific variables (LOG_LEVEL, ENABLE_SIGNUP).
  • Feature flags are config that changes behaviour without a deploy: the boolean above, or a flag service when you need per-user rollout. Remove flags once a feature is fully launched.

When something breaks in production, logs are your only witness. console.log("user " + id + " failed") is hard to search, impossible to filter by field, and carries no level or time. Structured logging writes one JSON object per line: {"level":30,"msg":"login failed","userId":7}. Log platforms (Loki, Elasticsearch, Datadog, CloudWatch) can then query userId = 7 AND level >= error. pino is the fastest and most used logger in Node: it writes JSON to stdout, and your platform collects it (your app never manages log files).

import pino from "pino";
import { Writable } from "node:stream";

const lines = [];                                                              // capture output so we can print it tidily
const sink = new Writable({ write(chunk, enc, done) { lines.push(chunk.toString().trim()); done(); } });

const logger = pino({
  level: "debug",                                                              // from config.LOG_LEVEL in a real app
  base: { service: "notes-api" },                                              // fields on every line (default: pid and hostname)
  timestamp: false,                                                            // off ONLY to keep this demo's output stable: keep it on in real life
  redact: { paths: ["password", "*.token", "user.email"], censor: "[REDACTED]" },    // masked wherever they appear
}, sink);

logger.info("server started");                                                 // message only
logger.info({ port: 3000, password: "hunter2" }, "listening");                // fields FIRST, message second; the password is masked
logger.debug({ userId: 7 }, "cache miss");
logger.warn({ user: { id: 7, email: "ana@example.com" } }, "login failed");   // the nested email is masked
logger.error(new Error("connection refused"), "query failed");                // an Error becomes err: { type, message, stack }
logger.error({ err: new Error("card declined"), orderId: 5 }, "payment failed");   // or pass it as err next to your own fields

const requestLogger = logger.child({ requestId: "req-42" });                   // a child adds fields to every line it writes
requestLogger.info("handling request");
requestLogger.info({ rows: 12 }, "query finished");

for (const line of lines) {
  const entry = JSON.parse(line);
  if (entry.err) entry.err.stack = "<stack trace>";                            // long and machine specific: shortened for the page
  console.log(JSON.stringify(entry));
}
console.log("level now:", logger.level, "| trace enabled:", logger.isLevelEnabled("trace"));

// what a default logger adds to every line:
const defaults = [];
pino(new Writable({ write(chunk, enc, done) { defaults.push(JSON.parse(chunk.toString())); done(); } })).info("hello");
console.log("default fields:", Object.keys(defaults[0]));
{"level":30,"service":"notes-api","msg":"server started"} {"level":30,"service":"notes-api","port":3000,"password":"[REDACTED]","msg":"listening"} {"level":20,"service":"notes-api","userId":7,"msg":"cache miss"} {"level":40,"service":"notes-api","user":{"id":7,"email":"[REDACTED]"},"msg":"login failed"} {"level":50,"service":"notes-api","err":{"type":"Error","message":"connection refused","stack":"<stack trace>"},"msg":"query failed"} {"level":50,"service":"notes-api","err":{"type":"Error","message":"card declined","stack":"<stack trace>"},"orderId":5,"msg":"payment failed"} {"level":30,"service":"notes-api","requestId":"req-42","msg":"handling request"} {"level":30,"service":"notes-api","requestId":"req-42","rows":12,"msg":"query finished"} level now: debug | trace enabled: false default fields: [ 'level', 'time', 'pid', 'hostname', 'msg' ]
LevelNumberUse for
fatal60The process cannot continue and is about to exit
error50An operation failed and somebody should look (5xx responses, failed jobs)
warn40Unexpected but handled: retry succeeded, deprecated call, 4xx spikes
info30Normal significant events: start, stop, request completed, job done
debug20Detail for developers. Off in production unless investigating
trace10Very noisy step by step detail

One log line per request, with a request id

pino-http is middleware that logs every request when it finishes (method, URL, status, duration), attaches a request id, and gives every handler a logger req.log that already carries that id, so every line your code writes while handling the request can be found together (and, with the correlation id from the Unit 8 entry, across services). Map status codes to levels yourself: by default everything is info.

import express from "express";
import pino from "pino";
import pinoHttp from "pino-http";
import { Writable } from "node:stream";

const lines = [];
const sink = new Writable({ write(chunk, enc, done) { lines.push(chunk.toString().trim()); done(); } });
const logger = pino({ base: undefined, timestamp: false }, sink);

const app = express();
app.use(pinoHttp({
  logger,
  genReqId: (req) => req.headers["x-request-id"] ?? "generated-id",            // reuse the caller's id, else create one (crypto.randomUUID() in real life)
  customLogLevel: (req, res, error) => (error || res.statusCode >= 500 ? "error" : res.statusCode >= 400 ? "warn" : "info"),
  serializers: {                                                               // choose exactly which request fields are logged: never dump all headers (cookies, tokens)
    req: (req) => ({ id: req.id, method: req.method, url: req.url }),
    res: (res) => ({ statusCode: res.statusCode }),
  },
}));

app.get("/notes/:id", (req, res) => {
  req.log.info({ noteId: req.params.id }, "loading note");                     // carries the request id automatically
  res.json({ id: req.params.id });
});
app.get("/crash", (req, res) => res.status(500).json({ error: "internal error" }));

const server = app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await new Promise((resolve) => server.once("listening", resolve));
const base = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`;
await fetch(base + "/notes/7", { headers: { "x-request-id": "req-abc" } });
await fetch(base + "/missing");
await fetch(base + "/crash");

for (const line of lines) {
  const entry = JSON.parse(line);
  delete entry.responseTime;                                                   // changes on every run
  if (entry.err) entry.err = { type: entry.err.type, message: entry.err.message };   // drop the stack for the page
  console.log(JSON.stringify(entry));
}
server.close();
{"level":30,"req":{"id":"req-abc","method":"GET","url":"/notes/7"},"noteId":"7","msg":"loading note"} {"level":30,"req":{"id":"req-abc","method":"GET","url":"/notes/7"},"res":{"statusCode":200},"msg":"request completed"} {"level":40,"req":{"id":"generated-id","method":"GET","url":"/missing"},"res":{"statusCode":404},"msg":"request completed"} {"level":50,"req":{"id":"generated-id","method":"GET","url":"/crash"},"res":{"statusCode":500},"err":{"type":"Error","message":"failed with status code 500"},"msg":"request errored"}

Pretty output for development only

JSON is for machines. On your laptop pipe the output through pino-pretty (never in production: it is slow and breaks the one-line-per-event rule):

$ printf '%s\n' '{"level":30,"time":1790000000000,"service":"notes-api","msg":"server started","port":3000}' '{"level":50,"time":1790000001000,"service":"notes-api","err":{"type":"Error","message":"db down"},"msg":"query failed"}' | npx pino-pretty --colorize=false --translateTime "UTC:yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM:ss"
[2026-09-21 14:13:20] INFO: server started
    service: "notes-api"
    port: 3000
[2026-09-21 14:13:21] ERROR: query failed
    service: "notes-api"
    err: {
      "type": "Error",
      "message": "db down"
    }
node --watch src/server.js | npx pino-pretty
What never goes in a logPasswords, tokens, session ids, API keys, full card numbers, and (depending on law and policy) personal data such as emails, phone numbers and addresses. Use redact as a safety net, but the real defence is not logging request bodies and headers wholesale. Also never log inside a hot loop at info, and do not log and rethrow the same error at every layer: that produces ten lines for one failure. Log it once, where you handle it.
  • Write to stdout and let the platform ship it (Docker, Kubernetes, systemd and every PaaS collect it). Do not rotate files from inside the app.
  • Log events with context ({ orderId, userId, durationMs }), not prose you will later parse with regular expressions.
  • Keep one consistent field name per concept (userId, not user here and uid there), so queries work across services.
  • Log at the edges (request in, request out, job start and finish, external call failed) and when you make a decision worth reviewing later (retry, fallback, circuit opened).
  • Alert on error volume, not on single lines, and send the details to an error tracker (Sentry or similar) that groups identical errors and shows the stack with the request context.

Logs tell you what happened to one request. Metrics tell you how the system is doing right now and over time: requests per second, error rate, latency percentiles, queue depth, memory. They are cheap numbers that a monitoring system (Prometheus plus Grafana is the standard) scrapes every 15 seconds from your /metrics endpoint, draws as graphs, and alerts on. The three metric types you need:

TypeBehaviourExample
CounterOnly goes up (resets on restart). Graph its rate.Requests, errors, emails sent
GaugeGoes up and downIn-flight requests, queue length, pool connections
HistogramCounts observations into buckets, so you can compute percentilesRequest duration (p50, p95, p99)

The RED method gives you the dashboard every service needs: Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed per second or percent), Duration (latency percentiles). The code below records all three for every route.

import express from "express";
import client from "prom-client";

const register = new client.Registry();
client.collectDefaultMetrics({ register });                                    // process CPU, memory, event loop lag, GC, active handles: free and valuable

const requests = new client.Counter({ name: "http_requests_total", help: "Completed HTTP requests", labelNames: ["method", "route", "status"], registers: [register] });
const duration = new client.Histogram({ name: "http_request_duration_seconds", help: "Request duration", labelNames: ["method", "route"], buckets: [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5], registers: [register] });
const inFlight = new client.Gauge({ name: "http_requests_in_flight", help: "Requests being handled right now", registers: [register] });

const app = express();
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  inFlight.inc();
  const stopTimer = duration.startTimer();
  res.on("finish", () => {
    inFlight.dec();
    const route = req.route?.path ?? "unmatched";                              // the route PATTERN ("/notes/:id"), never the raw URL (see warning below)
    requests.inc({ method: req.method, route, status: res.statusCode });
    stopTimer({ method: req.method, route });
  });
  next();
});

app.get("/notes/:id", (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.params.id }));
app.get("/metrics", async (req, res) => { res.type(register.contentType).send(await register.metrics()); });   // protect this route from the public internet

const server = app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await new Promise((resolve) => server.once("listening", resolve));
const base = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`;
for (const path of ["/notes/1", "/notes/2", "/notes/3", "/nope"]) await fetch(base + path);

const text = await (await fetch(base + "/metrics")).text();
const wanted = /^(# TYPE http_|http_requests_total|http_requests_in_flight|http_request_duration_seconds_count)/;
console.log(text.split("\n").filter((line) => wanted.test(line)).join("\n"));
console.log("default process metrics included:", ["process_cpu_user_seconds_total", "process_resident_memory_bytes", "nodejs_eventloop_lag_seconds"].every((name) => text.includes(name)));
server.close();
# TYPE http_requests_total counter http_requests_total{method="GET",route="/notes/:id",status="200"} 3 http_requests_total{method="GET",route="unmatched",status="404"} 1 # TYPE http_request_duration_seconds histogram http_request_duration_seconds_count{method="GET",route="/notes/:id"} 3 http_request_duration_seconds_count{method="GET",route="unmatched"} 1 # TYPE http_requests_in_flight gauge http_requests_in_flight 1 default process metrics included: true

Four requests produced three counter series for /notes/:id (all 200) and one for unmatched (404). The gauge shows 1 because the /metrics request that read it was itself in flight. A typical alert reads "5xx rate above 2% for 5 minutes" or "p95 duration above 500 ms for 10 minutes".

Label cardinality can take down your monitoringEvery distinct combination of label values is a separate time series stored in memory. Labels must have few, bounded values: method, route pattern, status. Never use user ids, emails, raw URLs (/notes/8271) or error messages as labels. A million users would mean a million series per metric. Put such detail in logs, not metrics.

Health checks: liveness and readiness

Orchestrators (Kubernetes, Docker, load balancers) ask your service two different questions and need two different endpoints:

ProbeQuestionChecksOn failure
Liveness /health/liveIs the process alive, or stuck beyond repair?Nothing external: it only proves the event loop answersRestart the container
Readiness /health/readyCan it serve traffic right now?Database, cache, anything required to answer requests, each with a short timeoutStop sending traffic (do not restart: restarting will not fix a down database)
Never put dependency checks in livenessIf the database goes down and liveness checks it, the orchestrator restarts every instance, which makes the outage bigger and slower to recover from. Liveness stays trivial; readiness carries the checks.
import express from "express";
import pg from "pg";
import { Redis } from "ioredis";

const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb", max: 2 });
const goodRedis = new Redis(6399, { lazyConnect: true, maxRetriesPerRequest: 0 });
const deadRedis = new Redis(6390, { lazyConnect: true, maxRetriesPerRequest: 0, retryStrategy: () => null });   // nothing listens on this port

const withTimeout = (promise, ms) => Promise.race([promise, new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error("timeout")), ms))]);
for (const connection of [goodRedis, deadRedis]) connection.on("error", () => {});   // ioredis emits "error" events: log them in real code, but always have a listener
async function check(name, fn) {
  try { await withTimeout(fn(), 500); return { name, status: "up" }; }       // 500 ms cap: a hanging dependency must not hang the probe
  catch { return { name, status: "down" }; }                                  // do not leak error details to the outside
}

function healthApp(redis) {
  const app = express();
  app.get("/health/live", (req, res) => res.json({ status: "alive" }));      // no dependencies on purpose
  app.get("/health/ready", async (req, res) => {
    const checks = await Promise.all([
      check("postgres", () => pool.query("SELECT 1")),
      check("redis", async () => { if (redis.status === "wait") await redis.connect(); await redis.ping(); }),
    ]);
    const ready = checks.every((c) => c.status === "up");
    res.status(ready ? 200 : 503).json({ status: ready ? "ready" : "not ready", checks });   // 503 tells the load balancer to stop routing here
  });
  return app;
}

async function probe(label, redis) {
  const server = healthApp(redis).listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
  await new Promise((resolve) => server.once("listening", resolve));
  const base = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`;
  const live = await fetch(base + "/health/live");
  const ready = await fetch(base + "/health/ready");
  console.log(label.padEnd(18), "| live:", live.status, "| ready:", ready.status, JSON.stringify(await ready.json()));
  server.close();
}

await probe("all dependencies up", goodRedis);
await probe("redis is down", deadRedis);                                       // liveness still 200, readiness 503

await pool.end(); goodRedis.disconnect(); deadRedis.disconnect();
all dependencies up | live: 200 | ready: 200 {"status":"ready","checks":[{"name":"postgres","status":"up"},{"name":"redis","status":"up"}]} redis is down | live: 200 | ready: 503 {"status":"not ready","checks":[{"name":"postgres","status":"up"},{"name":"redis","status":"down"}]}
  • Add a third probe, startup, for slow-booting apps (warming caches, running migrations), so liveness does not kill an app that is still starting.
  • Return 503 while shutting down from readiness (next entry) so the load balancer drains you before the process exits.
  • Expose /metrics and health endpoints on an internal port or behind the proxy, never open to the internet, and keep them cheap: a probe that runs a heavy query every second is a load problem of its own.
  • Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) is the third pillar beside logs and metrics: it shows one request's path and timing through every service and database call. Adopt it when you have several services (Unit 8 correlation ids are the manual version).

Your process will be stopped many times: every deploy, every scale-down, every node maintenance. The platform does not pull the plug at once. It sends a polite signal, waits a grace period (Docker: 10 s, Kubernetes: 30 s by default), then sends the unstoppable SIGKILL. A server that ignores the polite signal drops every request in flight at that instant: users see failed payments and half-finished uploads on every deploy. Handling it takes twenty lines.

SignalSent byMeaningCan you handle it?
SIGTERMdocker stop, Kubernetes, systemd, PM2, kill pid"Please shut down" (the one that matters in production)Yes
SIGINTCtrl+C in a terminalInterrupt from a userYes
SIGHUPTerminal closed; some daemons use it to reload configHang upYes
SIGUSR2nodemon and some toolsUser-defined (restart)Yes
SIGKILLThe platform after the grace period, the OOM killerDie nowNo: the process just disappears

Here is the difference, measured. The same slow endpoint (400 ms) is served by two child processes. A request is in flight, SIGTERM arrives, and then a new request tries to connect:

import { spawn } from "node:child_process";
import fs from "node:fs";
import os from "node:os";
import path from "node:path";

const naive = `
import http from "node:http";
const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => { await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 400)); res.end("finished"); });
server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => console.log("PORT " + server.address().port));
`;

const graceful = `
import http from "node:http";
let draining = false;
const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (req.url === "/ready") { res.statusCode = draining ? 503 : 200; return res.end(draining ? "draining" : "ready"); }   // readiness flips first
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 400));
  res.end("finished");
});
server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => console.log("PORT " + server.address().port));

function shutdown(signal) {
  if (draining) return;                                                       // a second signal must not start a second shutdown
  draining = true;
  console.log("got " + signal + ": refusing new connections, finishing in-flight requests");
  setTimeout(() => { console.log("grace period over: forcing exit"); process.exit(1); }, 3000).unref();   // never hang: exit before the platform kills us (unref so this timer alone cannot keep the process alive)
  server.close(() => {                                                        // runs when every connection has ended
    console.log("drained: closing database pool and queue workers here");
    process.exit(0);
  });
}
process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM"));
process.on("SIGINT", () => shutdown("SIGINT"));
`;

async function scenario(name, code) {
  const file = path.join(fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "shutdown-")), name + ".mjs");
  fs.writeFileSync(file, code);
  const child = spawn(process.execPath, [file], { stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "inherit"] });
  const log = [];
  const exited = new Promise((resolve) => child.on("exit", (code, signal) => resolve({ code, signal })));
  const port = await new Promise((resolve) => child.stdout.on("data", (chunk) => {
    for (const line of chunk.toString().split("\n").filter(Boolean)) line.startsWith("PORT ") ? resolve(Number(line.slice(5))) : log.push(line);
  }));

  const inFlight = fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}/slow`, { headers: { connection: "close" } })
    .then((res) => res.text(), (error) => "FAILED (" + (error.cause?.code ?? error.message) + ")");
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
  child.kill("SIGTERM");                                                      // what "docker stop" sends
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
  const newcomer = await fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}/new`).then((res) => res.status, (error) => "refused (" + (error.cause?.code ?? error.message) + ")");

  console.log(`${name.padEnd(9)} in-flight request: ${await inFlight}`);
  console.log(`${name.padEnd(9)} new request     : ${newcomer}`);
  console.log(`${name.padEnd(9)} exit            :`, await exited);
  if (log.length) console.log(`${name.padEnd(9)} process log     :`, log);
}

await scenario("naive", naive);
await scenario("graceful", graceful);
naive in-flight request: FAILED (UND_ERR_SOCKET) naive new request : refused (ECONNREFUSED) naive exit : { code: null, signal: 'SIGTERM' } graceful in-flight request: finished graceful new request : refused (ECONNREFUSED) graceful exit : { code: 0, signal: null } graceful process log : [ 'got SIGTERM: refusing new connections, finishing in-flight requests', 'drained: closing database pool and queue workers here' ]

The naive process was killed by the signal itself (signal: 'SIGTERM') and the user's request failed mid-flight. The graceful one finished the request, refused the newcomer (a real load balancer sends it to another instance, because readiness already failed), ran its cleanup, and exited with code 0.

let shuttingDown = false;

async function shutdown(signal) {
  if (shuttingDown) return;
  shuttingDown = true;
  logger.info({ signal }, "shutting down");
  setTimeout(() => { logger.fatal("graceful shutdown timed out"); process.exit(1); }, 25_000).unref();   // less than the platform's grace period

  try {
    await new Promise((resolve, reject) => server.close((err) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve())));   // 1. stop accepting, wait for requests
    await queueWorker.close();                                                                     // 2. let running jobs finish (BullMQ)
    await Promise.all([pool.end(), redis.quit()]);                                                 // 3. close connections cleanly
    logger.info("shutdown complete");
    process.exit(0);
  } catch (error) {
    logger.error({ err: error }, "error during shutdown");
    process.exit(1);
  }
}
process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM"));
process.on("SIGINT", () => shutdown("SIGINT"));

// readiness (previous entry) returns 503 once shuttingDown is true, so the load balancer stops routing here first
app.get("/health/ready", (req, res) => (shuttingDown ? res.status(503).json({ status: "shutting down" }) : /* run the checks */ res.json({ status: "ready" })));
  • PID 1 and signals in containers: signals go to the container's first process. Start Node directly (CMD ["node", "server.js"]), not through npm start or a shell wrapper, which may not forward SIGTERM, so your handler never runs and the platform waits the full grace period before SIGKILL. (The Docker entry below shows this.)
  • Keep-alive connections: server.close() waits for open connections, and since Node 19 it also closes the idle keep-alive ones. After your timeout use server.closeAllConnections() to cut the rest.
  • Long-lived connections (WebSockets, SSE) never finish by themselves: on shutdown, close them yourself with a code that tells clients to reconnect elsewhere (1001, going away).
  • Workers: close queue workers so running jobs finish and unfinished ones return to the queue (Unit 8). Jobs must be idempotent anyway, because SIGKILL can still happen.

Server timeouts: the defaults and when to change them

import http from "node:http";
const server = http.createServer();
console.log("keepAliveTimeout:", server.keepAliveTimeout, "ms   how long an idle keep-alive connection is kept open");
console.log("headersTimeout  :", server.headersTimeout, "ms   how long the client has to send the request headers");
console.log("requestTimeout  :", server.requestTimeout, "ms   how long the whole request (headers and body) may take");
console.log("timeout         :", server.timeout, "ms   socket inactivity timeout (0 means none)");
keepAliveTimeout: 5000 ms how long an idle keep-alive connection is kept open headersTimeout : 60000 ms how long the client has to send the request headers requestTimeout : 300000 ms how long the whole request (headers and body) may take timeout : 0 ms socket inactivity timeout (0 means none)

These protect you from slow clients (the "slowloris" attack opens many connections and sends data one byte at a time). One setting you must usually change: a load balancer closes idle connections after its own timeout (AWS ALB: 60 s, nginx: configurable). If Node's keepAliveTimeout (5 s here) is shorter, Node closes first, sometimes at the exact moment the balancer sends a request, which produces random 502 errors. Set Node's value higher than the balancer's (for ALB: server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000 and server.headersTimeout = 66_000).

Crashes: unhandled rejections and uncaught exceptions

Some bugs escape every try/catch: a promise nobody awaits rejects, or code in a timer throws. Since Node 15, an unhandled rejection crashes the process (exit code 1), the safe default. After an uncaughtException the process is in an unknown state (half-updated memory, locks held, connections open), so the only correct reaction is to log it and exit, and let the supervisor (Docker restart policy, Kubernetes, systemd, PM2) start a clean process. Never "swallow and carry on".

import { spawnSync } from "node:child_process";

const run = (code) => spawnSync(process.execPath, ["-e", code], { encoding: "utf8" });

const bare = run("Promise.reject(new Error('lost promise'))");
console.log("no handler        -> exit code", bare.status, "| error printed to stderr:", bare.stderr.includes("lost promise"));

const logged = run("process.on('unhandledRejection', (e) => { console.log('logging: ' + e.message); process.exit(1); }); Promise.reject(new Error('lost promise'))");
console.log("log then exit     -> exit code", logged.status, "| stdout:", JSON.stringify(logged.stdout));

const thrown = run("process.on('uncaughtException', (e, origin) => { console.log('fatal: ' + e.message + ' (' + origin + ')'); process.exit(1); }); setTimeout(() => { throw new Error('late bug'); }, 10)");
console.log("uncaughtException -> exit code", thrown.status, "| stdout:", JSON.stringify(thrown.stdout));
no handler -> exit code 1 | error printed to stderr: true log then exit -> exit code 1 | stdout: "logging: lost promise\n" uncaughtException -> exit code 1 | stdout: "fatal: late bug (uncaughtException)\n"

In an Express 5 app, errors thrown or rejected inside route handlers never reach these events: Express catches them and sends them to your error middleware (Unit 4). These handlers are the last safety net for everything outside a request: timers, event emitters, background tasks. Flush your logger and report to the error tracker inside them, then exit.

Node runs your JavaScript on one thread. That is fine, because most of a backend's time is spent waiting (for the database, the network, the disk) and waiting does not use the thread. But any synchronous work that takes 300 ms (a big JSON parse, a regex gone wrong, pbkdf2Sync, image resizing, a huge loop) stops every request for 300 ms, not just the one that caused it. The first rule of Node performance: keep the event loop free. The server below runs in its own process; the client sends a slow request and then, 100 ms later, a trivial /ping:

import { spawn } from "node:child_process";
import fs from "node:fs";

const serverCode = `
import express from "express";
import { Worker } from "node:worker_threads";

const app = express();
const spin = (ms) => { const end = Date.now() + ms; while (Date.now() < end); };   // synchronous CPU work: nothing else can run meanwhile

app.get("/ping", (req, res) => res.send("pong"));

app.get("/block", (req, res) => {          // BAD: 400 ms of CPU work on the main thread
  spin(400);
  res.send("done");
});

app.get("/offload", (req, res) => {        // GOOD: the same work on another thread
  const worker = new Worker("const { parentPort } = require('node:worker_threads'); const end = Date.now() + 400; while (Date.now() < end); parentPort.postMessage('done');", { eval: true });
  worker.once("message", (message) => res.send(message));
});

const server = app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => console.log("PORT " + server.address().port));
`;
const file = new URL("./event-loop-server.mjs", import.meta.url);               // next to this script so that it can import express
fs.writeFileSync(file, serverCode);
const child = spawn(process.execPath, [file.pathname], { stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "inherit"] });
const port = await new Promise((resolve) => child.stdout.on("data", (chunk) => { const match = /PORT (\d+)/.exec(chunk); if (match) resolve(Number(match[1])); }));
const base = `http://127.0.0.1:${port}`;

const timeIt = async (path) => { const start = performance.now(); await (await fetch(base + path)).text(); return performance.now() - start; };
await timeIt("/ping");                                                          // warm up

for (const route of ["/block", "/offload"]) {
  const slow = timeIt(route);                                                   // start the slow request...
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
  const ping = await timeIt("/ping");                                           // ...and ping the server while it is busy
  await slow;
  console.log(route.padEnd(9), "a /ping sent 100 ms later was", ping > 200 ? "STUCK for about 300 ms (waited for the blocked loop)" : "answered immediately");
}
child.kill();
fs.rmSync(file);
/block a /ping sent 100 ms later was STUCK for about 300 ms (waited for the blocked loop) /offload a /ping sent 100 ms later was answered immediately
WorkWhere it should run
Database, HTTP calls, file reads (async APIs)On the main thread: they only wait, so this is the intended use
Hashing passwords, crypto.pbkdf2, zlib, fs (async versions)Node's built-in thread pool (4 threads by default, UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to change): already off the main thread, just never use the *Sync versions in handlers
Your own CPU-heavy JavaScript (image processing, large parsing, report generation)Worker threads (node:worker_threads, or a pool such as piscina), or a queue and worker process (Unit 8)
Anything that takes secondsA background job, answered with 202 Accepted

Typical event-loop blockers to hunt for: JSON.parse or JSON.stringify of multi-megabyte data, a regular expression with nested quantifiers on user input (ReDoS, Unit 7), fs.readFileSync and other *Sync calls after startup, sorting or looping over huge arrays inside a request, and unbounded SELECT results processed in JavaScript. The default metrics from the previous entry include nodejs_eventloop_lag_seconds: alert when it grows.

Compression

Text compresses to 10 to 30 percent of its size, which is a large win on slow links. Browsers send Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, and the server answers with Content-Encoding. The compression middleware does it; skip tiny bodies (compression costs CPU, and the default threshold is 1 KiB) and never compress already compressed formats (images, video, zip). In production, many teams let the reverse proxy (nginx, a CDN) do it, which frees Node's thread.

import http from "node:http";
import express from "express";
import compression from "compression";

const app = express();
app.use(compression());                                                        // before the routes that send large responses
const notes = Array.from({ length: 300 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i, title: "note number " + i, done: i % 3 === 0 }));
app.get("/notes", (req, res) => res.json(notes));
app.get("/tiny", (req, res) => res.json({ ok: true }));

const server = app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await new Promise((resolve) => server.once("listening", resolve));
const port = server.address().port;

// raw http.get so that nothing decompresses behind our back
const get = (path, encoding) => new Promise((resolve) => {
  http.get({ port, host: "127.0.0.1", path, headers: { "accept-encoding": encoding } }, (res) => {
    const chunks = [];
    res.on("data", (chunk) => chunks.push(chunk));
    res.on("end", () => resolve({ headers: res.headers, bytes: Buffer.concat(chunks).length }));
  });
});

const plain = await get("/notes", "identity");
const gzipped = await get("/notes", "gzip");
console.log("without compression:", "content-encoding =", plain.headers["content-encoding"]);
console.log("with gzip          :", "content-encoding =", gzipped.headers["content-encoding"], "| vary =", gzipped.headers.vary);
console.log("gzip body is under 20% of the plain body:", gzipped.bytes < plain.bytes * 0.2);
console.log("tiny response (under the 1 KiB threshold) is left alone:", (await get("/tiny", "gzip")).headers["content-encoding"] === undefined);
server.close();
without compression: content-encoding = undefined with gzip : content-encoding = gzip | vary = Accept-Encoding gzip body is under 20% of the plain body: true tiny response (under the 1 KiB threshold) is left alone: true

Load testing with autocannon

Measure, do not guess. autocannon is a fast HTTP load generator written in Node (alternatives: k6, wrk, hey). You choose the number of connections (simulated concurrent clients) and a duration, and it reports requests per second, latency percentiles and errors. Run it against a production-like build, from another machine if you can (the load generator competes for CPU), and compare before and after a change. Below, two handlers do the "same" 5 ms of work, one by blocking the thread and one by waiting asynchronously (as a database call would):

import { spawn } from "node:child_process";
import fs from "node:fs";
import autocannon from "autocannon";

const serverCode = `
import express from "express";
const app = express();
const spin = (ms) => { const end = Date.now() + ms; while (Date.now() < end); };
app.get("/blocking", (req, res) => { spin(5); res.json({ ok: true }); });                               // 5 ms of CPU on the main thread
app.get("/waiting", async (req, res) => { await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 5)); res.json({ ok: true }); });   // 5 ms of waiting, like a query
const server = app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => console.log("PORT " + server.address().port));
`;
const file = new URL("./bench-server.mjs", import.meta.url);
fs.writeFileSync(file, serverCode);
const child = spawn(process.execPath, [file.pathname], { stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "inherit"] });
const port = await new Promise((resolve) => child.stdout.on("data", (chunk) => { const match = /PORT (\d+)/.exec(chunk); if (match) resolve(Number(match[1])); }));

const bench = (path) => autocannon({ url: `http://127.0.0.1:${port}${path}`, connections: 20, duration: 2 });
const blocking = await bench("/blocking");
const waiting = await bench("/waiting");

// exact numbers depend on the machine, so print what is stable: errors and the comparison
console.log("result fields include:", ["requests", "latency", "throughput", "errors", "non2xx"].every((key) => key in blocking));
console.log("errors / non-2xx (blocking):", blocking.errors, "/", blocking.non2xx);
console.log("errors / non-2xx (waiting) :", waiting.errors, "/", waiting.non2xx);
console.log("blocking handler is limited to about 1000 / 5 = 200 requests per second:", blocking.requests.average < 260);
console.log("waiting handler served more than 3 times as many requests:", waiting.requests.average > blocking.requests.average * 3);
child.kill();
fs.rmSync(file);
result fields include: true errors / non-2xx (blocking): 0 / 0 errors / non-2xx (waiting) : 0 / 0 blocking handler is limited to about 1000 / 5 = 200 requests per second: true waiting handler served more than 3 times as many requests: true
npx autocannon -c 50 -d 20 http://localhost:3000/notes             # 50 connections for 20 seconds
npx autocannon -c 50 -d 20 -m POST -H "content-type: application/json" -b '{"title":"x"}' http://localhost:3000/notes
  • Look at p99 latency (the slowest 1 percent), not only the average: users feel the tail.
  • The bottleneck is usually the database, not Node: slow queries, missing indexes (Unit 6), N+1 queries (Unit 8). Look there before micro-optimizing JavaScript.
  • Connection pools multiply: instances × pool.max must stay under the database's max_connections (PostgreSQL default 100). A pool of 10 across 20 instances is already 200.
  • Scale out, not just up: one Node process uses one CPU core for JavaScript. Run one process per core (the cluster module, PM2 in cluster mode, or, in containers, several replicas) behind a load balancer. This only works if the app is stateless: sessions, caches and WebSocket rooms in Redis, uploads in object storage.
  • Cache what is expensive and rarely changes (Unit 6 Redis entry, HTTP caching in the REST unit), and put a CDN in front of static and public content.
  • Pagination and limits on every list endpoint: a query that returns a million rows is a performance bug and a security bug.

Finding the slow code: CPU profiles

When the server is slow and you do not know why, record a CPU profile: Node samples the call stack many times per second and writes the result to a .cpuprofile file. Open it in Chrome DevTools (Performance or Profiler tab, "Load profile"), in VS Code, or turn it into a flame graph with npx clinic flame or npx 0x: the widest bars are where the time goes.

$ node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir=prof -e "let x = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 3e7; i++) x += i % 7; console.log('result', x)"
result 89999995
$ ls prof | grep -c '\.cpuprofile$'
1
Tool or flagShows
node --cpu-prof app.jsWhere CPU time goes (a flame graph)
node --heap-prof app.js, heap snapshots in DevToolsWhere memory is allocated, and what is keeping objects alive (leaks: compare two snapshots)
node --inspect app.jsAttach Chrome DevTools: breakpoints, profiler, memory (never expose the inspector port publicly)
perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()Event loop delay histogram: how long the loop was blocked
process.memoryUsage(), process_resident_memory_bytesMemory over time: steady growth that never falls back means a leak (unbounded caches and arrays, listeners added per request, timers never cleared)
APM (OpenTelemetry, Datadog, New Relic)Slow routes and slow queries in production, with traces

TLS (the protocol behind https://) gives three guarantees: encryption (nobody on the network can read the traffic), integrity (nobody can alter it) and authentication (the server proves it really is api.example.com, using a certificate signed by an authority your client trusts). Without it, passwords, tokens and cookies cross the network in readable form. HTTPS is not optional for anything beyond a toy.

Where TLS is handled

SetupHow
At the edge (most common)A reverse proxy or load balancer (nginx, Caddy, Traefik, a cloud load balancer, a CDN) holds the certificate and talks plain HTTP to your Node processes on a private network. Certificate renewal, TLS versions and HTTP/2 are its job. Your app sets app.set("trust proxy", ...) (Unit 4 and 7) so that req.protocol, req.secure and req.ip reflect the real client.
In Node itselfhttps.createServer({ key, cert }, app): fine for internal services, mutual TLS between services, or a small deployment without a proxy

Certificates for public sites are free and automatic: Let's Encrypt issues them, and Caddy, certbot, Traefik or your cloud provider obtain and renew them for you every 60 to 90 days. For local development, mkcert creates a certificate your own machine trusts. Below, we create a self-signed certificate with openssl (a certificate that signs itself, so no client trusts it by default), start a real HTTPS server, and see exactly what a client does with it:

import https from "node:https";
import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import fs from "node:fs";
import os from "node:os";
import path from "node:path";
import express from "express";

// 1. make a key and a certificate valid for localhost (subjectAltName is what modern clients check)
const dir = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "tls-"));
const keyFile = path.join(dir, "key.pem"), certFile = path.join(dir, "cert.pem");
execFileSync("openssl", ["req", "-x509", "-newkey", "rsa:2048", "-nodes", "-keyout", keyFile, "-out", certFile, "-days", "30",
  "-subj", "/CN=localhost", "-addext", "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost,IP:127.0.0.1"], { stdio: "ignore" });

// 2. an ordinary Express app, served over TLS
const app = express();
app.get("/", (req, res) => res.json({ secure: req.secure, protocol: req.protocol }));
const server = https.createServer({ key: fs.readFileSync(keyFile), cert: fs.readFileSync(certFile), minVersion: "TLSv1.2" }, app);   // refuse old, broken TLS versions
await new Promise((resolve) => server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", resolve));
const port = server.address().port;

// 3. three clients
const get = (options) => new Promise((resolve) => {
  const req = https.get({ host: "localhost", port, path: "/", agent: false, ...options }, (res) => {
    const facts = { tls: res.socket.getProtocol(), certificateCN: res.socket.getPeerCertificate().subject.CN };
    let body = ""; res.on("data", (chunk) => (body += chunk)); res.on("end", () => resolve({ status: res.statusCode, body, ...facts }));
  });
  req.on("error", (error) => resolve({ refused: error.code }));
});

console.log("1. default client (verifies):", await get({}));
console.log("2. client that trusts THIS certificate:", await get({ ca: fs.readFileSync(certFile) }));
console.log("3. client with verification switched off:", await get({ rejectUnauthorized: false }));
server.close();
1. default client (verifies): { refused: 'DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT' } 2. client that trusts THIS certificate: { status: 200, body: '{"secure":true,"protocol":"https"}', tls: 'TLSv1.3', certificateCN: 'localhost' } 3. client with verification switched off: { status: 200, body: '{"secure":true,"protocol":"https"}', tls: 'TLSv1.3', certificateCN: 'localhost' }

Client 1 does the right thing: it refuses with DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT, because nobody it trusts vouches for this certificate. Client 2 is how you handle internal certificates correctly: give it the certificate (or your company's CA) to trust, via the ca option or the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS environment variable. Client 3 works, and is a vulnerability:

Never disable certificate verificationrejectUnauthorized: false and NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 turn off authentication, so anyone on the path can impersonate the server and read everything (a man-in-the-middle attack). It is the most copied "fix" for a certificate error and it must never reach production. Fix the trust instead (add the CA), or fix the certificate (wrong hostname, expired, missing intermediate).

HSTS and redirecting HTTP to HTTPS

People type example.com and the browser first tries plain HTTP. Two defences: redirect HTTP to HTTPS (normally one rule in the proxy), and send Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) so that the browser remembers to use HTTPS only, for a period you choose, and never makes the plain request again. Helmet sets the header (Unit 7). Roll it out with a short max-age first, because a mistake is remembered by browsers for as long as you said.

import express from "express";
import helmet from "helmet";

const app = express();
app.set("trust proxy", 1);                                                     // we sit behind exactly one proxy that sets X-Forwarded-Proto
app.use(helmet({ hsts: { maxAge: 31_536_000, includeSubDomains: true } }));   // Strict-Transport-Security: one year

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  if (req.secure) return next();                                               // with trust proxy, req.secure reads X-Forwarded-Proto
  res.redirect(308, `https://${req.hostname}${req.originalUrl}`);              // 308 keeps the method, so a redirected POST stays a POST
});
app.get("/", (req, res) => res.json({ hello: "secure world" }));

const server = app.listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await new Promise((resolve) => server.once("listening", resolve));
const url = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}/notes?page=2`;

const plain = await fetch(url, { redirect: "manual" });                                                                         // no forwarded header: arrived over plain HTTP
console.log("plain HTTP      ->", plain.status, plain.headers.get("location"));
const proxied = await fetch(url.replace("/notes?page=2", "/"), { headers: { "x-forwarded-proto": "https" } });                  // the proxy says: client used HTTPS
console.log("via HTTPS proxy ->", proxied.status, "| HSTS:", proxied.headers.get("strict-transport-security"));
server.close();
plain HTTP -> 308 https://127.0.0.1/notes?page=2 via HTTPS proxy -> 200 | HSTS: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
  • Cookies: set Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly and SameSite (Unit 7), so a cookie cannot travel over plain HTTP.
  • Renewal is the usual outage: expired certificates take sites down. Use automatic renewal, and monitor the expiry date (an alert at 14 days).
  • Between services: encrypt internal traffic too when the network is not fully trusted, and consider mutual TLS, where the client also presents a certificate, so each service proves who it is.
  • Test your setup with an external scanner (SSL Labs) after deploying: it reports protocol versions, chain problems and missing HSTS.
Not run hereThis environment has the Docker command-line tool but no Docker daemon, so images cannot be built or started. What was run: the compose file was validated with docker compose config, and the application inside the image was started and stopped with a real signal. Everything about docker build and docker run below is standard behaviour that you should check on your own machine. For Docker in depth, see the companion Docker guide.

A container image is your app plus everything it needs (a Node version, system libraries, node_modules) frozen into one file. The same image runs on your laptop, in CI and in production, which removes "works on my machine". A container is a running instance of an image. Images are built from a Dockerfile: an ordered list of steps, each producing a cached layer. Order the steps from rarely changing to often changing, so that editing your code does not reinstall every dependency.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---- stage 1: install production dependencies (cached until package*.json change) ----
FROM node:22-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# ---- stage 2: the small final image ----
FROM node:22-alpine
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY package.json ./
COPY src ./src
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/health/live').then((r) => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1)).catch(() => process.exit(1))"
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]
LineWhy it is there
FROM node:22-alpine AS depsPick a base image with Node 22. Use a specific version (node:22.22-alpine) so rebuilds are reproducible. Alpine is small but uses musl: if a native module (bcrypt, argon2, sharp) misbehaves, switch to node:22-slim (Debian).
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ then RUN npm ci --omit=devCopy only the dependency files first: Docker caches this layer until they change. npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says (reproducible, fails on mismatch) and --omit=dev leaves out test tools.
Second FROM (multi-stage)The final image starts clean and copies in only the result. Build tools, caches and dev dependencies never reach production: a smaller image with fewer things to attack. (With TypeScript you would compile in a middle stage and copy only dist/.)
ENV NODE_ENV=productionExpress and many libraries switch to production behaviour
COPY src ./src lastYour code changes most often, so it comes last and only this small layer rebuilds
USER nodeRun as an unprivileged user (the official image includes one). If someone exploits your app, they are not root in the container.
EXPOSE 3000Documentation of the port. It does not publish it: -p 3000:3000 does.
HEALTHCHECK ...Docker polls the liveness endpoint (previous entries) and marks the container unhealthy when it fails. (Kubernetes ignores this and uses its own probes.)
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]Exec form (a JSON array) runs Node directly as process 1, so SIGTERM reaches your shutdown handler. CMD npm start or CMD node server.js (shell form) wraps it in another process that may swallow the signal.
 
node_modules
npm-debug.log
.git
.env
.env.*
Dockerfile
compose.yaml
coverage
test
*.md

The .dockerignore keeps node_modules (rebuilt inside the image for the right platform), .git, and above all your .env files out of the build context, so secrets cannot leak into an image layer.

The app the image runs is the small server with the probes and the shutdown handler from the earlier entries. Started here with a real SIGTERM at the end (the test harness stops it exactly as docker stop would):

import express from "express";

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
let shuttingDown = false;

const app = express();
app.get("/health/live", (req, res) => res.json({ status: "alive" }));
app.get("/health/ready", (req, res) => (shuttingDown ? res.status(503).json({ status: "shutting down" }) : res.json({ status: "ready" })));
app.get("/", (req, res) => res.json({ service: "notes-api", env: process.env.NODE_ENV ?? "development" }));

const server = app.listen(port, () => console.log(JSON.stringify({ msg: "listening", port })));

function shutdown(signal) {
  if (shuttingDown) return;
  shuttingDown = true;
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ msg: "shutting down", signal }));
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 25_000).unref();
  server.close(() => process.exit(0));
}
process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM"));
process.on("SIGINT", () => shutdown("SIGINT"));
$ curl -s localhost:3000/health/live
{"status":"alive"}
$ curl -s localhost:3000/health/ready
{"status":"ready"}
$ curl -s localhost:3000/
{"service":"notes-api","env":"development"}
{"msg":"listening","port":3000} {"msg":"shutting down","signal":"SIGTERM"}

Compose: the whole stack in one file

Real apps need a database and a cache. Docker Compose describes the set of containers, their networks and volumes in one YAML file, and docker compose up starts them all. Inside the compose network each service is reachable by its service name (db, redis), as the connection strings show.

services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      PORT: "3000"
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD}@db:5432/notes
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started
    restart: unless-stopped
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    read_only: true
    cap_drop: [ALL]

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD}
      POSTGRES_DB: notes
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d notes"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

volumes:
  dbdata:
$ docker compose config --quiet
error while interpolating services.api.environment.DATABASE_URL: required variable DB_PASSWORD is missing a value: set DB_PASSWORD
error while interpolating services.db.environment.POSTGRES_PASSWORD: required variable DB_PASSWORD is missing a value: set DB_PASSWORD
$ DB_PASSWORD=example docker compose config --quiet && echo "valid"
valid
$ DB_PASSWORD=example docker compose config --services | sort
api
db
redis

The first command fails on purpose: the :? in ${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD} makes compose refuse to start without the variable, instead of silently using an empty password. The same fail-fast idea as the config entry. In the file: depends_on with service_healthy waits until Postgres accepts connections, stop_grace_period gives your shutdown handler its 30 seconds, and read_only plus cap_drop take away what a web service never needs.

docker build -t notes-api:1.0.0 .                       # build the image from the Dockerfile
docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 -e NODE_ENV=production notes-api:1.0.0
docker ps                                                # running containers, with their health status
docker logs -f <container>                               # follow the JSON logs
docker exec -it <container> sh                           # a shell inside (alpine has sh, not bash)
docker stop <container>                                  # sends SIGTERM, waits 10 s, then SIGKILL
docker compose up -d --build                             # start the whole stack in the background
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose down                                      # stop and remove (add -v to delete volumes: DATA LOSS)
  • Never bake secrets into an image: not ENV, not COPY .env, not a build argument. Layers are readable by anyone who can pull the image. Inject secrets at run time (environment, mounted files, a secret manager).
  • Tag images immutably (the git commit hash or a version number) and deploy exactly that tag. latest means "something, unpredictable", and makes rollback guesswork.
  • Scan images for known vulnerabilities in CI (Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout) and rebuild regularly to pick up base-image patches.
  • One process per container, logs to stdout, stateless (data lives in volumes or external services). Scale by running more containers, not by clustering inside one.
  • Run migrations as a separate step (a one-off job before the new version starts), not at the start of every replica, or ten replicas race to migrate.
  • Resource limits (--memory, CPU limits) stop one container from starving the host. Node reads the container memory limit, but set --max-old-space-size to about 75 percent of it for large heaps.

In production, Node almost never faces the internet directly. A reverse proxy sits in front and takes on everything that is not your business logic: TLS termination, HTTP to HTTPS redirects, load balancing across several instances, buffering slow clients (so a phone on a bad connection does not tie up your Node process), compression, static files, rate limiting, and health-based routing (stop sending traffic to a dead instance). nginx is the classic choice; Caddy (automatic HTTPS), Traefik (container-aware), HAProxy, and cloud load balancers do the same job.

This is not a diagram of intentions: nginx is installed in this environment, so the next block starts a real nginx with a real config, two real Express backends, a self-signed certificate, and then checks each behaviour from the outside. (The odd *_temp_path lines exist only because this demo runs without root; on a real server you do not need them.)

import { spawn, spawnSync, execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import fs from "node:fs";
import os from "node:os";
import path from "node:path";
import net from "node:net";
import http from "node:http";
import https from "node:https";
import express from "express";
import { WebSocketServer, WebSocket } from "ws";

const freePort = () => new Promise((resolve) => { const s = net.createServer(); s.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => { const { port } = s.address(); s.close(() => resolve(port)); }); });

// two identical Node instances that report what they see
async function startBackend(name) {
  const app = express();
  app.set("trust proxy", 1);                                                   // exactly one proxy in front: believe its X-Forwarded-* headers
  app.get("/", (req, res) => res.json({ backend: name, secure: req.secure, host: req.hostname, sawForwardedFor: Boolean(req.get("x-forwarded-for")) }));
  app.get("/big", (req, res) => res.json(Array.from({ length: 300 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i, title: "note number " + i }))));
  app.post("/login", (req, res) => res.json({ ok: true }));
  const server = app.listen(await freePort(), "127.0.0.1");
  await new Promise((resolve) => server.once("listening", resolve));
  const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server });
  wss.on("connection", (socket) => socket.on("message", (data) => socket.send("echo: " + data)));
  return { port: server.address().port, stop: () => { wss.close(); server.closeAllConnections(); server.close(); } };
}

// a certificate for localhost, and the two instances
const dir = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "nginx-demo-"));
execFileSync("openssl", ["req", "-x509", "-newkey", "rsa:2048", "-nodes", "-keyout", `${dir}/key.pem`, "-out", `${dir}/cert.pem`, "-days", "30",
  "-subj", "/CN=localhost", "-addext", "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost,IP:127.0.0.1"], { stdio: "ignore" });
const [a, b] = [await startBackend("A"), await startBackend("B")];
const httpPort = await freePort(), httpsPort = await freePort();

// THE nginx CONFIGURATION (the variable parts are our random ports and temp folder)
const proxy = `
      proxy_pass http://notes_api;                                  # hand the request to the upstream group
      proxy_http_version 1.1;                                       # needed for keepalive and WebSockets
      proxy_set_header Host $host;                                  # keep the original Host header
      proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;  # the client's address, for req.ip
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;                   # "https": makes req.secure true
      proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;                       # pass WebSocket upgrades through
      proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
      proxy_read_timeout 60s;`;
const conf = `
worker_processes 1;
daemon off;
pid ${dir}/nginx.pid;
error_log ${dir}/error.log warn;
events { worker_connections 128; }
http {
  access_log off;
  client_body_temp_path ${dir}/body; proxy_temp_path ${dir}/proxy; fastcgi_temp_path ${dir}/fcgi; uwsgi_temp_path ${dir}/uwsgi; scgi_temp_path ${dir}/scgi;

  limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=login:1m rate=5r/s;       # at most 5 requests per second per client address
  map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade { default upgrade; '' ''; }

  upstream notes_api {                                              # the instances to balance across (round robin by default)
    server 127.0.0.1:${a.port};
    server 127.0.0.1:${b.port};
    keepalive 16;                                                   # reuse connections to the instances
  }

  server {                                                          # plain HTTP: only redirect
    listen 127.0.0.1:${httpPort};
    return 301 https://$host:${httpsPort}$request_uri;
  }

  server {
    listen 127.0.0.1:${httpsPort} ssl;
    ssl_certificate ${dir}/cert.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key ${dir}/key.pem;
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000" always;
    client_max_body_size 1m;                                        # reject big bodies before they reach Node
    gzip on; gzip_types application/json; gzip_min_length 1024;

    location / {${proxy}
    }
    location = /login {                                             # brute-force protection for one sensitive route
      limit_req zone=login burst=5 nodelay;
      limit_req_status 429;${proxy}
    }
  }
}`;
fs.writeFileSync(`${dir}/nginx.conf`, conf);

// always check a config before using it (this is what you run before every reload)
const check = spawnSync("nginx", ["-t", "-p", dir, "-c", `${dir}/nginx.conf`], { encoding: "utf8" });
console.log("nginx -t says the syntax is ok:", check.stderr.includes("syntax is ok"), "| test is successful:", check.stderr.includes("test is successful"));

const nginx = spawn("nginx", ["-p", dir, "-c", `${dir}/nginx.conf`], { stdio: "ignore" });
for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) {                                                  // wait until it accepts connections
  try { await new Promise((resolve, reject) => { const s = net.connect(httpsPort, "127.0.0.1", resolve); s.on("error", reject); }); break; }
  catch { await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 100)); }
}

// a client that trusts our certificate, and its helper
const ca = fs.readFileSync(`${dir}/cert.pem`);
const get = (urlPath, { method = "GET", headers = {} } = {}) => new Promise((resolve) => {
  const req = https.request({ host: "localhost", port: httpsPort, path: urlPath, method, ca, agent: false, headers }, (res) => {
    const chunks = []; res.on("data", (chunk) => chunks.push(chunk));
    res.on("end", () => resolve({ status: res.statusCode, headers: res.headers, body: Buffer.concat(chunks) }));
  });
  req.on("error", (error) => resolve({ error: error.code })); req.end();
});

// 1. TLS ends at nginx, and the app learns about it from the forwarded headers
const first = await get("/");
const seen = JSON.parse(first.body);
console.log("1. status", first.status, "| the app sees secure:", seen.secure, "| host:", seen.host, "| forwarded-for present:", seen.sawForwardedFor);
console.log("   HSTS header added by nginx:", first.headers["strict-transport-security"]);

// 2. load balancing
const who = [];
for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) who.push(JSON.parse((await get("/")).body).backend);
console.log("2. four requests alternate between the instances (round robin):", who.every((name, i) => i === 0 || name !== who[i - 1]));

// 3. compression done by nginx, not by Node
const plain = await get("/big", { headers: { "accept-encoding": "identity" } });
const zipped = await get("/big", { headers: { "accept-encoding": "gzip" } });
console.log("3. content-encoding:", zipped.headers["content-encoding"], "| under 20% of the original size:", zipped.body.length < plain.body.length * 0.2);

// 4. WebSockets pass through (Upgrade and Connection headers)
const socket = new WebSocket(`wss://localhost:${httpsPort}/ws`, { ca });
