const reply = await new Promise((resolve) => { socket.on("open", () => socket.send("hello")); socket.on("message", (data) => resolve(String(data))); socket.on("error", (error) => resolve("error: " + error.message)); });
console.log("4. websocket through nginx:", reply); socket.close();

// 5. plain HTTP only redirects
const redirect = await new Promise((resolve) => http.get({ host: "127.0.0.1", port: httpPort, path: "/notes?page=2", agent: false }, (res) => { res.resume(); resolve({ status: res.statusCode, location: res.headers.location }); }));
console.log("5. http request ->", redirect.status, redirect.location.replace(String(httpsPort), "<https-port>"));

// 6. rate limiting protects /login
const statuses = [];
for (let i = 0; i < 20; i++) statuses.push((await get("/login", { method: "POST" })).status);
console.log("6. 20 quick login attempts: some allowed:", statuses.includes(200), "| the rest rejected with 429:", statuses.filter((s) => s === 429).length > 5);

// 7. when every instance is down, nginx answers for them
a.stop(); b.stop();
await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 200));
console.log("7. both instances stopped ->", (await get("/")).status, "(Bad Gateway)");

nginx.kill("SIGQUIT");                                                          // graceful stop, like "nginx -s quit"
await new Promise((resolve) => nginx.on("exit", resolve));
nginx -t says the syntax is ok: true | test is successful: true 1. status 200 | the app sees secure: true | host: localhost | forwarded-for present: true HSTS header added by nginx: max-age=31536000 2. four requests alternate between the instances (round robin): true 3. content-encoding: gzip | under 20% of the original size: true 4. websocket through nginx: echo: hello 5. http request -> 301 https://127.0.0.1:<https-port>/notes?page=2 6. 20 quick login attempts: some allowed: true | the rest rejected with 429: true 7. both instances stopped -> 502 (Bad Gateway)
DirectiveWhat it does
upstream + proxy_passNames the backend instances and forwards requests to them. Failed instances are skipped for a while. Add max_fails and fail_timeout to tune, or use the platform's own balancing.
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-*Tells Node the original client address, scheme and host. Without them req.ip is the proxy's address, and rate limiting and logging are wrong.
Upgrade and Connection headersRequired for WebSockets: without them the handshake fails
limit_req_zone / limit_reqCheap, early rate limiting: abusive traffic is rejected before it costs Node any work
client_max_body_sizeThe proxy's upload limit. nginx's default is only 1 MB, so large uploads fail with 413 until you raise it (and keep Express's own limits too).
proxy_read_timeoutHow long nginx waits for your app to answer. For SSE and long polling raise it, and add proxy_buffering off for the event-stream route (Unit 8).
ssl_protocols, HSTSModern TLS only, and the browser remembers to use HTTPS
nginx -t then nginx -s reloadCheck the syntax, then apply without dropping connections. Never reload an unchecked config.

On a real server the certificate comes from Let's Encrypt (certbot --nginx writes the ssl_certificate paths under /etc/letsencrypt/live/your-domain/ and sets up renewal). Caddy does the same with a two-line config and no certbot.

PM2: several processes, restarts and zero-downtime reloads

One Node process uses one CPU core, and crashes when it hits a bug. A process manager runs several copies, restarts crashed ones, and reloads them without downtime. PM2 is the common one on plain servers and VMs (in containers, the orchestrator does this job, so skip PM2 there). Its cluster mode starts one process per core, all sharing the same port, using the same cluster mechanism from Unit 3.

module.exports = {
  apps: [{
    name: "notes-api",
    script: "./src/server.js",
    instances: "max",              // one process per CPU core
    exec_mode: "cluster",          // processes share the port, PM2 balances connections
    env: { NODE_ENV: "production", PORT: "3000" },
    max_memory_restart: "300M",    // restart a process that leaks past this
    kill_timeout: 30000,           // how long PM2 waits after SIGINT before SIGKILL: match your shutdown timeout
    listen_timeout: 10000,
  }],
};
import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import fs from "node:fs";
import os from "node:os";
import path from "node:path";

const dir = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "pm2-demo-"));
fs.writeFileSync(path.join(dir, "server.js"), `
const http = require("node:http");
const server = http.createServer((req, res) => res.end("answered by process " + process.pid));
server.listen(47821, "127.0.0.1");
process.on("SIGINT", () => server.close(() => process.exit(0)));            // PM2 sends SIGINT first: finish and exit
`);
fs.writeFileSync(path.join(dir, "ecosystem.config.cjs"), `module.exports = { apps: [{ name: "notes-api", script: "./server.js", instances: 2, exec_mode: "cluster", kill_timeout: 5000 }] };`);

const env = { ...process.env, PM2_HOME: path.join(dir, "pm2-home") };           // keep this demo's PM2 away from any other
const pm2 = (...args) => execFileSync("pm2", args, { cwd: dir, env, encoding: "utf8", stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "pipe"] });
const processes = () => JSON.parse(pm2("jlist")).map((p) => ({ name: p.name, mode: p.pm2_env.exec_mode, status: p.pm2_env.status, restarts: p.pm2_env.restart_time, pid: p.pid }));
const pause = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

try {
  pm2("start", "ecosystem.config.cjs");
  await pause(1500);
  const before = processes();
  console.log("started:", before.map(({ name, mode, status, restarts }) => ({ name, mode, status, restarts })));

  const answered = new Set();
  for (let i = 0; i < 12; i++) answered.add(await (await fetch("http://127.0.0.1:47821/")).text());
  console.log("requests to ONE port were answered by", answered.size, "different processes");

  pm2("reload", "notes-api");                                                    // restart the processes one after another, never all at once
  await pause(2500);
  const after = processes();
  console.log("after reload every process is new:", after.every((p) => !before.some((old) => old.pid === p.pid)), "| restart counter:", after.map((p) => p.restarts), "| status:", after.map((p) => p.status));
} finally {
  pm2("delete", "all");
  try { pm2("kill"); } catch { /* the daemon exits while answering */ }
}
started: [ { name: 'notes-api', mode: 'cluster_mode', status: 'online', restarts: 0 }, { name: 'notes-api', mode: 'cluster_mode', status: 'online', restarts: 0 } ] requests to ONE port were answered by 2 different processes after reload every process is new: true | restart counter: [ 1, 1 ] | status: [ 'online', 'online' ]
CommandEffect
pm2 start ecosystem.config.cjsStart the apps described in the file
pm2 reload notes-apiZero-downtime restart: processes are replaced one at a time (cluster mode)
pm2 restart notes-apiHard restart of everything at once (brief downtime)
pm2 logs, pm2 monitTail logs, live CPU and memory
pm2 startup then pm2 saveStart PM2 and your apps again after a server reboot
pm2-runtimeThe foreground variant to use inside containers if you want PM2 there at all

systemd: the operating system as your supervisor

On a Linux server you can skip PM2 and let systemd, which already starts everything else, run Node. You describe the service in a unit file, and get restarts, boot start, log collection (journalctl -u notes-api) and sandboxing for free. Run several copies by templating the unit (notes-api@3000.service) behind the load balancer.

[Unit]
Description=Notes API
After=network-online.target postgresql.service
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=notes
WorkingDirectory=/srv/notes-api
EnvironmentFile=/etc/notes-api.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node src/server.js
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
TimeoutStopSec=30
# sandboxing
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/notes-api

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
  • Install with sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now notes-api, watch with journalctl -u notes-api -f. (Not run here: this environment has no systemd.)
  • Restart=on-failure restarts after a crash, TimeoutStopSec is the grace period for your SIGTERM handler, EnvironmentFile keeps secrets out of the unit file (permissions 600, owned by root), and the sandboxing lines (NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem, PrivateTmp) limit the damage of a compromise.
  • Choosing: containers plus an orchestrator when you already run them or need many services; a managed platform (Render, Fly.io, Railway, Heroku-style, Cloud Run) when you want to avoid servers; systemd or PM2 behind nginx for one or two VMs. All of them need the same things from your app: stateless, configured by environment, health endpoints, graceful shutdown.

Continuous integration (CI) builds and tests every change automatically. Continuous delivery or deployment (CD) ships tested changes to servers by a script instead of by hand: the same steps every time, no "I forgot to run the migration". A good pipeline makes deploying boring, so you deploy small changes often, and each one is easy to understand and to undo.

name: deploy
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }

jobs:
  test:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/test.yml          # the workflow from the testing unit

  build-and-deploy:
    needs: test                                 # only after the tests pass
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read, packages: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with: { registry: ghcr.io, username: "${{ github.actor }}", password: "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" }
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}     # immutable tag: the exact commit
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh ${{ github.sha }}                      # run migrations, then roll the new tag out
        env:
          DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}                         # secrets live in the CI system, never in the repo

Deployment strategies

StrategyHowGoodWatch out
RollingReplace instances one at a time, waiting for readiness each timeNo extra capacity, no downtime (needs graceful shutdown and readiness)Old and new versions run together for a while: they must be compatible with the same database
Blue-greenStart a complete new copy (green) beside the current one (blue), switch the router, keep blue for instant rollbackInstant switch and rollbackDouble the capacity during the switch; same shared-database rule
CanarySend 1 to 5 percent of traffic to the new version, watch the error rate and latency, then increaseLimits the blast radius of a bad releaseNeeds good metrics and automated rollback
RecreateStop all, start newSimplestDowntime

Database changes without downtime: expand, then contract

During a rolling deploy, version N and version N+1 serve traffic against the same database. A migration that breaks the old code (dropping or renaming a column) crashes the old instances while they are still serving users. The safe pattern changes the schema in backward-compatible steps, over several deploys:

Goal: rename notes.text to notes.bodyStep
1. ExpandMigration: ADD COLUMN body text (nullable). Old code keeps working.
2. Dual writeDeploy code that writes both columns and still reads the old one
3. BackfillCopy old rows in batches (a job, not one giant locking UPDATE)
4. Switch readsDeploy code that reads and writes only body
5. ContractLater migration: DROP COLUMN text, once no running version uses it
  • Migrations run before the new code starts, once, from the pipeline (not from every instance on boot). Never edit a migration that has already run anywhere: add a new one (Unit 6).
  • Beware migrations that lock big tables (adding a column with a default on old PostgreSQL versions, creating an index without CONCURRENTLY, changing a column type): they block all queries. Test timing against production-sized data.
  • Test the migration on a copy of production data and keep a tested rollback plan. "Down" migrations rarely restore deleted data: the real safety net is the next point.
  • Backups that you have restored at least once. A backup you have never restored is a hope. Define how much data you can lose (RPO) and how fast you must recover (RTO), and rehearse it.

Rollbacks and feature flags

  • Rollback is "deploy the previous image tag", which only works because tags are immutable and the database stayed compatible (expand/contract). Practise it before you need it.
  • Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature: ship it dark, enable for staff, then 5 percent of users, then everyone, and switch it off in seconds without a deploy if it misbehaves.
  • Automate the verification: after each deploy the pipeline calls /health/ready and a short smoke test, and rolls back if they fail.

Staying current: dependencies and Node versions

  • Dependencies: npm audit in CI (fail on high severity), and let Dependabot or Renovate open small upgrade pull requests weekly, which your tests then vet. Small frequent upgrades are easy; a three-year-old lockfile is a project.
  • Lockfile and supply chain: commit package-lock.json, use npm ci, review new dependencies (maintainers, size, install scripts), and consider npm ci --ignore-scripts where you can.
  • Node itself: run an LTS (long-term support) release in production. Even-numbered releases become LTS and receive security fixes for roughly 30 months. As of the date of this guide: Node 22 is in maintenance (end of life 2027-04-30), Node 24 is the active LTS (end of life 2028-04-30), and Node 26 is the current release with LTS planned for 2026-10-28. Check nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases for the current table, and put your Node major version in engines, the Dockerfile, and CI so all three agree.

Monitoring, alerting and incidents

  • Define what "healthy" means: a service level objective (SLO) such as "99.9 percent of requests succeed and 95 percent finish within 300 ms, over 30 days". The gap between 100 percent and the objective is your error budget: spend it on shipping, and slow down when it is gone.
  • Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency, failed health checks, queue backlog growing, certificate expiring), not on every cause (one CPU spike). Every alert must be actionable and link to a runbook: what it means, how to check, how to fix. Alerts that are ignored teach people to ignore alerts.
  • Know before your users do: an external uptime check hitting a real endpoint from outside your network, plus error tracking (Sentry or similar) grouping exceptions with request context.
  • During an incident: first stop the bleeding (roll back, disable the flag, scale up), then diagnose. Keep a timeline, communicate status, and afterwards write a blameless postmortem: what happened, why the system allowed it, and what changes so it cannot recur (a test, an alert, a guard rail).

The production-readiness checklist

  • Config: validated at startup, secrets from a manager, none in git or in images (this unit, Unit 7).
  • Security: HTTPS only with HSTS, Helmet, CORS allow-list, input validation, parameterized SQL, hashed passwords, rate limits, upload and body limits, least-privilege database user, dependency audit (Unit 7).
  • Reliability: health and readiness endpoints, graceful shutdown, timeouts on every outbound call, retries only for idempotent operations, a circuit breaker for flaky dependencies, idempotent background jobs (Unit 8).
  • Data: migrations in CI, expand/contract, indexes for real queries, pool sized against max_connections, backups restored at least once, pagination everywhere (Unit 6).
  • Observability: structured logs with request ids, RED metrics, error tracking, dashboards, alerts with runbooks.
  • Testing and delivery: tests run in CI against a real database, immutable image tags, automated deploy, tested rollback, smoke test after deploy (Unit 9, this unit).
  • Operations: stateless instances (sessions, rate limits, caches and files outside the process), at least two instances behind a load balancer, resource limits, a documented way to run the app locally, and someone who knows who gets paged.
Start smallYou do not need Kubernetes, canaries and distributed tracing on day one. The honest minimum for a first real deployment: HTTPS, validated config, health endpoint, graceful shutdown, structured logs, automatic tests on every push, automated deploy of an immutable build, a backup you have restored once, and one alert on errors. Add the rest as the system and the team grow.
11

Unit 11: Capstone, the Notebox API

Everything so far, assembled into one real project: signup and login, JWT authentication, per-user notes with validation, pagination, search and tags, PostgreSQL migrations, structured logging, health checks, graceful shutdown, a full test suite, and a TypeScript version of the core types. Every file shown here was run, and every transcript is real output.

Notebox is a small but complete backend: people sign up, log in, and keep private notes with tags that they can search and page through. It is deliberately modest in features so that you can read every line, and deliberately complete in engineering: the same decisions you would make for a real service. Read it as a checklist of the previous ten units applied together.

The decisions, and where you learned them

DecisionWhyUnit
Express 5, ES modules, plain JavaScript with Zod typesAsync errors reach the error handler without wrappers; one schema validates and types the data (a TypeScript version is included)2, 4, 5
An app factory, createApp({ db, config, logger })Nothing listens on a port in tests; every dependency is replaceable4, 9
Raw SQL with pg, parameterized, plus SQL migration filesThe SQL is visible and teachable; $1 placeholders make injection impossible6, 7
Argon2id for passwords, injected hasherSlow on purpose; tests use cheap settings7
JWT access token (HS256) with issuer, audience and expiry, pinned algorithmStateless auth for an API; every verification option is explicit7
Authorization in the repository: WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2No route can forget the ownership check; another user's note looks like a missing one (404)7
Cursor pagination, capped page size, escaped LIKE search, GIN index on tagsStable pages under inserts, no unbounded lists, no wildcard surprises5, 6
One error shape { error: { message, details } }, bugs hidden and loggedClients can rely on it; no stack traces leak4, 5
Config validated at startup, pino logs, probes, graceful shutdownFail fast, observable, safe to deploy10
Tests against a real PostgreSQL, one rolled-back transaction per testThe SQL is really tested, tests are isolated and fast9

Setting it up

The database is created, then the migration runner applies migrations/001_init.sql. Running the migration a second time does nothing, which is exactly what you want from a deployment step:

-- users: one row per account. Emails are stored lowercase, so the UNIQUE constraint is case-insensitive in practice.
CREATE TABLE users (
  id            serial PRIMARY KEY,
  email         text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  password_hash text NOT NULL,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- notes: each belongs to exactly one user, and disappears with the user.
CREATE TABLE notes (
  id         serial PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    integer NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  title      text NOT NULL CHECK (length(title) BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  body       text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  tags       text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  pinned     boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- the list query is always "this user's notes, newest first, after a cursor"
CREATE INDEX notes_user_id_idx ON notes (user_id, id DESC);
-- tag filtering uses array containment (tags @> ARRAY['x'])
CREATE INDEX notes_tags_idx ON notes USING gin (tags);
// A tiny migration runner: applies migrations/*.sql in name order, once each, each inside a transaction.
import fs from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";
import pg from "pg";

const dir = path.join(import.meta.dirname, "..", "migrations");
const client = new pg.Client({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
await client.connect();
try {
  await client.query("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (name text PRIMARY KEY, applied_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now())");
  const done = new Set((await client.query("SELECT name FROM schema_migrations")).rows.map((r) => r.name));
  for (const file of fs.readdirSync(dir).filter((f) => f.endsWith(".sql")).sort()) {
    if (done.has(file)) { console.log(`skip   ${file} (already applied)`); continue; }
    await client.query("BEGIN");
    try {
      await client.query(fs.readFileSync(path.join(dir, file), "utf8"));
      await client.query("INSERT INTO schema_migrations (name) VALUES ($1)", [file]);
      await client.query("COMMIT");
      console.log(`apply  ${file}`);
    } catch (error) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");                              // a failed migration leaves nothing half-done
      throw error;
    }
  }
} finally {
  await client.end();
}

Start from the bottom. These modules have no knowledge of HTTP routes or SQL; each does one job and can be tested alone.

config.js: fail fast

import { z } from "zod";

const Schema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(["development", "test", "production"]).default("development"),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65535).default(3000),
  DATABASE_URL: z.url(),
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32, "must be at least 32 characters"),
  JWT_TTL_SECONDS: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(900),
  LOG_LEVEL: z.enum(["fatal", "error", "warn", "info", "debug", "trace", "silent"]).default("info"),
  CORS_ORIGINS: z.string().default("").transform((s) => s.split(",").map((o) => o.trim()).filter(Boolean)),
  LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(10),        // login attempts per minute per client
  ARGON2_MEMORY_KIB: z.coerce.number().int().min(1024).default(19456),     // OWASP minimum: 19 MiB
  ARGON2_TIME_COST: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(2),
});

export function loadConfig(env = process.env) {
  const parsed = Schema.safeParse(env);
  if (!parsed.success) throw new Error("Invalid configuration:\n" + z.prettifyError(parsed.error));
  return Object.freeze(parsed.data);
}

Exactly the pattern from the production unit: strings become typed values, missing secrets stop the process at startup with every problem listed, and the result is frozen. The Argon2 settings are config too, because tests need cheap hashing and production needs the recommended cost.

errors.js and validate.js: one error shape, one validation path

// Errors raised on purpose. The error handler in app.js turns them into JSON responses.
export class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(status, message, details) {
    super(message);
    this.status = status;
    this.details = details;
  }
}
export const badRequest = (message, details) => new HttpError(400, message, details);
export const unauthorized = (message = "Authentication required") => new HttpError(401, message);
export const notFound = (what) => new HttpError(404, `${what} not found`);
export const conflict = (message) => new HttpError(409, message);
import { badRequest } from "./errors.js";

// validate({ body, query, params }) with Zod schemas. The parsed, converted values land on req.valid.
// (In Express 5 req.query is a read-only getter, so results are stored on a new property instead.)
export const validate = (schemas) => (req, res, next) => {
  const valid = {};
  const problems = [];
  for (const part of ["params", "query", "body"]) {
    if (!schemas[part]) continue;
    const result = schemas[part].safeParse(req[part] ?? {});
    if (result.success) valid[part] = result.data;
    else problems.push(...result.error.issues.map((i) => ({ in: part, field: i.path.join("."), problem: i.message })));
  }
  if (problems.length) return next(badRequest("Validation failed", problems));
  req.valid = valid;
  next();
};
  • validate({ params, query, body }) turns Zod issues into one 400 with a list of { in, field, problem }, so a client sees every mistake at once.
  • The parsed, converted values (a query string "20" becomes the number 20) go on req.valid, because in Express 5 req.query is a read-only getter and cannot be replaced. Handlers read req.valid and never touch raw input.
  • Throwing an HttpError anywhere, even inside an async handler, reaches the error handler: Express 5 forwards rejected promises (Unit 4).

passwords.js: slow on purpose, and the same time for everyone

import argon2 from "argon2";

// Hashing is injected so tests can use cheap settings while production uses the recommended ones.
export function createPasswordHasher(config) {
  const options = { type: argon2.argon2id, memoryCost: config.ARGON2_MEMORY_KIB, timeCost: config.ARGON2_TIME_COST, parallelism: 1 };
  // verified once at startup against a throwaway hash: lets login spend the same time for unknown emails
  const dummyHash = argon2.hash("not-a-real-password", options);
  return {
    hash: (password) => argon2.hash(password, options),
    async verify(hash, password) {
      try { return await argon2.verify(hash ?? (await dummyHash), password); }
      catch { return false; }
    },
    needsRehash: (hash) => argon2.needsRehash(hash, options),
  };
}

Argon2id with the OWASP minimum cost by default. Two subtleties. verify returns false instead of throwing on a malformed hash. And when the user does not exist, verify(undefined, password) checks against a dummy hash, so a login attempt for an unknown email takes as long as one for a real email: otherwise response time would reveal which emails have accounts (Unit 7).

tokens.js and auth.middleware.js: verify everything explicitly

import { SignJWT, jwtVerify } from "jose";

const ISSUER = "notebox";
const AUDIENCE = "notebox-api";

export function createTokens({ secret, ttlSeconds }) {
  const key = new TextEncoder().encode(secret);
  return {
    sign: (userId) =>
      new SignJWT({})
        .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "HS256" })
        .setSubject(String(userId))
        .setIssuer(ISSUER)
        .setAudience(AUDIENCE)
        .setIssuedAt()
        .setExpirationTime(`${ttlSeconds}s`)
        .sign(key),
    async verify(token) {
      // pin the algorithm, issuer and audience: never accept whatever the token header claims
      const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, key, { algorithms: ["HS256"], issuer: ISSUER, audience: AUDIENCE });
      return { id: Number(payload.sub) };
    },
  };
}
import { unauthorized } from "./errors.js";

export const requireAuth = (tokens) => async (req, res, next) => {
  const [scheme, token] = (req.get("authorization") ?? "").split(" ");
  if (scheme !== "Bearer" || !token) throw unauthorized();
  try {
    req.user = await tokens.verify(token);                  // { id }
  } catch {
    throw unauthorized("Invalid or expired token");          // same message for bad signature, expired, wrong audience: no hints to attackers
  }
  next();
};
  • Verification pins the algorithm (HS256), the issuer and the audience. A token signed for another service, an expired token and an unsigned alg: none token are all rejected, and the tests below prove each one.
  • The token carries only the user id as sub: no email, no role, nothing that could go stale while the token is valid. Short life (15 minutes by default); a refresh-token flow is one of the exercises at the end.
  • Every failure gives the same 401 message, so an attacker learns nothing about why a token failed.

The repositories: where authorization lives

import { isUniqueViolation } from "./db.js";
import { conflict } from "./errors.js";

export const createUsersRepository = (db) => ({
  async create({ email, passwordHash }) {
    try {
      const { rows } = await db.query("INSERT INTO users (email, password_hash) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id, email", [email, passwordHash]);
      return rows[0];
    } catch (error) {
      if (isUniqueViolation(error)) throw conflict("Email already registered");   // the database decides: no check-then-insert race
      throw error;
    }
  },
  async findByEmail(email) {
    const { rows } = await db.query("SELECT id, email, password_hash FROM users WHERE email = $1", [email]);
    return rows[0] ?? null;
  },
  async findById(id) {
    const { rows } = await db.query("SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = $1", [id]);
    return rows[0] ?? null;
  },
});
// Every query is scoped by user_id: authorization lives in the data layer, so no route can forget it.
const COLUMNS = `id, title, body, tags, pinned, created_at AS "createdAt", updated_at AS "updatedAt"`;

export const createNotesRepository = (db) => ({
  // cursor pagination: "notes older than this id". Fetch one extra row to know whether another page exists.
  async list(userId, { limit, cursor, tag, q }) {
    const where = ["user_id = $1"];
    const params = [userId];
    if (cursor) { params.push(cursor); where.push(`id < $${params.length}`); }
    if (tag) { params.push([tag]); where.push(`tags @> $${params.length}::text[]`); }
    if (q) { params.push(`%${q.replace(/[\\%_]/g, "\\$&")}%`); where.push(`(title ILIKE $${params.length} OR body ILIKE $${params.length})`); }
    params.push(limit + 1);
    const { rows } = await db.query(`SELECT ${COLUMNS} FROM notes WHERE ${where.join(" AND ")} ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT $${params.length}`, params);
    const hasMore = rows.length > limit;
    const items = hasMore ? rows.slice(0, limit) : rows;
    return { items, nextCursor: hasMore ? items.at(-1).id : null };
  },

  async create(userId, { title, body, tags, pinned }) {
    const { rows } = await db.query(
      `INSERT INTO notes (user_id, title, body, tags, pinned) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5) RETURNING ${COLUMNS}`,
      [userId, title, body, tags, pinned]);
    return rows[0];
  },

  async get(userId, id) {
    const { rows } = await db.query(`SELECT ${COLUMNS} FROM notes WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2`, [id, userId]);
    return rows[0] ?? null;                                  // someone else's note looks exactly like a missing one
  },

  // partial update: only the provided fields change (COALESCE keeps the old value for the rest)
  async update(userId, id, { title, body, tags, pinned }) {
    const { rows } = await db.query(
      `UPDATE notes SET title = COALESCE($3, title), body = COALESCE($4, body), tags = COALESCE($5, tags), pinned = COALESCE($6, pinned), updated_at = now()
       WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2 RETURNING ${COLUMNS}`,
      [id, userId, title ?? null, body ?? null, tags ?? null, pinned ?? null]);
    return rows[0] ?? null;
  },

  async remove(userId, id) {
    const { rowCount } = await db.query("DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2", [id, userId]);
    return rowCount === 1;
  },
});
  • Every notes query includes user_id. Because ownership is part of the SQL, no route can forget to check it, and Ana's note requested by Raj returns null, which the route turns into 404: it does not even confirm that the note exists.
  • Cursor pagination: WHERE id < $cursor ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT n+1. The extra row is how we know another page exists without a separate COUNT. The cursor (an id here, an opaque token in bigger systems) stays correct when new notes arrive, unlike page numbers.
  • Search: the search text is a parameter ($n), never concatenated, and the characters %, _ and \ are escaped, so a search for % finds a literal percent sign instead of matching everything. The column names in the WHERE come from code, never from the client.
  • Duplicate email: no "does this email exist? then insert" (a race between two requests). The UNIQUE constraint decides, and the repository turns PostgreSQL error code 23505 into a 409.
  • Partial update: COALESCE($3, title) keeps the old value for every field the client did not send.

The routes and their schemas

import { Router } from "express";
import { z } from "zod";
import { validate } from "./validate.js";
import { requireAuth } from "./auth.middleware.js";
import { notFound } from "./errors.js";

const Id = z.object({ id: z.coerce.number().int().positive() });
const Tags = z.array(z.string().trim().toLowerCase().min(1).max(30)).max(10);

// the fields once, WITHOUT defaults: a create fills in defaults, a patch must not (an omitted field means "leave it alone")
const fields = {
  title: z.string().trim().min(1).max(200),
  body: z.string().max(20_000),
  tags: Tags,
  pinned: z.boolean(),
};
const NewNote = z.object({ ...fields, body: fields.body.default(""), tags: fields.tags.default([]), pinned: fields.pinned.default(false) }).strict();   // unknown fields are an error, not silently ignored
const NotePatch = z.object(fields).partial().strict().refine((patch) => Object.keys(patch).length > 0, "send at least one field to change");

const ListQuery = z.object({
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20),
  cursor: z.coerce.number().int().positive().optional(),
  tag: z.string().trim().toLowerCase().optional(),
  q: z.string().trim().min(1).max(100).optional(),
});

export function createNotesRouter({ notes, tokens }) {
  const router = Router();
  router.use(requireAuth(tokens));                           // every route below needs a valid token

  router.get("/", validate({ query: ListQuery }), async (req, res) => {
    const { items, nextCursor } = await notes.list(req.user.id, req.valid.query);
    res.json({ items, nextCursor });
  });

  router.post("/", validate({ body: NewNote }), async (req, res) => {
    const note = await notes.create(req.user.id, req.valid.body);
    res.status(201).location(`/notes/${note.id}`).json(note);
  });

  router.get("/:id", validate({ params: Id }), async (req, res) => {
    const note = await notes.get(req.user.id, req.valid.params.id);
    if (!note) throw notFound("Note");
    res.json(note);
  });

  router.patch("/:id", validate({ params: Id, body: NotePatch }), async (req, res) => {
    const note = await notes.update(req.user.id, req.valid.params.id, req.valid.body);
    if (!note) throw notFound("Note");
    res.json(note);
  });

  router.delete("/:id", validate({ params: Id }), async (req, res) => {
    if (!(await notes.remove(req.user.id, req.valid.params.id))) throw notFound("Note");
    res.status(204).end();
  });

  return router;
}
A bug the tests caught while this project was being writtenThe first draft built the patch schema with NewNote.partial(). In Zod, .partial() makes fields optional but keeps their defaults, so a PATCH with an empty body was silently parsed as { body: "", tags: [], pinned: false } and would have erased the note's body, tags and pin. The empty-patch assertion in the tests failed first, which exposed it. The fix, shown above, defines the fields once without defaults and derives both schemas: create adds defaults, patch makes everything optional with no defaults. This is what tests are for.
  • .strict() rejects unknown fields, which blocks mass assignment (a client sending userId or admin: true) instead of silently ignoring them.
  • Create returns 201 with a Location header, delete returns 204 with no body, a missing or foreign note is 404: the REST conventions from Unit 5.
  • router.use(requireAuth(tokens)) at the top of the router protects every route in it, including routes added later. Secure by default.

auth.routes.js

import { Router } from "express";
import { rateLimit } from "express-rate-limit";
import { z } from "zod";
import { validate } from "./validate.js";
import { requireAuth } from "./auth.middleware.js";
import { HttpError, unauthorized } from "./errors.js";

const Credentials = z.object({
  email: z.string().trim().toLowerCase().max(254).pipe(z.email()),
  password: z.string().min(12, "must be at least 12 characters").max(128),
});

export function createAuthRouter({ users, passwords, tokens, config }) {
  const router = Router();

  // slow down password guessing: 10 attempts per minute per client (store this in Redis when you run several instances)
  const loginLimiter = rateLimit({
    windowMs: 60_000,
    limit: config.LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT,
    standardHeaders: "draft-8",
    legacyHeaders: false,
    handler: (req, res, next) => next(new HttpError(429, "Too many login attempts, try again later")),
  });

  router.post("/signup", validate({ body: Credentials }), async (req, res) => {
    const { email, password } = req.valid.body;
    const user = await users.create({ email, passwordHash: await passwords.hash(password) });
    res.status(201).location("/auth/me").json({ user });     // never return password_hash
  });

  router.post("/login", loginLimiter, validate({ body: Credentials }), async (req, res) => {
    const { email, password } = req.valid.body;
    const user = await users.findByEmail(email);
    const ok = await passwords.verify(user?.password_hash, password);      // runs even when the user does not exist
    if (!user || !ok) throw unauthorized("Wrong email or password");       // one message for both cases: no account enumeration
    res.json({ accessToken: await tokens.sign(user.id), tokenType: "Bearer", expiresIn: config.JWT_TTL_SECONDS });
  });

  router.get("/me", requireAuth(tokens), async (req, res) => {
    res.json({ user: await users.findById(req.user.id) });
  });

  return router;
}
  • Emails are trimmed, lowercased and validated before they touch the database, so Ana@Example.com and ana@example.com are the same account.
  • Passwords are limited to 128 characters (hashing a megabyte would be a denial-of-service lever) and must have at least 12.
  • Login answers one message for "wrong password" and "no such user", and does the hashing work in both cases.
  • The login route has its own rate limit, in front of the validation. In-memory counters are per process: with several instances, give express-rate-limit a Redis store (Unit 7).

app.js: the order of middleware is the design

import express from "express";
import helmet from "helmet";
import cors from "cors";
import pinoHttp from "pino-http";
import { createAuthRouter } from "./auth.routes.js";
import { createNotesRouter } from "./notes.routes.js";
import { createUsersRepository } from "./users.repository.js";
import { createNotesRepository } from "./notes.repository.js";
import { createPasswordHasher } from "./passwords.js";
import { createTokens } from "./tokens.js";
import { HttpError, notFound } from "./errors.js";

// Builds the whole app from its dependencies. It never calls listen(): server.js does that, tests do not need to.
// `db` is anything with .query(): a Pool in production, a transaction client in tests.
export function createApp({ db, config, logger, isShuttingDown = () => false }) {
  const users = createUsersRepository(db);
  const notes = createNotesRepository(db);
  const passwords = createPasswordHasher(config);
  const tokens = createTokens({ secret: config.JWT_SECRET, ttlSeconds: config.JWT_TTL_SECONDS });

  const app = express();
  app.disable("x-powered-by");
  app.set("trust proxy", 1);                                // we run behind one reverse proxy
  app.use(helmet());
  app.use(cors({ origin: config.CORS_ORIGINS }));           // an allow-list; an empty list allows no cross-origin browser calls
  app.use(pinoHttp({
    logger,
    customLogLevel: (req, res, err) => (err || res.statusCode >= 500 ? "error" : res.statusCode >= 400 ? "warn" : "info"),
    serializers: { req: (req) => ({ id: req.id, method: req.method, url: req.url }), res: (res) => ({ statusCode: res.statusCode }) },
  }));
  app.use(express.json({ limit: "100kb" }));

  // liveness never touches dependencies, readiness checks the database and fails while shutting down
  app.get("/health/live", (req, res) => res.json({ status: "alive" }));
  app.get("/health/ready", async (req, res) => {
    if (isShuttingDown()) return res.status(503).json({ status: "shutting down" });
    try { await db.query("SELECT 1"); res.json({ status: "ready" }); }
    catch { res.status(503).json({ status: "database unavailable" }); }
  });

  app.use("/auth", createAuthRouter({ users, passwords, tokens, config }));
  app.use("/notes", createNotesRouter({ notes, tokens }));

  app.use((req, res, next) => next(notFound(`Route ${req.method} ${req.path}`)));

  app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
    if (res.headersSent) return next(err);
    const expected = err instanceof HttpError || (err.status >= 400 && err.status < 500);
    if (!expected) req.log.error({ err }, "unhandled error");
    res.status(expected ? err.status : 500).json({
      error: { message: expected ? err.message : "Internal server error", details: err.details },
    });
  });

  return app;
}
  • Security middleware first, so even error responses carry the headers. The body parser has a size limit. The request logger redacts by choosing fields (id, method, url, status), so no header or body ever lands in the logs.
  • The error handler is last. It sends HttpError messages to the client, logs everything unexpected with the request id, and replaces bugs with "Internal server error".
  • createApp receives db as anything with .query(), which is why the tests can hand it a transaction.

server.js: wiring, probes and a polite exit

import pino from "pino";
import { loadConfig } from "./config.js";
import { createPool } from "./db.js";
import { createApp } from "./app.js";

const config = loadConfig();                                // fails fast with a readable message if the environment is wrong
const logger = pino({ level: config.LOG_LEVEL, base: { service: "notebox" } });
const pool = createPool(config);

let shuttingDown = false;
const app = createApp({ db: pool, config, logger, isShuttingDown: () => shuttingDown });
const server = app.listen(config.PORT, () => logger.info({ port: config.PORT, env: config.NODE_ENV }, "notebox listening"));

async function shutdown(signal) {
  if (shuttingDown) return;
  shuttingDown = true;                                      // readiness now answers 503: the load balancer stops sending traffic
  logger.info({ signal }, "shutting down");
  setTimeout(() => { logger.fatal("shutdown timed out"); process.exit(1); }, 25_000).unref();
  server.close(async () => {                                // waits for in-flight requests
    await pool.end();
    logger.info("shutdown complete");
    process.exit(0);
  });
}
process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM"));
process.on("SIGINT", () => shutdown("SIGINT"));
process.on("unhandledRejection", (error) => { logger.fatal({ err: error }, "unhandled rejection"); process.exit(1); });

Only this file knows about the real world: it reads the environment, creates the pool, listens, and handles signals exactly as in the shutdown entry. On SIGTERM readiness flips to 503, the server stops accepting, finishes in-flight requests, closes the pool, and exits with code 0.

The server below was started with the environment a real deployment would provide (DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET, LOG_LEVEL=info, and a PORT), and every command is a real request. The token is saved to a file instead of printed, the way you would keep it in a shell variable, and notes are shown without their timestamps so the output is easy to read. Things to notice, in order: the unauthenticated GET /notes is a clean 401; signup lowercases the email and never returns the hash; the duplicate is a 409 even though the case differs; validation errors list every wrong field; the decoded token holds only sub, issuer, audience and a 900 second life; the note creation response carries a Location header and Helmet's security headers; the first page has nextCursor: 3 which is simply "continue after note 3", and the second page ends with nextCursor: null; the search for % finds only the note that really contains a percent sign; the patch changed only pinned; deleting twice gives 204 then 404; userId: 99 in the body is rejected, not ignored; and Raj, authenticated and valid, gets 404 for Ana's note and an empty list of his own. The log at the end is the same story as one JSON line per request, with warnings for 4xx responses and the request ids that tie everything together, followed by the two shutdown lines when the test harness sent SIGTERM.

The suite runs the real app against a real PostgreSQL. Each test starts a transaction and rolls it back, so tests are isolated and nothing needs cleaning up (Unit 9). The helpers build state through the public API (signupAndLogin calls the real endpoints), so a test reads like a client's story.

import { beforeEach, afterEach, after } from "node:test";
import pg from "pg";
import pino from "pino";
import request from "supertest";
import { loadConfig } from "../src/config.js";
import { createApp } from "../src/app.js";

export const hasDatabase = Boolean(process.env.DATABASE_URL);

const baseEnv = () => ({
  NODE_ENV: "test",
  DATABASE_URL: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  JWT_SECRET: "test-secret-that-is-at-least-32-characters-long",
  ARGON2_MEMORY_KIB: "1024",                 // cheap hashing keeps the suite fast; production uses the default
  LOG_LEVEL: "silent",
  LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT: "1000",
});

// Call inside a describe(): every test gets a fresh app running inside a transaction that is rolled back afterwards.
export function useTestApp(extraEnv = {}) {
  const ctx = {};
  const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL, max: 2 });
  beforeEach(async () => {
    ctx.client = await pool.connect();
    await ctx.client.query("BEGIN");
    ctx.config = loadConfig({ ...baseEnv(), ...extraEnv });
    ctx.app = createApp({ db: ctx.client, config: ctx.config, logger: pino({ level: "silent" }) });
    ctx.http = () => request(ctx.app);
  });
  afterEach(async () => {
    await ctx.client.query("ROLLBACK");
    ctx.client.release();
  });
  after(() => pool.end());
  return ctx;
}

export const PASSWORD = "correct horse battery";

// helpers that build state through the public API, the same way a client would
export async function signupAndLogin(ctx, email = "ana@example.com") {
  await ctx.http().post("/auth/signup").send({ email, password: PASSWORD }).expect(201);
  const res = await ctx.http().post("/auth/login").send({ email, password: PASSWORD }).expect(200);
  return { Authorization: `Bearer ${res.body.accessToken}` };
}
import { describe, it } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { SignJWT } from "jose";
import { hasDatabase, useTestApp, signupAndLogin, PASSWORD } from "../support/helpers.js";

describe("authentication", { skip: !hasDatabase && "set DATABASE_URL" }, () => {
  const ctx = useTestApp();

  it("signs a user up without ever returning the password hash", async () => {
    const res = await ctx.http().post("/auth/signup").send({ email: "Ana@Example.com", password: PASSWORD });
    assert.equal(res.status, 201);
    assert.deepEqual(res.body, { user: { id: res.body.user.id, email: "ana@example.com" } });     // email normalised to lowercase
    assert.ok(!JSON.stringify(res.body).includes("hash"));
    const { rows } = await ctx.client.query("SELECT password_hash FROM users");
    assert.match(rows[0].password_hash, /^\$argon2id\$/);                                          // stored as an argon2id hash, not the password
  });

  it("rejects a duplicate email, whatever its case, with 409", async () => {
    await ctx.http().post("/auth/signup").send({ email: "ana@example.com", password: PASSWORD }).expect(201);
    const res = await ctx.http().post("/auth/signup").send({ email: "ANA@example.com", password: PASSWORD });
    assert.equal(res.status, 409);
  });

  it("validates input and says which field is wrong", async () => {
    const res = await ctx.http().post("/auth/signup").send({ email: "not-an-email", password: "short" });
    assert.equal(res.status, 400);
    assert.deepEqual(res.body.error.details.map((d) => d.field).sort(), ["email", "password"]);
  });

  it("logs in and uses the token on a protected route", async () => {
    const headers = await signupAndLogin(ctx);
    const me = await ctx.http().get("/auth/me").set(headers);
    assert.equal(me.status, 200);
    assert.equal(me.body.user.email, "ana@example.com");
  });

  it("gives the same answer for a wrong password and an unknown email", async () => {
    await ctx.http().post("/auth/signup").send({ email: "ana@example.com", password: PASSWORD });
    const wrongPassword = await ctx.http().post("/auth/login").send({ email: "ana@example.com", password: "wrong password here" });
    const unknownEmail = await ctx.http().post("/auth/login").send({ email: "nobody@example.com", password: PASSWORD });
    assert.equal(wrongPassword.status, 401);
    assert.equal(unknownEmail.status, 401);
    assert.deepEqual(wrongPassword.body, unknownEmail.body);                                       // no account enumeration
  });

  describe("token checks", () => {
    const secret = new TextEncoder().encode("test-secret-that-is-at-least-32-characters-long");
    const forge = (options) => {
      const jwt = new SignJWT({}).setProtectedHeader({ alg: "HS256" }).setSubject("1").setIssuedAt();
      return jwt.setIssuer(options.issuer ?? "notebox").setAudience(options.audience ?? "notebox-api").setExpirationTime(options.exp ?? "5m").sign(secret);
    };
    const status = async (token) => (await ctx.http().get("/auth/me").set("Authorization", `Bearer ${token}`)).status;

    it("refuses requests with no token, garbage, or a non-Bearer scheme", async () => {
      assert.equal((await ctx.http().get("/auth/me")).status, 401);
      assert.equal(await status("garbage"), 401);
      assert.equal((await ctx.http().get("/auth/me").set("Authorization", "Basic abc")).status, 401);
    });
    it("refuses an expired token", async () => assert.equal(await status(await forge({ exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 60 })), 401));
    it("refuses a token for another audience or issuer", async () => {
      assert.equal(await status(await forge({ audience: "other-api" })), 401);
      assert.equal(await status(await forge({ issuer: "someone-else" })), 401);
    });
    it("refuses an unsigned token (alg none)", async () => {
      const b64 = (o) => Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(o)).toString("base64url");
      const unsigned = `${b64({ alg: "none", typ: "JWT" })}.${b64({ sub: "1", iss: "notebox", aud: "notebox-api", exp: 4102444800 })}.`;
      assert.equal(await status(unsigned), 401);
    });
    it("accepts a correctly signed token for the same secret (control test)", async () => {
      await ctx.client.query("INSERT INTO users (id, email, password_hash) VALUES (1, 'a@example.com', 'x')");
      assert.equal(await status(await forge({})), 200);
    });
  });
});

describe("login rate limiting", { skip: !hasDatabase && "set DATABASE_URL" }, () => {
  const ctx = useTestApp({ LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT: "3" });
  it("answers 429 after too many attempts", async () => {
    const attempts = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) attempts.push((await ctx.http().post("/auth/login").send({ email: "ana@example.com", password: PASSWORD })).status);
    assert.deepEqual(attempts, [401, 401, 401, 429, 429]);
  });
});
import { describe, it } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { hasDatabase, useTestApp, signupAndLogin } from "../support/helpers.js";

describe("notes API", { skip: !hasDatabase && "set DATABASE_URL" }, () => {
  const ctx = useTestApp();
  const createNote = async (headers, note) => (await ctx.http().post("/notes").set(headers).send(note).expect(201)).body;

  it("requires a token on every route", async () => {
    for (const [method, path] of [["get", "/notes"], ["post", "/notes"], ["get", "/notes/1"], ["patch", "/notes/1"], ["delete", "/notes/1"]])
      assert.equal((await ctx.http()[method](path)).status, 401, `${method.toUpperCase()} ${path}`);
  });

  it("runs the full life of a note", async () => {
    const headers = await signupAndLogin(ctx);

    const created = await ctx.http().post("/notes").set(headers).send({ title: "  Buy milk ", tags: ["Home", "home "] });
    assert.equal(created.status, 201);
    assert.equal(created.headers.location, `/notes/${created.body.id}`);
    assert.deepEqual({ title: created.body.title, body: created.body.body, tags: created.body.tags, pinned: created.body.pinned }, { title: "Buy milk", body: "", tags: ["home", "home"], pinned: false });

    const id = created.body.id;
    assert.equal((await ctx.http().get(`/notes/${id}`).set(headers)).body.title, "Buy milk");

    const patched = await ctx.http().patch(`/notes/${id}`).set(headers).send({ pinned: true });
    assert.equal(patched.status, 200);
    assert.deepEqual({ title: patched.body.title, pinned: patched.body.pinned }, { title: "Buy milk", pinned: true });   // other fields untouched

    assert.equal((await ctx.http().delete(`/notes/${id}`).set(headers)).status, 204);
    assert.equal((await ctx.http().get(`/notes/${id}`).set(headers)).status, 404);
    assert.equal((await ctx.http().delete(`/notes/${id}`).set(headers)).status, 404);
  });

  it("rejects bad input with details", async () => {
    const headers = await signupAndLogin(ctx);
    const post = (body) => ctx.http().post("/notes").set(headers).send(body);
    assert.equal((await post({})).status, 400);                                             // title is required
    assert.equal((await post({ title: "x", admin: true })).status, 400);                    // unknown field: mass assignment blocked
    assert.equal((await post({ title: "x", tags: "not-an-array" })).status, 400);
    assert.equal((await ctx.http().patch("/notes/1").set(headers).send({})).status, 400);   // an empty patch changes nothing
    assert.equal((await ctx.http().get("/notes/abc").set(headers)).status, 400);            // id must be a number
    assert.equal((await ctx.http().get("/notes?limit=1000").set(headers)).status, 400);     // page size is capped
  });

  it("a patch leaves every field it does not mention alone", async () => {
    const headers = await signupAndLogin(ctx);
    const note = await createNote(headers, { title: "Plan", body: "details", tags: ["work"], pinned: true });
    const res = await ctx.http().patch(`/notes/${note.id}`).set(headers).send({ title: "New plan" });
    assert.deepEqual({ title: res.body.title, body: res.body.body, tags: res.body.tags, pinned: res.body.pinned }, { title: "New plan", body: "details", tags: ["work"], pinned: true });
  });

  it("never lets one user see or change another user's notes", async () => {
    const ana = await signupAndLogin(ctx, "ana@example.com");
    const raj = await signupAndLogin(ctx, "raj@example.com");
    const note = await createNote(ana, { title: "Ana's secret" });

    assert.equal((await ctx.http().get(`/notes/${note.id}`).set(raj)).status, 404);                        // looks exactly like a missing note
    assert.equal((await ctx.http().patch(`/notes/${note.id}`).set(raj).send({ title: "hacked" })).status, 404);
    assert.equal((await ctx.http().delete(`/notes/${note.id}`).set(raj)).status, 404);
    assert.deepEqual((await ctx.http().get("/notes").set(raj)).body.items, []);                            // and absent from Raj's list

    assert.equal((await ctx.http().get(`/notes/${note.id}`).set(ana)).body.title, "Ana's secret");         // untouched
  });

  it("pages through the list with a cursor, newest first, without gaps or repeats", async () => {
    const headers = await signupAndLogin(ctx);
    for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) await createNote(headers, { title: `note ${i}` });

    const titles = [];
    let cursor, pages = 0;
    do {
      const res = await ctx.http().get("/notes").query({ limit: 2, cursor }).set(headers);
      titles.push(...res.body.items.map((n) => n.title));
      cursor = res.body.nextCursor ?? undefined;
      pages++;
    } while (cursor);
    assert.deepEqual(titles, ["note 5", "note 4", "note 3", "note 2", "note 1"]);
    assert.equal(pages, 3);
  });

  it("filters by tag and searches text, treating % and quotes as plain characters", async () => {
    const headers = await signupAndLogin(ctx);
    await createNote(headers, { title: "Groceries", tags: ["home"] });
    await createNote(headers, { title: "Sprint plan", body: "ship 100% of the backlog", tags: ["work"] });
    await createNote(headers, { title: "Reading list", tags: ["home", "fun"] });

    const titles = async (query) => (await ctx.http().get("/notes").query(query).set(headers)).body.items.map((n) => n.title).sort();
    assert.deepEqual(await titles({ tag: "home" }), ["Groceries", "Reading list"]);
    assert.deepEqual(await titles({ q: "plan" }), ["Sprint plan"]);
    assert.deepEqual(await titles({ q: "%" }), ["Sprint plan"]);                              // a literal percent sign, not "match everything"
    assert.deepEqual(await titles({ q: "'; DROP TABLE notes; --" }), []);                    // injection attempt: just text that matches nothing
    assert.equal((await ctx.client.query("SELECT count(*)::int AS n FROM notes")).rows[0].n, 3);   // the table is still there
  });

  it("reports health and answers unknown routes in JSON", async () => {
    assert.deepEqual((await ctx.http().get("/health/live")).body, { status: "alive" });
    assert.deepEqual((await ctx.http().get("/health/ready")).body, { status: "ready" });
    const missing = await ctx.http().get("/nope");
    assert.equal(missing.status, 404);
    assert.deepEqual(missing.body, { error: { message: "Route GET /nope not found" } });
    assert.equal(missing.headers["x-powered-by"], undefined);
    assert.ok(missing.headers["strict-transport-security"]);                                 // helmet is on
  });
});

The project is plain JavaScript so that nothing stands between you and the ideas. Here is the same core in TypeScript, as you would write it in a typed codebase (the syntax is from Unit 2). Three ideas matter most: the Zod schema yields the type as well as the validation, the NotesRepository interface is the contract between routes and data layer, and a function returning Note | null makes the compiler force every caller to handle "not found".

import { z } from "zod";

// 1. ONE schema is the single source of truth: it validates at runtime AND produces the static type.
export const NewNote = z.object({
  title: z.string().trim().min(1).max(200),
  body: z.string().max(20_000).default(""),
  tags: z.array(z.string().trim().toLowerCase().min(1).max(30)).max(10).default([]),
  pinned: z.boolean().default(false),
}).strict();

export type NewNote = z.infer<typeof NewNote>;          // what the code receives AFTER parsing: every field present
export type NewNoteInput = z.input<typeof NewNote>;     // what a client may SEND: defaulted fields are optional

// 2. The domain types: what is stored and returned.
export interface Note extends NewNote {
  id: number;
  userId: number;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
}

export interface ListQuery {
  limit: number;
  cursor?: number;
  tag?: string;
}

export interface Page<T> {
  items: T[];
  nextCursor: number | null;
}

// 3. The contract between the routes and the data layer. The PostgreSQL repository and the in-memory fake both implement it.
export interface NotesRepository {
  list(userId: number, query: ListQuery): Promise<Page<Note>>;
  create(userId: number, note: NewNote): Promise<Note>;
  get(userId: number, id: number): Promise<Note | null>;       // `| null` forces every caller to handle "not found"
}

export class MemoryNotes implements NotesRepository {
  private rows: Note[] = [];
  private nextId = 1;

  async list(userId: number, { limit, cursor, tag }: ListQuery): Promise<Page<Note>> {
    const matching = this.rows
      .filter((n) => n.userId === userId && (cursor === undefined || n.id < cursor) && (tag === undefined || n.tags.includes(tag)))
      .sort((a, b) => b.id - a.id);
    const items = matching.slice(0, limit);
    return { items, nextCursor: matching.length > limit ? items.at(-1)!.id : null };
  }

  async create(userId: number, note: NewNote): Promise<Note> {
    const now = new Date();
    const row: Note = { ...note, id: this.nextId++, userId, createdAt: now, updatedAt: now };
    this.rows.push(row);
    return row;
  }

  async get(userId: number, id: number): Promise<Note | null> {
    return this.rows.find((n) => n.id === id && n.userId === userId) ?? null;
  }
}

// A generic helper: walks every page of ANY paginated source, whatever the item type.
export async function collectAll<T>(fetchPage: (cursor?: number) => Promise<Page<T>>): Promise<T[]> {
  const all: T[] = [];
  let cursor: number | undefined;
  do {
    const page = await fetchPage(cursor);
    all.push(...page.items);
    cursor = page.nextCursor ?? undefined;
  } while (cursor !== undefined);
  return all;
}
import { MemoryNotes, NewNote, collectAll } from "./notes.ts";
import type { NewNoteInput, NotesRepository } from "./notes.ts";

const repo: NotesRepository = new MemoryNotes();          // code depends on the interface, not the class

// what arrives from a client is `unknown` until the schema has checked it
const incoming: NewNoteInput[] = [{ title: "  First  " }, { title: "Second", tags: ["Work"] }, { title: "Third", pinned: true }];
for (const raw of incoming) await repo.create(1, NewNote.parse(raw));

const titles = (await collectAll((cursor) => repo.list(1, { limit: 2, cursor }))).map((n) => n.title);
console.log("all notes, newest first:", titles);

const one = await repo.get(1, 2);
console.log("note 2 tags:", one?.tags);                  // optional chaining: `one` may be null
console.log("someone else's note:", await repo.get(99, 2));

const bad = NewNote.safeParse({ title: "", unknown: true });
console.log("invalid input:", bad.success ? "accepted?!" : bad.error.issues.map((i) => i.message));

Node strips the type annotations and runs the file (Unit 2), so there is no build step for this code; tsc --noEmit is the separate step that actually checks the types. Both belong in CI. The next file contains three realistic mistakes, and the compiler finds all of them before any test or user does:

import { MemoryNotes } from "../typed/notes.ts";
import type { Note, NotesRepository } from "../typed/notes.ts";

const repo: NotesRepository = new MemoryNotes();

// Mistake 1: using a value that may be null
const note = await repo.get(1, 7);
console.log(note.title);

// Mistake 2: wrong type for a field
await repo.create(1, { title: "x", body: "", tags: [], pinned: "yes" });

// Mistake 3: an implementation that forgets part of the contract
class Broken implements NotesRepository {
  async list() { return { items: [] as Note[], nextCursor: null }; }
  async get() { return null; }
}
$ npx tsc --ignoreConfig --noEmit --strict --module nodenext --moduleResolution nodenext --target es2023 --skipLibCheck --allowImportingTsExtensions --types node typed-mistakes/mistakes.ts
typed-mistakes/mistakes.ts(8,13): error TS18047: 'note' is possibly 'null'.
typed-mistakes/mistakes.ts(11,56): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'boolean'.
typed-mistakes/mistakes.ts(14,7): error TS2420: Class 'Broken' incorrectly implements interface 'NotesRepository'.
  Property 'create' is missing in type 'Broken' but required in type 'NotesRepository'.
  • TS2322 / TS18047: a wrong type, and a value that may be null. These two are the bulk of everyday TypeScript errors, and the second one prevents the classic "cannot read properties of null" crash.
  • TS2420: a class that does not fully implement its interface. Swapping the in-memory repository for the PostgreSQL one can never silently drop a method.
  • Types vanish at runtime. NewNote.parse(raw) is what protects you from bad client data; the type only describes what the schema already checked. Never cast (as NewNote) data from outside the program.
  • Typing the whole project with @types/express, @types/pg and the same schemas is a mechanical next step, and the Unit 4 TypeScript project showed the Express side.

You learn backend development by changing a working system. Each exercise below is small, uses something from the guide, and has a done when you can check with a test. Do them in order or pick the ones that scare you.

#ExerciseSkills and unitDone when
1Refresh tokens: short access token (15 min) plus a long-lived refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie, stored hashed in a table, rotated on each use, revoked on logoutCookies, JWT, hashing, tables (Units 6 and 7)A reused refresh token is rejected, and logout makes the old one useless
2Optimistic concurrency: return an ETag from GET /notes/:id, require If-Match on PATCH, answer 412 if it changedHTTP caching and concurrency (Unit 5)Two clients editing the same note cannot overwrite each other silently (write the test with two requests)
3Soft delete and restore: a deleted_at column, queries that hide deleted rows, a restore endpoint, a partial indexSchema changes, expand/contract (Units 6 and 10)Deleted notes vanish from lists and come back with restore, via a migration that does not break the old code
4Full-text search: replace ILIKE with a tsvector column, a GIN index and ranked resultsPostgreSQL (Unit 6)EXPLAIN shows the index used, and results are ranked
5Email verification and welcome mail through a queue: signup enqueues a job, a worker sends the email, the link verifies the accountBullMQ, nodemailer, idempotency (Unit 8)Signup answers in milliseconds, the job retries on failure, and a retry never sends two emails
6Attachments: upload an image to a note, validate its real type, store it outside the database, serve it with correct headersUploads, streams, security (Units 3, 5 and 7)A file that is a script renamed to .png is rejected, and large files stream without loading into memory
7Live updates: push "note changed" to the user's other open tabs over Server-Sent Events, across two server instances through RedisReal-time (Unit 8)Edit in one client, see it in another connected to a different instance
8Metrics and a dashboard: a /metrics endpoint with request rate, errors and latency, readable by an internal network onlyprom-client (Unit 10)The three RED numbers appear, labelled by route pattern
9Package and deploy: write the Dockerfile and compose file for Notebox, and a CI workflow that tests, builds, and deploys an immutable tag behind nginx with TLSDocker, nginx, CI/CD (Unit 10)docker compose up gives a working API, and a deploy can be rolled back to the previous tag
10OpenAPI documentation generated from the Zod schemas, with the examples checked by the testsREST, validation (Unit 5)The docs cannot drift from the code, because they are produced from it
How to work through themFor each exercise: write the failing test first, make it pass, then run the whole suite. When you finish one, read your diff as a reviewer would, and ask what could go wrong in production (Unit 10 checklist). Real backend skill is mostly this loop, repeated.

Unit 12: Revision and Mastery

Cheat sheets that actually run, the errors you will meet with their real messages, drills with answers, interview questions, and a learning path

This is the Unit 3 toolbox compressed into a single script. Every line ran, and the output underneath is what it printed, so you can use it as a reference for syntax and for what the results look like. For the explanation behind any line, search the guide for the module name.

import path from "node:path";
import os from "node:os";
import { mkdtemp, writeFile, readFile, readdir, stat, rm } from "node:fs/promises";
import { createWriteStream } from "node:fs";
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";
import { Readable, Transform } from "node:stream";
import { EventEmitter, once } from "node:events";
import { createHash, createHmac, randomUUID, scryptSync, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";
import { parseArgs, promisify } from "node:util";
