import { AsyncLocalStorage } from "node:async_hooks";

// PATH: always build paths with path, never by gluing strings together
console.log(path.join("/srv", "app", "..", "data", "a.txt"));          // joins and normalizes
console.log(path.resolve("/a/b", "../c"));                             // absolute result
console.log(path.basename("/x/report.final.pdf", ".pdf"), path.extname("archive.tar.gz"));

// FILES: use the promise API, and clean up what you create
const dir = await mkdtemp(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "cheat-"));
const file = path.join(dir, "notes.txt");
await writeFile(file, "line one\nline two\n");
console.log(JSON.stringify(await readFile(file, "utf8")));
console.log((await stat(file)).size, "bytes;", await readdir(dir));

// STREAMS: pipeline connects them, handles errors, and applies backpressure
const shout = new Transform({ transform(chunk, enc, cb) { cb(null, chunk.toString().toUpperCase()); } });
await pipeline(Readable.from(["a", "b", "c"]), shout, createWriteStream(path.join(dir, "out.txt")));
console.log(await readFile(path.join(dir, "out.txt"), "utf8"));
await rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });

// EVENTS: emit and listen, or await a single event
const bus = new EventEmitter();
bus.on("greet", (name) => console.log("hello", name));
bus.emit("greet", "Ana");
setTimeout(() => bus.emit("ready", 42), 5);
const [value] = await once(bus, "ready");                              // a promise for the next "ready"
console.log("ready with", value);

// CRYPTO: hash, sign, compare safely, derive keys
console.log(createHash("sha256").update("hello").digest("hex"));
console.log(createHmac("sha256", "secret").update("payload").digest("hex").slice(0, 16), "...");
console.log(randomUUID().length, "chars in a UUID");
const a = scryptSync("pw", "salt", 32), b = scryptSync("pw", "salt", 32);
console.log(a.length, "byte key; equal:", timingSafeEqual(a, b));      // never compare secrets with ===

// ARGUMENTS: parse command line flags without a library
const { values, positionals } = parseArgs({
  args: ["--port", "8080", "-v", "input.txt"],                         // normally this is process.argv.slice(2)
  options: { port: { type: "string" }, verbose: { type: "boolean", short: "v" } },
  allowPositionals: true,
});
console.log({ ...values }, positionals);

// CHILD PROCESSES: run another program and read what it printed
const { stdout } = await promisify(execFile)("node", ["-p", "6 * 7"]);
console.log("child printed", stdout.trim());

// TIMERS: sleep, and give up if something takes too long
await sleep(5);
try {
  await sleep(1000, null, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(20) });
} catch (err) {
  console.log("gave up:", err.name);
}

// ASYNC CONTEXT: data that follows a request through awaits (request ids in logs)
const als = new AsyncLocalStorage();
await als.run({ requestId: "req-7" }, async () => {
  await sleep(5);
  console.log("still know the request:", als.getStore().requestId);
});

// GLOBALS worth remembering
console.log(structuredClone({ when: new Date(0) }).when instanceof Date, process.versions.node.split(".")[0] >= 22);
/srv/data/a.txt /a/c report.final .gz "line one\nline two\n" 18 bytes; [ 'notes.txt' ] ABC hello Ana ready with 42 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824 b82fcb791acec578 ... 36 chars in a UUID 32 byte key; equal: true { port: '8080', verbose: true } [ 'input.txt' ] child printed 42 gave up: AbortError still know the request: req-7 true true
Memory hooks
  • Paths and files: node:path for names, fs/promises for content, streams/pipeline for anything big.
  • Never block the loop: no *Sync calls and no long CPU loops inside request handlers (use a worker thread or a queue).
  • Secrets: random with crypto, compare with timingSafeEqual, hash passwords with Argon2 or scrypt, never with a bare SHA.
  • Shutdown: on SIGTERM stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close the database, then exit.

One small Express 5 application using the pieces you reach for in almost every project, in the order a request meets them. Read it top to bottom as a map: middleware first, routes next, the 404 and the error handler last.

import express from "express";
const app = express();

app.disable("x-powered-by");                         // do not advertise the framework
app.use(express.json({ limit: "10kb" }));            // JSON body into req.body (only if Content-Type matches)
app.use((req, res, next) => {                        // your own middleware: do something, then call next()
  res.set("X-Request-Id", "req-1");
  next();
});

const items = express.Router();                      // a mini app for one resource
items.param("id", (req, res, next, id) => {          // runs for every route containing :id
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(id)) return next("route");       // not a number: skip this route, fall through to the 404
  req.itemId = Number(id);                           // params are strings, convert once here
  next();
});
items.get("/", (req, res) => res.json({ q: req.query.q ?? null }));
items.get("/:id", async (req, res) => {              // async handlers just work in Express 5
  const row = await Promise.resolve(req.itemId === 1 ? { id: 1, name: "pen" } : null);
  if (!row) return res.status(404).json({ error: "not found" });
  res.json(row);
});
items.post("/", (req, res) => {
  res.status(201).location("/items/2").json({ id: 2, ...req.body });
});
app.use("/items", items);                            // mount the router under a prefix

app.get("/boom", async () => { throw new Error("async failure"); });   // a rejected promise reaches the error handler
app.get("/old", (req, res) => res.redirect(301, "/items"));
app.get("/text", (req, res) => res.type("text/plain").send("plain text"));
app.get("/cookie", (req, res) => {
  res.cookie("sid", "abc", { httpOnly: true, sameSite: "lax" });
  res.sendStatus(204);
});

app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: "no such route" }));      // nothing matched
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {                                            // four arguments: the error handler, always last
  if (err.type === "entity.parse.failed") return res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid JSON" });
  if (err.status) return res.status(err.status).json({ error: err.message });
  res.status(500).json({ error: "server error" });                            // never leak err.message for unexpected bugs
});
> GET /items?q=pens < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"q":"pens"} > GET /items/1 < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":1,"name":"pen"} > GET /items/9 < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"not found"} > GET /items/abc < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"no such route"} > POST /items {"name":"ink"} < 201 Created < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"id":2,"name":"ink"} > POST /items {oops > content-type: application/json < 400 Bad Request < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"invalid JSON"} > GET /boom < 500 Internal Server Error < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < {"error":"server error"} > GET /old < 301 Moved Permanently < content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 < Moved Permanently. Redirecting to /items > GET /text < 200 OK < content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 < plain text > GET /cookie < 204 No Content
You want toWrite
Read data from the requestreq.params (path), req.query (after the ?), req.body (needs a parser), req.get("Header"), req.cookies (needs cookie-parser), req.ip
Send JSON with a statusres.status(201).json(obj)
Send nothingres.sendStatus(204) or res.status(204).end()
Set a header or cookieres.set("X-Name", "value"), res.cookie(name, value, options), res.clearCookie(name)
Redirectres.redirect(301, "/new") (permanent) or res.redirect("/login") (302)
Send a fileres.sendFile(absolutePath) or res.download(path, "name.pdf")
Pass control onnext() to the next handler, next("route") to skip the rest of this route, next(err) to jump to the error handler
Group routesexpress.Router() then app.use("/prefix", router)
Serve static filesapp.use(express.static("public"))
Behind a proxyapp.set("trust proxy", 1) so req.ip and req.secure are right
Start listeningconst server = app.listen(port) and keep server for graceful shutdown
The order ruleExpress runs middleware and routes in the order you register them. A parser registered after the route that needs it does nothing for that route, a 404 handler registered before your routes answers every request, and an error handler that is not last misses errors from the code below it.

curl is your backend debugger. These commands ran against the small playground server from Unit 1, so each line shows exactly what the flag does. Quoting matters: wrap any URL containing ? or & in quotes, and wrap JSON in single quotes.

$ curl -s localhost:3000/json
{"ok":true,"now":"a fixed time"}
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{content_type}\n' localhost:3000/json
200 application/json; charset=utf-8
$ curl -sI localhost:3000/ | grep -i '^content-type'
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
$ curl -s -X POST localhost:3000/items -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"ink"}'
{"id":3,"name":"ink"}
$ printf '{"name":"from a file"}' > body.json
$ curl -s -X POST localhost:3000/items -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @body.json
{"id":4,"name":"from a file"}
$ curl -s -G localhost:3000/echo --data-urlencode 'q=node js' -d 'page=2'
{"method":"GET","path":"/echo","query":{"q":"node js","page":"2"},"body":null,"type":null}
$ curl -s -X PATCH localhost:3000/items/1 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"fountain pen"}'
{"id":1,"name":"fountain pen"}
$ curl -s -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' -X DELETE localhost:3000/items/2

HTTP 204
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'redirects followed: %{num_redirects}, final status: %{http_code}\n' -L localhost:3000/old
redirects followed: 1, final status: 200
$ curl -s -c jar.txt localhost:3000/cookie/set && curl -s -b jar.txt localhost:3000/cookie/read
{"set":"theme=dark"}{"cookieHeader":"theme=dark"}
$ curl -s -u ana:secret localhost:3000/headers | jq -r .authorization
Basic YW5hOnNlY3JldA==
$ curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer abc.def.ghi' localhost:3000/headers | jq -r .authorization
Bearer abc.def.ghi
$ curl -sf localhost:3000/status/404; echo "exit code with --fail: $?"
curl: (22) The requested URL returned error: 404
exit code with --fail: 22
$ curl -s --max-time 0.1 'localhost:3000/slow?ms=800'; echo "exit code on timeout: $?"
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 102 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
exit code on timeout: 28
$ etag=$(curl -sI localhost:3000/etag | grep -i '^etag' | cut -d' ' -f2 | tr -d '\r'); curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'second request with If-None-Match: %{http_code}\n' -H "If-None-Match: $etag" localhost:3000/etag
second request with If-None-Match: 304
FlagMeaning
-sSilent: no progress meter (add -S to still show errors)
-i / -IInclude response headers / send a HEAD request and show only headers
-X METHODChoose the method (not needed for GET, and -d already implies POST)
-H 'Name: value'Add a request header
-d / -d @fileSend a body from the text or from a file; with -G the data goes into the query string instead
--data-urlencodePercent-encode a value (spaces, ampersands, unicode)
-o file / -OSave the body to a file (/dev/null to discard) / keep the remote file name
-w '%{...}'Print facts about the request afterwards: http_code, time_total, content_type, num_redirects, size_download
-LFollow redirects (curl does not by default)
-b / -cSend cookies from a jar / save received cookies to a jar
-u user:passBasic authentication header
-fExit with code 22 on a 4xx or 5xx, so scripts can detect failure
--max-time sGive up after a number of seconds (exit code 28)
-vVerbose: show the request and response headers and the TLS handshake
-kSkip certificate verification. Local experiments only, never in a script that touches real data

Status codes to know by heart

CodeNameUse it when
200OKSuccess with a body
201CreatedA POST made a resource (add Location)
204No ContentSuccess with nothing to return (DELETE, some PUTs)
301 / 302MovedPermanent / temporary redirect
304Not ModifiedThe cached copy is still good (conditional requests)
400Bad RequestMalformed or invalid input
401UnauthorizedNot authenticated: no or bad credentials
403ForbiddenAuthenticated, but not allowed
404Not FoundNo such resource (also the safe answer for "not yours")
409ConflictDuplicate, or the state does not allow it
412Precondition FailedIf-Match did not match: someone changed it first
413Content Too LargeBody over the limit
422UnprocessableWell-formed but semantically invalid (many APIs use 400 instead; pick one)
429Too Many RequestsRate limited (add Retry-After)
500Internal Server ErrorA bug of yours
502 / 503 / 504Bad Gateway / Unavailable / TimeoutA proxy could not reach your app, your app is shutting down or overloaded, or it was too slow

The SQL from Unit 6 as one script on a real PostgreSQL server. Read the statement, then the result printed under it.

CREATE TABLE authors (
  id   serial PRIMARY KEY,
  name text NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
CREATE TABLE books (
  id        serial PRIMARY KEY,
  author_id int  NOT NULL REFERENCES authors(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  title     text NOT NULL,
  pages     int  CHECK (pages > 0),
  tags      text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  meta      jsonb  NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);
CREATE INDEX books_author_idx ON books (author_id);

INSERT INTO authors (name) VALUES ('Le Guin'), ('Borges') RETURNING id, name;
INSERT INTO books (author_id, title, pages, tags, meta) VALUES
  (1, 'The Dispossessed',     387, '{scifi}',           '{"year": 1974}'),
  (1, 'A Wizard of Earthsea', 183, '{fantasy,classic}', '{"year": 1968}'),
  (2, 'Ficciones',            174, '{classic}',         '{"year": 1944}');

-- filter, sort, page
SELECT title, pages FROM books WHERE pages > 180 ORDER BY pages DESC LIMIT 5 OFFSET 0;

-- join and aggregate
SELECT a.name, count(*) AS books, sum(b.pages) AS total_pages
FROM authors a JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.name HAVING count(*) >= 1 ORDER BY a.name;

-- arrays and JSON
SELECT title, meta->>'year' AS year FROM books WHERE tags @> '{classic}' ORDER BY (meta->>'year')::int;

-- CTE
WITH long_books AS (SELECT * FROM books WHERE pages > 180)
SELECT author_id, count(*) FROM long_books GROUP BY author_id;

-- window function: rank without collapsing rows
SELECT title, pages, rank() OVER (PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY pages DESC) AS rank_for_author
FROM books ORDER BY author_id, rank_for_author;

-- upsert and update with RETURNING
INSERT INTO authors (name) VALUES ('Le Guin') ON CONFLICT (name) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name RETURNING id;
UPDATE books SET pages = pages + 1 WHERE id = 3 RETURNING title, pages;

-- a transaction you take back
BEGIN;
DELETE FROM books WHERE author_id = 2;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT count(*) AS books_after_rollback FROM books;

-- a cascade you do not take back
DELETE FROM authors WHERE name = 'Borges';
SELECT count(*) AS books_after_cascade FROM books;
CREATE TABLE authors ( id serial PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL UNIQUE ); CREATE TABLE books ( id serial PRIMARY KEY, author_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES authors(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, title text NOT NULL, pages int CHECK (pages > 0), tags text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}', meta jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}' ); CREATE INDEX books_author_idx ON books (author_id); INSERT INTO authors (name) VALUES ('Le Guin'), ('Borges') RETURNING id, name; id | name ----+--------- 1 | Le Guin 2 | Borges (2 rows) INSERT INTO books (author_id, title, pages, tags, meta) VALUES (1, 'The Dispossessed', 387, '{scifi}', '{"year": 1974}'), (1, 'A Wizard of Earthsea', 183, '{fantasy,classic}', '{"year": 1968}'), (2, 'Ficciones', 174, '{classic}', '{"year": 1944}'); -- filter, sort, page SELECT title, pages FROM books WHERE pages > 180 ORDER BY pages DESC LIMIT 5 OFFSET 0; title | pages ----------------------+------- The Dispossessed | 387 A Wizard of Earthsea | 183 (2 rows) -- join and aggregate SELECT a.name, count(*) AS books, sum(b.pages) AS total_pages FROM authors a JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id GROUP BY a.name HAVING count(*) >= 1 ORDER BY a.name; name | books | total_pages ---------+-------+------------- Borges | 1 | 174 Le Guin | 2 | 570 (2 rows) -- arrays and JSON SELECT title, meta->>'year' AS year FROM books WHERE tags @> '{classic}' ORDER BY (meta->>'year')::int; title | year ----------------------+------ Ficciones | 1944 A Wizard of Earthsea | 1968 (2 rows) -- CTE WITH long_books AS (SELECT * FROM books WHERE pages > 180) SELECT author_id, count(*) FROM long_books GROUP BY author_id; author_id | count -----------+------- 1 | 2 (1 row) -- window function: rank without collapsing rows SELECT title, pages, rank() OVER (PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY pages DESC) AS rank_for_author FROM books ORDER BY author_id, rank_for_author; title | pages | rank_for_author ----------------------+-------+----------------- The Dispossessed | 387 | 1 A Wizard of Earthsea | 183 | 2 Ficciones | 174 | 1 (3 rows) -- upsert and update with RETURNING INSERT INTO authors (name) VALUES ('Le Guin') ON CONFLICT (name) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name RETURNING id; id ---- 1 (1 row) UPDATE books SET pages = pages + 1 WHERE id = 3 RETURNING title, pages; title | pages -----------+------- Ficciones | 175 (1 row) -- a transaction you take back BEGIN; DELETE FROM books WHERE author_id = 2; ROLLBACK; SELECT count(*) AS books_after_rollback FROM books; books_after_rollback ---------------------- 3 (1 row) -- a cascade you do not take back DELETE FROM authors WHERE name = 'Borges'; SELECT count(*) AS books_after_cascade FROM books; books_after_cascade --------------------- 2 (1 row)
  • Always pass values as parameters ($1) from Node, never by building SQL strings.
  • Always write WHERE on UPDATE and DELETE, and try it as a SELECT first.
  • Index the columns you filter, join and sort by; check with EXPLAIN (Unit 6), not with guesses.
  • Money is numeric or integer cents, never float; times are timestamptz.
  • Several statements that must succeed together belong in one transaction.

Reading error messages well is most of debugging. Each message below was produced by actually causing the failure, so what you see here is what your terminal will show. Start with the language and Node errors:

import path from "node:path";
import http from "node:http";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { EventEmitter, once } from "node:events";

const attempt = async (label, fn) => {
  try {
    await fn();
  } catch (err) {
    const code = err.code ? ` [${err.code}]` : "";
    const message = err.message.replace(/ imported from .*/, "").replaceAll(import.meta.dirname, "<dir>").replace(/:\d{4,5}\b/g, ":PORT");
    console.log(`${label.padEnd(20)}${err.name}${code}: ${message}`);
    if (err.cause) console.log(`${"".padEnd(20)}caused by [${err.cause.code ?? err.cause.name}]`);
  }
};

await attempt("undefined property", () => { const user = undefined; return user.name; });
await attempt("not a function", () => { const repo = {}; repo.save(); });
await attempt("not defined", () => missingVariable);
await attempt("const reassigned", () => { const limit = 1; limit = 2; });
await attempt("bad JSON", () => JSON.parse("{oops"));
await attempt("empty JSON", () => JSON.parse(""));
await attempt("class without new", () => { class Repo {} Repo(); });
await attempt("endless recursion", () => { const f = () => f(); f(); });
await attempt("bigint mix", () => 1n + 1);
await attempt("require in ESM", () => require("node:fs"));
await attempt("wrong argument", () => path.join(undefined));
await attempt("bad URL", () => new URL("not a url"));
await attempt("missing file", () => readFile("/no/such/file.txt"));
await attempt("missing module", () => import("./does-not-exist.js"));
await attempt("unhandled event", () => new EventEmitter().emit("error", "bad"));

// network failures
const first = http.createServer().listen(0);
await once(first, "listening");
const { port } = first.address();
await attempt("port in use", () => new Promise((resolve, reject) => http.createServer().on("error", reject).listen(port)));
first.close();
await once(first, "close");
await attempt("connection refused", () => fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}/`));
undefined property TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name') not a function TypeError: repo.save is not a function not defined ReferenceError: missingVariable is not defined const reassigned TypeError: Assignment to constant variable. bad JSON SyntaxError: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2) empty JSON SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input class without new TypeError: Class constructor Repo cannot be invoked without 'new' endless recursion RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded bigint mix TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types, use explicit conversions require in ESM ReferenceError: require is not defined wrong argument TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]: The "path" argument must be of type string. Received undefined bad URL TypeError [ERR_INVALID_URL]: Invalid URL missing file Error [ENOENT]: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/no/such/file.txt' missing module Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module '<dir>/does-not-exist.js' unhandled event Error [ERR_UNHANDLED_ERROR]: Unhandled error. ('bad') port in use Error [EADDRINUSE]: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 0.0.0.0:PORT connection refused TypeError: fetch failed caused by [ECONNREFUSED]

Errors that stop the program before it even starts, run as real scripts so you see what Node prints (and with which exit code):

$ printf 'const fs = require("node:fs");\n' > esm.mjs; node esm.mjs 2>&1 | grep ReferenceError
ReferenceError: require is not defined in ES module scope, you can use import instead
$ printf 'import fs from "node:fs";\nconsole.log("import in an untyped .js file:", typeof fs.readFileSync);\n' > detect.js; node detect.js
import in an untyped .js file: function
$ printf 'export const answer = 42;\n' > lib.mjs; printf 'const lib = require("./lib.mjs");\nconsole.log("require of an ES module:", lib.answer);\n' > main.cjs; node main.cjs
require of an ES module: 42
$ printf 'const value = await Promise.resolve(1);\n' > tla.cjs; node tla.cjs 2>&1 | grep SyntaxError
SyntaxError: await is only valid in async functions and the top level bodies of modules
$ node nothing.js 2>&1 | grep 'Cannot find module'
Error: Cannot find module '~/demo/startup-errors/nothing.js'
$ node -e 'Promise.reject(new Error("nobody caught me"))' 2>&1 | grep -E '^Error|^Node'; echo "(the grep status is not the exit code)"
Error: nobody caught me
Node.js v22.22.0
(the grep status is not the exit code)
$ node -e 'Promise.reject(new Error("nobody caught me"))' 2>/dev/null; echo "exit code: $?"
exit code: 1

Database errors come with a five-character SQLSTATE code in err.code. Branch on the code, never on the message text. Everything below runs inside a transaction that is rolled back, with a savepoint around each deliberate mistake:

import pg from "pg";

const show = (label, err) => console.log(`${label.padEnd(20)}[${err.code}] ${err.message}`);
const client = new pg.Client({ connectionString: "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb" });
await client.connect();
await client.query("BEGIN");                                   // everything below is rolled back at the end
await client.query("CREATE TEMP TABLE users (id serial PRIMARY KEY, email text UNIQUE NOT NULL, age int CHECK (age >= 0))");
await client.query("CREATE TEMP TABLE posts (id serial PRIMARY KEY, user_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id))");
await client.query("INSERT INTO users (email, age) VALUES ('a@x.com', 30)");

const attempt = async (label, sql, params = []) => {
  await client.query("SAVEPOINT s");                           // an error aborts a transaction; the savepoint lets us continue
  try {
    await client.query(sql, params);
  } catch (err) {
    show(label, err);
    await client.query("ROLLBACK TO s");
  }
};

await attempt("duplicate key", "INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('a@x.com')");
await attempt("null in NOT NULL", "INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES (NULL)");
await attempt("check failed", "INSERT INTO users (email, age) VALUES ('b@x.com', -1)");
await attempt("foreign key", "INSERT INTO posts (user_id) VALUES (99)");
await attempt("no such table", "SELECT * FROM userz");
await attempt("no such column", "SELECT emial FROM users");
await attempt("syntax error", "SELEKT 1");
await attempt("wrong value type", "INSERT INTO users (email, age) VALUES ('c@x.com', 'abc')");
await attempt("missing parameter", "SELECT $1::int + $2::int", [1]);
await attempt("division by zero", "SELECT 1 / 0");
await client.query("ROLLBACK");
await client.end();

// problems before any query runs
for (const [label, url] of [
  ["wrong password", "postgres://dex:nope@127.0.0.1:5432/dexdb"],
  ["no such database", "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:5432/nodb"],
  ["nothing listening", "postgres://dex:dexpass@127.0.0.1:1/dexdb"],
]) {
  try {
    await new pg.Client({ connectionString: url }).connect();
    console.log(label.padEnd(20), "connected anyway");
  } catch (err) {
    show(label, err);
  }
}

Authentication and validation libraries tell you precisely what failed. Log the reason on the server, but send the client only a vague answer (Unit 7):

import { SignJWT, jwtVerify } from "jose";

  .setSubject("1").setIssuer("notebox").setAudience("notebox-api").setIssuedAt(now - 100).setExpirationTime(exp).sign(key);

};

await attempt("expired", async () => jwtVerify(await make(secret, now - 10), secret, rules));
await attempt("wrong secret", async () => jwtVerify(await make(other), secret, rules));
await attempt("wrong audience", async () => jwtVerify(await make(secret), secret, { ...rules, audience: "other-api" }));

And the Express and HTTP-layer mistakes. The error handler here deliberately records the real error so you can read it; a production handler would only log it:

import express from "express";
const app = express();
const seen = [];                                                           // what the error handler saw

app.post("/no-parser", (req, res) => { const { name } = req.body; res.json({ name }); });   // the parser is registered below: too late
app.use(express.json({ limit: "20b" }));
app.post("/parsed", (req, res) => res.json(req.body));
app.get("/twice", (req, res) => { res.send("first"); res.send("second"); });                  // two responses for one request
app.get("/seen", (req, res) => res.json(seen));

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  seen.push(`${err.name}${err.code ? " [" + err.code + "]" : ""}${err.type ? " {" + err.type + "}" : ""}: ${err.message}`);
  if (res.headersSent) return;                                             // too late to send an error page
  res.status(err.status ?? 500).json({ error: err.status ? err.message : "server error" });
});

The lookup table

You seeUsual causeFix
Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')A value you assumed exists is undefined: a missing field, a failed lookup, a forgotten await, a parser that never ranFind where the value should have been set; use ?. only when absence is truly allowed
repo.save is not a functionWrong name, wrong import (default vs named), or the object is a PromiseLog the value and its type, check the import line and the await
missingVariable is not definedTypo, missing import, or a variable used outside its scopeCheck spelling and scope
Assignment to constant variable.Reassigning a constUse let if it really changes, otherwise mutate the object or build a new value
Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 / Unexpected end of JSON inputInvalid JSON, or an empty body being parsedWrap JSON.parse in try/catch for outside data; in Express return 400
Class constructor Repo cannot be invoked without 'new'Calling a class like a functionWrite new Repo()
Maximum call stack size exceededRecursion with no base case, or two functions calling each otherAdd the base case, or loop instead
require is not defined in ES module scope, you can use import insteadrequire inside an ES module (.mjs, or "type": "module")Use import; for the rare CommonJS-only need, createRequire(import.meta.url)
await is only valid in async functions and the top level bodies of modulesTop-level await in a CommonJS fileUse ES modules, or wrap in an async function
Cannot find module '.../nothing.js' (ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND)Wrong path, missing .js extension in an ESM relative import, or a package that was never installedCheck the path and the extension; run npm install
ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '...'File does not exist, or the path is relative to the wrong directoryBuild paths from import.meta.dirname, not from the current directory
EADDRINUSE: address already in useAnother process (often your previous run) holds the portStop it, or choose another port (lsof -i :3000)
fetch failed caused by ECONNREFUSEDNothing is listening at that address and port, or it is the wrong host (localhost inside a container is the container itself)Start the service, check host and port, check the compose service name
Unhandled error. ('bad') (ERR_UNHANDLED_ERROR)An EventEmitter emitted "error" with no listenerAlways attach .on("error", ...) to streams, servers and emitters
Process dies with the error text and exit code 1 (a rejected promise nobody caught)An async function failed and no catch or error handler saw itCatch it, and log a process-level unhandledRejection handler as a last line of defense, then exit
Cannot destructure property 'name' of 'req.body' as it is undefined.No body parser ran for this route (registered after it, or the Content-Type did not match)Register express.json() before the routes; send Content-Type: application/json
400 with a JSON syntax message (entity.parse.failed)The client sent broken JSONMap it to your own 400 error shape in the error handler
413 request entity too large (entity.too.large)Body over the parser's limitRaise the limit for that route only if you mean to; otherwise tell the client
Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client (ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT)Two responses for one request: a missing return, or a handler that also calls next()return res.json(...) every time you respond early
Cannot GET /nothingNo route matched and you have no 404 handlerAdd a JSON 404 handler after all routes
[23505] duplicate key value violates unique constraintInserting a value that must be uniqueCatch code 23505 and answer 409; or use ON CONFLICT
[23502] null value violates not-null constraintA required column got null or was omittedValidate input before the query
[23503] violates foreign key constraintThe referenced row does not exist (or still has children when deleting)Check the parent exists, or define ON DELETE behavior
[23514] violates check constraintA value breaks a rule such as age >= 0Validate in the app too, so users get a clear 400
[42P01] relation does not exist / [42703] column does not existMigration not run, wrong database, or a typoRun migrations, check DATABASE_URL, check names
[42601] syntax error at or nearInvalid SQL, often a stray comma or a misspelled keywordRead the text right after "at or near"
[22P02] invalid input syntax for type integerA string that is not a number reached an integer columnValidate and convert ids before querying
[08P01] bind message supplies 1 parameters, but prepared statement requires 2The number of $n placeholders and values differCount them
[28P01] password authentication failed / [3D000] database does not existWrong credentials or database name in DATABASE_URLCheck the URL, and that the database was created
JWTExpired "exp" claim timestamp check failedThe access token's life endedAnswer 401 and let the client refresh
signature verification failed, unexpected "aud" claim valueWrong secret, tampered token, or a token meant for another serviceAnswer 401, log the reason, never reveal it to the client
Browser: blocked by CORS policyThe browser, not your server, refusing to let a page read your response; the server did not send the right Access-Control-Allow-* headersConfigure CORS for the exact origin (Unit 7); curl will never show this error
JavaScript heap out of memoryA leak, or loading something huge into memoryStream large data, find the leak with a heap snapshot (not run in this guide)
A debugging routine that worksRead the first line of the error and the first stack frame that is in your code. Reproduce it with the smallest request or script. Print the real values just before it fails. Change one thing at a time. Then turn the reproduction into a test so it never comes back.

Reading is not learning; predicting and checking is. For each drill, cover the output, decide what you expect, then compare. When you were wrong, work out why before moving on, because that gap is exactly what the drill exists to find.

Drills 1 to 6: JavaScript behavior

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";
import fs from "node:fs";

// Drill 1: two loops, two results. What do they collect?
const withVar = [];
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => withVar.push(i));
const withLet = [];
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => withLet.push(j));
await sleep(10);
console.log("1.", withVar, withLet);

// Drill 2: in what order do these run? (started inside an I/O callback so the order is fixed)
const order = [];
await new Promise((done) => {
  fs.readFile(import.meta.filename, () => {
    setTimeout(() => order.push("timeout"), 0);
    setImmediate(() => { order.push("immediate"); done(); });
    process.nextTick(() => order.push("nextTick"));
    Promise.resolve().then(() => order.push("promise"));
    order.push("sync");
  });
});
await sleep(10);
console.log("2.", order);

// Drill 3: one failure among three jobs. What does each combinator report?
const jobs = () => [Promise.resolve("a"), Promise.reject(new Error("b failed")), sleep(5, "c")];
console.log("3.", (await Promise.allSettled(jobs())).map((r) => r.status));
console.log("3.", await Promise.all(jobs()).catch((err) => `all() rejected with: ${err.message}`));

// Drill 4: group words by first letter without a library
const words = ["apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry"];
console.log("4.", { ...Object.groupBy(words, (w) => w[0]) });

// Drill 5: merge configuration. Which value wins, and what type is port?
const defaults = { port: 3000, host: "localhost", debug: false };
const fromEnv = { port: "8080", debug: undefined };
console.log("5.", { ...defaults, ...fromEnv });

// Drill 6: four classic surprises
console.log("6.", ["1", "2", "3"].map(parseInt), 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3, typeof null, [0 || "x", 0 ?? "x", null ?? "x"]);
1. [ 3, 3, 3 ] [ 0, 1, 2 ] 2. [ 'sync', 'nextTick', 'promise', 'immediate', 'timeout' ] 3. [ 'fulfilled', 'rejected', 'fulfilled' ] 3. all() rejected with: b failed 4. { a: [ 'apple', 'avocado' ], b: [ 'banana', 'blueberry' ], c: [ 'cherry' ] } 5. { port: '8080', host: 'localhost', debug: undefined } 6. [ 1, NaN, NaN ] false object [ 'x', 0, 'x' ]
  • 1: var has one variable for the whole loop, let makes a fresh one per turn. The timers ran after the loop ended.
  • 2: after the synchronous code, nextTick runs first, then promise callbacks (the microtask queue), then setImmediate (the check phase), and the timer last, because a timer waits for the next loop turn. Outside an I/O callback the timeout and the immediate can swap places, so never depend on it.
  • 3: allSettled always finishes and describes each result; all rejects as soon as one rejects.
  • 5: spreading an explicit undefined overwrites the default. Environment values are strings, so convert and validate them (Unit 10 does it with Zod).
  • 6: parseInt receives the array index as its radix, so use .map(Number); binary floating point cannot store 0.1 exactly; typeof null is a historical quirk; ?? only replaces null and undefined, while || replaces every falsy value including 0.

Drill 7: predict the middleware trail

Before running, write down the list returned by each request. Pay attention to next(), next("route") and next(error).

import express from "express";
const app = express();
const trail = [];
const mark = (name) => (req, res, next) => { trail.push(name); next(); };

app.use(mark("A"));
app.get("/ok", mark("B"), (req, res) => { trail.push("C"); res.json(trail.splice(0)); });
app.get("/skip", (req, res, next) => { trail.push("B"); next("route"); }, mark("never"));
app.get("/skip", (req, res) => { trail.push("second route"); res.json(trail.splice(0)); });
app.get("/fail", mark("B"), (req, res, next) => next(new Error("stop")), mark("never"));
app.use(mark("D"));                                          // registered after the routes
app.use((err, req, res, next) => { trail.push("error handler"); res.status(500).json(trail.splice(0)); });
app.use((req, res) => { trail.push("404"); res.status(404).json(trail.splice(0)); });
> GET /ok < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < ["A","B","C"] > GET /skip < 200 OK < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < ["A","B","second route"] > GET /fail < 500 Internal Server Error < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < ["A","B","error handler"] > GET /nothing < 404 Not Found < content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 < ["A","D","404"]

The rule: every request walks the stack from the top, and only the entries whose method and path match are run. A normal next() goes on to the next matching entry, next("route") abandons the rest of the current route, and next(error) jumps to the next entry with four arguments. A matched route that sends a response ends the walk, which is why D only appears for requests that fell through.

Drill 8: a SQL trap

Goal: list every author with the number of books over 180 pages, including authors with none. Two queries look almost the same. Which one answers the question?

CREATE TABLE authors (id serial PRIMARY KEY, name text);
CREATE TABLE books (id serial PRIMARY KEY, author_id int REFERENCES authors(id), pages int);
INSERT INTO authors (name) VALUES ('Le Guin'), ('Borges');
INSERT INTO books (author_id, pages) VALUES (1, 387), (1, 183), (2, 174);

-- A: condition in WHERE
SELECT a.name, count(b.id) AS long_books
FROM authors a LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE b.pages > 180
GROUP BY a.name ORDER BY a.name;

-- B: condition in the join
SELECT a.name, count(b.id) AS long_books
FROM authors a LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id AND b.pages > 180
GROUP BY a.name ORDER BY a.name;
CREATE TABLE authors (id serial PRIMARY KEY, name text); CREATE TABLE books (id serial PRIMARY KEY, author_id int REFERENCES authors(id), pages int); INSERT INTO authors (name) VALUES ('Le Guin'), ('Borges'); INSERT INTO books (author_id, pages) VALUES (1, 387), (1, 183), (2, 174); -- A: condition in WHERE SELECT a.name, count(b.id) AS long_books FROM authors a LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id WHERE b.pages > 180 GROUP BY a.name ORDER BY a.name; name | long_books ---------+------------ Le Guin | 2 (1 row) -- B: condition in the join SELECT a.name, count(b.id) AS long_books FROM authors a LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id AND b.pages > 180 GROUP BY a.name ORDER BY a.name; name | long_books ---------+------------ Borges | 0 Le Guin | 2 (2 rows)

B is correct. The LEFT JOIN keeps authors with no matching book by filling the book columns with NULL. A WHERE b.pages > 180 is false for those NULL rows, so it throws the authors away again and silently turns the outer join into an inner join. Conditions about the optional side belong in ON.

Drills 9 and 10: build it yourself, then compare

Write your own version of each function first. The checks at the bottom must all print true.

import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

// Drill 9: allow at most `limit` calls per key in every window of `windowMs`.
// The clock is a parameter, so the test does not have to wait.
function createRateLimiter({ limit, windowMs, now = Date.now }) {
  const windows = new Map();                                      // key -> { start, count }
  return function allow(key) {
    const t = now();
    let w = windows.get(key);
    if (!w || t - w.start >= windowMs) {
      w = { start: t, count: 0 };                                 // a new window begins
      windows.set(key, w);
    }
    if (w.count >= limit) return false;
    w.count++;
    return true;
  };
}

let clock = 0;
const allow = createRateLimiter({ limit: 2, windowMs: 1000, now: () => clock });
console.log("9.", allow("ana") === true, allow("ana") === true, allow("ana") === false);   // the third call is refused
console.log("9.", allow("raj") === true);                                                   // keys are independent
clock = 1000;
console.log("9.", allow("ana") === true);                                                   // the window has passed

// Drill 10: run an async function over many items, at most `limit` at a time, keeping result order
async function mapLimit(items, limit, fn) {
  const results = new Array(items.length);
  let next = 0;
  async function worker() {
    while (next < items.length) {
      const i = next++;                                           // safe: no await between reading and incrementing
      results[i] = await fn(items[i], i);
    }
  }
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, worker));
  return results;
}

let running = 0, peak = 0;
const doubled = await mapLimit([5, 1, 4, 2, 3, 6], 2, async (n) => {
  running++; peak = Math.max(peak, running);
  await sleep(n * 3);                                             // different durations finish out of order
  running--;
  return n * 2;
});
console.log("10.", doubled, "peak concurrency:", peak);
9. true true true 9. true 9. true 10. [ 10, 2, 8, 4, 6, 12 ] peak concurrency: 2

Drills 11 and 12: find the bugs

This handler has six problems. Find them before opening the answers.

app.post("/orders", async (req, res) => {
  const { userId, items } = req.body;
  const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM products WHERE id IN (${items.join(",")})`);
  let total = 0;
  rows.rows.forEach(async (p) => { total += p.price * 100; });
  const order = db.query("INSERT INTO orders (user_id, total) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING *", [userId, total]);
  if (!order) res.status(400).json({ error: "failed" });
  res.json(order);
});
  1. SQL injection: items.join(",") puts client text into the SQL. Use WHERE id = ANY($1) with an array parameter.
  2. No validation: items may be missing or not an array, so the handler crashes or misbehaves. Validate the body with a schema first.
  3. Broken authorization: userId comes from the body, so anyone can order as anyone. Take the user from the verified token.
  4. Async inside forEach: forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, and the sum is a floating-point calculation on money. Use a for...of loop, and do money arithmetic in integer cents or in SQL.
  5. Missing await: order is a Promise, which is always truthy, and res.json(order) would send a promise. Also nothing guards the multi-step work in a transaction.
  6. No return after the error response: it would continue and respond twice (ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT, shown in the errors table). And never send the whole database row back without choosing its fields.

Drill 12 (project): take the Notebox capstone and add one feature from "Where to Take Notebox Next" with its test first. The guide cannot run that one for you, and it is the drill that matters most.

Interviewers do not want a recital; they want to hear that you understand why. Each answer is the length you would speak. Open the ones you cannot answer yourself first.

What is Node.js, and why can one thread serve many users?

Node is a runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser, built on the V8 engine and a C library called libuv. Your JavaScript runs on one thread, but waiting (for the network, the disk, the database) is handed to the operating system or a thread pool, and a callback is queued when the wait ends. While one request waits, the same thread serves another. That is why Node is excellent at I/O-bound work and poor at long CPU-bound loops, which block everyone.

Explain the event loop.

It is the loop that takes finished work and runs its callbacks. Each turn goes through phases: timers, pending I/O callbacks, poll (waiting for and running I/O), check (setImmediate) and close callbacks. Between callbacks Node drains process.nextTick and then the promise microtask queue. The consequence you must remember: anything synchronous and slow inside a callback delays every other request.

What is the difference between process.nextTick, promises, setTimeout and setImmediate?

nextTick and promise callbacks run right after the current operation, before the loop moves on (nextTick first). setImmediate runs in the check phase of the current loop turn; setTimeout(fn, 0) runs in the timers phase of a later turn, at least a millisecond later. Only inside an I/O callback is the order immediate-then-timeout guaranteed.

How do you handle CPU-heavy work in Node?

Do not do it on the request thread. Options: a worker_threads pool for computation inside the process, a job queue with separate worker processes (BullMQ) for anything slow or retryable, or a different service for truly heavy work. For scaling across cores, run several processes (cluster, PM2 or containers) behind a load balancer.

What is middleware in Express?

A function (req, res, next) that runs between the request arriving and the response leaving. It can read or change req and res, end the response, or call next() to pass control on. Express runs them in registration order, so the order is part of the program. Body parsing, logging, authentication, CORS and rate limiting are all middleware; an error handler is the same with four arguments.

How does error handling work in Express 5 compared with 4?

In both, an error handler is a middleware with four arguments registered last. In Express 4 a rejected promise in an async handler was not forwarded, so you needed try/catch with next(err) or a wrapper. Express 5 forwards rejected promises and thrown errors from handlers and middleware automatically.

What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

Authentication answers "who are you?" (a password, a token, a session). Authorization answers "what may you do?" (roles, ownership of a resource). A very common bug is checking only the first: a logged-in user changes the number in /orders/42 and reads someone else's order. Always scope queries by the authenticated user, and answer 404 for resources that are not theirs.

How should passwords be stored?

Never in plain text, and never with a fast hash such as SHA-256. Use a slow, salted, memory-hard algorithm designed for passwords: Argon2id (preferred), scrypt, or bcrypt, with the library handling the salt. Verify with the library's compare function. On login, give identical answers for "unknown email" and "wrong password", and rate limit attempts.

Sessions or JWTs?

A session stores state on the server and gives the browser an opaque cookie; it is easy to revoke and a good default for a website. A JWT is a signed token the client carries, which the server can verify without a lookup; it suits APIs and several services, but it cannot be revoked before it expires unless you keep a deny list. Keep access tokens short (minutes) and pair them with a rotated refresh token. Never store sensitive data in a JWT: it is signed, not encrypted.

What is CORS, and does it protect my API?

CORS is a browser rule that decides whether a page from one origin may read responses from another. It does not stop requests from curl or other servers, and it does not authenticate anyone. It is configured on the server with Access-Control-Allow-* headers and should list exact origins. The error you see in the console is the browser refusing to hand the response to the page.

What is CSRF and how do you prevent it?

Cross-site request forgery: a malicious site makes the victim's browser send a request to your site, and the browser attaches the victim's cookies. It matters for cookie-based authentication. Defenses: SameSite=Lax or Strict cookies, anti-CSRF tokens for state-changing requests, checking the Origin header, and never changing state on GET. Bearer tokens in an Authorization header are not sent automatically, so they are not vulnerable to it.

What is SQL injection and how do you stop it?

Attacker-controlled text becomes part of the SQL command, so it can change the query. Stop it by passing values as parameters ($1), which the database never treats as code. Table and column names cannot be parameters, so choose them from an allowlist. The same idea applies to NoSQL operators, shell commands and HTML: separate code from data.

What is XSS and how do you prevent it?

Cross-site scripting: untrusted data is inserted into a page and runs as script in the victim's browser. Escape output for its context (template engines do this by default), never build HTML from user input by string concatenation, set HttpOnly on session cookies so scripts cannot read them, and add a Content-Security-Policy as a second layer.

What is an IDOR?

Insecure direct object reference: the API accepts an identifier and returns or changes the object without checking that this user may. Fix it by including the owner in the query (WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2), and test it with two users, as the Notebox suite does.

Design a REST endpoint for a collection: methods, status codes, pagination.

GET /notes lists, POST /notes creates (201 and a Location header), GET /notes/:id reads (404 if missing), PATCH /notes/:id changes some fields, PUT replaces, DELETE returns 204. Validate input and answer 400 with the fields at fault. For lists use a limit with a maximum and a cursor ("after id 30") rather than a big offset, because a cursor stays fast and does not skip or repeat rows when data changes.

What does "idempotent" mean, and which methods are?

Repeating the request leaves the system in the same state as doing it once. GET, PUT, DELETE and HEAD are idempotent; POST is not. Networks retry, so for operations like payments you accept an Idempotency-Key header and return the stored result for a repeated key.

401 or 403?

401 means the server does not know who you are (missing or invalid credentials). 403 means it knows exactly who you are and you are not allowed. For another user's private resource, 404 is often better than 403, because it does not confirm that the resource exists.

What is an index, and what does it cost?

An index is a separate sorted structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows without reading the whole table. It speeds up reads that filter, join or sort on the indexed columns and slows down writes and uses disk, because every insert and update must maintain it. Index what you query, confirm with EXPLAIN, and do not index everything.

What is a transaction? What does ACID mean?

A group of statements that succeed or fail together. Atomic: all or nothing. Consistent: constraints hold before and after. Isolated: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work (to a degree set by the isolation level). Durable: once committed, it survives a crash. Transferring money is the classic example: the debit and the credit must happen together.

What is the N+1 query problem?

One query loads a list, then the code runs one more query per item, so 100 items cost 101 round trips. Fix it with a join, a single WHERE id = ANY($1) query, or batching (DataLoader in GraphQL). It hides well in ORMs and in code that loops with await.

SQL or NoSQL?

Start with PostgreSQL unless you have a reason not to: relations, constraints, transactions and JSON columns cover most applications. Document stores such as MongoDB fit data that is naturally a self-contained document and read as a whole; key-value stores such as Redis fit caches, counters, rate limits and queues. Many systems use more than one, each for what it is good at.

How do you migrate a database schema safely?

With versioned migration files that run in order and are recorded, never by editing tables by hand. For zero downtime use expand and contract: first add the new column (old code still works), deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, and only later drop the old column. Never change a migration that has already run in production.

How would you cache API responses?

Closest to the client first: HTTP caching with Cache-Control and ETag so clients and CDNs can reuse or revalidate responses. Server side, put hot reads in Redis with a TTL, and decide how it is invalidated (on write, or by expiry). The hard part is not storing, it is knowing when the data is stale, so cache only what can tolerate it.

How do you scale a Node API?

Keep the app stateless (sessions and caches in Redis or the database, files in object storage), then run several instances behind a load balancer. Use all cores per machine with a process manager or containers. Move slow work to queues. Find the real bottleneck first (usually the database): add indexes, connection pooling, caching, and read replicas before adding servers.

What is a message queue for, and what must a job handler guarantee?

It moves slow or unreliable work out of the request: the API enqueues and answers at once, and a worker does the job with retries and backoff. Delivery is typically at-least-once, so a job can run twice; handlers must be idempotent (safe to repeat), for example by checking a unique key before sending an email.

WebSockets, Server-Sent Events or polling?

Server-Sent Events are the simplest for one-way pushes (notifications, progress) and work over plain HTTP. WebSockets give two-way, low-latency messaging (chat, games). Polling is the simplest and fine when updates are rare. With several server instances, a broker such as Redis must connect them so a message reaches clients on any instance.

How do you test a backend?

Unit tests for pure logic, fast and numerous; integration tests that run the real app (with supertest or fetch) against a real database, each test inside a rolled-back transaction; and a few end-to-end checks. Test the unhappy paths as much as the happy ones: validation, 401, 403, 404, duplicates. Mock only what is outside your control, and run everything in CI on every push.

What do you log, and what must you never log?

One structured (JSON) line per request with a request id, method, path, status and duration, plus errors with their stack. Use levels (info, warn, error) so you can filter. Never log passwords, tokens, full card numbers or other secrets and personal data; redact them at the logger.

What is graceful shutdown?

On SIGTERM (what deploys and containers send) the process stops accepting new connections, finishes the requests in flight, closes the database and queue connections, and then exits, with a timeout that forces exit if something hangs. Without it, every deploy cuts some users off mid-request. Health checks should report "not ready" during the shutdown so the load balancer stops sending traffic.

Liveness versus readiness checks?

Liveness asks "is the process alive?" and a failure means restart it, so keep it trivial. Readiness asks "can it serve traffic right now?" (database reachable, not shutting down) and a failure means stop routing to it, not restart it. Mixing them up causes restart storms when the database is briefly down.

Why put nginx or a load balancer in front of Node?

It terminates TLS, serves static files cheaply, spreads load across instances, buffers slow clients, applies timeouts and size limits, and lets you deploy or restart instances without dropping the public port. Remember to set trust proxy in Express and forward the original client address headers.

How do you manage configuration and secrets?

Read from environment variables, validate them once at startup with a schema, and fail fast with a clear message if anything is missing. Keep secrets out of the repository and out of images; inject them at runtime from the platform's secret store. Different environments differ only in configuration, never in code.

A production endpoint became slow. What do you do?

Measure before guessing. Check the metrics: is it every route or one, CPU or waiting, since which deploy? Look at the database (slow query log, EXPLAIN on the suspect query, missing index, N+1, connection pool exhausted). Check the event loop lag in Node for blocking code, and the logs for the request ids involved. Fix the biggest cause, then confirm with the same measurement, and add a test or an alert so it does not return.

Tick an item only when you can do it without looking, on an empty file. If you cannot, the entry to reread is named in brackets.

Can you do these?

  • Unit 1: Explain what happens between typing a URL and seeing a page, and read a raw HTTP request and response. Pick the right method and status code. Use curl for every method, with headers, JSON and cookies. [web-works, http-messages, status-codes]
  • Unit 2: Write functions, closures, destructuring, array pipelines, classes, async/await with try/catch and Promise.all, and ES module imports, without notes. Add basic TypeScript types to a function. [js-functions, js-async, js-modules]
  • Unit 3: Read and write files with the promise API, pipe a stream, use EventEmitter, hash and sign with crypto, read process.env and signals, and explain why blocking the event loop hurts. [event-loop, node-fs, node-streams]
  • Unit 4: Build an Express app with routers, parameters, a body parser, custom middleware, a 404 handler and an error handler, in the right order. Explain what changed in Express 5. [express-middleware, express-errors, express-migration]
  • Unit 5: Design resource URLs and error responses, validate every input with a schema, paginate with a cursor, accept an upload safely, and use ETag and If-Match. [rest-design, validation-zod, rest-pagination]
  • Unit 6: Design tables with keys and constraints, write joins, grouping, CTEs and upserts, read an EXPLAIN, use transactions, write a migration, and talk to PostgreSQL with parameters from Node. [sql-joins, sql-transactions, db-pg, db-migrations]
  • Unit 7: Hash passwords properly, issue and verify tokens, enforce ownership on every query, configure CORS, CSRF defenses and Helmet, rate limit, and name the OWASP top risks with a defense for each. [auth-passwords, auth-authorization, sec-injection]
  • Unit 8: Push events with SSE or WebSockets, run a background job with retries, verify a webhook signature, and explain timeouts, retries and idempotency between services. [rt-sse, adv-queues, adv-webhooks]
  • Unit 9: Write unit and integration tests, use a rolled-back transaction per test, mock a dependency or the clock, and run everything in CI. [test-fundamentals, test-http-db]
  • Unit 10: Validate configuration at startup, log structured JSON with request ids, expose health and metrics, shut down gracefully, and describe a Dockerfile, a reverse proxy and a safe deploy. [prod-config, prod-shutdown, prod-cicd-ops]
  • Unit 11: Build, test and run an API with authentication, ownership, validation, pagination and tests from an empty folder, and add a feature to it test first. [cap-plan to cap-next]

A practice path that works

  1. Weeks 1 to 2: foundations. Units 1 and 2. Do every drill. Write small scripts daily; do not just read.
  2. Weeks 3 to 4: Node and Express. Units 3 and 4. Build three tiny servers from memory: a to-do API with in-memory data, a URL shortener, a file-upload service.
  3. Weeks 5 to 7: real APIs and data. Units 5 and 6. Move the to-do API onto PostgreSQL with migrations, validation and pagination.
  4. Weeks 8 to 9: secure it. Unit 7. Add signup, login, ownership checks, and write the attack tests yourself (two users, forged tokens, injection strings).
  5. Weeks 10 to 11: tests and production. Units 9 and 10. Reach a test suite you trust, add logging, health checks and graceful shutdown, then containerize it and deploy it somewhere real.
  6. Week 12 and on: ship something. Rebuild Notebox without looking, then do the exercises, then build your own idea. Real users and real bugs teach what no guide can.

Where to go after this guide

  • Frameworks on top of the same ideas: Fastify (faster, schema-first), NestJS (structured, TypeScript-first), Hono (small, runs everywhere). Everything about HTTP, databases, security and testing transfers unchanged.
  • Depth: PostgreSQL internals and query tuning, designing for failure (retries, backoff, circuit breakers), observability with traces (OpenTelemetry), message brokers beyond Redis (Kafka, RabbitMQ).
  • Infrastructure: Docker and Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, a cloud provider's managed database and queue, CDNs.
  • Always: read the source and the changelog of the libraries you rely on, and re-read the OWASP list once a year.

This guide was built by a program that runs every example and pastes the real output next to it, so the output you see is not typed from memory. If a snippet had failed, the build would have stopped. Values that change on every run (timestamps, ids, ports, durations) are normalized so the pages stay stable.

Described, but not run here
  • Docker images and containers: the environment has the Docker command-line tool but no daemon, so the Dockerfile and compose file were checked for syntax (the compose file was validated) and explained, but no image was built.
  • MongoDB and Prisma: no MongoDB server and no Prisma engine were available, so those examples are labelled and were not executed.
  • systemd, GitHub Actions and cloud services (object storage, managed databases, registries): they need machines or accounts this environment does not have. The files shown are sketches that follow each tool's documented format.
  • Testcontainers, npm audit (its output changes daily) and heap snapshots are described only.
  • The outbox and saga patterns in the microservices entry are explained with diagrams; they need several real services to demonstrate.
Versions and your machineEverything ran on Node.js 22.22, Express 5.3, PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, Zod 4.6 and TypeScript 7. Node 24 is the current long-term-support line and Node 22 is in maintenance, so a new project today should start on 24, and the code here should work there with the same ideas (check each library's changelog). The diagrams are drawn by Mermaid, which is loaded from the internet, so they appear only when you are online; the text next to each is complete without them. Package versions move, so if something behaves differently on your machine, read the error against the lookup table in this unit first.
Last wordYou do not need to memorize this guide. Memorize the shape: a request arrives, middleware prepares it, validation checks it, authorization permits it, a transaction changes data, a response goes back, and logs and metrics tell you what happened. Everything else is detail you can look up. Go build something.
